A directed graph is semi-transitive when its adjacency relation satisfies transitivity without including strict cycles. In 2008, Bouchet demonstrated that every split graph possesses a semi-transitive orientation. This paper investigates specific classes of split graphs to determine which admit a semi-transitive orientation where multiple edges share the same direction (bidirectional orientation). We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for various graph types to ensure all their semi-transitive orientations are bidirectional. Furthermore, we introduce a significant and non-trivial class of split graphs characterized by the property that every one of its maximal cliques has a semi-transitive orientation that is entirely bidirectional. Combining our theorems with Bouchet's construction yields a large class of graphs in which every semi-transitive orientation is strictly bidirectional. As a consequence, we provide a substantial subset of the graphs discussed by Bouchet, whose bidirectional nature is guaranteed rather than merely assumed. Additionally, we examine practical applications of these findings in the context of conflict-free coloring of graphs. Finally, we present an algorithm that assigns a semi-transitive orientation to any given split graph with at least one such orientation, ensuring that every maximal clique receives a bidirectional orientation. This algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time and serves as a constructive proof of Bouchet's theorem. We further analyze the algorithm's output to identify a class of split graphs whose orientations minimize the count of bidirectional cliques among all possible semi-transitive orientations. Finally, we introduce a novel class of split graphs where every semi-transitive orientation is bidirectional, a finding that has inspired new research directions. Specifically, we have begun exploring whether a similar constructive proof exists for semi-transitive orientations of circle graphs. This paper is the result of that initial inquiry. Our practical algorithm not only confirms Bouchet's theorem but also significantly restricts the search space for bidirectional orientations of circle graphs. We demonstrate that several representative circle graphs are indeed bidirectional. The remainder of this work is dedicated to examining the relationship between circle arc representations and the bidirectionality of their semi-transitive orientations. We establish that for any circle arc representation of a circle graph, there exists a modification preserving the graph structure that makes all maximal cliques bidirectional. This result holds for maximal cliques within the circle arcs but does not extend to the entire set of arcs. We conclude by posing the question of whether a similar algorithm exists for all circle arcs and invite readers to consider this challenge. Our findings suggest that the answer is likely negative.

Identifying decays into tau leptons is essential for the physics investigations of the LHC and its future high-luminosity upgrades. This study presents the results of a deep neural network optimized for this identification process, generated via an end-to-end training approach that utilizes all information from $\tau^\pm$ decays. The analysis covers a dataset of 100,000 simulated $\tau^\pm$ decays and 100,000 simulated QCD jets. The resulting tau identification efficiency for decaying tau leptons is established at various fake rates for jets misidentified as tau leptons across different $p_\mathrm{T}$ intervals, with results presented for both 13 TeV and 14 TeV collision scenarios. These findings are directly applicable to physics analyses requiring tau identification. The neural network architecture, implementation details, and performance metrics can be accessed through a public web interface. Given their success in tau identification, these techniques are also being investigated for jet flavor tagging. Furthermore, the study examines how increased data statistics and improved data quality impact the method's performance. This work was conducted as part of the Machine Learning for High Energy Physics (ML4HEP) project, an initiative within the European Union's H2020 INFRAIA program. Neural networks (NNs) offer a promising solution for processing such vast datasets in real-time during the era of multi-TeV particle physics. This study explores Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) for classification tasks, comparing their performance on simulated data with that of standard drop-out based Neural Networks (NNs). The results indicate that, aside from slight reductions in speed and accuracy, BNNs present no significant differences from NNs for classification applications. Consequently, drop-out based NNs remain the more practical choice. Additionally, we demonstrate that dropout can be formulated as a Bayesian approach and examine how varying the prior distribution within BNNs affects both accuracy and convergence. Finally, we address strategies for reducing model parameters to enhance training speed and outline how McMC sampling can be employed to estimate uncertainties in classification results. Finally, we emphasize that these conclusions are specific to binary classification and may not extend to other applications. This study examines intermodal forward Brillouin scattering within a solid-core photonic crystal fiber (PCF), showcasing a record coherent power combination of 1.4 dB among the five lowest-order modes for a 30-cm fiber segment. The observed performance aligns with theoretical predictions, attributed to the PCF's high intermodal differential Brillouin shift, which facilitates effective backscattering even at low pump powers. These findings indicate that solid-core PCFs are promising for intermodal Brillouin sensing applications. Additionally, we demonstrate the first observation of degenerate intermodal forward Brillouin scattering in the same fiber type, alongside a detailed analysis of the resulting hybrid spatio-spectral Brillouin spectrum. Such detailed spectral data holds significant potential for applications in structural health monitoring. Finally, we discuss a mechanism for generating multiple mode coupling through side-mode resonance in this system. This mechanism is demonstrated in a photonic crystal fiber with a larger air hole near the modes' propagation path, resulting in strong coupling among the five lowest-order modes and a substantial reduction in intermodal crosstalk. The observed record-breaking performance in both experimental contexts underscores the value of carefully designed air holes near mode propagation paths as a viable strategy for managing intermodal coupling in solid-core PCFs. Ultimately, the proposed structural design offers a pathway to further enhance intermodal power combination using cost-effective solid-core PCF technologies. Furthermore, the combination of intermodal and coherent properties of these fibers may enable the development of a new class of photonic devices. Specifically, the combination of multiple modes could facilitate the creation of on-chip optical beam combiners and filters, while the high-intermodal isolation characteristic of these fibers offers a potential solution to the crosstalk problem inherent in intermodal Brillouin lasing devices. Consequently, solid-core PCF technologies are poised to advance the field of high-power, high-energy, and high-sensitivity Brillouin-based photonic devices. To this end, we have also characterized another solid-core PCF featuring a more complex air-hole pattern along its propagation path, which demonstrates even better intermodal isolation. This further underscores the critical role that air-hole design plays in managing intermodal power combination. Additionally, the study addresses the trade-off between intermodal differential delay and power combination efficiency in solid-core PCFs. We conclude by discussing the potential of this type of fiber for realizing a new class of devices that integrate high power, energy, and sensitivity. The Orbit algebra of a finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$, denoted $\Omega_\Lambda$, is a graded algebra where the grading corresponds to the internal degrees of linear combinations within $\Lambda$. When $\Lambda$ arises from a finite-dimensional hereditary algebra associated with a reduced finite-type Coxeter group $W$ of B-type, this paper investigates the graded structure of $\Omega_\Lambda$. The primary result establishes a basis for $\Omega_\Lambda$ analogous to the basis theorem for finite-type Coxeter algebras of A and D types, specifically tailored to the B-type case. Additionally, the authors explore the relationships between $\Omega_\Lambda$ and the Hecke algebra, a finite-dimensional Hermitian algebra, as well as the Morita stable equivalence classes of $\Lambda$. Through explicit calculations of $\Omega_\Lambda$ for the four non-simple roots of B and D types, the study demonstrates that the basis theorem is optimal and cannot be extended to other finite-dimensional Hermitian algebras. Furthermore, the paper examines the graded center and graded representation algebra of $\Omega_\Lambda$ as natural candidates for an inverse automorphism. Finally, the authors pose an open question regarding whether the basis theorem holds for Coxeter groups beyond the A, D, and B types. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP) are both NP-hard combinatorial optimization challenges where selecting the most effective items within a budget maximizes the coverage of unique elements. This study introduces a novel Effective and Efficient Local Search (EELL S) algorithm designed for both the SUKP and BMCP. To achieve this, we incorporate new operators that modify the decision variable matrix while maintaining the candidate set pool for algorithms to explore. Additionally, we implement methods to accelerate the evaluation of algorithm performance. Through extensive computational experiments on real-world datasets, we assess the advantages of our approach and its capacity to identify high-quality solutions. The dataset, along with the implemented algorithms, is available at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1980/SUKP. In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, photon-photon interactions generate electron-positron pairs. When these pairs occur near heavy nuclei, they experience significant electromagnetic interactions. This study investigates such processes within ultra-peripheral collisions of $^{208}$Pb beams and protons using the PYTHIA and ELITE event generators. By comparing these simulations with experimental data from the LHCb experiment at $p_{T} < 1$ GeV, we observe discrepancies. This suggests that the electromagnetic interactions of low transverse-momentum electrons and positrons with heavy nuclei may be more significant than currently modeled in these frameworks. Our findings indicate that the inclusive production cross-sections for these electrons and positrons could be enhanced by up to a factor of 100 when interacting with lead or by a factor of 4 when interacting with a proton. These interactions occur through the exchange of either single or two photons with the nucleus. While interactions with a single exchanged photon are typically considered negligible, we demonstrate that they can be substantial in this specific context due to kinematic effects. These enhancements could be verified in the near future using the same LHCb data. Additionally, we explore the potential for studying these phenomena in ultra-peripheral collisions of $^{82}$Pb+$^{208}$Pb, which could be achieved with the upgrade of the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Centre (FAIR). We conclude that these measurements could probe nuclear photon distributions at very low values, offering a complementary approach to other methods for studying the photon content of the nucleus. This would aid in understanding how photon distributions scale with the nuclear charge. We have also deposited our analysis code on GitHub. Our results indicate that these measurements are feasible within the next few years, utilizing existing experimental data from the LHC. Specifically, the current dataset should be adequate to confirm our findings, and the FAIR upgrade is expected to provide data sufficient to test the effects of double photon exchange. These measurements could establish a new channel for photon-tagged events, potentially enhancing the photon flux available for photon-photon interactions. This enhancement could be particularly significant for studying light-by-light scattering and vector boson pair production. Furthermore, these findings are relevant for understanding the production of low-$p_{T}$ electrons and positrons in heavy-ion collisions, which is crucial for measuring dilepton invariant mass spectra and searching for exotic physics. For cyclists, traffic constitutes the primary hazard. Consequently, accurately gauging road risk is vital to boost cycling attractiveness and achieve modal shift goals. Existing solutions often depend on user-reported risk ratings to gather subjective evaluations of dangerous situations. However, these ratings frequently suffer from low reliability due to an absence of contextual metadata, such as road type, speed, and lane availability. This study introduces a robust context-aware risk descriptor (CRD) designed to enable the objective context validation of cyclist risk assessments. The proposed system utilizes computer vision to automatically generate measurements of critical safety metrics, including lane width, speed, and obstacle detection. By relying on video-based data rather than subjective reports, the CRD enhances the reliability of cyclist risk evaluation. The study validates this descriptor through the automated measurement of CRD measurements (CD) across various traffic scenarios using both computer-simulated and real-world datasets. Results indicate that CRD effectively captures context changes and accurately infers risk levels across diverse traffic environments, demonstrating its utility as a reliable contextual risk descriptor. Furthermore, the CD shows high reliability in urban settings, meeting all criteria for valid context validation. Ultimately, this research provides a dependable method for assessing cyclist risk within traffic contexts. Additionally, the findings suggest that combining computer vision with machine learning can automatically measure or predict risk descriptors, thereby advancing the field of intelligent transportation systems. Future applications include the automated generation of risk maps and the development of smart cycling devices. These devices would assist cyclists in avoiding dangerous routes and inform policymakers to create safer infrastructure. Additionally, smart cycling helmets could facilitate real-time monitoring of critical descriptors like lane width, obstacle detection, and curvature, enabling intelligent systems to provide timely warnings to users. This could lead to the emergence of autonomous two-wheelers, where advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and automated functions are standard in the cycling industry. Ultimately, these technologies aim to improve the cycling experience, enhance safety, and promote a sustainable modal shift. To achieve this, the CRD and CD must be integrated into smart cycling devices, such as smart helmets, to enable the proposed applications. The current paper focuses on validating the CRD and CD to support the development of these devices. Specifically, the CD is integrated with an AR smart helmet prototype, which is currently being evaluated for its ability to measure and display CRD information to the cyclist. This integration marks a significant step toward realizing the described smart cycling devices and advancing intelligent systems for two-wheelers. The CD is expected to be fully operational within the next 12 to 24 months. This work

Control Barrier Functions (CBF) are extensively utilized to enforce safety-critical constraints on nonlinear systems, yet they have not yet been a primary component in motion planning for dynamic vehicles. This study addresses the challenge of generating feasible CBF constraints during planning for highly under-actuated systems, such as fixed-wing aircraft, which feature highly nonlinear and time-variant dynamics. We propose a robust and interpretable approach to create CBFs that tolerate modeling errors, sensor noise, and dynamic variations. Unlike many existing safety-planning methods, our technique does not depend on CBFs defined by lower-dimensional target sets. Instead, we derive CBFs directly from the vehicle's safety requirements and underlying physical principles. Furthermore, we incorporate these constraints into the planning process by defining a novel CBF-based cost function. By minimizing this cost, the resulting CBFs not only ensure safety but also promote progress toward the goal, avoid unnecessary maneuvers, and maintain reasonable flight paths. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed CBFs ensure safe, feasible, and robust planar flight paths and trajectories for an under-actuated aircraft, even in the presence of modeling errors, wind disturbances, and sensor noise. Additionally, we validate the method's robustness by showing that it maintains safe operation for a more complex, multi-vehicle formation trajectory following a different trajectory class. The corresponding CBFs are interpretable and can be readily adapted to physical constraints, such as minimum separation distances between aircraft. Finally, we tested the approach on a fixed-wing aircraft with a nonlinear autopilot, where CBFs derived from our planning method successfully ensured safe takeoffs and landings under various conditions. We believe this method represents a step toward safety-critical planning for advanced, multi-vehicle missions in dynamic environments. The CBFs derived from such planning can serve as the foundation for future research into real-time, on-board safety-critical planning and control for dynamic robotics and aircraft. Additionally, our CBF framework is compatible with other techniques for safety-critical planning and control, thereby enhancing their robustness and practicality. Our findings are supported by actual flight data demonstrating the method's efficacy. To foster further research, we have made our code and data available online. The code for the CBFs derived from our planning approach can facilitate safer, feasible, and robust trajectory generation for dynamic robotics and aircraft, thereby advancing the field of safety-critical planning and control in dynamic environments. A cover of an algebraic structure consists of a finite collection of proper substructures whose union equals the entire structure, and the covering number represents the minimum size of such a cover. This paper investigates all possible covering numbers for rings and, to a certain extent, for commutative rings, demonstrating that the two possibility sets differ. We also examine structural insights and symbolic applications, noting that for a fixed $n$, the maximum gap between consecutive elements in Ring$(n)$ is generally achieved when the covering numbers are close to their potential minimum. Furthermore, for specific values of $n$, we detail a symbolically computed basis for the ideal corresponding to the set of all possible covering numbers of rings of size $n$. Finally, we present a computationally intensive symbolically driven conjecture regarding the covering numbers of commutative rings, which requires verification for a specific, computationally intense value of $n$. Our inquiry into this possibility set originates from recent work on the linear and circular covering numbers of rings and the covering numbers of vector spaces and directed graphs. The resulting paper introduces several open-ended questions, with the final one being computationally intensive, as it concerns the covering numbers of commutative rings for a specific value of $n$. Our approach relies on computational techniques, leveraging the fact that rings of a fixed size form a computable structure. We have successfully computed all possible covering numbers for rings of size up to 12 and for commutative rings of size up to 10, with the latter case requiring only minor additional effort. The paper concludes with 110 conjectures, most of which are supported by the data available, alongside an outline of the procedures used to generate them. This extensive list serves as a foundation for future research, which will employ computational and symbolic methods to explore the structure of rings and their covering numbers. To facilitate this research, we have created an open-source library of routines for ring data and covering numbers, which will be made available via an open access publication. Our methodology utilizes computational algebra software, with much of the code available as an open-source library that can be adapted for various applications. This library, which employs a variety of algorithms, is accessible through an open-source publication. We have also developed application code for symbolically computing covering numbers, the results of which are presented in the paper. Deep learning models are susceptible to adversarial examples, which consist of images altered by subtle, human-imperceptible noise that causes these models to produce incorrect predictions. This study investigates the relationship between adversarial robustness and model memorization, demonstrating a strong correlation between a model's ability to generalize adversarial inputs and its training loss on that data. Furthermore, we propose a method called AdaMix to enhance adversarial robustness by mitigating memorization. The results indicate that our approach can substantially improve adversarial accuracy while leaving accuracy on clean test images largely unaffected. Additionally, our findings reveal that the training strategies considered adversarially robust are distinct from those robust to natural corruption. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our training-based defense against data poisoning attacks. Given that the test set remains unseen during training, the lack of performance degradation on clean data strongly suggests that our defense does not rely on memorizing clean examples from the test set. Consequently, our training scheme offers a natural form of robustness against adversarial examples. In contrast, adversarial training, which processes test-time adversarial examples during the training phase, risks overfitting to these test-time inputs and thus lacks this inherent robustness. We also highlight that our training-based approach is more effective against data poisoning attacks than adversarial training is. This is because the test-time robustness achieved by adversarial training stems from memorizing the training set, which does not extend to the validation or test sets in standard machine learning workflows. In summary, our research provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying adversarial robustness and memorization. Additionally, our training-based defense represents a promising alternative to adversarial training for enhancing model robustness against data poisoning. By modifying the training process to learn robust features, our approach enhances model robustness without requiring the collection of adversarial training data or the expensive computational costs associated with adversarial training. Furthermore, our findings underscore the critical need for developing training-based defenses to achieve natural robustness against adversarial examples. We believe this work offers valuable insights into the mechanisms of adversarial robustness and memorization. Training-based defenses provide a means to enhance robustness against adversarial examples without the need for generating adversarial training data or the substantial computational costs of adversarial training. Our results also highlight the importance of developing training-based defenses to achieve natural robustness against adversarial examples. Our findings offer valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying adversarial robustness. Nonlocal conservation laws, defined by fluxes that depend on the state history, offer a macroscopic framework for analyzing traffic dynamics. At a micro level, this nonlocality reflects the fact that vehicles influence one another over a finite distance. Unlike local conservation laws, these nonlocal models do not admit classical solutions. Instead, they are interpreted as partial differential equations featuring nonlocal coefficients—specifically measures—that may lack functional representation. This work establishes robust $L^1$-estimates for the singular limit as kernel nonlinearity vanishes for a prominent class of traffic models and demonstrates the convergence rate when the kernel is nonnegative and totally monotone. From a PDE perspective, these models are analyzed using the framework of entropy-admissible solutions for nonlinear conservation laws with measure-valued coefficients. This approach demands novel techniques to address the specific challenges posed by measure coefficients. We derive the entropy admissibility condition required for a solution and prove its stability. Finally, these theoretical findings are illustrated through a detailed traffic example. Key words: conservation laws, measure-valued coefficients, totally monotone, entropy-admissible, convergence rate. Dilation surfaces extend the concept of translation surfaces by allowing atlas transitions to include local dilation factors. These surfaces can arise as quotients of dilated translation surfaces, which admit a decomposition into translation dilation tiles. When this decomposition lacks invariant foliations, the resulting dilation surface exhibits horizon saddle connections. Assuming this absence of invariant foliations, we demonstrate that horizon saddle connections are dense on a translation dilation surface if and only if the dynamics are Morse-Smale. In this specific case, all orbits converge to fixed points or limit cycles, characterized by vectors with non-zero x-coordinates. This paper offers a comprehensive understanding of horizon saddle connections within translation dilation surfaces and establishes the first instance where the horizon saddle connection property holds for a class of dilation surfaces. Furthermore, this phenomenon represents the initial instance where the horizon saddle connection property facilitates the analysis of dynamics, even in the broader context of general dilation surfaces. To achieve these results, we develop a novel technique for constructing invariant foliations, which we believe will be a valuable instrument in the study of dilation surfaces. Additionally, we provide a complete classification of the horizon saddle connections and their associated dynamics for dilation surfaces derived from two-cusped thrice-punctured spheres and tori. These findings have significant implications for the dynamics of dilation surfaces arising from polygon gluing and from translation-cylinder bundles. The paper also includes an appendix that generalizes the theory of horizon saddle connections to dilation surfaces with non-trivial abelian parts. This appendix classifies such surfaces based on their horizon saddle connection behavior and connects the presence of these saddle connections to the existence of translation dilation tiles with dilation vectors possessing non-zero x-coordinates. Finally, the appendix explores the relationship between translation dilation tiles and the core sets of vector fields on dilation surfaces. Specifically, we characterize the core sets of vector fields on translation surfaces using translation translation tiles, thereby validating a conjecture by Chen and Zhuang. Additionally, we characterize the core sets for dilation surfaces arising from polygon gluing and translation-cylinder bundles. As a byproduct, we confirm several conjectures regarding the relationship between translation dilation tiles and the dynamical properties of the associated vector fields. These findings also address an open question regarding the existence of translation dilation tiles with dilation vectors having non-zero x-coordinates. This study functional connection model utilizes total correlation, a generalized entropy metric, to quantify complex interdependencies among various brain regions. We demonstrate that, compared to other models, the total correlation connection model more accurately captures long-range dependencies and enhances prediction accuracy for unseen data. Leveraging the interpretive power of connectionists, we illustrate that the regions linked in this connection model align closely with those identified through neurobiological research on brain connectivity. Furthermore, we show that the total correlation connection model achieves more precise predictions of future time series data. Finally, we validate the model's interpretability by establishing a correlation between the prediction accuracy of this connection model and empirical brain connectivity data. These findings underscore the potential of total correlation and connectionism for advancing next-generation AI applications in healthcare and medicine. Ravi, "Functional Connectome of the Human Brain with Total Correlation," in Proceedings of the 29th ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD'23), 2023. Total Correlation (TC) quantifies functional dependencies among multiple random variables, whereas Granger Causality (GC) captures pairwise causal links. The connection model defines a multivariate time process as a sequence of time series, where each series represents a vector of random variables. At any given time step, TC measures the total dependencies among all variables across the entire set, while connectivity networks are constructed using an algorithm that selects the most influential variables for each series. In this study, we apply the connection model to analyze dynamic brain regions using fMRI data. We find that the connectivity patterns derived from TC align well with existing neurobiological evidence regarding brain connectivity. Additionally, we establish a significant link between the prediction accuracy achieved by the connection model and real-world brain connectivity data. These results indicate that TC, alongside connectionism, holds promise for developing next-generation AI tools in healthcare and medicine. Specifically, TC identifies dependencies among all variables, whereas GC focuses on pairwise causality. This distinction suggests that TC-based connection models may outperform GC-based ones in predicting multivariate time processes. We empirically confirm that the TC connection model outperforms the GC connection model both in overall multivariate prediction accuracy and in predicting a specific target time series.

We demonstrate that for complex Clifford algebras, off-shell unitary representations of the Heisenberg group give rise to Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann spaces through the tensor product of $n-1$ copies of the 2-dimensional off-shell unitary representation. Furthermore, we show that the classical Segel-Bargmann transform on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ is isomorphic to a generalized Fourier transform under the identification of polynomial matrices with their noncommutative coefficients. This result yields an explicit formula for the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transform, which serves as the isometric extension of the classical transform. Additionally, we establish an analogue of the Taylor isomorphism theorem in the noncommutative setting. As an application, we derive a formula for computing the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transform of a polynomial matrix without invoking the generalized Fourier transform. We illustrate this approach with examples from the group of Euclidean motions. Finally, in a brief appendix, we provide an example of a Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann space associated with a finite group. This study introduces a conditional Gaussian process where each function incorporates an additional parameter integrated into the mean function. We demonstrate that marginalizing over this parameter yields the Gaussian process mean function. By applying this approach to full Bayesian inference for Gaussian process regression, we show that the resulting model can accurately forecast new inputs while simultaneously elucidating the primary input variables. This technique is particularly advantageous for tasks where understanding input features is as critical as accurate predictions. We validate the method's effectiveness for Gaussian process classification using a real-world dataset of handwritten digits. Furthermore, we extend the approach to Gaussian process regression and propose a variant designed to identify the most influential input features. Ultimately, we develop models capable of predicting both digital intensity and specific features, such as the digit's slant or input position, thereby enabling applications where knowing input properties is essential. To our knowledge, existing Gaussian process models do not offer this capability for prediction. The proposed method is broadly applicable to Gaussian process models that feature Gaussian priors over parameters within the mean function. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/kevinpfaendtler/gp-pathwise-conditioning. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of this approach for Gaussian process regression on arXiv:2002.00017. This practical version, while lacking the full Bayesian capability of our original formulation, is sufficient for regression applications where predicting input properties is desired. We have demonstrated its effectiveness on a regression task involving 2D sine waves with unknown phase shifts. Our contributions include: (1) a pathwise conditioning extension to Gaussian processes; (2) a method for Gaussian process model extension where the extended GP inherits the original kernel; and (3) strategies for inferring parameters within the mean function. Our original Bayesian approach to inferring GP parameters is detailed in our thesis [1], and our practical method for predicting GP inputs is described in arXiv:2002.00017. The original extension to Gaussian processes for predicting influential inputs is outlined in arXiv:2007.00017. This paper investigates a ground-based wireless sensor network (WSN) augmented by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that function as mobile relays. We demonstrate that a significant benefit of employing UAVs is their capacity to bridge isolated ground sensors, enabling these sensors to transmit data to a central base station. Our primary objective is to assess the performance of the proposed wailing-UAS system under the constraint that UAV movement is restricted by a specific energy consumption limit. Our initial analysis focuses on the probability of connectivity, which measures the likelihood of every sensor being linked to the base station. Subsequently, we examine the performance through the lens of communication capacity, which reflects the total volume of information a sensor network can convey to the base station. We find that the trade-off between connectivity (or capacity) and UAV movement energy is non-trivial, indicating that determining the optimal UAV trajectory to maximize connectivity (or capacity) is a complex optimization problem. To address this, we introduce an efficient algorithm for identifying the optimal trajectory. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression for the maximum achievable connectivity within a first-order approximation. We also highlight the non-monotonicity of this expression concerning the UAV's altitude, which implies the existence of an optimal flight height for a given UAV energy budget. Finally, we explore the trade-off between ground sensor density and UAV height from an energy consumption perspective. Our findings indicate that UAVs can substantially enhance the performance of ground WSNs, thereby offering a promising avenue for future applications. Additionally, we outline several promising directions for future research in this domain. Specifically, we suggest that the impact of random mobility on ground sensor connectivity should be investigated. We also recommend examining multi-hop communication scenarios where UAVs, acting as mobile relays, may serve as intermediate nodes between two ground sensors. Finally, we propose exploring the use of UAVs to mitigate the effects of eavesdropping on ground WSNs. This could be achieved by deploying UAVs as dedicated jamming nodes to disrupt eavesdroppers or as decoy nodes to divert their attention away from the legitimate ground-based WSN. These extensions could significantly advance research in this field. In summary, this study offers a foundational analysis of how UAVs can improve the performance of ground WSNs, considering both connectivity and capacity. The work establishes essential groundwork for future investigations into wailing-UAS systems. Our results indicate that UAVs can substantially enhance WSN performance, although random movement remains a critical factor influencing ground sensor connectivity. Top tagging has become a critical area of research for optimizing the CMS top signal, driven by the TopQuarkFuture Working Group's (TQFWG) recommendation to develop taggers utilizing complete event information. This work presents BoostedTopTagger (BBT), a top tagger trained on COMPLETEP data using the top-quark tagger based on Universal Graph Neural Networks (UGNN). The topology of UGNNS allows for the training of taggers on complete event data, enabling BBT to function as both a reconstruction and identification tool for jets originating from b-quarks. Trained on simulated data from the CMS proton-proton collider, BBT surpasses existing top taggers by approximately 10% in signal-to-background ratio improvement. Additionally, we provide an interpretation of the BoostedTopTagger through the use of Shapley values. Finally, we outline a path for the future development of the BBT algorithm. The BBT tagger is accessible via a public Jupyter Notebook at https://github.com/abernabeu/BoostedTopTagger. The source code for BBT, along with the data required to reproduce the results presented here, can be found at https://github.com/abernabeu/BoostedTopTagger/tree/master/paper_data. The algorithms are also available for import into CMS JetNet. Furthermore, the BBT model is available for universal adoption by all experiments. VO refinement is highly pertinent to various software engineering disciplines, particularly requirement engineering, design engineering, and verification. We extend this graph representation with specific annotations and utilize graph mappings to define refinement operations. Subsequently, we outline several useful properties of VOs and their refinements, which can serve as formal bases for defining sound and efficient analysis methods. Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success in sequential decision-making tasks across various domains. However, the core challenge lies in the non-stationary nature of the underlying learning process. Experience replay is a widely adopted technique designed to mitigate this challenge by storing past experiences and sampling small batches for parameter updates. Despite its popularity, we identify a significant flaw in the standard approach: it neglects temporal correlations between samples from the experience replay buffer. This oversight leads to the non-stationarity problem, which is the primary obstacle in deep learning-based reinforcement learning. To address this issue, we introduce VR-EVR, a novel algorithm that integrates variance reduction techniques with experience replay to effectively handle this challenge. VR-EVR incorporates a variance reduction step during the value function update phase and leverages the first-order correlation structure of the data to construct unbiased, rapidly converging gradient estimates. Our theoretical analysis proves that VR-EVR achieves linear convergence with a complexity of $O(T\log(T))$, where $T$ represents the number of iterations. Furthermore, we validate our method's effectiveness through extensive experiments on the Atari benchmark, where VR-EVR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms. Additionally, we have made our code and model available for public use. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/Chengda-Zhao1998/VarExpReplay.

"Volume" refers to the volume of a compact Lie group, which can be expressed as a path integral over Lie algebra-valued functions or, alternatively, as a Grassmann integral. The superbosonization formula provides a direct method to equate these two expressions for group volumes. Conversely, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation maps the path integral formulation to the Grassmann integral format. This article provides an explicit comparison between the superbosonization formula and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. Although both yield the correct group volume, the formulas produce significantly different integrands. For instance, applying these methods to the volume of a compact $SU(N)$ Lie group reveals that the integrands in the path integral and Grassmann formulations differ substantially; however, it is demonstrated that the path integral integrand can be expanded into a series that, when summed, accurately reproduces the integrand of the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. This finding suggests a deep connection between the integrands of the path integral and Grassmann formulations for the group volume. This insight is particularly significant for the study of chiral symmetry breaking in quantum chromodynamics, as the volume of a compact $SU(N)$ Lie group appears within the chiral effective action. In this context, the integrands of the path integral and Grassmann formulations for the group volume generate distinct contributions to the bosonization condition required to determine the dynamical $SU(N)$ $SU(N_f)$ fermion gap. Generating complex spatiotemporal data is a demanding challenge across various domains, such as autonomous driving and weather forecasting. Predicting movement trajectories from these data points is particularly difficult due to their spatiotemporal nature, characterized by dynamic patterns and frequent direction changes. We introduce a motion detail-aware generative model designed to predict long-term trajectories with high precision and accuracy regarding spatial and temporal details. Our method leverages advanced Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to extract features from spatiotemporal data and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) to generate future positions that preserve motion details. Specifically, the model utilizes the encoder architecture from ResNet50 to build a feature extractor that captures motion details from the environment. Subsequently, a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network is employed to predict trajectories by encoding both spatial and temporal dimensions of the data. Experimental evaluations show that our model outperforms existing baselines in predicting long-term trajectories from spatiotemporal data, achieving an R$^2$ score of 0.939 and a F1 score of 0.893. The source code and model are accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/MoDeRNN. This model holds significant potential for real-world applications requiring the accurate prediction of movement patterns from spatiotemporal data. Future research will focus on applying this model to complex real-world scenarios, including human pose prediction and object tracking in video feeds. Additionally, we plan to incorporate Transformer architectures to enhance model performance and explore the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to increase trajectory accuracy. Finally, we aim to extend the model to predict long-term trajectories in 2D video data.
Keywords: Motion Details, Encoder-Decoder, Generative Model, Neural Networks, Object Tracking.

We construct a concurrency model grounded in Rust's lifetime annotations and demonstrate its viability by formally specifying and implementing it in JavaScript. This implementation, named Josephine, integrates our proposed model into the language, complete with dynamic checks to guarantee safety. We provide examples in both data structures and user code to illustrate the model, demonstrate compatibility with existing Rust libraries, and highlight connections to other garbage collector designs. Furthermore, we executed property tests on blocks of code written in what is effectively Pure JavaScript, leveraging the demand-driven nature of our concurrency model. The paper begins by analyzing Rust's concurrency framework, followed by a review of related work and formalizations of garbage collection and concurrency. The concurrency model is defined using data types for references, shared references, and ref cells, built upon data structures for smart pointers and ref cells. Implementation details address choices regarding the ref cell representation and methods for garbage collection. Finally, the paper concludes with examples written in what is essentially Pure JavaScript. This approach offers several benefits: the concurrency model serves as an extension of JavaScript that simplifies programming concurrent code; its implementation ensures safety through dynamic checks; and the resulting demand-driven concurrency mechanism enables the use of existing functional programs as specifications for concurrent execution. To our knowledge, this represents the first execution of functional programs written in a pure language alongside the first implementation of demand-driven garbage collection and concurrency. The paper provides an execution model for concurrent data structures and methods for verifying their safety, followed by a demonstration of these concepts using JavaScript data structures. This work offers new opportunities for data structure research and introduces novel concepts for JavaScript concurrent programming. Ultimately, the paper shows that garbage collection and concurrency are feasible, thereby enhancing the language and advancing the field. While Standard Model neutral currents typically leave neutrinos unaffected, they can become significant in scenarios involving baryon number violation. This paper investigates such processes within frameworks extending the SM, specifically focusing on neutrinoless double-beta decay both at low and high energy scales. We demonstrate that multiple heavy states with TeV-scale virtual contributions can interfere in these regimes. This interpretation of double-sum data enables the reconstruction of effective neutrino properties, including the number of Majorana states, their average masses, and the magnitude of neutral couplings. Consequently, heavy states that do not interact via strong or electromagnetic forces can be characterized through purely neutral interactions. This study is motivated by emerging theoretical models that predict a spectrum of new heavy Majorana neutral states, a scenario supported by various phenomenological and cosmological observations. Ultimately, we emphasize that neutrino physics serves as a crucial component of a broader, multi-disciplinary search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. Finally, we outline experimental initiatives at colliders designed to probe heavy neutral states and their non-Standard Model interactions. These programs include SHiP at the (muon)CERN, P2MuM at Mu3e, and LHCb NuBE, all of which utilize neutrinoless double-beta decay as a primary search channel. By providing accessible experimental constraints, this work aims to encourage further research into neutrino properties utilizing data from high-energy colliders. Specifically, we aim to demonstrate that a comprehensive and adequate investigation of neutrino properties necessitates methods beyond those currently employed. Finally, we argue that high-energy neutrino research is an essential and necessary field of study. This article is the third in a series; the full context and the underlying theoretical framework were previously detailed in [1] and [2]. The remaining papers in this series will provide numerical results, theoretical implications, and an outline of the experimental programs utilizing colliders to search for heavy neutral states and their non-Standard Model interactions. Specifically, we will describe the experimental approaches to studying neutrino properties at colliders in [3], and the theoretical implications of these studies in [4]. The implications and potential of neutrino research at colliders will be the subject of our final paper in this series [5]. Keywords: Neutrino physics, Beyond the Standard Model, Majorana states. Permutation decoding has recently attracted significant attention for its ability to achieve near-capacity performance while maintaining linear-time decoding complexity. This framework is particularly significant because it validates the hypothesis that deterministic block codes can act as substitutes for random codes in list decoding algorithms. However, existing permutation decoding methods face a fundamental limitation: they rely on short subcodes with a small minimum distance, which severely restricts the set of correct codewords identified by the decoder. This paper introduces a novel subclass of subcodes derived from polar codes, which possess a minimal length for a given minimum distance but exhibit an unbounded minimum distance as the code expansion factor increases. By integrating polar subcodes with permutation decoding, we develop a new family of belief propagation list decoders capable of decoding large binary polar codes. We demonstrate the existence of subcodes with an unbounded distance parameter and establish a theoretical connection between polar subcodes and polar codes. Furthermore, we provide an explicit method for constructing subcodes with the desired parameters. Finally, we analyze the codeword set size and present a practical implementation of polar subcode-based permutation decoding, supported by numerical results. Our data indicates that polar subcodes can effectively replace short, high-distance codes in permutation decoding strategies, and that the resulting list decoders outperform standard belief propagation list decoders in terms of codeword set size. Additionally, we observe that the proposed decoder is among the first to support polar codes with a minimum distance exceeding 100. As an example, we detail the construction of a subcode with minimum distance 120 and demonstrate its successful application in a list decoder for a code ensemble with an expansion factor of 100. This results in an ensemble code with an minimum distance of 12,000, achieving an error probability of $10^{-3}$ at 0.125 bits/channel use, compared to 0.112 bits/channel use for standard polar coding. This performance surpasses that of recent suboptimal decoders designed for polar codes with minimum distances ranging from 1 to 1000. To our knowledge, this represents the first polar code subcode-based list decoding technique to achieve such results. The approach is also applicable to other subfield codes that are not strictly polar codes, such as Reed-Muller and Kerdock codes. In coadded image surveys, such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) associated with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the point-spread function (PSF) of the cumulative coadd must be accurately modeled to determine photometric redshifts and ensure precise photometry. However, the PSF of each individual survey coadd varies, primarily due to the evolving optical configuration of the telescope over time. This paper introduces a method to model these time-variable PSFs in a way that is computationally efficient enough for large-scale coadded image surveys. The approach models the PSF of a specific coadded image using the characteristics of the last four individual exposures. This technique was validated using the coadded images from the 30-band Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the public dataset from the Pan-STARRS 1 (PS1) survey. For a magnitude of $r = 20$, the relative root mean square (RMS) residuals between the model and the observed PSF width are approximately 0.005 arcsec for LSST coadds and 0.015 arcsec for PS1 coadds. The proposed method is computationally sound for LSST and is anticipated to be highly effective for other coadded image surveys, including Gaia, Euclid, and coadds derived from the combined data of both surveys. The code utilized in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/taekyungkim/PSF_model.git. The software is written in Python and utilizes NumPy, Scipy, and Astropy libraries. Additionally, the code includes a simple procedure to derive a PSF model from a single coadded image. We have employed this method in our photometric redshift (photo-$z$) simulations and will continue to do so in the future. The maximum computational cost is roughly 0.01 seconds per coadded image, which corresponds to approximately 1 second for 100 coadds. This represents a two-order-of-magnitude speedup compared to the time required to read the image file. We have also developed a procedure to fit model parameters using the `scipy.optimize` package, which can be easily adapted to fit model parameters against observed quantities using the `emcee` package for photo-$z$ estimation. This study examines the fracture toughness of brittle materials using molecular dynamics simulations within the framework of percolation theory. The investigation centers on the structural evolution of the damaged zone as it expands during crack propagation. Our findings reveal that fracture toughness is fundamentally linked to the characteristics of the frontally damaged region, specifically through the connection between these parameters and the crystal's lattice geometry. Additionally, numerical calculations indicate that the enlarged cluster exhibits an elliptical form, facilitating the rapid advancement of cracks at high stress intensities. Furthermore, we propose an alternative method for calculating stress intensity factors. By employing this approach, we successfully replicate the theoretical predictions of linear elastic fracture mechanics. Ultimately, the stress intensity factor can be expressed as a function of the stress four-point radius of the damaged zone and the stress intensity exponent, the latter of which is determined by the stress-strain curve. Consequently, our results facilitate a more practical and intuitive computation of fracture toughness for crystalline solids. The proposed methodology has been applied to various crystal structures, including body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed lattices. The paper concludes with a discussion on the potential extensions of these results to polycrystalline crystals and amorphous solids. These outcomes establish a groundwork for future research into predicting material failure in multigrain polycrystalline structures. Furthermore, the proposed approach offers a means to assess fracture toughness in materials where stress and strain data are obtained from molecular dynamics simulations or experimental techniques such as digital image correlation. Finally, the proposed approach can facilitate the prediction of failure in materials where stress and strain data are obtained from molecular dynamics simulations.

The practical deployment of quantum technologies necessitates the classical verification of their computational outputs. However, naive classical verification methods, which rely on re-running the computation, are prohibitively expensive because they scale quadratically with quantum memory. We introduce a novel classical verification protocol with linear scaling relative to quantum memory, applicable to the extensive class of quantum computations handled by any quantum circuit. Our approach relies on two fundamental capabilities: the capacity of a classical computer to sample from the current state of a quantum circuit, and the capacity of a quantum computer to validate this sampling process. We demonstrate the classical efficiency of our approach by implementing it on a publicly accessible web-based quantum computer, showing that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods regarding computational resources. Furthermore, we outline a path toward experimental realization using near-term quantum hardware. Ultimately, our work establishes that the classical verification of quantum computations is feasible with linear scaling in both time and space relative to the quantum computer's memory. This ensures that, although the quantum computer may be larger, the classical verifier will not be proportionally so. Consequently, our findings provide strong evidence for the stability of the complexity separation between the quantum and classical verification of distributed computation. Specifically, we show that the resource gap between the quantum and classical verifiers scales inversely with the quantum memory, a relationship that remains independent of the total computation time. This gap would otherwise be constrained by the difference in resource usage between the two verifiers during the computation itself. Our results also contradict the classical complexity conjecture suggesting that the classical verifier requires computational resources comparable to those of the quantum verifier. In contrast, we demonstrate that the classical verifier can be exponentially more efficient than the quantum prover, thereby refuting the classical complexity conjecture. Our findings also contradict another conjecture, which posited that a classical verifier requires more resources than a quantum verifier to verify the output of a quantum computation. We illustrate that, given sufficient quantum memory, the classical verifier can be orders of magnitude more efficient than the quantum verifier. This efficiency advantage is so substantial that the classical verifier can be smaller than the quantum verifier, contradicting the conjecture that the classical verifier is larger. Blockchain serves as a distributed technology designed to foster trust between parties lacking prior knowledge of one another. By leveraging smart contracts, blockchain enables the automatic execution of tasks when predefined conditions are met. Within the Internet of Things (IoT) domain, blockchain facilitates trust by ensuring data integrity, while smart contracts automate decisions based on pre-agreed rules. This paper introduces a new blockchain architecture for supply chains that integrates blockchain, IoT devices, and pre-sensors to monitor products throughout the distribution process. Utilizing a food supply chain as a case study, the study highlights benefits such as enhanced security, trust, and transparency, alongside improved efficiency driven by decision automation. We introduce a method for modeling the shape distributions of cell bodies (cell shapes) using explicit networks within an implicit generative framework based on neural representations. Implicit generative models represent 3D geometry as the implicit surface of a continuous 3D function, utilizing point-based distance representations to generate realistic cell shapes. These surfaces are defined by the zero-level sets of implicit functions. For shape generation, we employ Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to approximate implicit functions, while shape analysis utilizes 3D level sets derived from experimental segmentation of cells stained with fluorescent membrane markers. By training a segmentation network on labeled experimental data, we train a shape generator to produce realistic cell shapes with realistic geometries. The network is trained to reproduce segmentation shapes during the generative process. We validate this generator by assessing its ability to produce realistic cell shapes on held-out datasets. Our validation results demonstrate that the generator can reliably reproduce realistic cell shapes, even for rare and diverse forms. Furthermore, we show that 3D point clouds sampled from these generated surfaces can be used for various applications, such as training a 2D morphological classifier to distinguish between different cellular conditions. The approach integrates three key components: task recommendations, navigation strategies, and user feedback, all tailored to diverse learning preferences. We demonstrate the method's application across three document types—books, reports, and news articles—through case studies involving a user with a print disability. These examples highlight how different elements of the approach adapt to specific domains and texts, emphasizing the method's flexibility and scalability to other documents. Furthermore, the approach is expected to improve not only document navigability but also task performance and efficiency for people with print impairments. Denoising autoencoder-based pretraining has established a robust foundation for state-of-the-art performance in downstream tasks. This pretraining strategy, which includes unmasked, autoregressive, and masked autoregressive models, is standard in prominent transformer-based approaches like BERT and GPT. However, BERT's unidirectional autoregressive objective is constrained by the need for text generation, while GPT's lack of masking prevents the model from learning to infer missing context. We introduce XLNet, a model based on masked auto-encoding that utilizes a generalized autoregressive objective to overcome these limitations. On tasks such as language modeling, next sentence prediction, and question answering, XLNet achieves performance that surpasses BERT and GPT by significant margins. Additionally, our auxiliary task objective and "rental strategy" enable faster convergence and superior performance. On additional benchmarks including natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and natural language inference, XLNet continues to outperform its predecessors. In summary, XLNet demonstrates that a generalized autoregressive objective can simultaneously offer the advantages of unidirectional and masked autoregressive methods. The search for habitable exoplanets remains a central focus of modern exoplanet research. While low-resolution transit spectroscopy offers a method to analyze the atmospheres of such worlds, stellar activity poses a significant challenge, as active regions rotating in and out of view during a transit can mimic atmospheric spectral features. This study examines how such contamination affects low-resolution data and demonstrates that high-resolution observations can effectively mitigate these artifacts. We analyzed data from the most magnetically active G-type star in the Kepler field, KO-079, which exhibits strong H$\alpha$ emission, utilizing both TESS and ground-based spectroscopic data. The TESS instrument, operating at a resolution of approximately 100, was insufficient to filter active region contamination, resulting in measured transit depths varying with activity levels. In contrast, high-resolution observations allowed for the successful removal of these activity-induced signals. These findings indicate that achieving low-resolution spectral coverage at high resolution is essential for accurately characterosing the atmospheres of small exoplanets. Consequently, the paper advocates for a new large-scale, high-resolution transit spectroscopy mission. To support this proposal, we provide a simulation demonstrating the potential of such a mission to detect and study the atmosphere of a small planet. The analysis employs the ExoTransits code, which models the impact of stellar activity on transit spectra, and employs a Bayesian framework to determine the most probable molecular abundances. The results confirm that high-resolution observations can substantially reduce the influence of stellar activity, enabling the detection of major atmospheric components like water and methane on small exoplanets. Additionally, the study shows that high-resolution data can constrain the abundances of minor species, such as carbon monoxide. This research underscores the necessity of high-resolution measurements for both characterizing exoplanet atmospheres and searching for biosignatures. The ExoTransits code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/EliaSantoro/ExoTransits. By formulating an ordinary differential equation derived from a specific type of meromorphic 1-form, we present an explicit method for constructing certain conformal metrics of constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities. As a practical application, we classify one-dimensional constant curvature metrics on the sphere $S^{2}$ that possess two conical singularities, a result originally established by Troyanov in \cite{Tr89} via the use of projective connections. Furthermore, our approach extends to the case involving three singularities, offering a non-trivial classification of such conformal metrics on the sphere. This generalization was previously demonstrated by Bertini and Nelli in \cite{BN17} through a real variational problem, in a non-vacuum context. Additionally, we demonstrate that the one-form analyzed in \cite{BN17} is particularly suitable for our framework.

Additionally, the aerodynamic and hydrodynamic forces driving the locomotion are quantified using a force balance approach, while pressure measurements determine how pressure gradients influence acceleration during acceleration phases and deceleration during transitions between undulations. Finally, the air-water interfacial properties are characterized to explain how surface tension forces facilitate undulatory swimming. The findings indicate that the organism's length is the key factor in its undulatory motion, with both forward and reverse swimming achieved by altering the phase of mid-body undulations. Furthermore, *L. forficatus* demonstrates both momentum and stress-based interfacial behaviors, suggesting that its swimming mode can adapt based on its length. The paper concludes by discussing how these results offer a foundation for modeling and simulating similar locomotion in other water-surface dwellers. The study also examines the limitations of current modeling approaches and explores their potential for future applications in bio-inspired robotics. Predicting the consequences of space-body impacts on Earth relies heavily on accurately translating impact-generated surface deformations into dispersive propagation and run-up simulations. This study presents the inaugural fully coupled fluid-structure interaction (FSI) experiment within our CUBIC (Fluid-Impact-Buoyancy-Coupling) framework, designed to investigate dispersive tsunami propagation triggered by an asteroid impact. To achieve this, we conducted a series of numerical experiments that gradually increased the mesh refinement level in the far-field propagation zone. By the final step, the fluid mesh comprised approximately 1.5 million cells. We evaluated several mesh adaptation strategies, with the most successful approach involving the selection of the highest mesh level immediately following the initial impact and subsequently adapting the mesh based on a local Hessian-based indicator. The primary objective was to maintain a sufficiently small surface discretization near the impact site to capture surface wave dynamics, including dispersion effects, while employing coarser meshes in regions where such effects are negligible. Our results demonstrate that this adaptive mesh strategy effectively concentrates fine meshes around the surface wave without degrading solution quality. Furthermore, we observed that the Hessian indicator remains sufficiently small in near-field run-up regions, even as the tsunami wave traverses varying ocean depths. Finally, we examined the transition from the impact-generated water-mound phase to the subsequent propagation and run-up phases, noting that the fluid mesh must remain sufficiently refined to capture the evolution of the transient water mound. This research underscores the necessity of adaptive mesh strategies in numerical simulations of complex, multi-physics natural phenomena. We develop a novel seven-dimensional gravity theory by incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action. For specific values of the coupling constants, this theory yields two distinct field equations. In the absence of the topological terms, the theory simplifies to the Gauss-Bonnet gravity model, yielding a single field equation. We derive the corresponding AdS black hole solutions for both sets of equations and calculate their on-shell actions. Furthermore, we apply the holographic renormalization method to determine their entropies and temperatures. We examine the phase transition problem for these AdS black holes and compare the results obtained from the two sets of equations against the Gauss-Bonnet gravity solution, which serves as the unique limit where the topological terms yield equivalent equations. Finally, we conduct two numerical simulations to validate the first law of thermodynamics in seven-dimensional topological black hole solutions derived from the new theory. These simulations compare the results with those from the Gauss-Bonnet gravity solution, and in all cases, the two sets of results are consistent. Additionally, we explore the phase transition issue, which has been previously studied in lower-dimensional theories. We find that for both equations, horizontal phase transitions occur between black holes of different charges at constant temperature and AdS radius. We also investigate various equations of state for seven-dimensional topological black holes and their graphs, which closely resemble those of their lower-dimensional counterparts. Finally, we explore the holographic connection between these topological black holes and their dual conformal field theories. We derive the two-dimensional trace anomaly for seven-dimensional topological black holes and compare it with the Gauss-Bonnet gravity solution, finding that the two results are consistent. Finally, we explore the holographic connection between seven-dimensional topological black holes and their dual central charges. The analysis reveals that the ratios of the central charges in the Einstein frame to those in the Fefferman-Graham frame are consistent with the Gauss-Bonnet gravity solution. Two sets of disks, differing in size and mass, are arranged in a horizontal channel under individual horizontal gravitational forces. Previous research established that for channels free of obstructions, these disks self-organize into random mixtures when subjected to sufficiently strong forces. This study focuses on weighted disks within force-driven, non-obstructed channels, demonstrating that deterministic arrangements can form, specifically alternating sequences where larger disks possess greater mass. We identify the specific combinatorial structures of these alternating sequences and determine the minimum force required for their jamming. Furthermore, we distinguish between scenarios where sequences follow a first-in, first-out order versus a reverse order, and we note that jamming thresholds can vary based on the channel's initial configuration. Finally, we investigate the relationship between disk size and weight, revealing that while correlated parameters typically permit jamming, uncorrelated ones allow for jamming only when larger disks are heavier. Additionally, the study briefly examines jamming behaviors in obstructed channels. Keywords: Granular matter, jamming, packing, disks. This study investigates how distinct flavors of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) leave differential marks on global seasonal precipitation patterns. By analyzing 30-year climate model simulations, we examine the spatial characteristics of very low ($P_{min}$) and high ($P_{max}$) precipitation regimes across hemispheres. Our results indicate that these spatial patterns are primarily governed by the dominant cross-tropical meridional circulation during a year, which shifts direction based on the ENSO phase. Furthermore, ENSO-induced variations in $P_{min}$ and $P_{max}$ reveal significant spatial asymmetries between the two regimes. These asymmetries correlate with the strength of the cross-tropical meridional circulation and the zonal asymmetry of the Southern Hemisphere's subtropical high-pressure cells, allowing us to distinguish between different ENSO flavors through their respective imprints on precipitation extremes. Ultimately, our findings highlight the critical roles of the Hadley and Hadley–Ferrel cells in shaping global precipitation regimes and suggest that ENSO-related shifts in these circulation patterns are a key driver of global precipitation variability. \textit{Keywords:} Precipitation, Seasonal variability, Southern Oscillation phenomena. \textit{Subject classification:} 12.54.0. \textit{DOI:} 10.1134/S001239721806006X. \textit{Translation:} V.P. The concept of non-affine displacement, which quantifies the local deviation from macroscopic strain, is essential for comprehending plasticity in materials. Although non-affine expansion—the increase in material volume resulting from non-affine displacement—has been detected via high-resolution microscopy in amorphous metals and structural glasses, a theoretical connection to volume nonaffinity derived from linearized elasticity remains absent. This study investigates non-affine expansion in foams using a combination of $\mu$-CT imaging, scattering, and theoretical modeling. Our results indicate that to first order, nonaffine expansion in foams scales with their nonaffinity measure, defined as the variance of nonaffine displacements, and follows a power-law relationship with sample volume. We conclude that scattering techniques can effectively characterize nonaffine expansion across length scales exceeding the scale of individual structures. Finally, we propose that the emergence of nonaffinity in foams shares fundamental similarities with the plastic deformation observed in amorphous materials. These findings offer valuable insights into the microscopic origins of the Coble-Jones effect and the volume nonaffinity associated with shear transformation zones. {Keywords: colloidal foams, nonaffinity, volume nonaffinity, plasticity, elasticity, scattering} {PACS numbers: 61.43.Hk, 61.43.Lk, 83.10.Pp, 83.80.-f} {PACS numbers: 61.43.Hk, 61.43.Lk, 83.10.Pp, 83.80.-f}

We introduce a substructural logic featuring structural rules, particularly underlining, which allows for the contraction of highlighted formulas. We demonstrate that while the ordering sublogics HL and HSub, along with their underlined variants, possess undecidable logics by adapting Halldórsson's method, this undecidability does not apply to all underlined substructural logics, nor to any logic incorporating H-monotone or non-hyperstructural laws. The decidable cases include systems with purely multiplicative or purely additive connectives, as well as those incorporating the average connective. For these decidable systems, we calculate proof-theoretic complexity using hypersequent calculi enhanced with underlining and specific weakening and contraction laws. These enhanced calculi facilitate a single-step transition from multiset to multiset+multisequence premises during rule applications. We establish that these transition multisequences remain finite through dynamic analysis of proof height growth, thereby ensuring the system's decidability. Furthermore, we investigate various complexity classes—including recursive, primitive recursive, polynomial, exponential, factorial, double exponential, tripe, and tetrape—through complexity theorems, some of which rely on weight methods. Finally, specific examples are provided to illustrate how these theoretical results manifest. Notably, this paper marks the first instance of applying hypersequents to analyze complexity within substructural logics. Additionally, the proposed calculus and complexity theorems offer a framework extendable to other substructural or fuzzy logics, such as Lattice or Blasiak's Modal sublogics. While this work focuses on complexity, it also briefly touches upon modality, serving as a precursor to future research. Overall, this study serves as a foundation for extending hypersequent-based complexity theorems to a broader range of substructural logics. To achieve this, we propose that the concept of underlining—enhancing weakening and contraction laws to accelerate rule transitions and enable multiset growth analysis—should be explored and expanded within the hypersequent framework. Additionally, employing the method of abstract modal algebras could facilitate the application of these findings to other substructural logics. Finally, this work may contribute to the historical development of the field by providing the first instances of these advancements. Underlining was originally proposed by the author in 2011 to enhance weakening and contraction laws for decidability; this paper now fulfills its potential to deliver complexity theorems for these underlined calculi. Building on this insight, we introduce HyperExpan, a taxonomy expansion method that represents words in hyperbolic space to capture their hierarchical relationships. Given a word, HyperExpan identifies suitable parent nodes by re-ranking candidates based on the distance metric inherent to hyperbolic geometry. Furthermore, by leveraging the inherent properties of hyperbolic space, the method can also rank candidate child nodes. We evaluate this approach on the TUIREPO dataset, which contains industrial encyclopedias, and additionally apply it to the WikiLexicon dataset, comprising Wikipedia edit histories. Additionally, we assess HyperExpan's performance in supporting dialogue systems through experiments with two conversational assistants. This study examines the interaction between two S22 molecular pairs under electric fields. We compare various dimensionalities of Electric Field Perturbed Electronic Structure Methods (EFP), which serve as computational shortcuts for calculating chemical binding energies. The research employs a series of S22 dimers placed within an electric field. The results indicate that all EFEP methods accurately describe the interaction of hydrogen-bonded dimers in electric fields, with $\text{CCSD}(T)/\text{cc-pVQZ}$ errors ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 kcal/mol. However, for $\pi-\pi$ dimers, the errors of the standard EFP approach rise to 1.5–2.0 kcal/mol. These findings suggest that EFP methods are viable for studying molecular clusters involving non-covalent interactions. Additionally, the study confirms that electric fields can significantly influence binding energies. Specifically, fields polar to the molecular dimers can either enhance or diminish binding, with maximum changes reaching approximately 2.5 kcal/mol. These observations may have implications for applications such as molecular switches. Keywords: Electric Field Perturbed Electronic Structure, Electric Fields, Molecular Binding Energies.
