The current version of EFP utilized in this research is referred to as EFP2, accessible at http://efp2.net/. EFP2 is also available on the SIESTA website, SIESTA-efp, at http://www.siesta-efp.org/. EFP2's capability to calculate the electrostatic field generated by a molecular assembly is detailed in Ref. [1]. EFP also offers functionality for computing molecular quadrupoles, as described in Ref. [2]. EFP2 was utilized to calculate the electrostatic field acting on the molecular dimers. EFEP is a suite of EFP-based methods designed to compute the perturbation caused by an external field on electronic structure properties, including electron density, binding energy, and vibrational frequencies. EFEP achieves this by applying the external field to the EFP charge distribution and subsequently solving the Schrödinger equation for the resulting perturbed system. This study focuses on the effect of external fields on electronic structure properties, specifically electron density and binding energy. The fourth industrial revolution is fundamentally transforming manufacturing facilities, characterized by high flexibility, a vast array of diverse products, and rapidly fluctuating and unpredictable market demands. To address these dynamic conditions, this study introduces a novel multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model for scheduling in such environments, incorporating both non-deterministic uncertainty and a specific type of nondeterministic uncertainty known as "nondeterministic uncertainty with deterministic bounds" or ND-UB. While ND-UB is often overlooked in planning and scheduling, it is crucial for the highly flexible and agile product ranges typical of Industry 4.0 settings. The proposed model utilizes "betas"—ranges of probable values for parameters like processing times and due dates—to represent ND-UB. Unlike many existing approaches, this work demonstrates the advantages of handling ND-UB by developing and testing multiple robustness metrics based on schedule resilience to minor processing time variations. Additionally, we propose a new concept called "robustness efficiency," which guides the selection of the most appropriate robust schedule among all feasible options. The model is validated using two real-world case studies from the automotive and food packaging sectors, which serve as prototypical Industry 4.0 manufacturing settings. This paper introduces an algorithm for determining the resilience of cyber-physical systems (CPS) against cyberattacks. Resilience is quantified using signal temporal logic (STL), which defines a specific formula for the system and its intended behavior, while accounting for various attack types and associated costs. The attack evaluation function is derived from this formula, alongside models of system dynamics and attack impacts. We propose an algorithm that solves a resiliency optimization problem to identify the specific states where an adversary should target the system to maximize their utility. This approach demonstrates that the attack function is submodular, enabling the development of a greedy algorithm. Numerical examples illustrate the application and effectiveness of this proposed method. Furthermore, we present an evaluation of our approach against existing methods on a simple power grid resilience problem. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses current techniques in terms of both adversarial effectiveness and computational efficiency. Finally, we apply this algorithm to a more complex, realistic power grid scenario, where the attack function is computed within a reasonable timeframe. Numerical results confirm that the algorithm successfully identifies state and/or input attacks that maximize adversarial gains while adhering to prescribed constraints. The source code for this work is accessible at: https://github.com/ehsan-nejati/CPS-Attacks-and-CPS-Resilience. This paper examines how the accuracy of rs-fMRI connectivity predictions changes when using both pre- and post-processing multisite data. These results hold primary value for researchers designing and analyzing rs-fMRI studies, particularly those leveraging multisite data. This paper presents a visual relocalization approach that utilizes 3D surfel maps. Unlike prior methods that depend on template-based or handcrafted descriptors, our reliance on learned descriptors allows map-based relocalization to achieve greater robustness and accuracy. We employ global 2D-3D matching to identify visual features corresponding to surfels, subsequently refining the camera pose via non-linear optimization that integrates depth uncertainty into the matching cost function. Experimental results on the TUM RGB-D dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses the direct visual relocalization baseline in both robustness and accuracy. Furthermore, in scenarios where visual features fail to detect any surfel, our approach enables reliable relocalization within map-aided systems, outperforming state-of-the-art visual relocalization techniques that rely solely on image data by significantly enhancing robustness and accuracy. In this context, a direct verification theorem emerges as a particularly valuable instrument for characterizing optimal strategies derived from stochastic maximum principles. Specifically, a uniform convergence result can facilitate an iterative approach to approximating the value function. This approach involves sequentially solving simpler optimal control problems linked to approximate q-processes, followed by proving sufficient conditions to ensure the convergence of these approximate optimal strategies to the true optimal one. This represents a significant improvement over the method proposed in Lim and Sheu (2011). Additionally, this method allows for the determination of a sufficient magnitude for a model parameter that guarantees conditions necessary for uniform convergence, a step often overlooked in the literature. This parametric threshold may hold significant practical importance for practitioners. To underscore this, we include a numerical example showing that, outside this specific magnitude range, both the convergence of approximate optimal strategies to the true one and the associated error estimates fail. The interplay between antiferromagnetism and nematicity in iron-based superconductors is a subject of significant interest. Although pure LiFeAs exhibits nematicity at ambient pressure, its antiferromagnetic order is weak. Under high pressure, this magnetic order vanishes, prompting speculation that nematicity might serve as the underlying mechanism. To investigate this, we performed neutron scattering experiments on LiFeAs at pressures ranging from 0 to 12 GPa. Our results show that neither spin fluctuations nor a kagome resonance were detected, even at 8 GPa. These findings indicate that LiFeAs does not display nematic behavior and suggest that electronic nematicity is not the primary cause. Instead, the nematic phase in LiFeAs is likely driven by non-electronic factors, such as structural distortions or orbital ordering. Our data suggest that any such non-electronic order is suppressed at high pressures. Furthermore, we observed that the neutron cross section scales with q as $q^4$, a characteristic of ferromagnetic systems, implying that any nematic order in LiFeAs must be of the canted ferromagnetic type. This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that a kagome resonance was only detected in LiFeAs when both pressure and superconducting doping were applied. These results strongly suggest that nematicity in LiFeAs is not electronic in origin. Additionally, our measurements reveal that the ferromagnetic order parameter is substantially reduced at high pressures. These outcomes align with recent first-principles calculations indicating that pressure-induced nematicity in LiFeAs arises from non-electronic sources. Our work provides the first microscopic evidence supporting this long-standing hypothesis. Finally, the study of LiFeAs offers valuable insights into understanding nematicity in other iron-based superconductors. Specifically, our results suggest that nematicity in FeSe is likely non-electronic, as evidenced by the absence of kagome resonances in both undoped and doped FeSe. Similarly, our findings imply that nematicity in Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$Fe$_2$As$_2$ is non-electronic, as no kagome resonance was detected in Ba$_{0.88}$K$_{0.12}$Fe$_2$As$_2$ at 10 K or in Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$Fe$_2$As$_2$ at 2 K. This paper presents a comprehensive global analysis of Type-II two-Higgs-doublet models (2HDM), examining how anticipated precision measurements of SM-like Higgs bosons and Z-pole observables will influence the viable parameter space. Utilizing the GAMBIT framework, our study incorporates current constraints from theoretical requirements (unitarity, perturbativity, and vacuum stability), collider Higgs searches, electroweak precision tests, and flavor physics. Our results indicate that while the allowed parameter space is substantial, its boundaries are defined by 13 TeV LHC data. Furthermore, ILC and Z-fitter results are projected to identify the directions of the CP-even Higgs states by isolating the SM-like Higgs, potentially revealing the decoupling limit by 2025. Finally, we assess the impact of future collider data on 2HDM viability, demonstrating that significant information will be extracted from HL-LHC by 2039, while FCC-hh is poised to explore a distinct, currently inaccessible region. Overall, future collider outcomes will provide decisive insights into the 2HDM's compatibility with nature. Finally, we compare the sensitivity of upcoming colliders with projections from the SHiP and CE$\nu$CC experiments. Our analysis reveals that these future facilities will constrain the parameter space by approximately one order of magnitude, whereas colliders will achieve this reduction within about 15 years, followed by the other facilities in the subsequent 20 years. Furthermore, these setups will probe previously inaccessible regions of 2HDM parameter space, such as the charged Higgs mass range around 100 GeV, by conducting charged-current searches. In summary, these future experimental endeavors will yield critical information essential for understanding the 2HDM's fate. This work was conducted within the GAMBIT collaboration, and the GAMBIT package version 22.0 was employed for the global analysis. Additionally, the package supports Type-I 2HDM, allowing for future comparisons between the limits derived here and those from previous GAMBIT analyses. The underlying code and data are accessible via https://gitlab.com/GAMBITproject/GAMBIT. A primary objective in soft matter physics is understanding how isotropic fluids of soft particles organize into complex structures. Recent studies have sought to link assembly speed and the stability of the resulting structure to the shape of the assembly potential and the characteristics of the particles themselves. In this work, I demonstrate that neuroevolutionary algorithms (NEA) can surpass previous methods in optimizing these parameters for self-assembly. These algorithms prove versatile, enabling the design of materials capable of forming reversible structures, maintaining structural integrity under stress, and forming irreversible materials with stronger bonds. Furthermore, NEA facilitate the assembly of target structures from specific particle sets by identifying protocols of external fields that generate the required assembly potential. NEA offer a versatile platform for self-assembly that goes beyond merely discovering new materials; it provides a pathway to dynamically control the formation of functional materials with user-defined properties using external fields. This approach is particularly significant for emerging soft materials that exhibit external-field-responsive behavior, such as liquid crystals. Finally, I show that NEA remain effective across a broad range of soft materials that are unlikely to spontaneously assemble without assistance. These systems include both anisotropic particles and assemblies relying on non-Coulombic interactions, such as those found in colloidal assembly. The optimization methods presented here are expected to advance the field of self-assembly, aiding in the discovery of new materials and functionalities. Ultimately, this research aims to establish a comprehensive design principle for user-defined materials that can be readily applied to diverse soft matter systems. Furthermore, a web-based demonstration of a material assembly protocol is hosted at https://ashishkumar12345.github.io/NEA. Users can input a target structure and a particle set to obtain an assembly protocol that forms the target structure from the provided particles. Additional user-friendly demonstration videos are located at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/NEA/tree/master/videos/demos. Users may input either a target structure or a particle set to observe various user-defined user materials. We investigate potential energy densities within chiral gauge theories by leveraging the local effective action derived from fermion integration. A significant finding is the emergence of strong anomalies, which sharply distinguish between phases, notably segregating chiral symmetry breaking from the conformal fixed point. By examining a simple two-flavor model, we demonstrate the formation of a Debye mass, signaling the dynamical breaking of chiral symmetries, and determine the phase diagram using perturbation theory. Furthermore, we outline a numerical strategy based on hypercircle methods to map out the theory's phases. Finally, we explore the possibility of chiral magnetic condensation, which can occur near or within conformal phases, and link this phenomenon to baryon number violation in the context of electroweak theory. Additionally, we address the conjecture regarding a new type of symmetry in chiral gauge theories, which would necessitate the existence of matter-induced conformal phases even when chiral symmetry breaking appears feasible. Ultimately, we propose that the phases of chiral gauge theories can be systematically identified by examining the local effective action for bosons following chiral gauge fixing and performing bosonization. This approach reveals that strong and chiral magnetic condensation, along with confinement, correspond to the dynamical breaking of chiral symmetries. Consequently, chiral condensation and confinement can be understood as two facets of chiral gauge theory dynamics, governed by an equation analogous to the gap equation. This insight offers a potential resolution to the question of whether matter can induce conformal phases and provides a pathway to dynamically map the phases of chiral gauge theories. Finally, we suggest that the existence of matter-induced conformal phases could be verified by numerically solving the local effective action equation. This can be achieved by expanding the solution in terms of strong coupling and calculating the strong anomaly, thereby generating a nontrivial phase diagram even for simple two-flavor models. This method extends naturally to multi-flavor scenarios. Notably, in the electroweak context, this represents a dynamical mechanism for confinement, contrasting with the traditional view involving strong coupling and chiral condensation. Furthermore, it offers a dynamical explanation for why fermion families do not appear to form complete multiplets. Specifically, certain families are confined, while others remain deconfined and acquire masses through conformal condensation. We also examine the possibility of matter-induced confinement and highlight the relationship between chiral condensation and confinement as two aspects of chiral symmetry breaking. This study provides a theoretical analysis of how temperature influences magnon-magnon interactions and spectral properties in antiferromagnetic insulators. By employing a four-magnon perturbation theory based on the Holstein-Primakoff representation, we investigate temperature-induced magnon squeezing and spectral shifts. Our results indicate that thermal magnon-magnon interactions can generate coherent squeezed states of pairs with equal frequency. Specifically, pairing occurs between magnons that have absorbed and reflected thermal energy, leading to a separation between the two eigenfrequencies of the squeezed state. Additionally, we demonstrate that the nonlinear spectral shift of magnons is directly proportional to the pairing strength. These findings offer crucial insights for interpreting the thermal evolution of holistic magnon states and magnon spectra in antiferromagnetic insulators. Furthermore, the methodology used is also applicable to investigating magnon interactions in other quantum magnetic systems. Finally, this work holds significant potential for advancing the development of quantum technologies utilizing quasiparticles as information carriers. This paper introduces two enhancements to Loidreau's rank metric code-based cryptosystem, which utilizes Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework. Following a recent polynomial-time key recovery attack that compromises the original system, we propose two defensive strategies. Modification 1 involves employing subcodes of Gabidulin codes as secret codes, while Modification 2 involves using subspaces of Gabidulin codes as secret codes; this approach leverages metric subcode codes, which are demonstrated to be Gabidulin codes. Both modifications maintain compatibility with the original system's public matrix generation algorithm and signature verification process. Furthermore, the size of the syndrome decoding problem for Modifications 1 and 2 corresponds to that of decoding standard Gabidulin codes with equivalent parameters. Consequently, both proposed systems offer improved security compared to the original Gabidulin code-based scheme. A comparative analysis regarding parameter sets and computational complexity for encryption, decryption, and signature generation/verification is provided to aid in the selection of an appropriate code type. Experimental results support these comparisons. Ultimately, the goal of these modifications is to enable system parameter selection based on a trade-off between asymptotic security, communication overhead, and efficiency. The efficiency of all three systems is evaluated through comprehensive experimental results. Notably, the original Loidreau system offers the highest efficiency in terms of bit lengths for public and private matrices as well as message space size. However, Modification 1 achieves the best security/complexity balance, exhibiting performance comparable to Modification 2. In contrast, Modification 2 displays significantly lower communication overhead compared to both the original system and Modification 1. These results demonstrate that modifying the secret code can substantially enhance the security of rank metric code-based cryptosystems. Additionally, this work establishes a foundation for future research aimed at developing even more secure and efficient rank metric code-based cryptosystems. To achieve this, one must investigate subcodes or subspaces of Gabidulin codes that possess different parameters than the original code. The original L1 encoders were designed based on the structure of full-rank matrices over Fq, whereas the L1 encoders for Modification 1 were derived from full-rank matrices over Fq representing subspaces of rank r within the Fq^n space. For Modification 2, the L1 encoders utilize subspaces of rank r that are not necessarily full-rank over Fq. These modified L1 encoders were developed by analyzing subcodes of Gabidulin codes under metric rank metric decoding. These contributions provide a valuable basis for future research

Although pre-trained language models (PLMs) have driven significant advancements across numerous natural language processing domains, the development of robust PLMs remains a formidable challenge. Current state-of-the-art PLMs predominantly rely on vast corpora of raw internet text, yet this unstructured data is often insufficient to capture the rich linguistic knowledge humans acquire from dictionaries. To address this, we propose Dict-BERT, a language model pre-trained on a unique dataset combining cleaned Wikipedia articles with Chinese-English bilingual dictionaries. The integration of dictionaries provides an effective mechanism for infusing PLMs with the extensive, multi-lingual linguistic knowledge present in dictionary texts. Our pre-training process employs a multi-stage fine-tuning strategy that initially trains the base model using dictionaries and subsequent stages incorporates BERT as inputs to train the models in a self-supervised manner with dictionaries. Experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT surpasses existing state-of-the-art PLMs on 13 standard NLP benchmarks, including but not limited to SQuAD, MRPC, STS, and RTE. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the inclusion of dictionaries yields an enhancement of 1.1% in final model performance. The code and data for Dict-BERT are accessible at https://github.com/zhengyiyu/DictBERT. Our data can be found here: https://github.com/zhengyiyu/DictBERT/blob/master/data.zip. Finally, Dict-BERT models are available at https://github.com/zhengyiyu/DictBERT. Our results indicate that our pre-trained models excel in few-shot and zero-shot learning scenarios. While the evaluation covers English, the code supports evaluations in both English and Chinese. The evaluation results are available at https://github.com/zhengyiyu/DictBERT/tree/master/evaluation. Our evaluation scenarios examine few-shot and zero-shot learning performance in both English and Chinese. The source code for DictBERT models is located at https://github.com/zhengyiyu/DictBERT. Our results indicate that DictBERT outperforms existing PLMs in few-shot and zero-shot learning contexts for both English and Chinese. The code for few-shot and zero-shot learning evaluation is available at https://github.com/zhengyiyu/DictBERT/tree/master/evaluation. Our few-shot and zero-shot learning evaluation results show that DictBERT outperforms current state-of-the-art PLMs in both English and Chinese.

We present a probabilistic analysis of minimal spanning complexes, addressing issues within algebraic topology, statistics, and machine learning. This approach incorporates several novel techniques in random complex theory, including a continuous-time relaxation of the random triangulation process and new methods for analyzing random complexes. Our work establishes novel limit theorems for minimal spanning complexes, such as a central limit theorem for the weight of the "bulk" of the minimal spanning 1-complex in a homogeneous Poisson point process in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \geq 3$), alongside extensions of Mendelson's theorem regarding spanning forests and related structures. These methods also demonstrate upper and lower large deviations for this minimal weight. Furthermore, we reveal that certain characteristics of persistent homology computed on random point clouds can be characterized using random polytopes and 1-median problems. These structural insights significantly advance random complex theory and hold significant implications for the statistical analysis of topological data analysis. Specifically, they clarify the sources of both qualitative and quantitative errors inherent in topological machine learning algorithms. Finally, we introduce the concept of minimal spanning acycles to extend the framework of minimal spanning trees on graphs. This generalization enables us to prove that the weight of the persistent homology associated with a Poisson point process in $\mathbb{R}^d$ converges in distribution to a Gaussian under mild conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the large deviations of the 1-dimensional homology are governed by a mean field problem in probability theory. These findings represent a first step toward developing topological statistical learning methods. The paper includes numerical simulations that validate these novel theoretical results. Overall, this work marks a significant advancement in random complex theory and provides a new perspective on topological data analysis. It serves as a foundation for developing topological statistical learning techniques. To ensure accessibility for researchers in statistics, topological data analysis, and machine learning, all code is provided in Jupyter notebooks. These materials facilitate the implementation of these methods in standard machine learning software, enabling their application to real-world datasets. The availability of the code and notebooks supports efforts to enhance the reproducibility of research in topological data analysis. Supporting materials are also available to assist in teaching these methods in undergraduate and graduate courses. A key example involves the application of persistent homology to the famous Iris dataset, which illustrates the practical utility of these techniques. This case study offers a comprehensive example for students and practitioners to understand and apply the methodology. By providing these educational resources, we aim to broaden the community engaged

Federated learning (FL) is a privacy-preserving framework designed to train machine learning models using data held locally by multiple participants without sharing the actual information. In vertical FL, participants possess different features for the same entities, whereas horizontal FL involves participants with data on different entities. This paper concentrates on the vertical FL scenario and presents three practical privacy attacks: (1) a generalized version of a recently proposed re-identification method from a specific horizontal FL study, demonstrating that such attacks are also feasible in vertical settings; (2) an improved member inference attack with broader applicability that can deduce whether a participant's input data contains a specific label; and (3) a generalized version of an input data reconstruction attack, proving that knowledge of the input label distribution is unnecessary for successful reconstruction. These findings reveal potential security vulnerabilities in FL, particularly regarding the sensitivity of aggregation operations and the risk of participant replay attacks. To mitigate these threats, we propose two countermeasures: adding noise to aggregation outputs and restricting the number of participants. Evaluation results indicate that these countermeasures effectively reduce the success rates of the proposed attacks. Additionally, to assess the trade-off between utility and privacy, we quantify the impact of these countermeasures on the final model performance. Extensive experiments confirm the practicality of our attacks and the efficacy of our proposed countermeasures. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi-2001/FL-Practical-Attacks}. Finally, we conclude by suggesting directions for future research. Given the current limitations of FL, further investigation is essential to enhance its security and privacy guarantees. This includes exploring more robust encryption schemes, developing more efficient countermeasures, and conducting more comprehensive evaluations of the trade-offs between privacy and utility. Our work aims to raise awareness of the potential risks associated with FL and stimulate research in this critical area. Our findings also have potential applications beyond the primary focus of this paper, such as in the fintech industry, where financial institutions and other organizations can collaborate to train ML models for fraud detection and credit scoring while preserving privacy. Our research can serve as a foundation for this application by providing a framework for evaluating the privacy risks of FL and offering countermeasures to mitigate them. Our conclusions also suggest potential applications in other fields, such as healthcare and education, where FL can be used to train ML models for disease prediction and personalized learning without compromising privacy. Contemporary smart cities rely on integrated information, communication, and communication technologies to enhance infrastructure, optimize resource usage, and boost overall efficiency. However, as these systems grow, they become increasingly vulnerable to cyber, information, and physical threats. Consequently, the primary challenge for city managers involves the strategic allocation of resources to counter these diverse attack vectors. This study introduces the Smart City Defense game, an extensive-form game designed to model the decision-making processes of smart city systems in mitigating such attacks. We provide a detailed analysis of key properties, including the game's size, the existence of equilibrium solutions, and the complexity associated with computing a Bayes-Nash equilibrium. Additionally, we propose a novel learning algorithm, Smart City Defense, which utilizes an extensive form graph to facilitate the convergence of fictitious play toward this equilibrium. The approach is validated through a case study applying it to a smart grid framework, demonstrating its effectiveness in minimizing energy loss and cost during attacks. The proof-of-concept implementation successfully highlights the algorithm's potential to reduce vulnerabilities and strengthen security protocols.

This study examines the Hawking--Page phase transitions of Schwarzschild and AdS$_3$ black holes formed within a cavity influenced by radiation. For a Schwarzschild black hole, the transition corresponds to the phase change of the cavity wall from a gas to a liquid. In the case of a cavity containing a black hole and a bath of AdS$_3$, two distinct transition scenarios are identified. The diameter of the cavity and the temperature of the surrounding environment significantly influence these transitions. These findings offer potential applications for understanding information recovery in the context of the black hole information paradox. Notably, the sudden release of a large amount of environmental heat during these transitions could represent a potential pathway for the recovery of lost information. Consequently, this presents a promising method for addressing the black hole information paradox. Furthermore, this framework may hold implications for the holographic complexity paradox. It is also possible that this model represents the simplest representation of the paradox. Future research will explore these and other related aspects. Finally, this study may contribute to the broader objective of achieving quantum gravity. Since the commercial release of the S2 dataset, numerous label noise ranking algorithms have been developed to address noise in large-scale search log data. However, most existing methods rely on pairwise comparisons, which often lead to overfitting on training data and poor generalization to test data. This study proposes a novel algorithm that combines bag sampling and group-wise loss to enhance label noise ranking. By partitioning query-document pairs into bags and processing each bag individually, the algorithm reduces direct comparisons between noisy and clean labels, thereby improving robustness to label noise. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the S2 dataset. Furthermore, the approach scales effectively to super-large datasets, requiring only a few hours to train on 32 GPUs. The source code is available at: https://github.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for node classification tasks, yet acquiring extensive labeled data for many real-world applications remains costly. To overcome this, semi-supervised learning approaches utilizing pseudo-labeling leverage the vast amount of available unlabeled data to boost performance. Existing methods typically identify high-confidence unlabeled nodes based on current model predictions and add them to the labeled set to facilitate training. However, this configuration often results in sparse and disconnected labeled graphs, causing model predictions to become overly reliant on local neighborhood information. To address this, we propose a novel approach that employs graph connectivity as a regularizer to guide the selection of a better-confidence subset of unlabeled nodes. Furthermore, we enhance the confidence of this newly selected subset by incorporating a graph-based confidence propagation mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuan1992/icml-2021-pseudolabeling. Although numerous distributed decision tree algorithms exist, they often compromise on either privacy or performance. This study introduces two efficient, distributed decision tree learning methods that provide differential privacy guarantees through secure multiparty computation. These approaches maintain high performance with minimal loss in privacy and accuracy compared to centralized methods. When applied to a realistic distributed dataset from the 2018 Data Challenge, our methods achieve nearly the same accuracy as a centralized algorithm. Additionally, we propose two provably private and scalable protocols for learning differentially private decision trees in distributed settings. Experimental results demonstrate that these protocols can process millions of data points within a day on 16 machines. Furthermore, by integrating a noise-scheduling strategy, our methods can lower the overall noise level by up to 40% while preserving differential privacy guarantees. We open-source these methods and their privacy proofs as the DP-DT library, available at https://github.com/DeepSBC/DP-DT. The library also includes privacy proofs for other noise mechanisms, such as Gaussian and $(\epsilon, 0)$-differential privacy. The source code for the experiments is available at https://github.com/DeepSBC/DP-DT/tree/master/data_challenge. The library can be installed via pip using `pip install DP-DT`. The DP-DT library is also featured in the 2022 NIPS tutorial on "Differential Privacy for Tree Models." The tutorial's code and exercises are accessible at https://github.com/DeepSBC/DPT2022. The DP-DT library can also be downloaded from the NIPS Tree Model Privacy Code repository at the same link. Additionally, the library supports differential privacy guarantees for various noise mechanisms, including the Exponential mechanism, Gaussian mechanism, and adaptive composition. Our methods are also showcased in two other NIPS tutorials: the 2021 and 2022 workshops on "Differential Privacy for Tree Models." The 2021 tutorial is available at https://github.com/DeepSBC/DPT2021, and the 2022 tutorial can be found at the same repository at https://github.com/DeepSBC/DPT2022. This paper addresses the minimization of the regularized Rényi divergence (RD) subject to constraints, a function recognized for encompassing KL, $\alpha$-order, and Fisher information divergences as specific instances. We demonstrate that the Rényi divergence functions constitute a class of generalized Bregman divergences, enabling the application of Bregman Proximal Gradient (BPG) algorithms to regularized RD minimization, with proven convergence guarantees. Specifically, we introduce two variants: the BPG and its regularized counterpart, the RBPG. Additionally, we propose two Weighted Proximal Gradient (WPG) variants that generalize standard BPG methods; these are derived by establishing that the application of a Bregman matrix results in a generalized Bregman matrix, thereby facilitating the transition from BPG to WPG. Finally, we establish the convergence of the proposed algorithms for the general RD case, and for the power mean generalized Bregman divergence, we provide stronger convergence theorems, including global linear convergence. Experimental results on real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of the proposed methods. The computational complexity analysis indicates a dependency on the power $\alpha$ of the RD, with proposed upper bounds for all matrix operations. Furthermore, we examined the relationships among various generalized Bregman divergences, their connections to $\alpha$-divergences, and their utility in addressing practical problems, specifically clustering and regression. All results were validated through experiments on the MNIST and California Housing datasets. Additionally, we explored a potential application of these algorithms in privacy-preserving machine learning, specifically for horizontal federated learning, and conducted numerical experiments to evaluate their performance. Chain event graph models offer significant potential for modeling and analyzing sequential decision-making processes. However, full probabilistic modeling at the micro-level introduces considerable complexity. This study examines two models that differ only in their available information sources, specifically comparing analysis based on the entire trajectory versus the history up to the current decision point. Both models are defined by parameters and an implicit network structure. By applying Bayesian hierarchical priors to the parameters, we introduce a Bayesian Markov random field over the networks. A Markov chain sampling the posterior distribution of this Bayesian model network is analyzed using standard Markov chain sampling theory. This approach provides a framework for model selection based on marginal likelihoods, which are estimated via the harmonic mean estimator within a fully Bayesian context. The framework is demonstrated through an analysis of the Swedish Social Services Board's investigation into child abuse cases. The results indicate that the "with history" model outperforms the "without history" model, as it more accurately captures the dependencies between analysis decisions and the variables accessible at each step. Furthermore, the proposed framework proves more efficient than existing methods for model comparison involving latent variables. Finally, the study underscores the practical importance of accounting for dependencies between decisions and accessible information in complex decision-making contexts. The code used to generate the theoretical results is publicly accessible. (Data available at: https://www.soc.se/data/). (Software available at: https://github.com/bragehansen/CEGtools). (Code, datasets, and documentation are also accessible via cran::install.packages("CEGtools")). The software is fully open-source. (Development initiated in 2018; released in 2020).

We introduce a new dynamic method designed to converge strongly toward the minimum norm solution of a convex minimization task within a Hilbert space. This approach represents a Thieffry-Thibault-type inertia-damped-viscously-damped system incorporating Tikhonov regularization, featuring a linear friction term with a non-constant, non-convex, non-regular friction exponent $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and a regularization parameter $\lambda$ that decreases over time. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of this visco-inertial regularization scheme, providing a complete description of its long-term dynamics and proving global convergence toward the minimum norm solution in both continuous and numerical frameworks. The findings generalize previous work by Su-Boyd-Penot et al., focusing on the case where $\alpha \neq 2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the added Tikhonov regularization does not impede global convergence; instead, it ensures strong convergence toward the target minimum norm solution, contrasting with standard findings where convergence typically occurs only in the weak sense. Finally, through a bridge between continuous and discrete settings, we develop a numerical algorithm based on the proximal Gauss-Seidel method, which is proven to implement a discretized inertia-damped system with regularization. Numerical experiments are included to illustrate the method's performance. These results extend the work of Su-Boyd-Penot et al. and Bojanov-Pasik-Panagiotopoulos. Notably, our approach does not rely on assumptions regarding the coercivity of the objective function or the boundedness of the minimizer. The methodology is broadly applicable to finding the minimum norm solution in convex optimization problems across various fields, including machine learning, control theory, and image processing. This research is part of the first author's Habilitation thesis at the University of Athens. The contributions here extend the findings of Su-Boyd-Penot et al. and Bojanov-Pasik-Panagiotopoulos. Furthermore, it identifies the conditions under which chaotic transients emerge and demonstrates that both periodic and quasi-periodic transients can also occur. Additionally, the study explores how adding a degree of freedom to the agent's motion generates complex behaviors, including a new mechanism for the onset of chaos. Finally, the research establishes a direct link between these dynamical systems characteristics and the agent's visual sensory capabilities. Overall, this research investigates basic motor intelligence in both simple and slightly more complex agents to demonstrate how their behavioral capabilities are constrained by their visual perception. Specifically, the agent's complex behaviors are shown to be bounded by the information quantity within its visual field. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the design of intelligent agents. Investigating the impact of extended impurities on the microwave conductivity of superconductors driven by kinetic energy leads to novel phenomena and distinctive features. In clean limits, the conductivity is universal, independent of chemical potential, and displays a linear dependence on frequency at low frequencies. Introducing impurities with finite size modifies this behavior in two key ways. First, under heavy doping conditions, the conductivity transitions to an energy-scale dependent regime. In this scenario, the zero-frequency conductivity is determined by the superconducting gap maximum, which is dictated by the impurity size, resulting in an energy-dependent and non-universal conductivity. Second, at moderate impurity concentrations, the conductivity becomes doping and energy-dependent, revealing a complex doping-induced crossover from the kinetic-energy-driven state to a Drude-like limit. This transition is marked by the collapse of the Drude peak and the emergence of a broad conductivity peak. The peak position is governed by the competition between the Drude peak width and the frequency-dependent conductivity. The kinetic-energy-driven state is characterized by a universal conductivity, a universal collapse field, and a field-induced crossover to the normal state. In contrast, kinetic-energy-driven superconductors with large impurities exhibit non-universal conductivity, a non-universal collapse field, and a more intricate field-induced crossover involving both the normal and superconducting states. These findings are derived from a self-consistent numerical solution of the kinetic equation. The theoretical predictions are validated by experimental microwave data, with the collapse field serving as a critical observable for distinguishing between the Drude and kinetic-energy-driven regimes. Furthermore, the proposed method for identifying the kinetic-energy-driven state is applicable to various materials, including cuprates, iron-based, nickelate, and twisted bilayer systems. Ultimately, this study establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework for detecting kinetic-energy-driven superconductivity in the microwave frequency range. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to investigate the kinetic response of kinetic-energy-driven superconductors under the influence of magnetic fields. The code used in this work is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhongqiangwang/Conductivity. The findings presented here were originally published in arXiv:2109.03577v1. In that earlier publication, the collapse field was not discussed, and the transition between the Drude and kinetic-energy-driven limits was not identified as a field-induced crossover between these two limits. Plants are vital for human survival, yet they have not been intentionally bred for specific shapes. We present GrowSpace, a simulated environment where agents can influence plant morphology through light control. This system is built upon Biopyx, a physical simulator that applies real biological principles to plant growth. By training agents within GrowSpace, we can decode the space's parameters, gaining new insights into plant biology. Our initial analysis reveals that an auto-regressive model effectively predicts root length based on it, suggesting this trait is shaped by gradual growth decisions. Additionally, we identify non-linear relationships between the light sensor field and shoot growth, indicating the system's capacity to manipulate plant shape. These findings demonstrate the environment's utility for both biological insight and emerging AI research. The GrowSpace software is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/grow-space. The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative (IBSI) functions as an independent global collaboration dedicated to standardizing the extraction of image biomarkers from extensive imaging datasets across diverse clinical environments. A primary obstacle in this domain is the lack of consensus on key definitions and methodologies, which hampers the reproducibility of imaging studies. To address this, the IBSI seeks to unify terminology and protocols for training, validation, verification, and the reporting of image-based biomarkers. These initiatives encompass multi-planar windowing and window/level adjustments, as well as strategies for handling missing data and outliers. Dr. Janneke Leijenaar serves as the IBSI Director, representing the Radiation Oncology Image Analysis Society (ROIS) and the Image Analysis & Mathematical Modeling (IAMM) group of the Canadian Association of Radiation Oncology (CARO). Further information is available at www.ibsi.org. This paper series presents image processing techniques and reporting standards aligned with IBSI recommendations. While the dominant focus has been on PET, although not exclusively so, these papers aim to facilitate the harmonization of image analysis methodologies currently prevalent in oncology. We anticipate that the collective output of this series will assist researchers in standardizing their image analysis workflows and ensuring that resulting reports are compatible with external validation efforts. Additionally, the IBSI organizes regular challenges to evaluate the impact of standardization on research reproducibility. Details regarding these initiatives can be found at www.ibsi.org/ibsi-challenges. We invite readers to explore the IBSI website for guidance on implementing these standards and to join our community to contribute to its ongoing development. We propose a mechanism for generating the power spectrum of primordial black holes by utilizing a running curvaton. Assuming the total energy density comprises both the standard model and a hidden sector, we demonstrate that inflation ends when the curvaton decays into the hidden sector. This process induces a running of the $\epsilon$-parameter, which in turn causes a time evolution in the power spectrum. We establish that parameters within this running curvaton framework can satisfy observational constraints while accounting for the baryon asymmetry of the universe. Furthermore, we show that the model can simultaneously explain dark matter density and generate primordial black holes in the mass range of $10^{16} - 10^{23}~{\rm g}$. Finally, we illustrate how variations in the curvaton mass can account for the observed stochastic gravitational wave background. Our proposed running curvaton model offers a viable alternative to the conventional curvaton scenario, which typically predicts a power spectrum with a sharp peak. Additionally, our model provides a solution to the tensor-to-curvature ratio problem without relying on late-time inflationary features. The model also predicts an isocurvature component in dark matter, which can be tested by future satellite and direct detection experiments. Notably, this isocurvature signal differs from those arising from inflation within the curvaton framework. Overall, our findings suggest that the curvaton framework holds significant promise for addressing multiple cosmological challenges simultaneously. Furthermore, our analysis of stau dark matter reveals a region compatible with LHC data that exhibits a distinctive annihilation cross-section behavior. This contrast with Higgs portal dark matter allows us to predict a specific mass range for the stau that is likely to be observed. In conclusion, our study successfully establishes a comprehensive framework that integrates primordial black holes, baryogenesis, dark matter, and the gravitational wave background. Our findings indicate that the curvaton model can effectively resolve various cosmological problems at once. Finally, we have provided detailed predictions regarding the stau dark matter mass range, which can be tested using data from upcoming LUX-ZEPLIN and XENONnT experiments. We anticipate that these predictions will contribute to a systematic investigation of the curvaton framework. In summary, our work successfully establishes a framework for addressing multiple cosmological issues simultaneously, with the curvaton model playing a pivotal role in resolving these challenges. Analyzing how students progress through university and defining their major selection trajectories are intricate challenges within higher education. This study introduces a new methodology for learning low-dimensional latent transition models (LTMs) using Gaussian mixture models, demonstrating that this approach captures the core characteristics of these pathways. The proposed framework is applied to examine degree transitions, the timing of them, and the influence of initial college choices. Results indicate that a three-group model best describes decision-making processes, with distinct parameters for each group. Furthermore, students in each group exhibit different transition pathways and demonstrate varying degrees of myopia. Although limited to a single institutional setting, the method's capacity to uncover multiple university progression paths suggests its potential as a powerful tool for decision-making in this domain. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a widely used optimization technique in machine learning, particularly for logistic regression (LR) and similar models, due to its ability to navigate large-scale problems more efficiently than standard gradient descent. However, SGD can be highly sensitive to the selection of hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and feature scaling. This paper presents a variant of SGD that is less responsive to specific hyperparameter choices. The proposed approach is derived from the average mirror method proposed by Juditsky et al. (2011) and aligns with the proximal average method by Kim and Kim (2007). We demonstrate that this updated method maintains the same theoretical convergence guarantees as original SGD. Furthermore, we illustrate the benefits of this convergence analysis regarding the selection of challenging hyperparameters, such as the initial point and step sizes. Finally, we validate the potential of this convergence analysis through numerical experiments on logistic regression. Misinformation spreads rapidly across various platforms, including news and social media, often in the form of headlines. To facilitate further dissemination, these headlines are sometimes automatically accompanied by AI-generated summaries. However, such summaries can unintentionally propagate false details found in the original articles. Since detecting misinformation is challenging, it is more effective to prevent its spread by identifying text as automatically generated through natural language generation. This study introduces a task that classifies headlines as either automatically generated or human-written using Transformers. We constructed a dataset by scraping and filtering headlines from three news websites in South Korea, achieving a balance of human and AI-generated samples with an average set size of 1,400 headlines per website. We conducted experiments employing various Transformers architectures, including BERT, RoBERTa, and ELECTRA, to fine-tune them for this classification task. The results demonstrate that BERT-based models are highly effective, reaching an F1-score of 0.913 on our test set. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of the dataset and explored alternative classification strategies. Ultimately, this research underscores the utility of pre-trained language models in automatically distinguishing between AI-generated and human-written text. By providing insights into the linguistic features of automated headlines, our findings contribute to the field of text generation and enable the development of more effective detection and prevention strategies. We demonstrate that chiral spin liquids (CSLs) can be achieved in both amorphous and polycrystalline materials through the application of external strain. This method is validated using the J1-J1' model, a prominent candidate for hosting CSLs. Our findings indicate that uniaxial strain can stabilize the CSL even when it is energetically unfavorable in the relaxed state, provided the energy gap to the second excited state remains sufficiently large. These results imply that implementing CSLs in experimental settings may not require precise atomic-level control over the lattice or the thermodynamic stability of the ground state. Instead, it is adequate to ensure that excitable states with a significantly larger gap to the ground state are suppressed. These discoveries offer guidance for future experiments aimed at realizing CSLs in amorphous and polycrystalline systems, such as those achieved through thin-film growth or by applying mechanical strain. Furthermore, we examine how these conclusions extend to other models, including the chiral Kitaev model and the chiral $J_1$-$J_2$ model. Notably, for these systems, we identify a scenario where CSLs emerge in fully disordered amorphous lattices without the need for external strain. This occurs when the chiral parameter exceeds a critical threshold, a condition that can be satisfied in amorphous geometries through careful design of the local bond-arrangement distribution. This approach expands the range of realizable quantum phases in amorphous systems and suggests a pathway to generating new topological phases through the deliberate engineering of the distribution of local bond configurations. Finally, we analyze the Kramers degeneracy of the CSL and its implications for the excitation spectrum. We observe that while the bulk spectrum remains gapless, the surface excitations in a multilayer system exhibit gaplessness only at discrete discrete-time momenta. This distinct excitation spectrum is expected to be a generic feature of discrete-time CSLs. Additionally, we investigate the field-theoretic description of the CSL, revealing that it differs from the conventional bosonic Chern-Simons field theory by including a term that modifies the statistical angle of the emergent gauge field. The Chern-Simons field theory also describes the phase when a small amount of frustration is introduced; however, this theory breaks down at the boundary between the CSL and the field-theoretically realized gapless phase. This boundary corresponds to the point where a low-lying excitable state, with a smaller gap than in the CSL, becomes accessible

Future radio observatories will be limited by the time required to correlate signals from thousands of base stations, making the $O(N^2)$ scaling of traditional self-calibration methods unsustainable. This paper introduces a multi-stage approach for large-array self-calibration with $O(N\log{N})$ complexity, leveraging the convolution theorem. Our method begins with fast self-calibration by convolving the visibilities' Fourier transform with itself. To mitigate residual correlated noise, we implement fast self-calibration across frequency and time, followed by the removal of remaining correlated noise via spatial and polarimetric multiplexing. The final stage involves determining remaining correlated noise using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to solve the resulting matrix equation. We demonstrate the efficacy of this scheme in convolving and self-calibrating simulated data from a 1024-antenna array with $O(N\log{N})$ complexity on standard hardware, alongside a computational complexity analysis. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the algorithm, including a self-calibration module utilizing the SciPy solver. This work serves as a proof of concept for the $O(N\log{N})$ self-calibration of large arrays with 1000+ base stations, demonstrating that the proposed approach is computationally feasible on current hardware. The associated code is available at https://github.com/Aniruddha-12345/Calibration-Schemes-with-O(NlogN)-Scaling-for-Large-N-Radio-Interferometers-Built-on-a-Regular-Grid. Future research will focus on extending this method to non-grid geometries, such as those found in the Murchison Widefield Array and the Square Kilometre Array. To tackle data scarcity, we integrate a generator with a discriminator, where the discriminator is optimized to reconstruct conditional information and market factor values for every generated return vector. This approach allows the generator to synthesize realistic return vectors given market factors, even under extreme market conditions. We analytically determine the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ at the 3-loop level in Quantum Chromodynamics for general values of the Mellin variable $N$, within both fixed-flavor and variable-flavor number schemes. This transition function connects the Mellin moments of polarized quark and gluin distribution functions across different numbers of active flavors, a prerequisite for analyzing the Mellin moments of polarized parton distribution functions at higher orders. We also examine specific cases: $N=1$, relevant for quark charges under isospin $I_3$, and $N=0$. For $N=0$, we provide numerical estimates of our results. Additionally, we discuss the large-$N$ asymptotic behavior of the findings in the Mellin plane. Our results are based on extensive numerical evaluations of a broad array of polylogarithmic functions and their generalizations. We have cross-checked all numerical outcomes using our independent computational framework, which relies on the analytic continuation of polylogarithmic functions in the Mellin plane. This validation underscores the necessity of such checks in higher-order calculations involving numerous polylogarithmic functions. Furthermore, we address the issue of spurious singularities in the Mellin plane caused by the poles of the $\Gamma$-function, a topic previously explored in our work. We also touch upon potential future generalizations of our results to even higher orders. Finally, we apply our findings to investigate the evolution of the Mellin moments of the quark component of the gluon distribution function at three loops. We also examine the evolution kernel $P_{qq}^{(3)}(N)$ in the large-$N$ limit, demonstrating that it exhibits a specific form in both regions of $N$ and at $N=0$. In the $N=0$ case, we show that the evolution of the quark component of the gluon distribution function is governed by a single evolution equation. This contrasts with the evolution of the quark component of the quark distribution function, which, in both the unpolarized and polarized contexts, is described by a system of coupled evolution equations. This difference stems from the distinct color structures of the quark and gluon distributions. We also discuss the behavior of the quark component of the quark distribution function in the large-$N$ limit. User-generated content is central to social media, yet existing interfaces for creating that content often lack essential accessibility features required by individuals with disabilities. This research investigates how people with visual, motor, and cognitive disabilities experience social content authoring. Through a mixed-methods study involving interviews with 20 participants and the analysis of 20 first-hand accounts, we identify specific accessibility barriers and propose design opportunities to lower the entry threshold for social media participation. These findings are validated by observations from first-hand experiences and are supported by existing literature and accessibility guidelines. Ultimately, our study offers valuable insights for guiding future accessibility research and practice in the domain of social content creation. By facilitating content authoring for a broader range of individuals, our work aims to assist content consumers and content creators in building an accessible online community. This paper presents three tensor-based operations on hypergraphs, which we demonstrate are equivalent and collectively refer to as the tensor join of hypergraphs. We establish that any hypergraph can be expressed as the tensor join of a set of pairwise disjoint stars. Furthermore, we derive an explicit relationship between the eigenvalues of a hypergraph and those of its constituent stars under the tensor join, based on the number of edges. This allows for the explicit calculation of the spectrum for various hypergraph classes formed by the tensor join of disjoint stars. Additionally, we investigate several properties of the tensor join, including connections to other known operations, formulae for standard parameters, and the line graph transformation. We also examine and compare the spectral radius and characteristic polynomial across different operation types for specific hypergraph families. The paper concludes by compiling a list of open problems. Finally, we introduce and examine multiple types of fuzzy tensor joins of hypergraphs. Given the equivalence of classical tensor joins of fuzzy hypergraphs, we explore methods for decomposing fuzzy hypergraphs into such joins of pairwise disjoint stars. We present and analyze two distinct types of these decompositions, providing illustrative examples. Finally, we outline and compare the standard adjacency, line, and intersection matrices for both classical and fuzzy tensor joins of hypergraphs. These results contribute to an emerging field focused on the structural and spectral analysis of fuzzy hypergraphs. Specifically, this work addresses the representation of fuzzy hypergraphs through elementary components (stars) and facilitates the study of properties that emerge from the interaction between structural features and spectral characteristics. We anticipate that these findings will generate further inquiries and contribute to solving additional problems within this domain. In this context, the term "elementary hypergraph" refers to a hypergraph that cannot be decomposed into the tensor join of two non-trivial hypergraphs. It is natural to investigate whether elementary hypergraphs possess specific properties, such as being line graphs of other graphs, being perfect, or having line graphs with positive semidefinite adjacency matrices. This study demonstrates the utility of natural cubic splines for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials using time-to-event analysis. We show that these splines effectively model non-linear relationships between continuous covariates, such as age, and the hazard of progressing from Alzheimer's to severe dementia. Employing natural cubic splines offers the benefit of avoiding arbitrary choices regarding the number of categorical levels to which a variable is assigned. Furthermore, we introduce the Global Hazard Ratio test, which provides a single p-value to detect any form of non-linearity, thereby preventing data-driven, post-hoc categorization. The method is illustrated with results from the ADNI clinical trial. Our approach is particularly advantageous when dealing with highly predictive covariates like age, where distinct biological effects may occur across different ranges. Additionally, the natural cubic spline model remains straightforward, containing no extra parameters. We argue that this flexible method should become the standard for analyzing non-linear effects in Alzheimer's disease trials. Our findings have broad applicability to various disease-related effects, including cognition, biomarkers, and neuroimaging. We conclude that natural cubic splines represent the preferred method for handling non-linear relationships in clinical trials. By adopting this approach, researchers can prevent data dredging, enhance reproducibility, and improve the generalizability of their results. We introduce Action-CVADE, a novel machine learning framework designed to explore the potential of variational autoencoders (VAEs) in identifying dominant pathways for both simple and complex chemical systems. By optimizing the random variable distribution of the VAE's latent space with the action functional as the objective, we derive trajectories that represent the system's dominant pathways. Validation on the simple $C_{60}$ fullerenes and the Q1500 complex peptide model demonstrates that the method successfully pinpoints known reaction pathways for these systems. Furthermore, within the context of $C_{60}$, we illustrate the method's capability to discover multiple dominant pathways by adjusting hyperparameters. Finally, by simulating the nitramine Q1500 oxidation reaction, we show that the approach can yield diverse reaction trajectories. The results indicate that trajectories possessing the lowest action values align with those obtained from transition path sampling (TPS) and the minimum energy path (MEP) method. Additionally, when compared to typical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the computational cost of our method is comparable to that of the MEP approach, while offering the advantage of simultaneously identifying multiple pathways. These findings confirm that our technique can effectively screen dominant transition pathways for chemical reactions. This paper investigates a variant of parabolic complex Monge-Ampère equations, employing a PDE methodology akin to that of Phong et al. to derive $L^{\infty}$ and Hölder estimates. Furthermore, we extend these $L^{\infty}$ bounds to the context of parabolic Hessian equations. Notably, our proof of the parabolic Hölder estimate relies on the maximum principle applied to an appropriate operator, representing a distinct approach from the PDE technique utilized by Zhang. We demonstrate that one estimate fundamentally derives from the other. Additionally, our findings remain applicable to non-complete solutions. Finally, examples and counterexamples are provided to elucidate how our results depend on specific conditions. These results generalize those of Li and Zhang. Through the analysis of parabolic complex Monge-Ampère equations and parabolic Hessian equations, we establish regularity theorems that generalize the corresponding results of Dinu. However, our work does not address the question of smoothness. We conclude with remarks on potential extensions and future research directions. Finally, to enhance the readability of the proofs, the paper incorporates several lemmas and theorems that may serve as independent interest. We suggest employing Church encodings within typed lambda-calculi to establish an automata-theoretic parallel to Rogers' formulation of type theory as a logic of computation. This approach leverages the established duality between Turing machines and type theory to create a novel, fine-grained parallel. Specifically, we introduce a regular function, defined as a sequence of real numbers exhibiting omega-regularity, and demonstrate that the set of lambda-terms strongly-typed in a multi-type system can be encoded within the omega-regularity of these functions. Furthermore, we prove that the functions typable by any multi-type system form a superclass encompassing all regular functions, thereby offering precise characterization and classification results for lambda-calculi based on the regularity of their term sequences. This methodology extends to more sophisticated functions, such as P-rates and Blum-Shub-Smale functions, provided that sufficiently expressive type systems are utilized. Additionally, we present practical examples of lambda-terms derived from the proof-theoretic analysis of Peano arithmetic and construct typable sequences of functions from beyond classical computability theory, such as the fast-growing hierarchy and transfinite epsilon numbers. Finally, we outline an algebraic perspective on the foundations of type theory, suggesting that the fine-grained parallelism identified in this paper may elucidate significant open problems in constructive mathematics and foundations. These contributions collectively represent the first steps toward developing fine-grained hierarchies and understanding the fine-grained expressiveness of lambda-calculi and type theory. **Keywords:** lambda-calculus, type theory, regular functions, automata, computability theory, computability logic.

This brief note explicitly establishes the relationship between Itô and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components appear within the integrands. The associated correction term incorporates Lions-type measure derivatives and identifies the necessary cross-correlations to consider. We frame this approach within the context of mean-field stochastic differential equations that depend on conditional measure flows, noting that the result becomes trivial under full measure flows. Furthermore, we demonstrate this relationship in a simple scenario where a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation is involved. This example illustrates the connection between Stratonovich and Itô integrals when a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation serves as the integrand. The resulting dynamics are linked to nonlinear Perron-Wiener-Hopf equations through their empirical solutions, and we derive an explicit solution in the case of a constant initial condition. This specific instance provides insight into the broader challenge of explicitly converting a Stratonovich integral to an Itô integral when a nonlinear Fokker-Planck equation is present in the integrand. Finally, we derive a nonlinear Wong-Zakai type theorem for a conditional measure flow. To achieve this, we utilize the concept of conditional measure flows and employ the concept of conditional Young integrals. The resulting Theorem presents an explicit correction term that includes empirical Hilbert space derivatives of the empirical measure flow. This Theorem represents a conditional extension of Wong-Zakai Theorems that were previously established for full measure flows. Additionally, it serves as a nonlinear extension of a Wong-Zakai theorem, as it does not require nonlinear PDEs to be interpreted in the weak sense. Instead, it accommodates PDEs that are both weak and non-weak, provided an appropriate definition of integrals is used. This approach aligns with findings by Ayala, Rodriguez, and Torres (2019), who demonstrated that a non-weak (non-linear) Fokker-Planck equation can serve as a valid integrand for Young integrals. To our knowledge, this represents the first Wong-Zakai result explicitly employing Stratonovich integrals alongside a (non-linear) Fokker-Planck equation within the integrand.

Autonomous ground vehicles (AGVs) are increasingly deployed in shared environments, making the prevention of collisions and entry into restricted zones critical. While existing methods often depend on precise models or accurate state estimates, safety-guaranteed Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising alternative by relying on the system's actual dynamics. This paper introduces a data-driven MPC framework designed to ensure safe navigation and avoidance among multiple robots. Unlike traditional approaches, our method requires only online access to discrete-time state and input data, eliminating the need for precise models or sensors. Furthermore, the proposed formulation handles both fully and partially known risk-sensitive sets. Extensive simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed MPC, which outperforms model-based alternatives when the model is inaccurate. The results also highlight improved collision avoidance and fewer trajectory violations compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Grant-free access serves as a foundational concept for massive machine-type communications (mMTC) within the 5G era. This approach enables multiple devices to transmit without obtaining prior permission from the base station, thereby drastically cutting down control signaling overhead and latency. This paper introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm (TSGA) designed to generate high-correlation robust non-orthogonal sequences for mMTC in 5G networks. The TSGA operates in two distinct phases: the first searches for robust sequences that are immune to low power levels, while the second identifies non-orthogonal sequences with a sufficient count to support a large number of devices. The second phase utilizes the sequence pool created by the first phase as its initialization basis. Through a crossover and mutation process, the TSGA generates high-correlation sequences with a minimal number of Hamming zeros. Experimental findings indicate that the TSGA outperforms existing access code generation methods, achieving superior detection rates under low transmit power and supporting a higher device density. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates robustness against jamming attacks, maintaining strong detection performance under both non-coherent and coherent conditions. Additionally, the proposed method outperforms orthogonal sequences in terms of detection rate and excels over high-capacity non-orthogonal sequences by allowing a greater number of simultaneous device transmissions. Simulation results confirm that the TSGA generates high-capacity, robust access codes, significantly enhancing detection performance in dense mMTC scenarios. The algorithm produces sequences with lengths of 255, 511, and 1023, offering high capacity with lengths only slightly longer than the theoretical lower bound of $\lceil \log_2 N_d \rceil$, where $N_d$ represents the number of devices. This results in a reduced number of Hamming zeros, which the simulation verifies leads to improved detection performance. Additionally, the TSGA exhibits resilience to low SNR and remains effective even when a device count exceeds network capacity. Finally, the computational complexity of the TSGA is negligible compared to traditional access code generation techniques. Consequently, the TSGA is a promising solution for grant-free access in massive connectivity scenarios. To validate this, the paper details the design of sequences for grant-free access using the TSGA and compares the algorithm's performance against other sequence types. The study concludes that the TSGA outperforms other sequence types in detection performance and supports higher network capacity. The source code for the TSGA is available at: https://github.com/ahmed

We examine common modeling approaches for the phase transitions between moist air and ice, frost, and liquid water, specifically focusing on chemical potential and Gibbs energy expansions. These methods vary in whether they include a mean field term and in how the energy is calculated—either through direct computation based on current state variables or via expansion using variables that deviate from the mean. We examine the consistency of these approximations with thermodynamic principles, identifying key differences between transitions involving liquid water versus those involving ice, frost, and steam. Consistency is assessed in two ways: first, by ensuring the derived kinetic relation adheres to the second law of thermodynamics; second, by verifying that the resulting phase diagram is both convex and symmetric, ensuring a unique equilibrium state regardless of the initial conditions. We conclude that thermodynamic consistency is generally not achieved unless the mean is computed directly or the model is otherwise adjusted. Finally, we explore how incorporating additional terms into the expansion can improve results, offering recommendations for models used to study frost and frozen soil mechanics. These suggestions aim to provide a more accurate description of the thermodynamics governing the liquid/steam/ice and ice/ice-water transitions in moist air. Specifically, we recommend including a $\ln(\mathfrak{h})$ term and a $\mathfrak{h}$ term, where $\mathfrak{h}$ represents relative humidity. Furthermore, we propose including an $\mathfrak{h}^2$ term when modeling the transition between ice and frost. We also address the necessity of surface energy in the mean field term, noting that while it is essential for consistency in capillary systems, its role remains unclear in modelling frost. Finally, we examine the implications of using different chemical potentials for ice and frost, highlighting the impact of this choice on the computed phase diagram. Finally, we discuss the challenges associated with applying these models to phases involving steam. In summary, we have explored the various ways to approximate the thermodynamic description of phase transitions in moist air and assessed the trade-offs involved in these approximations. This work serves as a foundation for developing new models for frost and ice mechanics, as well as for investigating phase equilibrium using non-perturbative expansions. It also addresses the challenges of non-consistency found in existing literature. Additionally, the derived phase diagrams can assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate model for their specific applications.
