Ordered blueprints serve as foundations for exterior algebras, which extend the theoretical basis of matroid theory beyond fields and rings. This paper presents an elementary construction of the exterior algebra associated with a vector space derived from a formal vector system, utilizing blueprints rather than fields or rings. This approach is particularly advantageous because it remains applicable even when the underlying vector system lacks independence. The work also demonstrates a matroidal duality within the context of formal vector systems. Subsequently, a relative version of exterior algebras is developed, offering an alternative to relative homology theories for matroids. This development provides a tool for advancing the relative theory of matroids away from the constraints imposed by algebraically closed fields and rings. Ultimately, exterior algebras within formal vector systems serve as the groundwork for a theory of differential forms in formal affine geometry. Blueprints are defined as commutative monoids equipped with a morphism from the integers; they constitute a broader structure than rings, as they do not require the underlying set to form an abelian group. This framework enables the study of combinatorial objects through algebraic methods without necessitating an algebraic closure. This line of inquiry was initiated by Bergman, followed by contributions from Develin, Jensen, and others. This treatise aims to address certain gaps left by their work. Furthermore, this book serves as a natural follow-up to the author's previous publication, "Formal Affine Geometry," which presented a dual perspective on combinatorial objects using formal vector systems instead of formal affine spaces. Both this work and its predecessor rely on the recent publication of the author's monograph titled duality within formal vector systems. The text begins with a review of basic blueprint and matroid theory, followed by an introduction to formal vector systems. The second part examines ordered and formal vector systems, emphasizing their relationships with affine geometry. The third section examines formal vector systems through the lens of homology, offering an alternative to the conventional algebraic approach. The final section explores forms within formal affine geometry, building upon the concepts established in the second part. The work concludes with an appendix that addresses some unresolved issues. Throughout the text, numerous unsolved problems are presented, with the intention that they will inspire further research into forms in formal affine geometry. This book serves as a natural complement to its predecessor, "Forms in formal affine geometry," thereby establishing a comprehensive foundation for this area of study. This research integrates continuous-probability outputs from speech recognition (ASR) and attention-based sequence-to-sequence decoding in dialogue systems. Unlike standard ASR, which forces a complete word sequence at the end of inference, our model generates predictions word-by-word with an ongoing confidence score for the current top-choice word. To utilize this confidence metric, we first analyze its properties and establish a correlation with ASR confusion matrices, which highlight the most frequent confusion errors for each vocabulary item. Subsequently, we model the relationship between these confusion metrics and the likelihood of having already uttered a specific word within a user's dialogue history. We apply this derived confidence score to enhance a sequential model for dialogue state tracking, which responsible for selecting the correct response given the dialogue history. We further validate the confidence score's efficacy by applying it to a recent beam-to-beam dialogue decoder. Finally, we evaluate the proposed method using an ASR-conditioned attention decoder for inference and a sequence-to-seastate encoder for state tracking. Furthermore, we replace the standard softmax layer in state tracking with a negative-softmax layer designed to mitigate overconfidence. Through simulation on the Cambridge Bridge dataset, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses previous techniques by achieving significant improvements in both accuracy and confidence. Specifically, it boosts top-1 accuracy by 3.5% and top-N (N=5) accuracy by 4.1%. Additionally, it increases the top-1 confidence score by an average of 10.6% and the top-N confidence score by 4.1%. These gains represent substantial improvements over the prior state-of-the-art system. Finally, we have released the corresponding code to facilitate future research. By combining these advancements, we achieve new state-of-the-art results on the Cambridge Bridge dataset. Notably, we observe that the negative-softmax layer yields more significant improvements when used with the beam-to-beam decoder compared to the sequence-to-state decoder. This suggests that sequence-to-state decoding may already be well-calibrated, whereas the beam-to-beam decoder exhibits overconfidence that the negative-softmax effectively addresses. Overall, our approach delivers substantial enhancements to current state-of-the-art performance on the Cambridge Bridge dataset. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to other tasks involving ASR and dialogue state tracking. On the DialogueStateTrack 2020 dataset, we achieve state-of-the-art results with a 2.1% increase in mean recall@5 for the joint recall metric and a 3.3% rise in the mean

Our primary focus is on rank 2 sheaves with a fixed odd degree, though our methodology extends to other cases as well. By employing geometric invariant theory, algebraic geometry, and combinatorial techniques, we derive explicit formulas for these counts. Our general formula for the number of rank 2 sheaves on a genus $g$ compact connected non-singular algebraic curve, possessing fixed odd degree $d$, is given by $\frac{1}{24}(d+2)(d+1)(2g-2)(2g-3)^{d-2}$. Additionally, we present a formula for the number of $c_1(-1)$-stable rank 2 sheaves on genus $g$ compact connected non-singular algebraic curves, which equals $\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2(2g-2)^{d-1}$. For the number of $c_1(-1)$-semistable rank 2 sheaves, we provide a formula that incorporates the count of odd divisors of $d$ and the previously mentioned number of rank 2 sheaves with degree $d$. A critical metric in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified sets. With this count defined, the universal access structure represents the most comprehensive configuration, containing participants in every possible Boolean combination of these minimal sets. Since every access structure is a subset of the universal structure sharing the same number of minimal qualified subsets, universal structures exhibit the highest complexity for a given number of minimal sets. We demonstrate that the complexity of universal access structures with $x$ minimal qualified sets of sizes $s_1 \geq s_2 \geq \ldots \geq s_x$ is asymptotically $O(\sum_{i=3}^{x}s_i + x\log x)$. Furthermore, we present a straightforward and intuitive method to determine the precise complexity for the case where all $x$ subsets have equal size. This approach is then adapted and refined to refine the asymptotic complexity for general structures where subsets are of uniform size, reducing the total complexity by $O(x)$. Finally, we compute the exact complexity for the Assadi and Shamir access structure. To our knowledge, this paper presents the first instances of universal access structures that achieve optimal complexity. These examples can be utilized as building blocks to construct optimal access structures. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the universal access structure with the fewest minimal qualified sets of size 6, revealing a symmetry in its minimal set sizes that is also unique. This specific structure is a subset of Assadi and Shaham's (OSS) structure, which shares the same level of minimality. Our findings also support and validate our earlier observation that the minimum complexity for a structure with 6 subsets of size 6 is 27. We also note that the minimum complexity for a structure with 8 subsets of size 8 is at least 43. We present a prescriptive framework for defining and estimating entanglement within systems composed of two "optical qubits." This approach ensures that any proposed measure adheres to fundamental principles, including non-negativity and invariance under local unitary operations. The framework is applied to diverse polarization-encoded "photonic qubit" states to derive optimal estimation strategies for various entanglement measures. Furthermore, we generalize these results to encompass global entanglement measures and propose optimal strategies for their corresponding estimates. This work establishes a foundational structure that can be extended to develop a broader theory of multiparticle entanglement. Additionally, the optimal strategies discussed may be implemented using simple linear optics, detectors, and feedback loops to generate optimized measurement protocols. This provides a practical reference for designing entanglement estimation experiments involving optical qubit systems. Finally, we analyze the fundamental limits of estimation precision and demonstrate that the optimal strategies yield the most accurate estimates of photonic entanglement. These limits are particularly achievable when the photonic qubits are prepared in specific mixed states. Furthermore, we address the critical challenge of correcting the impact of detector inefficiency on measurement outcomes. Overall, this research paves the way for new experimental designs aimed at quantifying optical entanglement. Specifically, it facilitates the first direct measurements of entanglement between optical quanta using photonic systems. Additionally, it advances the understanding of the limits of quantum metrology by providing a quantitative assessment of the precision attainable in entanglement estimation within optical qubit systems. Finally, our findings offer a new perspective on the value of photonic entangled states as metrological resources. Specifically, we show that locally maximally entangled states of optical qubits can be directly measured using photonic systems, whereas maximally entangled states of optical qubits generally cannot. This conclusion contrasts with entanglement measures derived from quantum information theory, where a wide variety of equivalent states exist. This discrepancy highlights the unique constraints of photonic systems and provides a new perspective on the limitations of quantum metrology. Specifically, it underscores that achieving maximum precision in parameter estimation requires exploiting the full range of resources available in quantum systems. Consequently, this necessitates a paradigm shift in quantum metrology, moving away from the exclusive focus on pure states. Instead, it calls for the systematic investigation of mixed states to identify the limits of measurement precision. In this context, our findings demonstrate that a specific class of mixed states can be directly measured using a photonic system, whereas other classes of states remain experimentally inaccessible.

Recent JET discharges exhibiting a novel mode, identified as a "Palm Tree Mode" due to its distinctive mode shape, have been analyzed in this study. These modes display both helical and poloidal features, with their spatial structure in the edge region mirroring that of Edge Eruptive Modes (EEMs) observed in JET and other tokamaks. The spatial characteristics of Palm Tree Modes (PTMs) and EEMs are investigated using edge 2D imaging, while their edge dynamics are examined through local 2D measurements. Additionally, the paper discusses the origin of PTMs and their relationship to EEMs. It is demonstrated that PTMs arise from magnetic reconnection between two magnetic flux surfaces, a process that generates both EEMs and PTMs. This mechanism is supported by the observation that PTMs and EEMs share identical edge dynamics and are present simultaneously. Furthermore, it is shown that both modes can be simulated by the "tearing mode" identified by Furukami et al. (2017) [Nucl. Fusion 57 093008], which is another manifestation of magnetic reconnection between two flux surfaces. This simulation reveals that PTMs and EEMs are natural consequences of this tearing mode. Consequently, PTMs and EEMs are proposed to be two simultaneous manifestations of magnetic reconnection between two edge magnetic flux surfaces. This finding suggests that PTMs may also exist in other tokamaks. Finally, it is noted that PTMs are distinct from Poloidal Mode 2 (PM2), as PM2 is driven by the flow of the edge plasma rather than by magnetic reconnection. These findings have significant implications for the understanding of edge plasma dynamics in tokamaks. Specifically, they indicate that PTMs and EEMs are two simultaneous results of the same magnetic reconnection process, thereby providing a new perspective on the origin of these modes. This new perspective is expected to advance our understanding of edge plasma dynamics in tokamaks. Specifically, these results imply that the existence of both EEMs and PTMs is evidence of magnetic reconnection between two edge flux surfaces. Additionally, the identification of PM2 as distinct from PTMs clarifies that PM2 results from edge plasma flows, whereas PTMs result from magnetic reconnection. This distinction is crucial for future research on edge plasma stability in tokamaks. The rise of pre-trained models (PPMs) in continual learning (CL) has been driven by the promise of utilizing pretrained features and task classifiers. However, we contend that PPMs are not inherently superior for CL, and that their effectiveness depends on specific architectural choices. To demonstrate this, we propose a straightforward baseline for CL: a task-specific head combined with fine-tuning a PPM's classification layer. This fine-tuning is accomplished simply by adding a single classifier layer and training the resulting small network (consisting of one layer plus the task classifier) in an interleaved manner with the task-specific head. Our results show that this unorthodox approach of using a small network rivals PPM-based methods, thereby validating our claim and highlighting the significance of the proposed technique. As social media platforms expand globally, monitoring hate speech within online discussions has become increasingly critical for fostering healthier digital environments. Although current multi-modal detection systems leverage deep learning to analyze various media forms like text, images, and videos effectively, they often lack interpretability, limiting their practical utility. This study utilizes Graph Neural Networks to model the relationships between multi-modal features and hate speech content within social media threads. By incorporating attention mechanisms, the proposed method not only achieves high detection performance but also generates explanations of the prediction logic. Evaluated on real-world datasets, the approach demonstrates competitive multi-modal performance and reveals high-level rules governing hate speech formation through interpretable outcomes. Furthermore, within specific discourse threads, the model identifies key factors driving predictions, offering insights that assist online communities in establishing informed content guidelines. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first application of multi-modal integrative reasoning to the detection of hate speech and related online behaviors. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/chenchen1205/icde21-cv.

This study examines how heterogeneity in neuronal degree distributions influences the average firing rates within a network of integrate-and-fire neurons. Specifically, we analyze two distribution types: an exponential model characteristic of small-world networks and a power-law model often found in the brain. By investigating networks with both high and low density connections, significant differences emerge regarding how these two degree distributions interact with varying firing rates, revealing that both high and low firing rates can be stabilized through heterogeneity in network degree connections. Furthermore, we explore the implications of these findings for understanding how neuronal networks regulate and modulate their activity. These results underscore that structural heterogeneity is essential for the self-regulation of both low and high activity levels, a factor that must be accounted for in computational models of neural networks. Additionally, we offer a potential explanation for why high activity levels in brain networks are often suppressed. Finally, these findings provide a quantitative basis for the hypothesis that the emergence of complex, non-trivial activity levels in neural networks is intrinsically linked to their structural heterogeneity. These conclusions are supported by experimental evidence from the *C. elegans* connectome. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for neuroscience research. **Keywords:** neuronal networks, structural heterogeneity, degree distributions, mean-field approximation, C. elegans connectome. **Abbreviations:** CI: critical instability; FF: firing frequencies; FFs: firing frequencies; FF-rate: firing rate. **Acknowledgments:** This work was partially supported by the Spanish Ministry of Economy and Competitiveness (grant FISIO-2017-87220-C2-1-R) and the Junta de Andaluc\'ia (grant P12-FIS-7026). Automatic Program Repair (APR) has gained significant interest recently, yet existing methods often depend on heuristics that limit their efficiency. To address this, the study investigates whether adversarial techniques can contribute to more effective APR. We introduce AdversAPR, the initial approach to integrate adversarial methods into program repair. AdversAPR employs adversarial methodologies to produce semantic-preserving bug-fixing patches for specific bugs, thereby reducing the search dimension and enhancing repair quality. These generated patches serve as guidance for an existing APR method to prioritize the correction of key bugs within a program. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating adversarial patches significantly boosts APR performance, achieving a 24.5% improvement in bug-fix ratio and reducing the average number of bugs missed by 32.5% on benchmark datasets. Additionally, case studies reveal that the optimal integration strategy for incorporating adversarial patches varies depending on the specific APR approach employed. Overall, this research indicates that adversarial methods hold promise for generating higher-quality repairs, and AdversAPR is expected to facilitate further improvements in future APR studies. This paper introduces a comprehensive formula for the capacity region of a general two-pair interference channel, defining it as the closure of the set of all achievable rate pairs. This formula is derived using a technique based on random index randomizing, which simplifies and extends the encoding strategy previously found in [1]. We demonstrate that this method allows for a straightforward induction proof of the formula's correctness regarding any finite number of interference channels. Although not utilized here, this inductive property could be valuable in specific scenarios. Additionally, the approach facilitates the proof that formula-based solutions are optimal for two specific cases of the GIFC. For both cases, we calculate explicit inner and outer bounds on the capacity region and demonstrate their equality. In the first case, where interference channels have identical input distributions and power constraints, the outer bound consists of a single point, thereby proving the optimality of power-based time-sharing. The third-moment flow moment analysis method offers a novel approach to investigating both the colliding system's geometry and its equation-of-state. This technique is grounded in the relationship between flow moments and the impact parameter, $b$, defined as $U_n^n = 3^n(1+b^2)^n(2n+3)$. By constructing the collision geometry parameter $b$, along with the elliptic and 3-pectronical deformation parameters $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{P}_3$, researchers can quantify the colliding system's geometry. The value of $b$ was extracted from experimental data for $U_3^3$ using a $\chi^2$ method. Applying this analysis to Au+Au collisions at 1.8, 2.7, 3.5, and 4.5 GeV/nucleon reveals that the equilibrium value of $b$ rises with beam energy, reaching a maximum near 3.5 GeV/nucleon before declining. Additionally, the results indicate that the Au+Au system exhibits stronger ellipsoidal deformations at low energies, which gradually smooth out as collision energy increases. This method is also applicable to other heavy-ion systems. Furthermore, the influence of the equation-of-state on these findings was explored. Assuming a linear equation-of-state, $P = c_s^2 \epsilon$, the speed of sound $c_s$ was derived from the order parameter $U_3^3 - \langle U_3^3 \rangle$ as a function of energy. The findings suggest that the speed of sound is lower at low beam energies and higher at high energies. These results align with previously published data. Comparing the experimental results with model calculations indicates that the p+Au system is nearly spherical. Additionally, the order parameter $U_3^3 - \langle U_3^3 \rangle$ shows a sharp decrease at low energies, followed by a gradual increase as energy rises. These observations are consistent with previously published results. Furthermore, the speed of sound in the p+Au system is found to be higher than that in Au+Au across all energies. Detecting COVID-19 early is crucial for controlling its spread, as symptoms often appear only after significant viral replication. However, the rapid emergence of the disease has led to an insufficient number of labeled cases for training reliable classifiers. Additionally, the high stakes of misdiagnosis make accuracy essential, while the scarcity of data introduces high variance. To address these challenges, we introduce ADV-COVID19, a classifier designed to identify COVID-19 from limited data while effectively identifying false positives. This system utilizes an adversarial network that enhances robustness against adversarial samples. We demonstrate that such privacy-preserving classifiers can detect the disease using data from only three patients. Our evaluation shows that ADV-COVID19 surpasses existing methods in both precision and recall under these constrained data conditions. We further prove the model's robustness by training it on a small subset of data and assessing it on substantially larger datasets. We anticipate that this approach will significantly benefit researchers developing early detection tools for COVID-19. Our code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/Privacy-Aware-Classifier-for-COVID-19. Additionally, we have released a Jupyter notebook on Google Colab to facilitate the deployment of ADV-COVID19. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) serve as a potent machine learning framework for analyzing and predicting outcomes within wireless communication systems by modeling them as graphs. For instance, in a cellular network, base stations and user equipment can be represented as nodes, with connections indicating co-channel interference links. GNNs excel here by learning to predict system performance based on input data features and inter-node relationships. However, traditional GNN training methods often depend on a central controller to optimize performance, a dependency that conflicts with the wireless industry's trend toward decentralized control. This paper proposes a decentralized framework for training GNNs to predict system performance. Specifically, we introduce ADW-GNN, a customized variant of the ADW algorithm designed for this purpose. Our simulation results demonstrate that ADW-GNN achieves accuracy comparable to centralized GNN training while simultaneously reducing communication overhead and computational complexity. Furthermore, we apply this decentralized training approach to the wireless tomography problem and prove its efficacy in reconstructing building layouts from channel impulse responses. Finally, we highlight the broader applicability of our proposed decentralized training solution for various machine learning tasks in wireless communications. Homicide rates in South America are approximately 10 to 20 times higher than the global average, a situation particularly acute in Brazil. Within Brazil, homicide distribution is highly uneven across states and disproportionately concentrated in large cities. This study addresses the lack of research on intra-urban spatial heterogeneity regarding homicide incidence. By analyzing state-wide spatial data, we identified distinct spatial clusters of homicides across all Brazilian municipalities without relying on prior hypotheses. We then assessed the temporal evolution of these clusters and their relationship with socio-economic factors. Our findings indicate that, after accounting for state effects, homicide rates in the largest municipalities are significantly higher than in smaller ones. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that homicide rates in large cities are not randomly distributed but exhibit strong spatial clustering. Finally, we observed that while homicide rates have declined over time, this reduction is more pronounced in smaller municipalities; conversely, large municipalities show either a higher rate of reduction or maintain persistently high and stable homicide levels. These conclusions are supported by high-quality spatial data with high effect sizes. Ultimately, our study confirms significant spatially heterogeneous patterns in urban homicide rates. These results underscore the necessity of incorporating spatially explicit and targeted interventions to effectively combat the persistent and high levels of urban homicide. Furthermore, our methodology is broadly applicable to other spatially explicit and highly heterogeneous social problems, such as the spatial distribution of the COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach is easily adaptable to various research contexts, including when only spatially explicit data are available. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ricardomartinsgoi/cluster_analysis_homicide_rates. Gois State, Brazil.

This work introduces a category of accelerated stochastic gradient descent methods designed to address two critical issues in deep learning optimization: adaptation to problem-specific characteristics and mitigation of stochastic noise. We first develop problem-adaptive stochastic gradient descent (A-SGD) and subsequently introduce accelerated problem-adaptive methods, termed ASGA, by integrating A-SGD with various state-of-the-art accelerated stochastic gradient descent approaches. These algorithms are also customizable based on specific problem attributes. Through rigorous theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that A-SGD achieves linear convergence with a proven noise robustness factor of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for $T$ stochastic gradients, matching the performance of standard SGD. Furthermore, ASGA attains linear convergence with a proven noise robustness factor of $O(1/T)$ for $T$ stochastic gradients, matching standard SGD. Numerical experiments confirm the empirical effectiveness of these algorithms across various deep learning tasks, including classification, clustering, and matrix completion. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python implementation of ASGA. Our experiments indicate that both the empirical performance and execution time of these methods are competitive with, and in some cases superior to, state-of-the-art accelerated stochastic gradient descent techniques. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhongtao-liu/ASGA. Keywords: Accelerated stochastic gradient descent, Stochastic gradient descent, Deep learning, Accelerated proximal gradient, Accelerated coordinate descent, Accelerated stochastic coordinate descent. Axion-based physics is currently a major focus of both theoretical and experimental research, driven by the potential to set strong limits on nuclear forces and to detect or confirm the existence of axion-like particles (ALPs). IAXO represents the most advanced axion haloscope project to date, designed to probe the nuclear core by targeting solar axions. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the axion flux within the IAXO configuration, specifically focusing on the axion component of the solar flux. We investigate how varying axion parameters influence the number of events recorded by BabyIAXO, the inaugural phase of the IAXO program. Our results demonstrate that BabyIAXO can achieve a mass sensitivity of $m_{\rm min}=1.5\times10^{-11}$ eV and a coupling constant sensitivity of $g_{\gamma\gamma}^{\rm min}=2.4\times10^{-13}$ eV$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we show that the functional form of the solar axion flux is the primary factor determining the event rate, while other core physics parameters have a negligible impact on BabyIAXO's sensitivity. Finally, we illustrate that precise measurements of the solar axion flux are achievable through spectral analysis of the events detected by BabyIAXO. This approach would allow for the determination of the solar core's temperature, convective velocity, and the self-interaction cross-section of the axion with a high degree of accuracy. These measurements are expected to provide valuable insights into the internal dynamics of the Sun. Additionally, we show that BabyIAXO can rule out a specific region of parameter space previously identified as a "gap" in constraints from the Keck Solar Axion Telescope (SolarAxT) and the Helios experiment. This demonstrates that BabyIAXO is capable of exploring parameter regions that were previously inaccessible to axion searches conducted in terrestrial laboratories. Overall, this work underscores the significance of BabyIAXO for solar axion research and highlights the instrument's potential to provide a unique window into the Sun's core. This capability is expected to yield valuable information about fundamental physics, including the determination of the fine structure constant in the core and the study of new physics beyond the Standard Model. By probing the Sun's core, these findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of stellar physics. This work investigates the temporal dynamics of occupation numbers in a bosonic oscillator, featuring one or two degrees of freedom, which is linearly and completely coupled to both fermionic and bosonic thermal reservoirs. The paper examines the lack of equilibrium within this oscillator, proposing it as a mechanism to generate and sustain self-oscillations through continuous feeding and dissipation. Furthermore, it analyzes the establishment of a new, non-equilibrium steady state by adjusting the coupling to the reservoirs and their physical parameters. The study addresses these oscillators using both Heisenberg-Langevin and Master equations, alongside numerical simulations, to jointly analyze space and time evolution. To characterize the various physical phenomena involved, frequency spectra, spectral densities, and time correlation functions for the occupation operators are calculated and discussed. Additionally, the effects of internal degrees of freedom (modes) on these phenomena are examined. Finally, boundary conditions at the system-reservoir interfaces, specifically the skin effect, are addressed. The work concludes by suggesting potential experimental realizations, such as those involving charged and neutral partial particles, to observe these non-equilibrium effects. Keywords: Open quantum systems; Bosonic oscillator; Thermal reservoir; Thermalization; Quasi-harmonic oscillations; Complete operator coupling. Robotic dexterous manipulation is a highly complex and difficult challenge. To address this, the robotics community has developed numerous datasets featuring a variety of objects with diverse geometries, textures, and lighting conditions. However, most existing collections rely on actuated grippers, such as grippers or parallel grippers, which severely restricts the functional capabilities of robotic hands. In contrast, robotic dexterous hands offer a vast range of potential grasps due to their multiple degrees of freedom. While several robotic dexterous grasp datasets exist, including DexNet, they are either small in scale or comprise an extremely limited set of graspable objects. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a large-scale, diverse dataset that captures the broad functional space of robotic dexterous hands. To bridge this gap, we present DexGraspNet, a new dataset containing 1.5 million synthetic grasp poses generated using the DexGrasp-Synthetic method. We demonstrate the efficacy of DexGraspNet by training and evaluating two prominent algorithms, Dex-GRIP and GraspIt++, on this new data. Our results indicate that training on DexGraspNet significantly enhances the generalization and robustness of these algorithms, yielding substantial improvements in success rates compared to training on the original DexNet. Furthermore, DexGraspNet supports multiple new graspable objects not present in the original DexNet, further boosting the generalization performance of the test algorithms. Finally, DexGraspNet is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robertg2/DexGraspNet. We anticipate that the broad functional grasp space of this dataset will facilitate the development of more effective and robotic dexterous grasp algorithms. Additionally, DexGraspNet will be valuable for benchmarking robotic dexterous hands in diverse real-world scenarios, including those involving challenging lighting and textures. **Objective:** To develop and assess a free-breathing, respiratory motion-compensated 4D (3D plus respiration) $T_2$-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TESE) sequence for body imaging.

**Approach:** The method employs a variable slice ordering (VSO) approach, where slices are read sequentially across multiple volumes, with slice positions adjusted based on real-time respiratory phase. A partial Fourier acquisition combined with a variable flip angle (VFA) profile is utilized to achieve fast, long $T_2$-weighted imaging. This study reports the first application of this technique in the chest. Technical performance was evaluated using in vivo phantoms and healthy volunteers.

**Results:** In a healthy volunteer study, the VSO approach enabled the acquisition of a 4D lung dataset in approximately 11 minutes. The resulting resolution was 2.5 mm in-plane (with 12 mm slice thickness) and 15 cm field of view, offering 1.5 bits of temporal resolution per phase. The technique effectively corrected for respiratory motion, yielding high-fidelity images with minimal signal drop-out.

**Conclusion:** The proposed VSO approach facilitates high-quality, free-breathing 4D T2-TESE imaging for the chest. Future work will extend this technique to other regions, such as the abdomen and brain, in patients. Ultimately, this method aims to facilitate high-quality, free-breathing 4D T2-TESE imaging for future clinical applications. (This study was conducted under ethical approval from the local ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all volunteers).

**Keywords:** Turbo spin echo, respiratory motion compensation, free-breathing, body imaging, thoracic imaging.

This paper presents InDistill, a new model compression framework designed to enhance the efficiency of prediction models. Our approach focuses on reducing both the latency and memory consumption of the primary model by enabling the extraction of intermediate computations and data during prediction, rather than waiting for the final output. We demonstrate how models can be compressed while maintaining the integrity of intermediate processes, ensuring no loss of information flow. To achieve this, we developed a unified, general-purpose compression method applicable to various model types and architectures through a straightforward, generic compilation process. We have validated the method's effectiveness across a broad spectrum of models and architectures, as well as on diverse hardware platforms. Our findings indicate that InDistill is effective across different model classes and can significantly reduce model size and latency without compromising accuracy. Let $f$ and $g$ be two submersion functions mapping $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}$, where $\mathscr{F}(f)$ and $\mathscr{F}(g)$ denote the regular foliations of $\mathbb{R}^2$ formed by the connected components of the level curves of $f$ and $g$, respectively. We demonstrate that if $f$ and $g$ are topologically equivalent at infinity, then their functions and corresponding foliations are globally topologically equivalent, provided that $f$ satisfies specific conditions characteristic of "linear-like" behavior. Distinct from "radial-like" or "quasi-radial" submersion functions, "linear-like" functions are defined as follows: $f$ is considered "linear-like" if, for every point $p$ where the gradient $\nabla f$ vanishes, the Hessian matrix $H(f)$ has rank 2, and the set of all such points constitutes a collection of points lying on finitely many distinct lines.

The significance of this result is as follows: While global topological equivalence between submersion functions is generally too strong to be useful in most applications, local notions of equivalence—such as $C^0$, $C^1$, or affine—are often too strong. Therefore, it is highly desirable to establish intermediate concepts, exemplified here by the "linear-like" equivalence, which closely relates to the concept of "tame" submersion functions. Furthermore, while our primary focus is on submersion functions, the resulting equivalence also applies to vector fields, as there is a natural correspondence between them. Specifically, a vector field is considered "linear-like" if its associated submersion function is "linear-like."

Key words: Submersion function, Topological equivalence, Regular foliation.

CountSketch is a well-known linear dimensionality reduction method that utilizes randomized linear projections to reduce the dimension of vectors while preserving specific structure. This projection enables the recovery of both cardinality and frequency functions from the reduced data. Previous research has demonstrated that CountSketch effectively handles input distributions to satisfy these constraints. However, in adaptive adversarial settings, existing CountSketch variants can fail completely. We present counterexamples illustrating how an adaptive adversary can disrupt prior CountSketch designs. Furthermore, we propose a new CountSketch variant that employs a randomized projection step to address adaptive inputs and ensure effective dimensionality reduction. Our findings indicate that this adaptive version of CountSketch can also preserve additional structure beyond cardinality and frequency estimates. Additionally, our work offers a unified analysis that generalizes several previous CountSketch variants as special cases. Finally, we validate our theoretical results using real-world applications. In summary, this research establishes both theoretical and empirical evidence for the critical importance of adaptive robustness in dimensionality reduction techniques. We contend that this perspective will foster further research and development in this domain. We have made our code and data available at: https://github.com/ashwinbhatia/AdaptiveCountSketch. High-frequency trading (HFT) serves as a vital indicator for the maturity of financial systems, as the strategies employed within the famous Prisoner's Dilemma (PD) can model its dynamics. This study investigates a frequency-dependent Nash equilibrium in an HFT scenario where two agents, representing opposing financial firms, collaborate to establish an agreement. The payoff matrix for this game is derived from the profits and losses of their coordinated HFT activities. When they cooperate, they establish a frequency for switching strategies in the PD, while their individual choices—cooperate or defect—determine the outcome based on the resulting profit. We examine the PD's behavior within a quantum framework and simulate this quantum game to investigate how the quantum coin operator influences the dynamics of the quantum HFT PD. Furthermore, we execute this simulation using remote quantum computers on the quantum cloud. Our findings demonstrate that, unlike classical HFT, Quantum HFT exhibits a single, stable Nash equilibrium at a fixed frequency. Additionally, the quantum coin operator significantly impacts the nature of the Nash equilibrium and the nature of HFT, specifically regarding the frequency at which strategies are switched. These insights may offer a pathway to a more stable HFT system. This paper advances our understanding of HFT by exploring the application of the PD to this field and investigates the potential of quantum computing to address problems in this domain. Additionally, we demonstrate the viability of quantum cloud computing for HFT, highlighting its role in fostering innovation and deepening our comprehension of financial systems. Finally, the methodologies and concepts discussed hold promise for other fields, such as ecology, where analogous dynamics to HFT are observed. This could pave the way for new research initiatives in both theoretical and practical quantum HFT. Additionally, our work may contribute to the development of quantum financial mathematics, a field that has recently begun to emerge. This paper investigates the optimal pricing strategy for a seller employing an auction mechanism to maximize revenue, accounting for the presence of intermediaries. Specifically, $n$ intermediaries are permitted to participate in the auction on behalf of multiple end-users. The study analyzes two distinct scenarios: (i) costless intermediairyies, who are free to accept or reject incoming orders, and (ii) costly intermediaries, who are compensated only for successfully traded orders. We demonstrate that under both conditions, a risk-neutral seller can secure a revenue equivalent to the classical "single-click" model. Furthermore, with risk-averse intermediaries, a first-price sealed-bid auction yields the seller's optimal revenue. However, when intermediaries possess different risk preferences, we find that a uniform reserve price applied across all auction formats constitutes the seller's unique optimal strategy. This approach may involve setting the reserve price to zero in certain cases. Additionally, we examine the impact of end-user participation on seller revenue. Our findings indicate that allowing end-users to join the auction increases the seller's optimal reserve price, with this increase being more pronounced when the auction format is revenue-equivalent. Finally, the proposed pricing strategies are benchmarked against the Vickrey auction. Our results show that the seller's optimal revenue from this uniform reserve price strategy exceeds that achieved by the Vickrey auction. Notably, this advantage is more significant when the number of intermediaries and end-users increases. These insights are validated through numerical experiments. Finally, we outline potential applications of the derived pricing strategies within the cryptocurrency sector. To our knowledge, no research has previously addressed seller pricing strategies for auctions. Our study offers a comprehensive framework for optimal pricing when intermediaries and end-users coexist. We introduce a straightforward yet powerful framework designed to control abstractive summarization models through a plan generated from task-specific entity representations, or prompts. This planned summarization strategy yields state-of-the-art results on the CNN/DailyMail dataset for both accuracy and diversity. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the model effectively integrates task prompts into the summary by utilizing them as additional contextual information. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach remains effective across domain-adaptive tasks, where it continues to deliver performance that exceeds previous state-of-the-art methods. Significantly, our highest-performing model utilizes no fewer than 90% of the planned summaries as structures to guide the abstractive generation process. In contrast, existing state-of-the-art models rely on context generated during training, which lacks the relevance needed to effectively constrain on-policy summarization. Our results indicate that plans are the most effective means of limiting what a model can say while simultaneously providing the most relevant information to the model for immediate task execution. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/josh-lee/plan-with-prompts. This work was accepted for presentation at ACL 2020.

This paper establishes several sufficient conditions for the differentiability of an $n$-variable real-valued function, relying on the differentiability of an $(n-1)$-variable real-valued function, and provides examples illustrating these theorems. The study addresses a problem initially raised by A. Koohestani and M. Vaezi, who proposed sufficient criteria for the differentiability of an $n$-variable function based on the differentiability of its partial derivatives. In this context, an $(n-1)$-variable real-valued function is defined as follows: for any fixed values of $n-2$ variables among the first $n-1$ variables of $f$, it represents the derivative of $f$ with respect to the $n$-th variable. Their findings were later extended to an "$(n-1)$-variable real-valued function defined inside $n$." In this scenario, for any fixed values of $n-1$ variables (regardless of their position), the function denotes the derivative of $f$ with respect to the remaining variable. The authors demonstrated that differentiability conditions regarding these $(n-1)$-variable real-valued functions are sufficient for the differentiability of $f$. Building upon this framework, the current work introduces several sufficient conditions for the differentiability of $n$-variable real-valued functions. Furthermore, examples are provided to show that these theorems cannot be extended to the case involving $(n-1)$-variable real-valued functions defined within $n$. Additionally, the theorems remain valid when replacing the term "differentiable" with "continuously differentiable." Finally, specific criteria are established to ensure the existence of higher-order derivatives and their continuity. Specifically, if the first-order partial derivatives of $f$ exist and are continuously dependent on one variable while remaining differentiable with respect to the others, then $f$ possesses first-order partial derivatives that are differentiable with respect to all variables. Consequently, $f$ is differentiable, implying that higher-order partial derivatives of $f$ exist, and either the first or second order of continuity is guaranteed. This work is dedicated to Professor Mohammad Vaezi. Keywords: Differentiability, Continuous Differentiability, Partial Differentiability, Continuous Partial Differentiability, Higher-Order Differentiability, Higher-Order Partial Differentiability. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 26B05, 26B20.

This study introduces a computationally efficient method to accurately measure vocal entrainment within dyadic conversations. By modeling entrainment as a regression problem, the approach employs linear regression to assess how closely the fluctuations in fundamental frequency ($f_0$) of one's own speech align with those of their conversation partner. Evaluated on the Utterance Entrainment in Face-to-face Interaction (UEFFI) dataset, which comprises approximately 1,000 hours of transcribed audio from 2,000 dyadic conversations, the ensemble of encoders outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, qualitative results highlight the significance of social context in entrainment, particularly regarding how interaction partners influence each other's speech. Ultimately, the paper underscores how measuring entrainment can deepen insights into human social interactions and their communication processes. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwin-krishnan/vocal-entrainment. The one-parameter family of lambda-spheres includes the well-known lambda-matrix and Mehta-sphere. This work demonstrates that lambda-spheres possess categorical properties analogous to those of lambda-matrices. Specifically, they exhibit an identity functor, a duality functor, a spherical functor, and an omega-functor. Additionally, lambda-spheres serve as spherical objects within the category of lambda-sphere matrices. The paper details the categorical and diagrammatic properties of lambda-spheres and provides a quantum circuit model for lambda-sphere gates. Furthermore, we investigate quantum sphere clustering and conditional lambda-sphere clustering, demonstrating that these phenomena can be interpreted as specific projections of multi-sphere gates. Ultimately, this study addresses the categorical structure of quantum spheres, their role as spherical objects in the category of multi-sphere matrices, and their application in generating multi-sphere gate circuits. These developments pave the way for new spherical lambda-sphere gates capable of generating multi-sphere cluster states. Additionally, we explore the implementation of generalized cluster states, multi-sphere cluster states, and lambda-sphere conditional clustering using multi-sphere gates. These advancements offer new quantum spherical objects and efficient methods for constructing multi-sphere gates. The paper concludes by outlining the lambda-sphere sphere and presenting a categorical model for multi-sphere matrices. These results provide a foundation for constructing spherical gates and efficient multi-sphere gates, thereby enabling the development of a new class of spherical circuits. Such circuits hold significant potential for quantum information processing, including the implementation of multi-sphere cluster states and lambda-sphere conditional clustering. These contributions advance the understanding of spherical circuits and facilitate the practical implementation of multi-sphere cluster states and lambda-sphere conditional clustering. Furthermore, this work deepens the connection between categorical quantum mechanics and quantum circuit models, while also establishing a foundation for the categorical and diagrammatic description of spherical circuits. These insights contribute to the design and analysis of spherical circuits, ultimately enhancing our comprehension of their computational capabilities. The paper also introduces the spherical lambda-sphere cluster state, which encapsulates the lambda-sphere cluster state, and presents a categorical model for multi-sphere matrices. These findings offer new quantum spherical objects and deepen the link between categorical quantum mechanics and spherical circuit models. The work also highlights the relationship between multi-sphere gates and multi-sphere cluster states, as well as lambda-sphere conditional clustering. These insights contribute to the design and analysis of spherical circuits, further advancing the field of quantum information processing. The lambda-sphere quantum model presented in this work holds significant potential for quantum computing

This study analytically computes exact results for two quasiparticle excitations within fractional quantum Hall effect wavefunctions. It derives the complete analytical expression for the fractional charge associated with single quasiparticle excitation in the 1/3 fractional quantum Hall state and obtains exact, analytical formulas for changes in correlation functions between various particles upon quasiparticle excitation in general filling fractions. Additionally, the formulation for quasiparticle fractional charge in general filling fractions is presented, building upon earlier work by the first author regarding the 2/p states. This research is essentially computational, utilizing computer algebra systems to execute extensive symbolic calculations and generate results that are either fully analytical or semi-analytical. Furthermore, extensive computer algebra analyses are conducted to derive results that are largely or completely analytical, with significant portions of the paper consisting of computer algebra outputs and discussions of their implications. Finally, new insights into fractional charge and quasiparticle interactions are achieved through localized correlation functions. These detailed analytical findings offer significant new perspectives on excitation properties in the fractional quantum Hall effect, and the computational approach employed opens avenues for further investigations into excitation properties in both the bosonic and fermionic fractional quantum Hall effects. Finally, this work introduces novel concepts and results that substantially advance our understanding of the excitation properties within the fractional quantum Hall effect. Specifically, it achieves the following: (i) It provides an exact analytical formula for the fractional charge of a quasiparticle excitation in the FQHE, a result previously unknown; (ii) It establishes a new method for calculating fractional charge that offers deeper insight into quasiparticle excitation properties in the FQHE; (iii) It generates new results and insights regarding quasiparticle interactions in the FQHE; and (iv) It develops new theoretical tools for computing fractional charge and quasiparticle interaction properties in the FQHE.

Stokes variational inequalities are essential for modeling glaciological processes, specifically the movement of ice sheets sliding over rough bedrock. In the 1990s, Penev developed a specific Stokes variational inequality featuring a semicoercive bilinear form to address this sliding motion. The primary objective of this work is to establish existence and uniqueness proofs for the variational inequality, examine the properties of the solution, and demonstrate a convergent finite element approximation based on a recent existence theorem. Additionally, numerical computations are included to illustrate these findings. As an extension of prior research, this study presents the first analysis of a semicoercive Stokes variational inequality and offers a more comprehensive solution analysis compared to existing literature. Furthermore, it utilizes larger values for model parameters, resulting in more extreme physical scenarios. The work begins with notations and definitions followed by an overview of relevant background material. Subsequently, it provides the statement of the main result regarding a weighted Hilbert space where the Stokes variational inequality resides. Following the derivation of estimates for this inequality, the proof of existence is constructed using the theory of Riesz maps. An analysis of the inequality's properties precedes an extension to a situation where sliding occurs only on a portion of the boundary. Finally, the proof for a finite element approximation based on the Nitsche method is completed, accompanied by numerical computations. These computations validate the numerical analysis and illustrate the physics of the problem, including the impact of varying model parameters. Notably, the numerical results reveal that the sliding function is not necessarily continuous. This finding is particularly significant because it contradicts established literature, which typically assumes the sliding function is either continuous or piecewise continuous. This discrepancy arises because most existing studies employ penalty methods, whereas the approach used here utilizes the Nitsche method. To address this, an alternative formulation of the Stokes variational inequality is proposed, where sliding is modeled as a pointwise constraint. This new inequality is analyzed using Nitsche methods, though only for the case where sliding occurs on the entire boundary. Finally, an appendix provides a proof for the uniqueness of this alternative inequality. This proof relies on demonstrating that the associated operator is monotone, thereby establishing that a monotone operator exists whose fixed point solves the inequality. Furthermore, the proof confirms that the sliding function is piecewise continuous, contrasting with the sliding function in the non-constrained Nitsche method formulation. This outcome aligns with expectations derived from penalty method approaches. The uniqueness of the alternative inequality is proven without relying on monot

The spatial resolution of these images allows us to investigate how star formation is regulated by feedback from both individual stars and supermassive black holes. We identify 11 compact nuclear active galactic nucleus (AGN) candidates, with 10 exhibiting strong ultraviolet emission from the hot gas surrounding the accretion disk. A prominent nuclear jet extends approximately 10 kpc across the galaxy, manifesting as a compact jet head and a diffuse tail. We detect 10 compact star-forming regions (SFRs) with masses between 1 and 10 Myr, and 11 extended SFRs spanning 10 to 100 Myr. Notably, the compact AGN nuclei are located within or adjacent to the compact SFRs, while the extended AGN nuclei are situated within the extended SFRs. We demonstrate that the nuclear jet aligns with a ridge of extended SFRs, suggesting that AGN feedback may suppress star formation in this region. Furthermore, we find that the SFRs are distributed along a filamentary structure, and we show that the nuclear jet and its associated pressure front intersect this structure, potentially channeling outflows through the galaxy. Our findings indicate that the ultraviolet emission from the compact AGN nuclei is primarily powered by the most massive young stars rather than the AGN itself. We conclude that DUVET represents a unique system for studying the simultaneous impact of stellar and AGN feedback on star formation, as well as how these outflows shape the distribution of star formation across the galaxy. This study underscores the necessity of high-resolution, high-sensitivity UV observations to capture the interplay between stellar and AGN feedback and to resolve the intricate connection between AGN and star formation. We posit that DUVET is part of a broader population of starbursting disk galaxies where stellar and AGN feedback are tightly linked, and we advocate for the use of next-generation space telescopes to observe similar objects. We introduce SyncR, a new framework designed to solve the motion planning problem. Its primary objective is to develop joint motion plans for a group of robots that share the same base configuration while ensuring obstacle-avoidance for their extended configurations. The framework addresses two distinct motion planning challenges: first, determining joint plans for robots possessing non-convex body geometries, and second, planning joint motions for a multi-armed robotic manipulator with fixed, non-pivoting arms. Sport robots are cited as the ideal use case for the latter application. Built upon the Generalized Collision Detection framework, the proposed solution operates across a four-dimensional space comprising base, left-right, up-down, and up-down (z) dimensions. We present two algorithms: the first performs joint motion planning for robots with non-convex bodies, while the second plans joint motions for a multi-armed manipulator featuring fixed arms. The framework's efficacy is validated through a real-world sport robot designed to clear snow from a curved path, a system composed of a mobile base carrying snow blowers on both sides of the platform. The proposed algorithms are implemented using this snow clearing robot as a practical demonstration. The resulting joint motion plans demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed solution. Current research in monocular depth estimation predominantly targets scenarios where semantic segmentation is also necessary. However, it remains unclear whether the depth estimation task inherently yields superior pre-training performance for semantic segmentation compared to the classification task usually employed in such pre-training. This study addresses that question by conducting a systematic evaluation of two widely used depth estimation datasets: KITTI and NYUDepthV2. Our findings indicate that pre-training on depth estimation does not consistently outperform classification-based pre-training for semantic segmentation. Instead, the effectiveness of pre-training is more strongly determined by the extent of unlabeled data available during the experiment, rather than the specific type of pre-training task. Additionally, we analyze the impacts of dataset choice, training objectives, and model architecture on pre-training outcomes. Finally, we demonstrate that combining pre-training strategies can yield results that significantly exceed the performance of any individual approach alone. Throughout this research, all code and models will be made publicly accessible. Additionally, we have developed a new python package to facilitate monocular depth estimation. This package supports a wide range of models, datasets, and optimization techniques, streamlining experimental workflows and reducing development time. We intend to maintain an open-source repository of our state-of-the-art models to enhance reproducibility and enable direct comparison across different depth estimation methods. The rise of self-driving and connected vehicles has driven significant advancements in communication and computing technologies for mobility. To effectively manage the massive data volumes generated by these vehicles, a distributed edge intelligence framework is proposed to deliver low-latency, data-driven services. However, this necessitates the development of privacy-preserving solutions to safeguard data and ensure compliance with regulations. This paper introduces a unified framework for privacy-preserving edge intelligence in vehicular networks. Specifically, we investigate two scenarios: one where vehicles and road side units (RSUs) utilize pre-trained model check points, and another where they collaboratively train models without sharing raw data. Furthermore, we examine a joint framework for model training and inference. Based on these scenarios, we analyze the trade-offs between model accuracy and the communication overheads of computation, configuration, and training data. Additionally, we assess how the number of participating nodes and network topology impacts the performance of edge intelligence services. Finally, we explore the trade-off between edge intelligence efficiency and energy consumption, suggesting that energy harvesting vehicles could contribute data to the framework. Ultimately, we introduce an optimization problem for executing edge intelligence services and propose a model for such services. To our knowledge, this framework represents the first comprehensive approach to enabling edge intelligence services in vehicular networks. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing solutions in terms of accuracy, energy usage, and latency. Given that no closed-form solution exists for this joint optimization problem, we develop an efficient algorithm utilizing a greedy search method. Compared to traditional edge computing architectures, our framework achieves a 10% improvement in energy efficiency and an 8% reduction in latency. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to jointly optimize energy and latency for edge intelligence services. The Hirsch Conjecture asserted that the diameter of any $d$-dimensional polytope with $n$ facets does not exceed $n - d$. In 2011, Santos refuted this conjecture. Subsequent research has increasingly focused on investigating analogous limits for the number of pivot iterations in the simplex method across various linear programming facet pivot algorithms. In the inaugural paper of this series, we demonstrated that the number of facet pivits using the dantzig rule, centering rule, or log-barrier cutting plane method is bounded by $O(n^3)$. However, for certain families of matrices associated with the Hopf, Daniels, and Stanley polytopes, these methods may require $\Omega(n^{2.5})$ iterations. In this follow-up paper, we establish that the facet pivot simplex method utilizing the dantzig or centering rule admits an iteration bound of $O(n^2)$. Furthermore, we provide a quadratic lower bound for the centering rule and demonstrate that the dantzig rule possesses an $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound within the family of matrices linked to the Daniels polytope. Finally, we prove that no polynomial iteration bound exists for the relabeled random pivot simplex method employing the log-barrier cutting plane method. Additionally, we examine the implications of these findings for the pivot choice-independent Hirsch conjecture and the polynomial kernel conjecture. Notably, our proposed counterexample to Hirsch's conjecture also serves as a counterexample to the polynomial kernel conjecture. Our findings suggest that the quadratic lower bound for the centering rule is likely tight, and the proposed counterexample to Hirsch's conjecture may likewise be tight regarding the quadratic lower bound for the centering rule and the cubic lower bound for the log-barrier cutting plane method applied to the relabeled random pivot algorithm. Furthermore, the quadratic lower bound for the dantzig rule presented in this paper appears to be tight. We also address the polynomial facet pivot primal-dual path method with ellipsoid cuts, proving it has no polynomial iteration bound. The susceptibility of face recognition systems to presentation attacks, such as photos or videos, necessitates effective anti-spoofing (AS) mechanisms to ensure system security. Unlike previous approaches that rely on extensive AS labels, our method leverages self-supervised knowledge inherent in large-scale image datasets. By utilizing fine-grained spatial information from the ViT encoder and incorporating an attention mask to represent recognition privacy, we transform the AS task into a classification problem. This innovative framework allows the model to detect presentation attacks without requiring specific AS training data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot AS applications. Additionally, we analyze the impact of fine-grained self-supervised patches and the attention mask on AS effectiveness. The source code will be made available upon request. Given its zero-shot capability, the system can be easily integrated into existing face recognition pipelines. Furthermore, the model generalizes across different data distributions, successfully detecting unseen attacks like 3D masks in AS tasks. Consequently, this method facilitates the deployment of highly effective AS solutions for various deep learning-based face recognition systems. Parallel evolutionary algorithms (PEAs) are recognized for their superior computational efficiency, scalability, and performance compared to parallelized non-evolutionary algorithms. The primary challenge in designing PEAs lies in balancing parallelization against inter-individual interactions. In asynchronous multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (AEMOEAs), these individuals are evaluated and simulated at varying time intervals. However, existing AEAEA methodologies often suffer from unfair fitness evaluations caused by temporal disparities, leading to biased assessments. This bias stems from individuals being selected or discarded based on the timing of their fitness assessment. To address this, we introduce a novel parent selection strategy based on the concept of "effective time." This mechanism ensures that individuals are chosen based on the duration elapsed since their last evaluation rather than the absolute time at evaluation. By utilizing a frequency-based approach, the method mitigates evaluation timing biases, thereby enhancing the overall performance of AEMOEAs. Extensive experiments were conducted to validate the efficacy of this proposed strategy. The comprehensive empirical analysis demonstrates that the proposed method significantly improves the performance of AEMOEAs in terms of both convergence and diversity. Furthermore, the strategy is algorithm-agnostic and can be readily adapted to any AEMOEA. The gravitational microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 was identified by the OGLE survey and later observed by the Subaru Telescope, leading to the initial detection of a planet with a mass ratio of $q \sim 10^{-4}$ (An et al. 2020). This study presents follow-up monitoring using Keck/NIRC2, which provides additional constraints on the lens system's mass and separation. By combining data from this work with prior analyses, we determined that the planet's mass lies between $1.7-2.3 \times 10^{9}$ kg, corresponding to a radius of approximately $1.0-1.3$ Earth radii. The planet orbits at a distance of $1.0-1.3$ AU from a low-mass star ($M_{\star} \sim 0.10-0.13 M_{\odot}$). This confirmation represents the second coldest exoplanet discovered via microlensing, following K2-188b (Gaudi et al. 2021). Additionally, we report the first measurement of the lens parallax $\pi_{\mathrm{E}}$ and mass distance parameter $\pi_{\mathrm{M}}$ for a microlensing planet. These findings highlight the effectiveness of Subaru/HSC and Keck/NIRC2 in identifying and verifying low-mass planets through high-resolution microlensing finite-source modeling. Future observations using these facilities may allow for the direct imaging of such a cold, close-in exoplanet. This discovery underscores the potential of microlensing to probe the population of cold, low-mass planets around low-mass stars. The planet K2-188b, which shares similar characteristics, may be the only other member of this group currently known. The study of quantum systems interacting with environments typically relies on the quantum master equation, which describes their evolution via a quantum dynamical semigroup governed by a Lindblad generator. The parameters defining this generator are often difficult to determine, though they can be derived from underlying system Hamiltonians and environmental interactions at the quantum level. While numerical methods exist for extracting these parameters, they are computationally intensive and restricted to low-frequency error estimates. To address this, a frequency expansion has been developed for time-periodic Lindblad generators, offering high accuracy across all relevant frequencies. This work establishes the well-posedness and stability of such expansions, establishes error estimates using non-commutative Hölder spaces, and demonstrates how to apply them in practice. As an illustration, the time-periodic Lindblad generator for a driven two-level system is computed up to second order. These findings are particularly relevant for analyzing quantum driving protocols, the open dynamics of cavity quantum electrodynamics, and the characterization of noisy quantum devices. Finally, the accuracy of the frequency expansion is validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, an implementation of the Lindblad generator derivation is provided via the open-source software package `qulib`. The methodology is also extended to fractional frequency expansions. While it is well-established that deep neural networks (NNs) achieve high accuracy in image classification when trained extensively on vast datasets like ImageNet, these resources are often inaccessible. Although domain adaptation methods promise to enhance performance by reducing the gap between source training data (e.g., ImageNet) and target data, their specific efficacy across different scenarios remains unclear. This study assesses multiple domain adaptation techniques by applying them to distinct combinations of source and target datasets. The results reveal a strong correlation between dataset domain similarity and adaptation success, indicating that source datasets derived from CUB or similar domains yield the most effective outcomes. Furthermore, domain randomization and multi-domain training were found to be beneficial for general NN robustness. Finally, to mitigate the reliance on large-scale datasets, we propose pre-training on smaller, domain-specific collections such as CIFAR or TinyImageNet. This approach yields substantial improvements on TinyImageNet and comparable gains on larger datasets like COCO. Overall, our findings demonstrate that with strategically selected sources and appropriate methods, domain adaptation can significantly boost the generalization capabilities of deep NNs on target data. This wordless proof establishes that a regular triangular grid with $n$ vertices per side contains $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles by defining a mapping from four-element subsets of $\{1,2, \dots, n+2\}$ to the set of these triangles. Specifically, we demonstrate the triangle associated with the subset $\{4,5,8,11\}$ under this bijection for the case where $n = 10$. This approach naturally extends to other geometries, such as the regular $n$-gonal grid, yielding counts like $\binom{n+4}{6}$ for equilateral six-pointed stars in a regular 10-gon's grid. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in both node and graph-level prediction tasks, explaining their behavior remains underexplored. While various methods have been developed to interpret GNNs, they lack the ability to explain the model's underlying architecture and the rationale behind the learned parameters. This paper introduces ParInter, the inaugural explanation framework designed to interpret the parameters of a parameterized neural network. Specifically, we apply this approach to GNNs, offering the first comprehensive interpretation of the model's parameters. The core concept involves representing parameters as virtual layers integrated into the actual network structure. ParInter synthesizes these virtual layers with the original GNN architecture into a interpretable neural pathway that illuminates how parameters contribute to predictions. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that ParInter outperforms existing baselines in generating accurate explanations while offering superior interpretability regarding the model's parameters. Additionally, we find that these explanations provide actionable insights for improving prediction performance, as highlighted in our case studies. We conducted a joint analysis combining Chandra X-ray data and optical imaging to investigate the substructure within the RXCJ0232.2-4420 galaxy cluster. Utilizing the CHANDRA SUBARCSEC SUBSTRUCTURE SEARCH (CHASSS) code, we examined the cluster's emission properties, while applying the caustic technique to its projected distribution. Our findings reveal that the cluster is not relaxed, with the northern region exhibiting more significant substructure than the southern. The sub-peak in the northern sector aligns with the eastern side of the caustic, suggesting it may be accreting onto the main cluster. Conversely, the southern area displays multiple X-ray peaks situated away from the caustic's gas distribution; however, these features appear to lie along the caustic's elongation, indicating they could be substructures projected onto the main cluster rather than distinct clumps. Furthermore, we identified two groups of substructures—one within the northern region and one southwest of the main cluster—that show signs of interaction. Finally, we present the morphological characteristics of the cluster's substructures. These results collectively indicate that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is an ongoing merger involving multiple clusters. Additionally, we identified a previously unknown dwarf cluster located approximately 1.5 arcminutes from RXCJ0232.2-4420. This dwarf cluster is situated along the elongation of an X-ray sub-peak and a group of red galaxies within the northern region, suggesting a potential physical connection. Future studies are required to further investigate this relationship. Finally, we provide the coordinates of the identified substructures for reference. (Abridged)

This paper details the strategies, techniques, and facility-specific approaches used to search for feebly interacting particles (FIPs), which experience only weak, hypercharge-mediated forces. Consequently, standard channels that rely on non-standard interactions are excluded, necessitating instead the detection of rare processes that deviate from known Standard Model physics. The study examines current and upcoming experimental efforts across various facilities, including the LHC, LHCb, SHiP, ESS, ILC, FCC-ee, SuperKEKB, B-factories, LEP2, LEP, LEP200, HERA, SuperKEKB-B, Belle II, BESIII, Super $\phi$, Super $\tau$-A, Super $\mu$-A, Super $\mu$-P, Mu3e, COMET, NAB, Super $\beta$-A, Super $\beta$-B, Super $\beta$-P, Super $\beta$-C, Super $\beta$-D, Super $\beta$-E, Super $\beta$-F, Super $\beta$-G, Super $\beta$-H, Super $\beta$-I, Super $\beta$-J, Super $\beta$-K, Super $\beta$-L, Super $\beta$-M, Super $\beta$-N, and Super $\beta$-O. The authors conclude that a comprehensive and coordinated experimental program, utilizing all proposed next-generation flavor and Higgs machines alongside high-intensity hadron facilities, offers the most promising path toward identifying FIPs and fully unraveling the mysteries associated with dark matter, matter-antimatter asymmetry, and the nature of dark energy. Furthermore, this program will significantly advance our understanding of the fundamental structure of the universe. Finally, the text explores the theoretical and experimental motivations driving these searches, as well as the anticipated scientific outcomes of potential future discoveries in this domain.
