Language, as a fundamental element of human civilization, is characterized by a vast array of words for common objects and the ability to encode complex ideas through these words. While the former reflects linguistic richness and the latter demonstrates linguistic power, the power of a language within the statistical physics framework of naming games is measured by the volume of the state space defined by its word inventory. This study investigates how a word library evolves to maximize linguistic power in scenarios involving multiple agent populations. To address this, we introduce a migration mechanism into the naming game that allows agents to switch between different language varieties. In this network-driven framework, agents randomly select neighbors to exchange names; if they already know each other's name, they assign it correctly. Conversely, if one agent lacks the name, both draw from each other's respective word libraries with equal probability. Our findings indicate that, although the total number of words across all libraries remains constant, the distribution of the word library's size follows a power-law distribution rather than a uniform one, resulting in a language that is both powerful and coherent. Furthermore, agents with high-degree connectivity tend to possess a larger vocabulary, while those with low-degree connectivity possess a smaller one, thereby enhancing the language's power. Additionally, the emergence of a coherent language, defined as every high-degree agent knowing every word, is significantly accelerated compared to single-library scenarios. This outcome underscores the effectiveness of the migration mechanism in fostering multi-library languages and holds promise for developing theoretical models to guide the creation of natural languages. Ultimately, our research provides theoretical backing for the hypothesis that human language evolved not merely for the practical communication of arbitrary information, but also to foster social cohesion and stability. By reducing the cost of word acquisition and boosting the speed of learning, the power and coherence of a language serve as the twin engines driving the evolution of human language. Consequently, this study may offer guidance for artificial intelligence initiatives aimed at developing machine languages. Specifically, a migration mechanism could be a viable approach to constructing machine languages that are both powerful and coherent, thereby facilitating the communication of complex information between humans and machines. To achieve this, we propose a straightforward and effective learning algorithm grounded in the naming game with migration. Given the inherent complexity of human language, this proposed algorithm may prove effective for the various sub-domains of natural language. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a growing method for addressing difficult differential equations, yet the dynamics underlying PINN training remain poorly understood. This study demonstrates that momentum optimization techniques substantially accelerate standard gradient descent (GD) within the PINN framework. Our findings indicate that this acceleration is particularly pronounced in regions affected by the spectral bias of implicit neural networks (INNs), which utilize fixed-frequency sinusoidal activations. We attribute this phenomenon to the superior ability of momentum methods to mitigate the ill-conditioning arising from varying-frequency eigenvalues of the training loss's Hessian. Through analyses of both synthetic and real-world problems, we illustrate how momentum significantly diminishes spectral bias effects by facilitating more rapid updates in highly conditioned directions indicated by INNs. Furthermore, we show that momentum allows GD to overcome spectral bias limitations by employing larger step-sizes in well-conditioned directions toward which PINNs converge more rapidly than INNs. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how momentum methods can mitigate the limitations imposed by spectral bias in INNs, thereby enhancing PINN performance. The entire study is released as an open-source software package, enabling reproducibility and further exploration. Additionally, to facilitate experimentation with momentum methods, we have updated our PINN library, DeepXDE, to support ADAM and other momentum-based optimizers. In sequential decision-making contexts, reinforcement learning (RL) serves as a highly effective mechanism for deriving policies directly from data. Nevertheless, deep RL approaches frequently encounter challenges including unstable convergence, sub-optimal outcomes, and a lack of interpretability. To address these issues, we introduce a hierarchical RL framework that utilizes a tree-structured search method enhanced with symbolic explanations. At the hierarchical level, the agent employs a symbolic return predictor to rapidly identify a symbolic goal for the subsequent task segment. By modeling the cumulative return as a tree-structured search problem, the agent can efficiently converge on an optimal policy given a defined task goal. On the lower level, the agent focuses on mastering the skills necessary to achieve this specific objective. Symbolic explanations are subsequently attached to the learned low-level policy through an inductive logic programming process. These explanations facilitate human understanding and enable the agent to select suitable high-level goals based on their low-level capabilities. Experimental evaluations across various domains demonstrate that our proposed method achieves competitive performance with human-level samples, while also generating interpretable representations of the resulting policies. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness in learning from a reduced number of features. The integration of interpretable representations at the hierarchical RL level presents a promising avenue for developing more sample-efficient and robust agents. We introduce an all-optical method for realizing on-chip optical nonreciprocity by applying quantum squeezing to one of two coupled resonator cavities. By appropriately adjusting the squeezing strength and phase, we demonstrate that an incoming classical optical signal can traverse the device in one direction while being entirely reflected in the opposite direction. This approach eliminates the need for magnetic fields, thereby enabling chip-scale integration. Furthermore, we show that applying squeezing to both cavities enhances device performance and stability. Our findings hold significant promise for developing on-chip nonreciprocal photonic circuits. In experimental applications, modest squeezing levels are expected to be readily achievable using current quantum technologies. Our results are validated by good agreement between theoretical predictions and numerical simulations. We anticipate that these findings will pave the way for future research into quantum-squeezing-driven nonreciprocal photonic circuits. Our approach involves establishing Lipschitz-type inequalities for SOT functions and analyzing the regularity concerns of their Fourier transforms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SOT functions, which are constants outside a bounded interval, constitute the kernel for a specific Banach space within a generalized Paley-Wiener theorem. Additional findings include local maximum properties, the resolution of generalized moment problems, and the resolution of generalized Markov problems. We also present a comprehensive theory grounded in the indefinite Stieltjes transform. Ultimately, we address Fenton-type minimax problems for both real and complex-valued SOT functions. The methodologies employed integrate techniques from harmonic analysis, approximation theory, and operator theory. These results find applications in Banach algebra theory, particularly regarding the structure of the ideal of functions vanishing at infinity within a generalized Fourier algebra. Additionally, we derive a significant inequality for positive definite functions and provide an optimal approximation theorem via a convex combination of functions. We introduce a novel method for investigating spin-dependent dark matter (DM) nucleon interactions by analyzing the $\gamma$-spectra from neutron capture on $^6$Li for the first time. Leveraging recent measurements of relativistic electron transition matrix elements, we calculate absolute gamma-ray fluxes. Subsequently, we derive the expected event rate for a direct detection experiment by integrating these fluxes with the detector's efficiency function. Finally, we establish limits on the DM-nucleon spin-dependent cross section (SDSC) as a function of DM mass, assuming a specific dark matter density profile. Our analysis demonstrates that this approach yields competitive sensitivity to SDSC, particularly in the sub-GeV mass region where current direct detection methods struggle to set limits. We conclude that a $^6$Li-enriched target, combined with high-precision $\gamma$-spectroscopy, holds significant promise for exploring light dark matter with spin-dependent interactions. This new pathway for direct detection research could be realized through an upgrade of the existing GRETINA/Gammasphere facility at the National Superconducting Cyclotron Laboratory. We have provided open-source tools to facilitate future explorations of this methodology. Additionally, we outline prospects for enhancing sensitivity via $\beta$-decay studies and discuss the potential for achieving similar results using $\beta$-delayed neutron capture on $^7$Li. These findings are intended to encourage further research into the $\gamma$-spectra of relevant nuclear reactions, which could unlock novel strategies for detecting dark matter. Finally, we suggest that future direct detection efforts should incorporate novel nuclear observables, such as those examined here, to fully exploit the unique features of dark matter interactions. Such an expansion is crucial for establishing a comprehensive and unified framework for the direct detection program. We have also demonstrated that our methodology is applicable to other nuclei, including $^{133}$Cs, $^{139}$La, and $^{176}$Yb. Blind image deblurring aims to simultaneously estimate the blur kernel and recover the latent image from a blurred input. This task is inherently ill-posed, as the latent image and blur kernel are highly correlated. Conventional approaches typically rely on prior knowledge of image structures, such as smooth regions and sharp edges, to reconstruct the latent image. However, the prior assumption that all smooth areas must exist in the latent image often leads to the formation of artificial smooth zones, which degrades image quality. To address this, we propose a blind deblurring method based on kernel-mixture modeling. This prior allows each latent image patch to be represented as a kernel-mixture prior, enabling the image to dynamically adapt its structure by combining a blur kernel with an unblurred patch. This flexibility facilitates the creation of smooth regions and the preservation of edges within the latent image. Additionally, the prior demonstrates robustness against overfitting to the blurred input. Experimental results on benchmark datasets confirm the effectiveness of the proposed kernel-mixture prior, showing superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we present a real-world demonstration utilizing this method. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/Kernel-Mixture. Our methodology has been accepted for presentation at SPIE Intelligent Systems Imaging and Holography 2021.

Formal verification ensures high assurance that software adheres to its specifications, yet a significant barrier remains the difficulty of expressing requirements and ensuring they are unambiguously implemented. While natural language is intuitive for stating software requirements, it lacks the formal expressiveness needed for automated verification. Hoare logic offers a suitable intermediate language for conditions involving software states, while recent natural language inference models demonstrate both the feasibility and effectiveness of translating natural language to and from logical forms. This paper introduces natural language Hoare logic, a framework designed to facilitate the formal verification of software against natural language requirements. We construct this framework using established Hoare logic and natural language inference, and we demonstrate its utility through several software verification examples. Additionally, we outline a research agenda and identify open challenges associated with this approach. Distributed consensus serves as a cornerstone for diverse distributed systems, such as databases, distributed trace systems, and blockchains. Canopus is a new consensus system tailored for fault-tolerant streaming data services, designed to accommodate network partitions and Byzantine faults. Its core mechanism relies on time-bounded multi-valued voting, where all valid votes for a specific value within a defined time window constitute the value output for that interval. Canopus offers linearizability, facilitates single-producer single-consumer (1P1C) streaming, and supports high throughput. However, its original design could not endure certain client and network failures. Canopus' primary limitations include: (1) the potential for multiple clients to send conflicting commands to the service; (2) susceptibility to client network partitions that could trigger a fatal consensus failure; and (3) the risk of consensus halting due to temporary network partitions around specific clients. To address these issues, RCanopus enhances Canopus to withstand various failures and Byzantine behaviors. RCanopus introduces two new components: the client quorums module and the Byzantine client detection mechanism. The former ensures that all quorums of clients within a time window form a subset of a single set, while the latter safeguards the 1P1C property even in the presence of Byzantine clients. Evaluation results demonstrate that RCanopus maintains Canopus' capabilities for fault tolerance, high availability, and high throughput, even when handling conflicting client requests. Furthermore, RCanopus has been deployed in production at Baidu. This RSystem is the first to combine fault tolerance with high availability and the ability to absorb client conflicts, all while supporting high-performance data services. Additionally, RCanopus supports fault injection testing for distributed consensus systems. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first system capable of effectively testing fault tolerance under client network partitions. Our experiments reveal that, unlike other systems, RCanopus exhibits robust resilience to such failures. Finally, RCanopus supports multiple consensus algorithms, including Time-based Ordering (TO), Gabriel's Optimistic Time (GOT), and Gabriel's Virtual Clock (VC). By adjusting the timeout parameter, users can balance fault tolerance and fault recovery time to suit specific service requirements. Furthermore, by modifying the voting rule, users can customize the consensus algorithm to meet particular needs. This research also contributes to the broader understanding of how to design fault tolerance for distributed consensus systems with conflicting clients. To verify this, we conducted molecular dynamics simulations on cholesterol-containing bilayers of cholesterol and choline-1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphatidylcholine (DMPC). Our analysis of spontaneous curvature and fluctuations revealed that the bilayer's bending modulus declines as the cholesterol fraction increases. Additionally, we examined the orientation distribution function (ODF) of cholesterol to correlate its molecular alignment with the measured mechanical properties. Finally, we compared these simulation results with experimental data and previously published simulated values. This study confirms that molecular dynamics simulations can effectively investigate how cholesterol influences the mechanical properties of lipid bilayers. This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian, specifically focusing on a spatially flat, homogeneous FRW universe. The resulting modified Friedmann equation retains the same structure as the APS LQC model; however, the critical matter density required for the bounce is exactly half that of the APS model, regardless of the particle number density or the graph's link density. Furthermore, this model indicates that quantum geometry effects are significantly lower than those in the APS model, implying that loop quantum cosmology is less viable when derived from the ADM Hamiltonian. Finally, we demonstrate that the ADM Hamiltonian, when applied as a quantum constraint, is not involutional, a finding that challenges the consistency of ADM quantization. These conclusions suggest that selecting an appropriate Hamiltonian is fundamental for the successful application of loop quantum cosmology. Additionally, our findings align with those of other researchers who have employed alternative Hamiltonians, such as the Thiemann square method or the Holst action. The article concludes with a discussion on the historical and practical reasons for the predominant use of the ADM formalism within the loop quantum gravity community.

**Keywords:** Loop quantum cosmology; ADM Hamiltonian; Quantum constraint; Holst action; Thiemann square method.

This paper presents a catalog detailing the highest-energy cosmic rays identified through the full array of the Pierre Auger Observatory during Phase I of its operation. It provides the energy estimates for the 14 events with the greatest energies and the 29 events that exceeded energies of $10^{19}\,$eV. These energy estimations rely on the average results derived from the complete set of methods employed by the Auger Collaboration. Additionally, the paper offers fundamental information regarding the recorded events, including their fluxes, isotropy, and anisotropies, along with comparisons to predictions from isotropic and anisotropic cosmic-ray models. The cataloged events are utilized to establish the minimum energy threshold for the large-scale, wide-angle, and high-energy (LWAHE) anisotropy analysis. This analysis was conducted to investigate the potential connection between ultra-high-energy (UHE) extensive air showers and active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The study confirms the previously reported correlation between the most energetic UHECR events and nearby AGNs, while also identifying a significant excess of UHECR arrival directions pointing toward GRB 080314C. The paper concludes with the current status of the UHECR point-source model and the findings of the latest searches for UHECR-GRB associations. Furthermore, the data supports a strong correlation between UHECR events and both blazars and non-blazars. Finally, the study confirms a significant large-scale dipole anisotropy in the UHECR sky, with its pole directed toward the constellation of the Virgo cluster. This dipole is also observed when restricting the sample to energies above $2\times10^{19}\,$eV. The Virgo direction is noted as a preferred direction for BL Lac objects, leading to the conclusion that UHECRs may originate from a population of relativistic extragalactic sources. The catalog is available at http://www. PierreAuger.org/Science/Data/. Integrating deep neural networks into autonomous systems necessitates estimating prediction uncertainty to ensure system safety. While various methods exist for uncertainty estimation, most rely on statistical assumptions, fail within deep model contexts, or neglect network-dependent factors. We introduce a Bayesian uncertainty estimation technique that analyzes feature map reliability through extensive ablation studies. By utilizing a point-wise Bayesian approach, our method achieves superior accuracy and generalizability when applied to generic deep object detectors. Furthermore, because this method is computationally efficient, it can be integrated into online learning systems without incurring significant overhead. Experimental results on the Microsoft COCO dataset demonstrate that our approach enhances the detection AP of the underlying detector by 1.5 points. The code and model card are available at https://github.com/ashishkumar100/bayesOD. Additionally, the methodology can be extended to other deep perception tasks, such as segmentation and pose estimation, by adapting the loss function to utilize ground truth masks or angles. Overall, BayesOD offers a versatile solution for uncertainty estimation across a broad range of deep detection models and datasets. For instance, when applied to the YOLOv4 detector, it improves mAP by an additional 2.5 points. Furthermore, the approach supports online uncertainty calibration, improving the method's performance. This capability is particularly advantageous for autonomous vehicles, where uncertainty estimates inform decision-making processes. The proposed framework can also be paired with uncertainty-aware planning algorithms to mitigate potential risks. In summary, our approach offers a pathway to safer, more reliable deep perception systems by providing accurate uncertainty estimates that integrate seamlessly into end-to-end autonomous workflows. Real-world traffic flows are intricate, non-stationary systems characterized by various mechanisms, including the propagation of traffic jams and shockwaves. Consequently, short-duration traffic recordings, often termed "moving snippets," serve as practical data points for modeling and predicting traffic evolution. This study introduces various machine learning techniques to forecast the trajectory and density profiles of these snippets, employing regression and classification tasks alongside temporal data augmentation and modern deep learning architectures like U-Nets. Additionally, we present a comprehensive data generation pipeline to create synthetic moving snippets for data augmentation and implicit data balancing. Experiments conducted on over 100,000 snippets from the Chicago Traffic Dataset demonstrate that our deep learning approach yields state-of-the-art results in both regression and classification domains. Furthermore, the proposed pipeline facilitates the balanced generation of synthetic snippets across extreme density levels, significantly enhancing the performance of snippet-based traffic forecasters at both density extremes. We have released all data processing code, allowing for the reproducible generation of synthetic snippets and the replication of our findings. The associated code repository can be accessed at: https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffer/TrafficForecastingOnSnippets. The dataset, including all pre-processed and balanced snippets, is available on OpenML at: https://www.openml.org/data/activerequest?id=18002. Ultimately, this work represents a foundational step toward developing data processing pipelines for traffic moving snippets, a critical component for training deep neural networks on such data. We anticipate that these methods will serve as a strong basis for subsequent research in snippet-based deep learning for traffic forecasting.

This demonstration serves as an introduction to proving a coherence result utilizing rewriting techniques. Specifically, we examine rewriting within weak weak higher categories, also known as g-categories. To achieve this, we develop a theory of rewriting systems and rewrite relations tailored for g-categories. The primary instrument for this endeavor is the concept of a display g-category, which functions as a g-dimensional analogue to display categories in dimension 1; these latter structures are fundamental to modern approaches in rewriting. Furthermore, we leverage the established connection between display categories and fibrations to define g-dimensional fibred rewriting systems, describing rewrites as g-simplices residing within specific fibrations. Finally, we apply these newly defined rewriting systems to rederiving the coherence of g-categories, which asserts that every potential-defining set of 2-cells is equivalently reducible to a single higher simplex. This proof adheres to the established pattern of integrating rewriting with weak higher category theory. Additionally, we explore an alternative approach to coherence that relies on type theory. Both methodologies are presented from a categorical perspective. To facilitate this demonstration, we have also prepared a corresponding lecture based on homotopy type theory. This time, the focus shifts to defining and implementing rewriting systems using dependent type theory, which is known to be coherent. We also provide an informal overview of the connections between category theory, rewriting, and type theory. Through these efforts, we establish a bridge between existing works on rewriting in type theory and the realm of higher category theory. Ultimately, our objective is to illustrate how higher category theory can contribute to and enhance the field of rewriting. Accurate segmentation of the hippocampus is critical for diagnosing and monitoring various forms of epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. This study introduces a two-stage Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) approach to address these challenges. In the first stage, the method estimates a bounding box for the hippocampus and classifies it into one of four conditions: healthy, hippocampal sclerosis (HS) of right or left origin, or HS of both sides. Since the model predicts the same bounding box regardless of the disease type, it effectively serves as a hippocampus detector. In the second stage, an HS detection model operates within the region defined by the detected bounding box from stage one. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves an HS detection accuracy of 91.5% and a hippocampus detection accuracy of 96.1%. The source code and the HLH2021 dataset are accessible at https://github.com/taehyounkim1222/HippocampusSegmentation. Additionally, this work has been utilized to estimate the performance of various segmentation methods on the Hippocampal Lesion Hippocampus Segmentation 2021 (Part 1) dataset organized by the Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Surgery (MICCAI) Epilepsy and Alzheimer's Disease Segmentation and Analysis Workshop. The results indicate a Dice score of 0.776 and a Dice+HDC score of 0.804. The corresponding paper and results are available at https://github.com/taehyounkim1222/HippocampusSegmentation. We examine the interferometric arrangement employed to demonstrate the quantum pigeonhole effect, which asserts that three particles traveling within a single mode can interact without ever occupying the same spatial location. Using both quantum and classical frameworks, we analyze this setup, revealing several overlooked features and proposing several potential improvements. Our results indicate that experimental uncertainty regarding the mode count in earlier studies is significant, and we suggest several refinements aimed at mitigating this issue. Furthermore, we highlight a classical simulation of the phenomenon that relies on random number generators rather than truly deterministic dynamics, thereby questioning the fairness of concluding that this specific experiment has been uniquely determined by quantum mechanics. Finally, addressing the involvement of transversal modes, we suggest that their impact was likely negligible, as they would need to remain empty for quantum effects to dominate; consequently, we recommend that truly transversal modes should be reevaluated and better understood. Overall, we conclude that the quantum pigeonhole effect has not been definitively demonstrated. Nevertheless, we believe this paper will stimulate further research and help establish a solid foundation for future investigations into this fascinating concept. The accompanying supplementary material offers additional details and simulations. Furthermore, our code is made publicly accessible to ensure full reproducibility, while our supplementary content, although not essential for replicating the results, provides extra detail and context. Addressing this issue is essential for clarifying the true nature of the experiment and its outcomes. Additionally, the supplementary material examines the trade-off between the number of particles and modes, which is essential for optimizing the experiment. Finally, the supplementary content explores the use of truly transversal modes, which could be considered as a potential alternative to better understand the true nature of the experiment. We believe that these contributions will stimulate further research and help establish a solid foundation for future investigations into this fascinating concept. The Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) mechanism is widely regarded as the primary driver for generating the inner radiation belt (IRB) of protons at low Earth orbit (LEO). However, prior studies have struggled to explain the formation of specific ions within the IRB due to limitations in existing methods, which typically relied on single or limited CRAND events and failed to account for the complex, time-dependent physical processes involved. This research introduces a novel simulation framework that integrates multiple CRAND events with time-varying ion loss and acceleration mechanisms. By employing a Monte Carlo approach, the study evaluates how varying numbers of CRAND events and time-dependent acceleration influence the spatial and temporal evolution of protons trapped in the IRB. The results indicate that time-dependent acceleration is critical for forming protons in the IRB, while the number of CRAND events primarily affects the initial population of protons already within the belt. Furthermore, simulations utilizing the 2001 solar cycle peak as an acceleration event demonstrate that this number of CRAND events is sufficient to generate the protons observed in the IRB. These findings provide a comprehensive explanation for the existence of the IRB and its source population of protons. Additionally, the study offers a new perspective on the physics governing the formation of the IRB, with the simulation code available for future investigations into trapped radiation. The widespread adoption of Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) has spurred extensive research into modeling techniques that aim to enhance understanding of data generation and underlying processes. However, existing studies often fail to comprehensively address how various structural elements influence DGNN performance. This paper introduces a novel architecture called PLSKLink, which systematically integrates key features such as global skeleton, local topology, and specific links. We first investigate the impact of graph degree distributions on DGNNs, revealing that regular distributions hinder learning by overemphasizing path-based features, whereas heavy-tailed distributions better capture real-world patterns. Building on this insight, we propose an algorithm that generates graphs with multi-scale global pyramid-like shrinkage skeletons from real-world datasets, ensuring robustness and accuracy while highlighting scale-free characteristics. Subsequently, specific local topologies are embedded into these skeletons to further investigate how local structures affect DGNNs, leading to the development of PLSKLink. Extensive experiments across 13 real-world datasets demonstrate that PLSKLink surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, thereby enhancing interpretability and providing a solid foundation for understanding intricate real-world phenomena. The code will be made publicly available at \url{https://github.com/zhongyuanliu/PLSKLink}.

Recent developments in privacy-preserving matrix completion demonstrate that differential privacy (DP) can safeguard user data while enabling the recovery of missing entries. However, these existing approaches are often computationally demanding and restricted to specific noise models, such as Gaussian, Gaussian-Exponential, and Laplace. This limitation is significant because Gaussian, Gaussian-Exponential, and Laplace mechanisms are only valid for full-rank matrices; applying them to low-rank matrices leads to excessive noise and degraded utility. To address this, we introduce the Huber mechanism, the first DP algorithm for low-rank matrix completion that employs a symmetric, heavy-tailed distribution. This mechanism is fully characterized, including a closed-form expression for its probability density function, and, unlike prior methods, supports the release of multiple perturbed matrices without requiring re-optimization. Experimental results indicate that the Huber mechanism, when applied to both full and low-rank matrices, utilizes approximately 50% less sample complexity compared to the Gaussian mechanism while maintaining equivalent utility. Furthermore, we find that DP-based matrix completion is viable even under extremely stringent privacy constraints. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedmohr/DP-MatrixCompletion. Our findings suggest that heavy-tailed distributions are a promising avenue for enhancing the utility of DP matrix completion. Additionally, we have made our code public to facilitate the deployment of Huber noise in practical scenarios. Future research will explore other heavy-tailed distributions, such as Student-t, to further improve the utility of this approach. Finally, we aim to extend these results to other applications, including regression and classification. To support this, we have developed a general-purpose tool for analyzing the influence of various noise distributions on the loss function of any given task. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahmedmohr/DP-Influence-Analysis. This general tool will be instrumental in advancing research on noisy optimization tasks, allowing for the systematic evaluation of different noise impacts on any specific objective function. In summary, the Huber mechanism represents a foundational step toward noisy low-rank matrix completion, and our supporting tools offer a framework for investigating the effects of alternative noise distributions. This work paves the way for new research directions, such as comparing the efficacy of various heavy-tailed distributions in noisy matrix completion and extending these findings to other tasks like regression and classification. Furthermore, utilizing these tools to determine the optimal number of components for noisy low-rank matrix completion could significantly enhance its performance, thereby opening avenues for future inquiry. We report the detection of a giant planet within the disk surrounding the very low-mass star CIDA 1, a system previously identified as a candidate for massive planet formation via gravitational instability. By combining ALMA observations of dust continuum emission at 1.3 and 0.8 mm with 1.3 and 3 mm gas emission, we observed dust ring structures at radii of 1.1 and 0.5 au, along with a gas ring at 0.25 au. These features indicate that the dust and gas rings are not free-floating but are trapped by a giant planet orbiting at approximately 0.6 au. This discovery marks the first instance of a massive planet detected within a disk via planet-dust interaction at such a close proximity to the central object, thereby expanding the understanding of the conditions necessary for giant planet formation through gravitational instability around very low-mass stars. Additionally, the presence of this planet at 0.6 au suggests that free-floating planets in the range of 5–10 $M_{\rm Jup}$ are unlikely to be a likely outcome of the gravitational instability model.

This paper examines the Most Clicks Problem, which involves determining the maximum number of clicks needed to extinguish all lights on an $m \times n$ grid with the fewest possible clicks per cell. Let $\mu(m,n)$ represent this minimum number of clicks. We derive a formula for $\mu(m,1)$ and demonstrate that for a fixed $m$, $\mu(m,n)$ follows a quasi-polynomial pattern with a period of $m$. Additionally, we explore properties of this sequence through the lens of the adjacency matrix of the light grid. Specifically, we prove that if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of this matrix corresponding to an eigenvector where every component has a magnitude of at least 1, then $\lambda$ is either 0 or negative and rational. We provide examples of such vectors and an infinite family of vectors that establish the existence of 0 or negative eigenvalues with the stated properties. Finally, we introduce a new graph invariant, $\eta(G)$, defined as the minimum number of clicks required to turn off all lights in graph $G$ using zero or one clicks per cell; we establish that $\eta(L_{p,q}) = O(q^2)$ for the lattice graph $L_{p,q}$ and for the path $P_n$ and cycle $C_n$. Furthermore, we prove that $\eta(P_{m \times n}) = \Theta(m^2)$ whenever $m$ is prime. We also present upper and lower bounds for the minimum number of clicks needed to solve a general grid graph, and in the appendix, we connect the Most Clicks Problem to the Set Cover Problem. Image segmentation and restoration are fundamental tasks in computer vision. This paper introduces a new variationally driven segmentation framework that incorporates image restoration principles, specifically leveraging total variation (TV) minimization and its variants. We develop two novel models, RISS1 and RISS2, which utilize modified TV terms as data fidelity components. The level set method is employed for the level-wise numerical implementation of these models. Extensive numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real images demonstrate that these proposed frameworks outperform numerous state-of-the-art level-set-based and variational segmentation methods. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies and benchmark tests validate that our proposed models are highly effective and robust. Finally, we illustrate the application of our models in removing salt-and-pepper noise from images prior to segmentation. In this context, our models generate more accurate segmentations with smoother and more logical boundary contours compared to other state-of-the-art techniques. Source code and numerical results are accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-chen2019/TV-based_image_restoration_and_segmentation.

Abstract Interpretation simulates a program's dynamic behavior at a reduced scale and a higher level of abstraction. This paper introduces two novel optimization techniques designed specifically for the phases of computation that typically consume the most time: those responsible for generating and resolving (when necessary) the large volumes of data—such as sets of tuples or constraints—produced during the phase to compute the best solution. These techniques are not restricted to sets; they can also be applied to other data structures like intervals or zones. Furthermore, they are inherently generic and independent of the specific domain interpreter. When implemented within the SPOT program analyzer, these optimizations demonstrate significant reductions in both computational time and the size of the simulated programs. Additionally, we outline a broader category of programs that exhibit similar space and time complexities in their descending and ascending phases. This broader class encompasses not only those addressed by our specific optimizations but also others, such as those involving the simulation of pointer aliasing. Our approach relies on a decoupling mechanism that enables the descending phase to access and simulate program portions more efficiently than traditional methods allow. Finally, our experimental results validate the effectiveness of these two techniques across various applications. Oxide perovskites are widely recognized for hosting diverse topological phonon phases. In this study, we demonstrate that these phases can be further enriched by endowing phonons with photonic characteristics. Through the non-perturbative coupling of acoustic and optical phonons with light, we successfully integrate photonic topology with the intrinsic properties of oxide perovskites. This approach, facilitated by a hybridization-deformation framework, reveals novel photonic topological phenomena. We illustrate this with a concrete example involving thin films, where we observe the emergence of the higher-order photonic quadrupole moment and the associated corner states. Furthermore, we highlight the ability to dynamically manage these states via external electromagnetic fields and the geometric configuration of the light-phonon coupling. These findings underscore the significant potential of our research for advancing research into photonic oxide perovskites and their novel photonic functionalities. Additionally, our proposed methodology for hybridizing photonic topology with acoustic and optical phonons is expected to yield new functionalities in both photonic and phononic systems. This is achieved by leveraging the strong interactions between photons, phonons, and light, alongside the rich topological landscape of oxide perovskites. Such devices could be realized through the hybridization of photonic crystal and phononic crystal platforms, offering superior performance compared to their individual counterparts. This is made possible by the unique properties of oxide perovskites, including their high dielectric constants, ferroelectric characteristics, and rich topological phases. Consequently, our work paves the way for a new class of hybrid photonic-phononic devices, data centers, and information processing systems. These advancements are driven by the abundant resources of oxide perovskites, their capacity for remote control, and their extensive functional capabilities. We investigate the dynamics of an atom adjacent to a thin conducting mirror by incorporating both electromagnetic radiation and the atom's electric polarizability into the coupling between the atom and the electromagnetic field. Our findings indicate that initial excitation can occur due to the polarizability-induced interaction with the electromagnetic vacuum field, with an associated timescale that scales across different atomic energy transitions and system configurations. Furthermore, we detect additional radiation emitted by the atom, driven by both the polarizability-based interaction with the vacuum field and the coupling with its excited state. We present quantitative results for various atomic systems, including hydrogen and alkali atoms, positioned near the mirror. These emissions can be attributed to both spontaneous emission and the vacuum polarizability effect. We also explore potential experimental methods for detecting these phenomena and estimate the potential signal strength. Notably, we observe that when the atom is sufficiently close to the mirror, both induced excitation and emission are significantly amplified, with the resulting signal reaching levels detectable by current experimental capabilities. These effects stem from the atom's interaction with image charges within the mirror, which are substantially stronger than atomic dipoles, thereby enabling detection. Consequently, our results suggest that atomic motion induced by the quantum electrodynamic vacuum field, previously hypothesized for an atom in a standing wave directly above a mirror, may be more readily observable in configurations involving a thin mirror. Furthermore, our predictions regarding motion and decoherence induced by the electromagnetic vacuum field may be testable through atomic interferometry or other suitable experiments. This work provides a foundation for exploring the noninvasive detection of purely quantum phenomena and for conducting fundamental tests of quantum electrodynamics. Finally, the discovered mechanisms of vacuum-induced atomic excitation and polarization could offer new avenues for quantum information processing and energy harvesting. Specifically, we propose a method to coherently excite atoms using solely their interaction with the electromagnetic vacuum field, without requiring an external source. This proposal is based on the phenomenon of vacuum polarization, which we have demonstrated can be significantly amplified by placing the atom in close proximity to a mirror. We also address potential challenges in implementing this proposal. Our results suggest that vacuum polarization could be harnessed to achieve excitation and manipulation of atoms without material contact, thereby opening new avenues for quantum information processing and energy harvesting. Achieving fairness in decision-making across diverse domains has become a significant research priority. While various definitions and algorithms have been proposed to address this, they frequently encounter practical and theoretical challenges when applied to graph-based data. To address these issues, we introduce a unified framework for fair graph learning by decentralized collaboration through neighborhood constraints, ensuring that fairness is maintained during the graph learning process. To enhance the efficiency of computing such neighborhood constraints, we develop multiple approaches for determining the most efficient definition and formulation of these constraints. Furthermore, we extend these methods to support graph fair classification and graph fair clustering, demonstrating that our solutions are both general and extensible. Finally, we evaluate the proposed graph fairness solutions using both synthetic and real-world datasets, with experimental results confirming the effectiveness of our approaches. This study investigates supersymmetry (SUSY) within final states characterized by jets and missing transverse momentum, utilizing proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis encompasses final states featuring one or more jets, alongside those with isolated electrons, muons, or photon-electron pairs. The observed data are compared against predictions for both the natural SUSY scenario and split-SUSY models. The study reports no significant discrepancies between the data and the standard model background. Consequently, various signal regions are excluded at the 95% confidence level, with the constraints on natural SUSY models varying from 1.1 to 2.5 TeV depending on the specific signal. Furthermore, for split-SUSY models, the excluded ranges for gluino, top squark, and chargino masses vary from 1.5 to 2.2 TeV, 1.0 to 2.0 TeV, and 1.0 to 1.2 TeV, respectively, based on the specific signal. This work represents the most stringent limits to date on natural SUSY and split-SUSY mass spectra derived from final states with jets and missing transverse momentum in split-SUSY, and the most restrictive limits on gluino mass achievable in this signal category. The study also establishes the most stringent natural SUSY limits in final states containing jets and missing transverse momentum combined with electrons or muons, as well as the tightest constraints on chargino and stop masses within the natural SUSY framework. For the natural SUSY scenario, a signal is observed with an observed local significance of 3.0 standard deviations and a global significance of 2.2 standard deviations. For the split-SUSY scenario, local significances of 2.8 and 3.1 standard deviations are found for a high gluino and chargino mass model, respectively, alongside a global significance of 2.6 standard deviations. These significant excesses are observed in signal regions featuring a high number of jets and high missing transverse momentum. The analysis also addresses potential new physics contributions from the dark sector, with the dark photon model yielding the strongest constraints for dark photon masses between 1.5 and 3.5 GeV and kinetic mixing parameters $\epsilon$ up to approximately $1.5\times 10^{-3}$. This study proposes a class of models featuring rational expectation financial bubbles, where the mean-reverting dynamics are governed by a stochastic time that transitions from an exponential growth phase to a bubble burst phase at a stochastic switching time. Within this framework, the expected termination time of the bubble can be either finite or infinite, contingent upon the parameters of the stochastic time. We analyze the fundamental characteristics of this bubble model and evaluate several related variants. Furthermore, we demonstrate a connection between this framework and models containing private information. The research's primary motivation stems from a recent rational expectation bubble model that we critically examined; that model's termination time distribution is a mixture of a uniform distribution and a Pareto distribution with shape parameter $\kappa=1$, resulting in both a finite expected termination time and linearity with respect to the initial condition. We also explore the implications of finite versus infinite expected bubble lifetimes. Additionally, we consider the case of a deterministic switching time and develop a series of nested models that incorporate private information. Finally, we examine the stochastic Euler-Lagrange equations associated with each of these frameworks. Overall, this paper offers a comprehensive exploration of various frameworks exhibiting rational expectation financial bubbles, with this phenomenon being a significant aspect of various financial markets. The proposed models are versatile and can be adapted to diverse contexts, including but not limited to foreign exchange markets, cryptocurrency markets, and the technology sector. Furthermore, we have established several extensions, such as introducing jumps into the financial bubble framework. These materials will be the subject of our future research. The stochastic switching time, or equivalently the stochastic termination time, is a common feature in many systems, including those with mode switching, which makes the methodologies discussed in this work applicable to a broad range of systems. Consequently, this research holds potential application value beyond the domain of financial bubbles. Our approach utilizes the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, which is a first-order nonlinear partial differential equation. We have developed several extensions to this work, including various numerical methods for solving the resulting nonlinear PDEs, which will also be the subject of our future investigation. Numerical simulations are available from the corresponding author. This work was partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 11971397 and 11771327). We simulated a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to arbitrary driving forces employing the path integral formulation. By employing world-line Monte Carlo methods, we treated the system's imaginary time coordinate as an additional spatial dimension. Our findings demonstrate that the method yields accurate results for both static two-point correlation functions and dynamic observables under various driving conditions, including a constant force (free fall), a back-and-forth driving protocol, and a potential that scales with time. These outcomes align excellently with analytical solutions for the specific cases of constant force and back-and-forth driving. Ultimately, the path integral approach proves highly effective for simulating quantum systems immersed in environments with arbitrary background fields. Additionally, this methodology facilitates the study of quantum many-body systems through the lens of background fields. To illustrate this potential, we also simulate a one-dimensional fermionic system featuring both spin-orbit coupling and a time-dependent pairing potential. Determining the ground state of this system reveals a transition from a topological superconducting phase to a trivial one. The path integral method proves particularly advantageous in this context, as it allows for the direct Monte Carlo simulation of time-dependent pairing potentials without necessitating the explicit calculation of the time-dependent ground state. This capability enables the investigation of topological invariants, such as the Majorana zero mode, which remain challenging to obtain via other techniques. Ultimately, the path integral approach offers a viable alternative to other driving methods for quantum systems embedded in arbitrary background fields. Finally, we also simulate the mean-field properties of the mean-field Hubbard model using the same methodology. This model exhibits a quantum phase transition between Mott insulating and superfluid phases, which we successfully simulated as a time-dependent problem. We observed the quantum phase transition within the pairing potential and examined the relationship between the pair gap and the superfluid order parameter. Ultimately, this path integral approach demonstrates significant advantages in studying both single-particle and multi-particle systems in time-dependent environments. Furthermore, it holds great promise for investigating driven many-body systems, offering a solution to the longstanding challenge of numerically simulating ground states in time-dependent environments. Specifically, this method enables the direct calculation of the ground state for pairing systems in time-dependent environments, thereby revealing the pair gap and other pair-related properties. In contrast, other driving techniques for quantum systems in time-dependent environments remain ineffective for directly obtaining the ground state. Consequently, the path integral approach emerges as a highly promising avenue for the simulation of quantum systems in time-dependent environments. Recent research in recommendation systems has increasingly focused on modeling the relationship between an recommender's interests and available resources. However, existing methods typically fail to incorporate the sentiment polarity of reviews, which is crucial for identifying a user's core preferences. To address this limitation, we introduce the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SiFN), a novel architecture for review-based recommendation that explicitly encodes review sentiment polarity. SiFN integrates raw review data through a two-stage process: first, it encodes raw reviews into latent vectors using neural networks, and second, it fuses these vectors with their corresponding sentiment polarities via a gating mechanism. We evaluated SiFN across three large-scale Amazon datasets to assess its efficacy in generating high-quality recommendations. The experimental results demonstrate that SiFN achieves superior recommendation accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/chenchen1993/SiFN. SiFN serves as a robust and versatile item recommendation model, particularly suited for scenarios where items are described by textual reviews and sentiment scores. Furthermore, we plan to deploy SiFN as a real-time API for product recommendation in a leading e-commerce search platform. Currently, the system is in the testing phase, and future work will involve deploying it into production to enhance real-time item recommendations. Additionally, we intend to explore advanced user profiling techniques, leveraging user browsing and purchasing history to refine personalized recommendations. Finally, we aim to extend the current review-based approach into a user-review-item rating system that incorporates user, review, and item embeddings, alongside developing a real-time query interface for embedding retrieval. This interface would accept user, review, and item inputs and return a ranked list of items. Additionally, we plan to implement real-time user embeddings by analyzing query and click data, such as search history and page views, to improve the accuracy of personalized recommendations. Finally, we will investigate the impact of product categories on review sentiment, aiming to develop a unified embedding space across different categories to further boost recommendation accuracy. This could be achieved by training a shared embedding model across categories or by mapping category IDs into a unified embedding space. By addressing these areas, we aim to further extend the SiFN system's capabilities and performance. Overall, SiFN represents a solid foundation for future research and practical applications in the field of recommendation systems. Its success in various datasets and its potential to address new challenges in the industry make it a valuable contribution to the advancement of this field. This paper details our methodology for enhancing Arabic-English code-switching (CSW) text through code-switched data unilingualization (CSDU). Our approach involves generating augmented CSW sequences from seed data by replacing code-switching points with whole words from the other language. To our knowledge, this marks the inaugural effort to investigate such text augmentation in CSW domains. We evaluated our generated data within a masked language model (MLM) framework, comparing our results against a baseline that samples only the non-CSW language for augmentation. Our findings indicate that the proposed method yields a 3.5% performance boost compared to the baseline, highlighting the critical role of leveraging cross-lingual code-switching points in CSW data augmentation. Additionally, we examine our results in the context of existing literature to demonstrate the significance of our work for future research in this area. Our code and model are made available online at https://github.com/ahmedelshafei123/CSDU. This work was supported by a grant from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. We demonstrate that no subgroup of the homeomorphism group of a compact surface, which fixes the boundary and acts with sufficient transitivity on the interior, can be Roelcke precompact when equipped with the topology inherited from the compact-open topology. Consequently, this Roelcke precompactness property is not preserved under homeomorphism. This finding contrasts with a result by P. K. M. Wong, who proved that every non-abelian free group is Roelcke precompact. Furthermore, we establish that for any compact surface $S$, the group $\mathrm{Homeo} (S)$, when given the compact-open topology, fails to admit an exact sequence involving two non Roelcke precompact groups. This result implies that $\mathrm{Homeo} (S)$ itself cannot be Roelcke precompact. An analogous argument demonstrates that the free group $\mathrm{Homeo} (\mathbb{T}^2)$ on the space of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms of the torus is also non Roelcke precompact. These results stand in sharp contrast to non-abelian free groups, which are both topologically simple and Roelcke precompact. The surface case, however, exhibits the opposite traits: $\mathrm{Homeo} (S)$ is neither property nor precompact. Our proofs rely on a variation of a theorem by A. B. Kechris and B. Pym, which states that the homeomorphism group of an infinite set, under the discrete topology, forms a topologically simple group. In this work, we generalize that theorem to contexts where the automorphism group exhibits similar simplicity. We also explore applications of this generalized theorem to the study of topologically simple groups. Additionally, our approach yields independent findings about the transfer of topological properties between a topological space and its homeomorphism group, as well as insights into groups generated by their conjugates within the framework of the compact-open topology. These topics represent significant areas of research that have recently garnered substantial attention. Finally, to address specific questions, we extend the definition of precompactness in the sense of Roelcke to the setting of topological groups with non-Hausdorff topologies. In this broader context, the property is termed "quasi-Roelcke precompactness." We examine this notion in detail for groups arising from the second formulation mentioned earlier, specifically within the exact sequences of topological groups. The computational efficiency of the hexagonal icosahedral (HIC) mesh format relies on its capacity to represent complex geometries using minimal data. However, these meshes are frequently generated via straightforward algorithms that fail to address the inherent complexities of the modeled objects, resulting in poor quality elements. Furthermore, the HIC constraint necessitates the inclusion of special data structures to manage non-conforming faces, which, although practical, diminish the mesh's structural elegance and complicate finite element analysis. This paper introduces the Tets/Hex transformation, a recent format proposed by the authors, which enables the straightforward regularization of HIC meshes by eliminating the need for special structures and facilitating the conversion of hex elements into tetrahedral elements. Each complete hex element is mapped to five tetrahedrons, while each non-conforming face in the original mesh corresponds to exactly one tetrahedron in the resulting mesh, thereby preserving the format's compactness. A straightforward algorithm is presented to identify and locate these special structures within a given mesh. By integrating this algorithm with the Tets/Hex transformation, we achieve an average performance rate of 58 tetrahedrons per second and each processed hex element, effectively minimizing the number of required special structures. This approach forms the foundation for the TetFix application, which serves as a user-friendly interface for automating the process. The methods demonstrated herein provide a pathway for developing user-friendly tools that enable scientists and engineers to more effectively tackle the challenges of mesh generation. The code and software associated with this work are publicly accessible. Relation extraction focuses on identifying the relationship between two entities within a specific sentence. Building on the finding that relation labels are often interdependent, we introduce a new knowledge-graph-driven Link Prediction (KP-LP) task designed to model these label dependencies. This task utilizes sentence representations and entity pair relationship labels as inputs to predict the entities within a given sentence. We argue that effectively modeling label interdependence enhances natural language understanding and boosts relation extraction performance. Building on this KP-LP task, we develop a unified framework that simultaneously handles link prediction and relation extraction by integrating them through mutually reinforcing cycles of learning. Experiments on three public datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in relation extraction and outperforms other approaches across various link prediction tasks. Additionally, an analysis of the learned knowledge graph reveals that the proposed method captures rich semantic information regarding entity classes and their mutual relationships. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhujingya98/KP-LP. Furthermore, the knowledge graphs associated with ISRCN and RE-SCi datasets are available at https://github.com/zhujingya98/KP-LP/tree/master/data/relation_graphs. Finally, to facilitate future research in relation extraction and knowledge graphs, we are releasing the newly constructed RE-KP dataset, which combines real-world knowledge graphs with relation-extraction sentences. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/zhujingya98/KP-LP/tree/master/data/RE-KP. Reference: Jingya Zhu, Yufeng Zhang, and Yong Li. This study introduces a novel analytical propagation delay model tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Recognizing that inverter delay depends on various parameters—including width ratios, load capacitance, supply voltage, temperature, and transistor dimensions, which in turn function of inverters and technologies—researchers have developed numerous models utilizing different calculation techniques. The proposed model is developed using Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox, which provides an efficient framework for deriving analytical delay equations. The results indicate that this model achieves high accuracy, with a maximum error of 4.2% across a wide parameter spectrum. When compared to both the analytical model and SPICE simulations, the findings validate the model's reliability. Consequently, the developed equations are well-suited for utilization within electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhaleem/Analytical-Propagation-Delay-Model-for-Deep-Submicron-CMOS-Inverters. Keywords: CMOS, Inverter Delay, Analytical Delay Model, CMOS Technology.

Principled decision-making in continuous state-action spaces relies on the assumption that environmental rewards and transitions vary smoothly with respect to states and actions. We demonstrate, however, that this conventional smoothness is insufficient for effective learning in such settings. Instead, we propose an alternative, coarse-grained smoothness tailored for continuous spaces, which is significantly more potent than traditional methods. Unlike prior approaches, our framework does not depend on specific learning rules or function approximators. Instead, it identifies broad regions in state-action space where relative Q-values maintain consistency, thereby guiding the learning process toward these areas. The framework's simplicity ensures that our theoretical guarantees are strong and universally applicable. Furthermore, experimental results on novel tasks demonstrate that this framework facilitates learning in complex continuous control problems that were previously unlearnable using existing techniques. We also illustrate its application in planning and few-shot reinforcement learning, showing that it advances the state of the art in these domains. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/alexsilver/continual-q.

The mechanisms that enable humans to generate, acquire, and utilize an extensive vocabulary remain a central focus in cognitive science and neuroscience. A key unresolved issue is how the brain organizes semantic knowledge, particularly regarding animacy, which has been widely considered a fundamental dimension of semantic space. This study investigates the neural basis of animacy dimensions using representational similarity analysis (RSA) on data from the human ventral temporal cortex. By applying generalized null models, we demonstrate that no single cortical region exhibits an animacy dimension, and quantitative analysis reveals that animacy representations are not robust within any individual region. Furthermore, we find that no region shows a statistically significant correlation between animacy similarity and behavioral distance across tested vocabularies. These findings challenge the traditional view of distinct cortical regions containing animacy dimensions and suggest that animacy representations are instead distributed and highly variable in the human ventral temporal cortex. Our results align with recent, more nuanced models of semantic knowledge that account for idiosyncratic variations in how individuals acquire and use language. Finally, the use of generalized null models offers a novel approach for validating hypotheses about neural representations of semantic dimensions. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to explicitly test whether a specific dimension corresponds to a location within the human ventral temporal cortex. We provide the R code used in this analysis as supplementary material. We introduce a structure-preserving filter designed for high-order finite element simulations involving complex geometries and multi-dimensional mesh distortion. This filtering technique preserves the original function's values, monotonicity, and curvature extremum, making it ideal for structure interactions where these physical attributes must be retained. The method is grounded in convex optimization theory, and its mathematical formulation and proof are presented. To enhance computational efficiency, we develop a practical algorithm based on the proof process, which is applied to various multidimensional simulation scenarios. First, we examine a 2D finite deformation large strain problem where the filtered stress results are compared against those from meshless methods and analytical solutions. Next, we analyze a 3D finite deformation problem with nonlinear material properties, presenting comparisons against 2D simulations, linearized solutions, and a more computationally intensive meshless method. Finally, we address a 3D wave propagation problem, comparing our results with a traditional filter. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is highly efficient and maintains high accuracy even under severe mesh distortion. Furthermore, in comparison to the traditional filter, our approach delivers comparable or superior accuracy while requiring significantly less computational time. Finally, we demonstrate the method's robustness in handling discontinuous functions. By formulating a convex optimization problem based on mean-value properties, we successfully smooth shockwaves in function values while also preserving jump size. This results in structure interactions with smoother shockwave effects and improved accuracy. The entire algorithm is implemented in C++ and made available on GitHub. [https://github.com/ChenchenLi2017/Structure-preserving-filter] (Li C., Chen C., Li X., 2021). The code is also accessible through an accompanying video. Our results demonstrate that a 5th-order scheme suffices for our method, whereas the traditional filter necessitates a 9th-order scheme. Overall, our approach offers higher accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. Our work provides a new perspective on simulating physics and establishes a foundation for developing more accurate and efficient numerical methods. Type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the hard state of black hole X-ray binaries are primarily located in the soft state and are characterized by low-frequency fluctuations in the 0.5–1.0 keV energy band. The evolutionary trajectory of type-C QPOs from the hard state to the soft state remains unclear. This study investigates the evolution of type-C QPOs in the black hole system MAXI J1535-571 using data from the Chinese Hard X-ray Modulation Telescope (HXMT). We identified type-C QPOs in 10 out of 17 observations, revealing a significant increase in frequency and a decline in amplitude as the source approached the low-hard/soft transition. Furthermore, we observed a notable shift in the frequency of type-C QPOs during the transition from the hard state to the soft state. This transition coincides with notable changes in the spectral shape and the amplitudes of low-frequency QPOs, indicating a change in the inner accretion flow structure. These findings suggest that type-C QPOs may serve as an indicator of low-hard/soft transitions in black hole binaries. Additionally, we determined that the type-C QPO frequency in MAXI J1535-571 is approximately 0.1–0.3 Hz, consistent with other black hole X-ray binaries. Finally, we examined the relationship between the frequencies of type-C and type-I X-ray fluctuations, finding that both exhibit a minimum around the low-hard/soft transition point. These results imply that both fluctuation types are linked to changes in the accretion flow structure, with type-I fluctuations potentially serving as a more precise indicator of the transition. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into the behavior of type-C QPOs during low-hard/soft transitions in black hole X-ray binaries. (Astronomy Astrophysics, 2022)

This study explores cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MRL), where agents engage in repeated interactions within a shared task environment, adapting their behaviors in response to one another's moves. In such scenarios, agents must reliably react to a partner's actions to achieve shared objectives. To address this, we introduce a method employing a social intrinsic motivation of transfer empowerment. This approach encourages an agent to generate diverse responses to its partner's actions by Empowering the set of its own responses relative to observations of the partner's recent actions. We successfully applied this framework to two CoRL 2020 benchmark tasks: the Multi-Agent Predator-Prey game and the Multi-Agent Starcraft Battle Map. The former illustrates a straightforward pre-trained CoRL task, while the latter models the application of transfer empowerment in a complex, real-world multi-agent StarCraft III environment. Our results demonstrate that the method effectively increases the variety of an agent's responses, leading to significantly higher scores in both benchmark tasks. Furthermore, we find that the method supports learning reliability by maintaining high performance even during randomizations of partner behaviors. The Python source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/taikiwatari/Transformation_of_Self-information_through_its_neighbors_actions. This work is based on the preprint available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07075. This paper has been included in the CoRL 2021 workshop and conference proceedings. This work is based on the preprint at arXiv:2103.07075 [cs.LG].

Keywords: multi-agent reinforcement learning, intrinsic motivation, empowerment, CoRL 2020 Multi-Agent StarCraft Battle Map, CoRL 2020 Multi-Agent Predator-Prey, randomization, CoRL 2021, preprint, arXiv:2103.07075 [cs.LG]

We introduce MatSim, a straightforward yet potent framework designed to generate synthetic images for one-shot material recognition. The process begins by rendering a material from numerous viewpoints and illumination angles, storing these as a material template for subsequent simulation uses. At runtime, the renderer accepts a single input image, the target material template, and a set of task parameters, then performs material recognition to deduce the simulation's material parameter. Our results demonstrate that MatSim excels at recognizing a vast array of real materials in real-world settings, achieving a 94.5% accuracy rate on a dataset comprising over 10,000 materials. Furthermore, we utilize MatSim to drive physics simulations, enabling realistic virtual shopping experiences within virtual reality environments. A video demonstration can be found at https://youtu.be/41111111111. The project source code and parameters are available at https://github.com/11111111111/MatSim. Our methods are released under the Apache 2.0 license and are accessible at https://github.com/11111111111/MatSim. The authors' user ID is 11111111111 on YouTube. We begin by revisiting two equivalent characterizations of Lie 2-algebras, namely the categorification of Lie algebras and 2-term $L_\infty$-algebras. Subsequently, we introduce key concepts categorified from standard Lie algebra theory, including exact 2-algebras, cohomology, central extensions, and abelian extensions. Finally, we present specific examples of each type of extension.

We introduce a new approach for local image feature matching that bypasses the traditional stages of detection, description, and vote generation. Instead, our method establishes direct pixel-to-pixel correspondences between images using a loftr module that comprises a common backbone and two feature landmark localization networks (FL-LN). Unlike conventional methods that rely on keypoints, FL-LN features are derived from global image representations; consequently, the backbone alone enables basic matching, while the specific configurations of the FL-LN modules determine the module's overall performance. We present two FL-LN designs: the basic and the upsampling versions. The common backbone combined with the basic FL-LN constitutes the LoFTR basic variant, which is optimized for speed. In contrast, the combination of the common backbone with the upsampling FL-LN creates the LoFTR upsampling variant, which prioritizes accuracy. Our results demonstrate that LoFTR achieves a 10x speed improvement over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) while maintaining comparable performance in the basic mode, and it surpasses SOTA in both performance and memory efficiency when using the upsampling mode. Furthermore, we evaluate the entire module across three datasets—Scene Match, PyramMatch, and Live1D—showcasing its versatility across both texture-rich and texture-poor image scenarios. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/MVHSV/LoFTR. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.04476. Given its simplicity and versatility, LoFTR is highly adaptable to various computer vision tasks beyond matching, such as feature point localization and segmentation. The matching outputs generated by LoFTR also serve as an effective pre-training task for downstream applications. Our evaluation confirms that LoFTR outperforms existing methods like SuperGlue and D2-Net in terms of matching quality and memory efficiency. Additionally, LoFTR is more lightweight than these methods, offering a significant computational advantage. Finally, LoFTR is versatile across different training conditions, including self-supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised pre-training. Our loop closure module outperforms existing methods like ORB-SLAM2 and LFD, delivering superior performance across various benchmarks. This study examines the bias inherent in the "two-point correlation" technique used to derive inferred solar vector magnetic field data. We establish a vector expression for this bias, demonstrating how it causes underestimation of horizontal vector field magnitudes within magnetic holes. Additionally, we present two strategies to address this issue: first, correcting magnetic hole magnitudes after data retrieval, and second, mitigating the bias during the inference process by selecting magnetic holes as initial values. These approaches were evaluated using two datasets: global inferred data from Schrijver et al. (2009) and Petrov et al. (2010), and synthetic data generated by applying a 3D coronal magnetic field model to inferred maps from Schrijver et al. (2009). Our results indicate that both methods effectively reduce the bias in inferred global data, with the synthetic dataset analysis confirming the validity of these solutions. Consequently, the magnitude of horizontal vector field vectors in the inferred data is significantly improved. These findings have important implications for understanding the relationship between inferred global magnetic field data and solar-driven space weather.
