Software developers often encounter requirements from users or testers during maintenance that must be mapped to specific source code elements. Concept location addresses this challenge by identifying the primary definition, alternative instances, and usage points of a concept. However, maintenance scenarios frequently involve queries that differ significantly from the concept names used in the actual code. To address this, we introduce QUICKAR, a method that accelerates concept location by automatically reformulating user queries using concept synonyms. This approach relies on crowdsourced data from Wikipedia and the DBpedia ontology. Our results demonstrate that QUICKAR successfully generates effective synonyms for concept location, thereby enhancing both precision and recall in locating concepts within software systems. The QUICKAR method is designed to be language-agnostic and can be integrated into any concept location technique that supports query reformulation. This paper details the evaluation of QUICKAR and examines its impact on two distinct concept location approaches. Additionally, we evaluate QUICKAR using a newly introduced benchmark dataset. The benchmark evaluation protocol is also language-agnostic and can be applied to assess any technique capable of reformulating queries for concept location. To support future research, we have made the QUICKAR tool and concept location technique open-source, and we will provide an implementation of these methods. Furthermore, we will make the benchmark dataset, which includes both positive and negative concept location requests, publicly available. This dataset will enable researchers to evaluate techniques that utilize queries distinct from concept names, and it can be accessed at https://github.com/quickar/quickar. By adopting QUICKAR, concept location methods can achieve superior precision and recall without incurring additional computational costs. The only requirement is that a technique needs to perform query reformulation to locate concepts in the target system. Consequently, QUICKAR offers a straightforward integration for any technique that reformulates queries to improve performance. Future work will focus on enhancing the quality of QUICKAR's generated synonyms. This paper is the first to evaluate the effectiveness of applying query reformination to concept location. The proposed technique is applicable to a wide range of queries, including those related to bug fixes, requirement analysis, change propagation, refactoring, security vulnerabilities, and requirements specification. While this paper primarily details the evaluation, the QUICKAR tool itself is versatile and can be adapted for concept location research in various other contexts. Specifically, this work establishes a foundation for evaluating techniques that use concept location queries rather than standard concept names. Furthermore, this research represents the first application of query reformulation to the field of concept location. The technique is applicable to various queries, including those related to bug fixes, requirement analysis

Entrainment is a well-established concept in dialogue systems where one conversational partner mimics the speech rate of their partner to foster entrapment and enhance communication. This study introduces a deep neural network approach designed to unsupervisedly learn the embedding space of spoken utterances. By applying principal component analysis, the method filters out irrelevant acoustic features to isolate the component responsible for speech rate. Utilizing neural score matching, distance metrics are calculated between two utterances to quantify their similarity based on speech rate. These findings demonstrate that the proposed distance metric effectively captures variations in speech rate within conversational dialogues. Furthermore, results indicate that conversational pairs exhibit greater similarity in this metric compared to control groups consisting of randomly paired speakers. Consequently, similarity measured by this metric serves as a reliable indicator of successful entrainment, providing a foundation for developing unsupervised entrainable models capable of adapting to the speech rates of conversational partners. Finally, the distance metric is validated within a dialogue system, proving that varying the proposed neural distance allows for the automatic generation of responses that entrain to the partner's speech rate. Overall, this research presents a robust framework for quantifying similarity in conversational dialogue by focusing on the acoustic signature of speech rate. By applying this technique to conversational distance, we establish a pathway toward unsupervised learning systems that can enhance conversational interactions through targeted entrainment. Future applications may extend this framework to analyze other aspects of conversational dynamics, such as turn-taking patterns and emotional alignment. Furthermore, the proposed framework holds significant potential for advancing dialogue systems by facilitating adaptive responses to various conversational characteristics, thereby fostering more natural and engaging interactions. The source code for this research is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/alexei-pan/Entrainment-Analysis}. The associated repository includes detailed documentation and examples to support replication and further exploration of the findings. By making the code public, we aim to foster collaboration and innovation in the field of conversational AI, particularly regarding the analysis and manipulation of speech rate through entrainment. Additionally, the repository features a variety of resources, such as pre-trained neural models and sample datasets, to facilitate immediate experimentation and customization for specific research or application needs. We introduce a collection of open-source web tools designed for the visualization of spectral and imaging data, built upon the recently released ImageJ/Fiji plugin, RCSEDv2. This suite includes three applications: RCSEDv2 Web, Spectral Viz, and Hyperspectral Viz. Built as single-page applications, these tools are accessible via web browsers, requiring no local installation. Developed using JavaScript, they can be easily customized and deployed on any web server. Their primary utility lies in the rapid exploration of image datasets, particularly through spectral dimension visualizations such as line plots, stacked line plots, and principal component analysis. These tools are ideal for pre-experiment planning and post-experiment analysis. By enabling the selection of samples, pixels, spectral bands, and sample groups, users can interactively monitor changes in pixel values. Furthermore, the inclusion of web-based tools for hyperspectral image analysis within the open-source software ecosystem fosters collaboration and enhances accessibility. This work demonstrates how pre-existing scientific software can be adapted to create interactive web applications for spectral analysis. The tools are freely available for use, which is crucial for remote access to scientific software. This development underscores the growing trend of hyperspectral analysis shifting from traditional desktop and laboratory settings to web-based platforms. To support this transition, we outline how RCSEDv2 and the associated web tools facilitate analysis and data visualization. Additionally, we address how these applications overcome specific challenges related to user interface design, interactivity, and remote access. Finally, the tools serve as a foundation for further development, including the creation of new analysis methods and the integration of machine learning techniques. This work demonstrates how scientific software built on established, open-source platforms can be extended with new features and functionalities. This approach to software development is gaining traction, as it promotes collaboration, transparency, and accessibility. To support this paradigm shift, the article details how to create new web applications from existing software, how to integrate new analysis methods, and how to incorporate machine learning capabilities. This fosters a collaborative environment where software can be continuously improved and enhanced. Additionally, the article provides a user guide for RCSEDv2 and its web tools, as well as a developer guide for extending these tools with new analysis methods. This comprehensive guide assists both new users and experienced users of scientific software in utilizing the tools effectively. For developers, it outlines how to contribute to the software and ensure its continued evolution. Ultimately, this work highlights a new paradigm for scientific software development, where tools are increasingly accessible through web interfaces, fostering a more collaborative and transparent community

Temporal action segmentation involves identifying action boundaries within videos and segmenting the frames according to the performed actions. While deep learning has driven the field's evolution, it depends on annotated data, which is costly and time-intensive to create. To address this, we introduce SSCAP, an entirely self-supervised approach that leverages the co-occurrence relationships between video segments and actions to achieve segmentation without any annotations. Specifically, we partition unlabeled videos into small fragments, encode them using a contrastive language-image pre-training model, and employ contrastive learning to align text and video feature spaces. The model automatically learns the correlation between semantic information in these representations and the "action boundary" concept, utilizing this knowledge for segmentation. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that SSCAP successfully generates high-quality annotations and achieves competitive performance in unsupervised temporal action segmentation. This study investigates the impact of Traditional Detailed Feedback (TF) versus Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback (IBCF) on undergraduate students during software testing education. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time these two feedback types are directly compared within the context of educational research. The research involves recruiting 111 fourth-semester undergraduate students and randomly assigning them to one of three groups: TF, IBCF, or a control group receiving no feedback. All participants were administered a pre-test followed by a testing quiz to establish a baseline, after which they received either TF or IBCF for each subsequent quiz until reaching the final assessment. Post-final quiz, a follow-up test was administered. Data from these pre, post, and follow-up assessments were analyzed to determine the effectiveness of each feedback approach. Results indicate that TF yields better outcomes than no feedback (NBF), while IBCF produces outcomes comparable to TF. Consequently, the paper concludes that IBCF serves as a viable alternative to TF for teaching software testing. Finally, the practical implications of these findings for software testing education are discussed. In summary, IBCF is a successful feedback mechanism in software testing education and should be widely adopted by instructors. Additionally, the paper outlines several avenues for future research. Finally, we provide sample problems from the testing quizzes used in this study on our GitHub repository to assist readers in replicating the experiment. Awaiting replication, we believe this example will assist others in understanding the educational value of software testing. Our objective is to demonstrate the practicality of testing education and its significance to the industry. We believe that more instructors will engage with testing education following the availability of these samples. Domain adaptation is a prevalent technique for addressing distribution shifts across vision, language, and multimedia domains. While most existing approaches rely on learning domain-invariant features using model parameters from both source and target domains, this paper proposes adapting hyperparameters of a pre-trained generative model exclusively with data from the source domain. We introduce a method to systematically explore hyperparameter spaces across different data distributions. Specifically, we reframe generative model pre-training as a hypothesis transfer task by casting it as a source-to-target domain adaptation problem. To address label scarcity in the target domain, we propose a self-supervised representation learning strategy utilizing generative models, alongside implementing source domain knowledge transfer through hypothesis-specific self-supervised learning. Experimental results across multiple vision tasks demonstrate that adaptively selecting a hypothesis based on target domain performance can recover a model's capabilities even with minimal target data. Consequently, this approach reduces the need for target data in generative model pre-training, yielding a more streamlined and interpretable methodology. The framework is flexible and can be applied to various self-supervised learning scenarios. Code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashishdixit/sfsdf. Paper available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.04015. Keywords: Domain Adaptation, Hyperparameter Search, Hyperparameter Optimization, Source-Free Domain Adaptation, Generative Models.

The analysis examines reactor design parameters, including a spherical core measuring 2.5 meters in diameter, surrounded by a moderator and reflector, with a power output of 100 MW. The study explores various concepts for high-specific-power on-board power generation, such as thermoelectric, Brayton, and Stirling cycles, alongside high-thrust expansion nozzles. Additionally, the implications of this nuclear rocket design on a sample return mission from the Martian moon Phobos are assessed. The mission architecture involves a launch from Earth parking orbit, a deep space maneuver (DSM) upon reaching escape velocity, a Phobos sample return journey, and a final DSM to re-enter Earth's atmosphere. Furthermore, the paper addresses safety concerns regarding potential reactor malfunctions and their impact on crew safety. The proposed reactor design demonstrates a high margin of safety, with estimated crew radiation doses of 100 mSv over a 150-day transit period. Finally, the feasibility of this architecture is evaluated, with a recommendation to proceed with preliminary design studies. This recommendation stems from the observation that Earth-to-Mars transit times could be reduced by approximately 50% compared to current chemical propulsion capabilities. The analysis also reviews alternative architectures, such as those employing both nuclear thermal rockets and electric propulsion, which offer higher specific impulse but require significantly longer transit durations. The only constraint is the time required, with a development period of 10 to 20 years being sufficient. The paper concludes with a summary of the work and provides recommendations for future research. This study evaluates the efficacy of domain-informed neural networks (DINNs) for identifying interaction points (IPs) within astroparticle experiments. As a specific application, the analysis targets the identification of muon neutrino (MN) interactions inside the IceCube detector. To facilitate this, a straightforward DINNN framework is established for IP detection. The model is trained using both realistic data and data generated through simulation. Performance is assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, which compare DINNN outputs against two baseline models: a neural network trained solely on simulated data and an experimental method based on a $\chi^2$ function. Results indicate that DINNNs achieve superior performance, exhibiting only a 1% reduction in accuracy relative to baseline models while utilizing 30% less training data. Furthermore, the IP localization capabilities of DINNNs are validated by examining the distribution of MN interaction distances from the detector's center, a metric that aligns with expectations derived from Monte Carlo simulations. The study concludes that DINNs hold significant promise for enhancing the accuracy of IP localization across various particle physics experiments. Additionally, this work establishes a foundational basis for developing DINNNs to detect candidates for charged current (CC) and neutral current (NC) neutrino interactions within the same framework. Future research will explore strategies to mitigate the influence of secondary IP generation processes on the accuracy of IP localization. Ultimately, this approach holds great potential for improving the precision of interaction localization in astrophysics. Atmospheric retrievals serve as a critical instrument for both characterizing exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres and benchmarking planet-formation theories. These retrievals necessitate a database of line-by-line radiative transfer calculations that encompasses a comprehensive array of molecules prevalent in these environments. While the exoplanet and brown dwarf communities have previously relied on databases derived for stellar atmospheres, such resources are inadequate for planets due to their inability to account for molecules like H$_2$O, CH$_4$, TiO, VO, and Na. This paper introduces the first database specifically designed for exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres, featuring line-by-line radiative transfer calculations for H$_2$O, CH$_4$, TiO, VO, and Na across pressures ranging from 0.01 bar to 100 bar and temperatures between 300 K and 3000 K. Utilizing the exoPLUTO code, we computed the pressure broadened cross sections required for line-by-line radiative transfer calculations, incorporating homogeneous broadening effects caused by H$_2$O, H$_2$, and CO. The database, named EXOPLINES, is accessible via the exoplanet retrieval package exoRMS. We applied EXOPLINES to generate synthetic transmission spectra for the hot Jupiter WASP-18b, comparing the results against the widely used public database from the Center for Astrophysics | Haverford College. Our findings indicate that EXOPLINES offers superior resolution and a significantly expanded temperature range. The EXOPLINES project is a collaborative effort by the Exoplanet Retrieval Working Group (exoRWW) of the Exoplanet Working Group (Exo). The group's website, www.exorww.org, provides access to EXOPLINES along with additional documentation and molecular data. Future developments will expand the database to include a wider variety of molecules and non-thermal heating mechanisms. This work offers a detailed theoretical examination of variable instantiation, or grounding, within Answer Set Programming (ASP). By leveraging the semantics of ASP's modeling language, we present a formal definition of grounding models grounded in fixed point theory. Central to this approach is a grounded version of the immediate predecessor operator, which we demonstrate is monotonic and continuous. Utilizing the reduct technique from classical ASP and integrative ASP, we specify a complete immediate predecessor operator for reduct-based grounding models. Furthermore, we propose a novel grounding method that is computationally equivalent to the widely used modern ASP grounder, GRoundUP. Additionally, we extend these theoretical concepts to fully capture the grounding of integrative ASP programs, thereby supporting multi-paradigm ASP modeling. Our findings are evaluated through proof obligations and implementation assessments, with all grounding methods available as open-source tools. We conclude that for programs free of default negation, our proposed grounding algorithms are computationally optimal. Specifically, we establish that the problem of determining whether a variable instance is part of the grounded Herbrand model is NP-complete, matching the complexity of standard ASP program verification. This conclusion holds true for integrative ASP programs as well. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the theoretical background; Section 3 details our main contributions; and Section 4 presents our conclusions. Subsequently, Sections 5 through 8 address existing grounding methods, while Sections 9 through 12 present our proposed approaches. Finally, Section 14 explores several open research questions. These criteria enable the construction of first-law relations, which serve as quantum analogues to the first law of thermodynamics. Introducing the concept of information measure from moments, we develop its theory alongside power variation from moments and establish its analytical expressions. The resulting information measure is distributed, enabling analysis of both lower and higher components within a variable. Furthermore, we derive the analytical formulas for single-layer and multi-layer moment discriminant tests. These findings are applied to analyze the information content of various distributions and their transformations, as well as to assess the similarity between different distribution types. Finally, several applications are proposed to demonstrate the advantages of this new information measure. Notably, moments of any order can yield meaningful information metrics, offering greater flexibility in selecting an optimal order. Additionally, moments capture only central tendencies, allowing the extraction of central tendency information from a single moment and facilitating the analysis of interdependencies among different moments. Overall, the moment-based information measure introduced here represents only a preliminary exploration of cumulative facts (CF), and its significant potential for future research is highlighted. This work paves the way for extending the concept of information measures to other statistical quantities and for developing new methods to calculate distribution information. Specifically, it advances the historical evolution of information measures, which has progressed from entropy to various forms (including those derived from CF) and is now advancing toward more generalized information measures. Furthermore, the moment-based information measure opens a new research direction for quantifying the randomness of transformed variables, thereby expanding the scope of information theory. Finally, this approach offers a promising alternative to traditional methods for analyzing distribution properties and distributional data. By directly calculating moment-based information measures, researchers can avoid the computational burden of maximum likelihood estimation required to determine traditional information measures for transformed variables. Consequently, this simplifies the analysis of transformed variables and provides a novel, alternative perspective on distributional data research. This paper investigates inference regarding non-stationary time series characterized by heavy tails and/or long-range dependence, as well as vectorized time series exhibiting such features. We introduce a time-domain method for estimating the infinite variance covariance matrix in non-stationary, heavy-tailed multivariate time series, deriving the asymptotic normality of the resulting estimator under appropriate conditions. Furthermore, we develop a frequency-domain approach for the non-stationary estimation of the spectral density matrix of non-deterministic multivariate non-stationary time series; this matrix is frequently utilized for non-parametric inference in such settings. Our approach is specifically designed for heavy-tailed non-stationary time series and employs the spectral matrix derived from the stationary component of the process. We demonstrate that, for the specific case of linear processes with linear trends, the proposed frequency-domain estimator yields the same estimates as our time-domain estimator. In the field of distributed computing, multiple nodes collaborate to resolve computational problems. This work investigates the distributed equivalence between Dominating Set and Distance-$2$ Dominating Set, a result that previously extended to Distance-$3$ Dominating Set. We demonstrate that this equivalence holds for Distance-$r$ Dominating Set when the graph contains no $(2r+1)$-cycles. Leveraging this equivalence, we establish a distributed lower bound for Dominating Set on $k$-out graphs, which is the first such bound reported for this specific graph class. Furthermore, utilizing a general property, we extend our findings to the equivalent problems of Distance-$r$ Dominating Set and Irrelevant Node Distance-$r$ Dominating Set. Additionally, our analysis reveals a connection between the equivalence of Dominating Set and Distance-$3$ Dominating Set, as well as Equivalent Degree on random $k$-out graphs. Finally, we introduce a new model known as Multiple Distributed Multiple Query, which establishes an upper bound for Distributed Dominating Set. Our proofs rely on the Graph Theoretic Lemma and a recent upper bound regarding the equivalence of Distributed Dominating Set and Distributed Distance-$3$ Dominating Set. Finally, by employing the concept of $r$-coloring, we prove the equivalence between Distributed Distance-$r$ Dominating Set and Distributed Distance-$2r$ Dominating Set. Through multiple lemmas, we show that for any $r \geq 1$, Distributed Distance-$r$ Dominating Set is strictly harder than Distributed $(r-1)$ Dominating Set, thereby implying that Distributed Distance-$1$ (equivalent to Standard Dominating Set) is the simplest instance of Distributed Dominating Set. This research was conducted within the context of the 2021 ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing (PODC). The paper includes proofs and sketches for these contributions. Keywords: Dominating Set, Distributed Computing, Lower Bound.

This study investigates how disorder impacts the bulk-boundary correspondence in two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs), focusing specifically on corner modes. Our findings reveal that localized zero-frequency corner states preserve the robust bulk-boundary correspondence, whereas localized sub-gap modes result in its violation, a phenomenon attributed to extended boundary-thickness modes. To overcome this violation and restore the bulk-boundary correspondence, we propose applying a spatially modulated external field. Furthermore, our work examines the localization transition of corner modes and the splitting of topological corner states induced by disorder, alongside the influence of boundary thickness on boundary-thickness modes. These insights deepen our comprehension of the robustness of topological corner states within highly disordered HOTIs and their stability under increasing disorder strength. Finally, we suggest potential applications for quantum devices operating in strongly disordered HOTI regimes. Over the past five to six years, the CMS experiment at LHC has conducted an extensive search for supersymmetry (SUSY) across various production modes. This review succinctly outlines the experimental methodology employed and details recent findings across a broad spectrum of SUSY models generated by tools such as PHENIX. Furthermore, I will present the latest results covering nearly all explored production scenarios, effectively providing an update on results from 2016 through 2018. Ultimately, this compilation demonstrates the significant potential of SUSY searches, which have not yet yielded any significant discoveries. Consequently, future investigations must delve deeper into the unexplored regions of the SUSY parameter space. This can be achieved by either increasing the integrated luminosity of the experiment or, more effectively, by enhancing the collision energy. Specifically, the LHC is scheduled to resume operations at 13 TeV in 2021, with a future upgrade planned to reach 14 TeV. Furthermore, the installation of the CMS High-Luminosity Upgrade is anticipated to deliver an integrated luminosity of 300 fb$^{-1}$ at 13 TeV over the next few years. This review aims to illustrate the opportunities and challenges associated with conducting SUSY searches under these high-luminosity conditions. Finally, I intend to highlight the specific strategies employed by the CMS experiment to uncover the physics phenomena concealed within the high-multiplicity, high-luminosity environment of the future LHC. We introduce a new frame-reuse technique that allows the efficient rendering of scenes captured via multiple views. Unlike previous methods, we apply the transformation from frame-reused video to 3D space directly within the network, effectively operating in a 3D convolution space. This approach enables the generation of novel views, videos, and full 3D light fields directly from the output of a convolutional layer. Additionally, we demonstrate how to integrate Spherical Harmonics into the output convolutional space for efficient lighting, thereby facilitating view and appearance synthesis. We validate the efficacy of our light field-based representation by utilizing it for model-based rendering, specifically for view and appearance synthesis. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on both single-camera and multi-camera datasets. On the multi-camera DfD dataset, our method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art by 0.29dB in PSNR and improves SSIM by 0.04. Furthermore, we show that this representation excels in light field-based rendering applications. On the Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) dataset, we exceed the previous state-of-the-art by 0.29dB in PSNR and 0.03 in SSIM. Finally, we demonstrate that the trained weights can be directly employed for model-based rendering. We demonstrate that this functional stochastic framework is equivalent to a classical quantum model describing vortex simulation in a single superconducting thin film, where the quantum state of the film corresponds to a Gaussian white noise field. This equivalence establishes a bridge between the classical simulation of 3-D vortex dynamics and standard circuit quantum hardware. To validate the approach, we present results from a new simulation of a specific vortex event previously recorded by experimental measurements. Our findings indicate that modeling this specific experimental record using our algorithm requires more than ten times the computational resources compared to the original measurement. This discrepancy underscores the inherent complexity of 3-D vortex dynamics and the substantial challenge of developing efficient simulation methods. Our work represents the initial step toward the ultimate goal of fully reproducing 3-D vortex dynamics experimentally. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed circuit can be utilized to develop new, efficient simulation techniques for specific vortex events, such as those involving a single vortex crossing the superconductor. Boson sampling is a quantum computational model designed to expose the power of quantum many-body systems. It relies on the interference of bosons within many-body entangled states to produce a random distribution of probability amplitudes that resists efficient classical simulation. Prior research typically examined early-time entanglement dynamics, suggesting an area law for entropy. In this study, we investigate the complete time evolution of the system, demonstrating that the entropy of individual modes approaches the maximum value, $\ln(d)$, where $d$ represents the dimension of the single-particle Hilbert space. The deviation from this maximum scales with the boson number $N$ and mode dimension $d$ according to $\ln(d)\times N^{2/3}d^{-1/3}$. This finding contrasts with the entanglement between pairs of modes, which follows a different scaling law. Our results indicate that the area-law behavior observed in earlier works likely stems from the finite size of the systems analyzed. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this scaling law for the efficiency of classical approximation algorithms. Finally, we calculate the entanglement entropy using the random tensor network framework. This approach relies on the hypothesis that the system's wave function is well-approximated by a random tensor network featuring entropy scaling properties similar to those of the boson sampling system. The entropy of a single mode in this framework follows a Gaussian distribution with a mean of $\ln(d)$ and a variance of $d^{-2/3}N^{2/3}$. This hypothesis is supported by the statistical properties of entropy and the entropy-area scaling laws, which align with the predictions of the random tensor network framework. The probability of observing early-time area-law entanglement decreases as the system size grows, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the entanglement structure of the boson sampling system. The entanglement structure of boson sampling systems is characterized by low entropy at early times, high entanglement at late times, and weak correlations between different modes. This structure is essential for the computational advantage of boson sampling over classical systems. Our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the entanglement structure in boson sampling systems, which is crucial for both fundamental research and practical applications. For instance, it has significant implications for the calibration of optical networks in photonic quantum computing experiments, where the entanglement structure must be carefully controlled to ensure the reliability of the computed results. Additionally, our findings may inform the design of new quantum algorithms that exploit the unique entanglement structures

Reinforcement learning focuses on agents navigating unknown environments within a Markov decision process framework. In scenarios where observations are partial, an agent's belief about its state is defined as the posterior distribution over possible states given its history. This study demonstrates that recurrent neural networks can effectively approximate decision policies by capturing dependencies between current and past inputs, yet it highlights that standard LSTM architectures fail to represent beliefs in partially observable settings because their internal forget mechanisms do not align with the agents' actual dynamics-related beliefs. Conversely, Recurrent Policy Networks, originally designed as function approximators, successfully model these beliefs due to their inherent state dependencies. To enhance scalability, we introduce policies based on Gaussian process recurrent neural networks, maintaining high performance while reducing parameter counts. Our results indicate that these recurrent policy networks surpass acyclic neural network baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to other leading approaches, including those utilizing particle filters and dynamic belief models. Furthermore, we derive a no-go theorem demonstrating that neural networks employing a recurrent architecture are necessary to approximate policies that depend on partially observable states. Finally, we apply our recurrent policy networks to a simulated autonomous vehicle environment, successfully learning a policy for obstacle avoidance. The prevailing approach to spatio-temporal action detection involves performing object detection and temporal action localization on each frame, followed by feature aggregation and decomposition. However, this method necessitates computationally intensive temporal processing and high-dimensionality learning. Furthermore, it typically requires a large number of sample-level annotations, which are costly and time-consuming to produce. To address these challenges, we propose an end-to-end framework for action detection that leverages the complementary strengths of spatial and temporal cues. Our method utilizes spatio-temporal graph convolutional networks to model within-object and cross-object interactions, enabling the system to identify contextually relevant objects and their bounding boxes. By incorporating a weak-supervision module, the approach can also localize actions based on loosely-bounded video segments. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function designed to mitigate class imbalance and ensure bounding box tightness. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance in both detection and weak-supervised detection tasks. Notably, it significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques that rely on similar supervision levels. Furthermore, our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in video-based detection while requiring substantially fewer annotations. Finally, we evaluate the method's computational efficiency, showing that it is well-suited for real-time action detection applications. This research examines diffusion processes halted by either absorption or exit, governed by degenerate parabolic equations that include negative eigenvalue terms of the form $-\lambda u$ and $-\lambda \sigma \cdot \nabla u$. The initial value problem for such equations, subject to various boundary conditions, yields a solution representable as a series expansion involving generalized eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint extension of a degenerate elliptic operator. In the context of boundary-value dynamics and perturbation theory, this series formulation offers superior analytical properties compared to alternative representations, such as those derived via the method of steps. Furthermore, this approach enables a comprehensive resolution of metastability questions, specifically determining both the slowest decay rate and the quasi-stationary distribution within a bounded domain. These findings are applicable to diverse operators and scenarios, including those exhibiting periodic drift. Additionally, this framework facilitates the derivation of effective boundary conditions for perturbed homogenization problems within degenerate domains. Specifically, for weakly periodic operators where degenerate diffusion occurs within a narrow channel, it provides an exact solution for the homogenized operator. These findings extend and complement earlier work by the authors and others regarding the asymptotic behavior of degenerate diffusion across varying scales. Finally, the methodology is also relevant to scenarios involving multiple domains where boundary conditions differ across each partition. This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the lowest-order constraint variational (LOCV) method with the $AV18$ two-body potential. Our findings indicate that while the LOCV energy remains largely unaffected by the magnetic field, the contributions from Coulomb and Pauli terms vary differently, resulting in their total contribution to the energy to change significantly. These results demonstrate that the LOCV energy and its components exhibit complex behaviors in the presence of such fields. Additionally, we observe that the symmetry energy, effective masses, and momentum of protons and neutrons all show distinct responses to strong magnetic fields. Furthermore, the symmetry energy calculated via the LOCV method shows good agreement with those derived from the M3I two-body potential and the Chiral Effective Field Theory (CH85) force. Finally, we note that the LOCV framework proves to be computationally efficient for analyzing nuclear matter properties under strong magnetic fields. Ensuring privacy and communication efficiency remains a significant challenge in federated learning. To address the growing concern of privacy leakage, this study employs information-theoretic leakage to evaluate the privacy efficacy of federated principal component analysis. Results indicate that training with a limited number of communications per round offers strong privacy guarantees, yet federated learning often violates this constraint due to the high frequency of local updates required for convergence. We address this by proposing a privacy-preserving refreshment mechanism that limits information transfer between rounds while reducing communication overhead. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that DP-REC achieves superior privacy efficiency and convergence with significantly fewer communications per round compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, these refreshments can be executed securely within the federated learning framework. Finally, we discuss the practical implications of this approach for training large-scale models. Our experiments confirm that DP-REC substantially reduces the communication burden in large-scale federated learning environments, thereby enhancing the system's practicality. Additionally, we show that this privacy-refreshment mechanism can even offer performance improvements in certain large-scale scenarios. Overall, our findings suggest that the proposed privacy-refreshment mechanism is both practical and effective for large-scale federated learning. To our knowledge, this is the first work to explicitly examine the trade-off between privacy and communication efficiency in this context. We introduce the initial results from the Far Ultraviolet Survey of the Taurus-Perseus-Auriga complex, conducted using the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE). This survey targeted approximately 100 young stellar objects (YSOs) and their surrounding disks, along with about 100 nearby T Tauri stars lacking disks. The selected sample prioritized sources with previously detected infrared excess emission, indicating the presence of disks. Of the 200 observed sources, 100 were chosen randomly to represent YSOs with disks across the full spectral energy distribution range, while the other 100 were selected specifically for their far-ultraviolet continuum emission to facilitate accurate disk temperature measurements. These observations provide the first comprehensive far-UV spectral data for a group of YSOs and disks at the main sequence age. The spectral coverage allowed for the identification of numerous atomic and molecular lines originating from both the disks and the YSOs themselves. We present spectral classifications for all 100 YSOs and compare their far-UV spectra with those of 100 nearby T Tauri stars. The analysis reveals that YSOs with disks exhibit significantly higher far-UV continuum emission than those without disks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that far-UV observations can be utilized to determine the temperatures of these disks. Finally, we propose that far-UV spectroscopy can serve as a diagnostic tool to identify and characterize the physical conditions of both the disks and the young stars themselves. The complete spectral library is accessible via the IUE Data Archive at STScI. This paper serves as an overview of the survey results, with detailed analyses of individual sources to be published separately. Future work will address the implications of these results for the physical conditions and evolution of disks and YSOs. (The sample used in this survey is also available for study). Table extraction involves identifying documents containing tables and ascribing labels to various regions within them. This task is challenging due to the diverse structures of tables and the complex, disorganized layouts of documents. Existing methods often treat table regions as independent entities, neglecting their intricate relationships. This study introduces an approach utilizing graph neural networks to model document layouts and extract tables, specifically to overcome the limitation of isolated relationship processing. We also propose a novel graph-based loss function that addresses the difficulty in modeling relationships among numerous regions. A thorough analysis of representation embeddings reveals that while tables share similar characteristics, documents exhibit greater variability, thereby explaining the difficulty in table extraction. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method is effective and can significantly outperform state-of-the-art baselines on major PDF table extraction benchmarks. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhenghaozhang/GraphNetTable.

We investigate the dynamic cognitive hierarchy (CH) framework within the context of multi-stage games characterized by imperfect information. In this setting, players at different levels of the hierarchy construct conditional belief hierarchies regarding others' levels and update them as new information emerges. These updated perceptions inform their assessment of the game's normal form at each stage, thereby determining their strategic choices. Under this understanding, we provide sufficient conditions ensuring that the dynamic CH has a unique fixed point, which represents a credible equilibrium for the entire game. Furthermore, we apply the dynamic CH model to signaling games, contributing to the understanding of how the concept of divinity arises from cognitive hierarchies. Additionally, we explore a series of open questions concerning dynamic CH and its potential to advance the field of quantal response equilibrium. Finally, we conduct an experimental study to evaluate the predictive accuracy of the dynamic CH model. Our findings indicate that the QRE and CH models fail to individually account for the data; however, the dynamic CH model successfully predicts the observations. These results highlight the critical role of timing in strategic thinking and suggest that dynamic cognitive hierarchies offer a more comprehensive prediction of human behavior in multi-stage games under imperfect information. Finally, we discuss the extension of the dynamic CH model to settings involving incomplete contracts. By generating predictions for the duration of relationships, the dynamic CH framework holds significant promise for addressing real-world problems. Specifically, it can address issues such as how long it takes for trust to develop in business partnerships and why relationship breakdowns often occur after an initial period of intense activity. These contributions aim to deepen our comprehension of the evolution of trust in dynamic environments and its impact on the sustainability of long-term relationships. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the dynamic CH model, while Section 3 examines its application to signaling games. Section 4 applies the model to the design of long-term business partnerships, and Section 5 reports on our laboratory experiments. The study concludes with Section 6. Accurate and timely population estimates are essential for formulating effective policy decisions. In numerous developing nations, including Mozambique, the absence of regular censuses or their limited sustainability has led to fragmented efforts by various organizations to estimate populations, often with little coordination. This study proposes a two-stage approach to achieve accurate and sustainable population estimates in Mozambique by integrating the Bayesian Area-to-Linear Geostatistical Model (BTLM) with Generalized Additive Models (GAMs). Initially, we employed DTW-MAP to derive population growth rates from the 2007 National Population and Health Survey (DSE 2007) and the 2017 Census. These census mean rates were subsequently extrapolated to 2021 using the latest UN data, which was then utilized as priors for a Bayesian analysis. Finally, a GAM was employed to adjust these mean rates for their reliance on women's data, incorporating covariates such as population density, distance to water, distance to roads, and distance to health centers. The efficacy of this methodology was evaluated by comparing estimated population figures against recent UN estimates. Results indicate that our approach yields accurate population estimates, suggesting its methodological viability. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the potential for advancing the sustainability of future censuses in Mozambique. By utilizing recent population estimates as priors, the model can be deployed every five years to generate accurate population data, thereby supporting effective government planning. Ultimately, this research offers a robust methodological foundation for achieving both accurate and sustainable population estimates in the country. Approximate membership (AM) data structures are popular in big data processing for reducing computational load through the sacrifice of exactness, specifically by allowing duplicate elements to be treated as members. This paper introduces and evaluates multiple methods to maintain such filters while identifying "true" members to eliminate duplicates. We frame this as a data cleaning problem, where duplicate removal is crucial for systems utilizing data structures like Bloom filters to trade exactness. Our findings indicate that our proposed algorithms outperform current state-of-the-art filters by up to 1,000 times in speed, though they require approximately 1.5 times more memory. Finally, we outline future research directions to extend this work. By demonstrating the viability of new duplicate-free filters, our work paves the way for future applications. Specifically, these filters can streamline data preprocessing for machine learning by enabling the use of one-hot encoding and minimizing the impact of class imbalance. Additionally, they facilitate data pre-filtering for classification tasks, thereby lowering the computational demands of big data processing. Finally, these filters offer significant advantages in privacy-preserving data sharing scenarios, such as federated learning, where duplicate-free datasets reduce the risk of re-identification attacks. The various approaches for duplicate elimination are grounded in established data cleaning techniques, with our methods adapted from existing solutions. Our implementation is available on GitHub. This study theoretically examines the conversion of spinor atoms into molecules within cold atomic gases, focusing on three-body recombination. The research addresses the reduction of entanglement between atomic spin and internal molecular rotation. To address the local nature of laser-induced recombination, a three-body model is established where spatial and spinor degrees of freedom are coupled. In the one-dimensional framework, the system is described by a system-bath Hamiltonian featuring local coupling to atomic spin, with bath modes representing two positive-energy scattering states. The spinor model is rigorously analyzed using both exact numerical methods and perturbation theory. Results demonstrate that laser-induced recombination successfully suppresses atomic spin entanglement, with the extent of spin-polarization control depending on the specific scattering state. Furthermore, the study confirms the existence of a phase transition from a system-polarized to a system-nonpolarized phase, control over atomic spin entanglement, and the establishment of spin superfluidity. Finally, in the thermodynamic limit, the spinor system is characterized by an exact Hamiltonian that is translationally invariant in space and rotationally invariant in internal space. By extending prior research on spinor molecules, this work offers a novel approach to controlling spinor three-body recombination and offers direct implications for spinor gases. The provided theoretical and numerical findings are expected to guide future experimental investigations into laser-induced three-body recombination. Additionally, the discussion includes insights into body-effect theory, highlighting its limitations regarding conservation laws and the necessity of incorporating kinetic energy. These outcomes underscore the critical role of quantum spin-orbit coupling and entanglement control during the recombination process. The developed theoretical and numerical methodologies can be readily extended to analyze recombination processes involving more than three bodies. Overall, this work establishes a new research direction on laser-induced three-body recombination, offering fundamental and practical value for future experimental and theoretical studies. The findings may also hold significant implications for cold atom physics, chemical physics, and quantum information science. Specifically, the results provide new perspectives on understanding spinor atom-molecule recombination, spinor entanglement control, and the spin superfluidity phase transition. These outcomes could facilitate future experiments on spinor atom-molecule recombination, entanglement control, and the investigation of superfluidity phase transitions. Furthermore, the theoretical and numerical approaches can be applied to explore superfluidity phase transitions, entanglement control, and entanglement generation in spinor systems. This study introduces a multi-resolution Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach that leverages the inherent adaptivity of the method to resolve complex geometries and challenging features within fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems. The framework is further extended to multi-phase scenarios, specifically modeling free surface phenomena in fFSI contexts. A key innovation is the integration of a new, adaptive neighbor thresholding technique for the Hamilton-Patera large density filter, which eliminates the need for a free-surface thickness parameter at the free surface. This advancement facilitates the construction of a robust multi-phase fFSI framework. The proposed approach is evaluated through three distinct fluid-structure cases: a flow over a flexible cylinder demonstrating fluid-elastic interaction (FEI), a flow over a flexible beam, and a flag flutter scenario. Additionally, the method is applied to two free surface problems: a falling water droplet and a fluid sloshing tank. Numerical results indicate that this framework offers a promising solution for simulating intricate flows in complex fFSI problems. Finally, the study underscores the necessity of multi-resolution capabilities for accurately modeling such scenarios. The code utilized in this research is publicly accessible via GitHub. Machine learning algorithms are fundamental to data analysis, pattern recognition, and decision-making. Although quantum computing offers a promising avenue for accelerating these tasks, many existing quantum learning algorithms remain constrained by the demand for quantum memory. This paper introduces a quantum supervised and unsupervised learning algorithm suite designed for near-term quantum processors, which operates without requiring quantum memory. Additionally, for the first time, we explore the application of quantum batch gradient descent in quantum machine learning. We validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations on near-term hardware, covering scenarios with and without mid-circuit measurements. Processors supporting mid-circuit measurements, such as the IBM Falcon and Ruesel systems, can execute these algorithms in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ iterations, delivering a quadratic advantage compared to the $\mathcal{O}(\log(N))$ iterations required by state-of-the-art classical machine learning methods, where $N$ represents the feature space dimension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed quantum batch gradient descent algorithm is more efficient than existing quantum machine learning algorithms for both unsupervised and supervised learning tasks. These results are supported by comprehensive numerical simulations utilizing quantum kernels based on various quantum circuit structures. Ultimately, we conclude that quantum batch gradient descent offers a robust and versatile framework for quantum machine learning. The source code for this project is publicly accessible at \href{https://github.com/Ankit-123456789/qmlearn}{https://github.com/Ankit-123456789/qmlearn}. Although the recently introduced pitch-controllable text-to-speech (TTS) system, FastPitch, is conditioned on pitch contours, its synthesized speech quality deteriorates significantly when pitch values deviate substantially from the training data. To overcome this limitation, we introduce pitch augmentation, a novel technique that blends the original pitch contour with a random, pitch-shifted version of another sequence to enhance FastPitch's pitch controllability. This approach ensures controlled pitch in generated speech while maintaining natural speech quality. We evaluate Timbre-preserving pitch augmentation (T-PA) against two baseline methods, showing it outperforms them in both objective metrics—specificer (Spec), Intelligibility, and Voice quality—and through human listener evaluations. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of various pitch augmentation strategies to elucidate the method's mechanisms for improving generated output. Extensive experiments confirm that T-PA enables FastPitch to produce speech with both the desired pitch contour and high speech quality. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/taehyunglee/pitch_augmentation. The paper can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.09000. This paper introduces Hopper, a Transformer-based model designed for reasoning within multi-step spatiotemporal contexts, specifically addressing future prediction in dense urban areas. While recent Transformer approaches have primarily focused on immediate t+1 prediction, this work extends the scope to multi-hop reasoning encompassing both space and time. We address this by developing a Multi-hop Attention mechanism that effectively aggregates multi-hop trajectories and multi-hop temporal features. Furthermore, we enhance performance by introducing a Multi-hop Residual mechanism that directly incorporates multi-hop contextual information into the model's predictions. Extensive experiments across real-world datasets, including CityFlow and TOSCA, show that Hopper significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both absolute and relative metrics. Additionally, we validate Hopper's ability to generate diverse multi-hop reasoning paths and its generation quality through qualitative assessments. We investigate lepton-pair production alongside bottom quarks at the LHC within both the Standard Model and a specific BSM framework incorporating extra neutral gauge bosons ($Z^{\prime}$). Focusing on the $ZZ^{\prime}$ cross section, we demonstrate that the observed spectrum in the subdominant one-lepton-one neutrino plus bottom quarks channel results from incoherent interference between Standard Model $WW$ and BSM $ZZ^{\prime}$ production. This channel exhibits a distinct feature: a significant enhancement of the cross section at high energies relative to the Standard Model. We analyze the impact of current experimental data and assess the sensitivity of deriving the $Z^{\prime}$ mass from the observed missing transverse energy distribution in one-lepton-plus-bottom quark events. Finally, we determine that the current precision of missing transverse energy measurements precludes determining the $Z^{\prime}$ mass, even with the full LHC dataset. Furthermore, we note that while missing transverse energy is sensitive to $Z^{\prime}$ production, other variables such as missing transverse mass fail to suppress the large high-energy contribution in one-lepton-plus-bottom quark final states, thereby showing no significant sensitivity toward constraining the $Z^{\prime}$ mass. To address this, we propose an alternative observable: the transverse mass of the lepton-neutrino system. This variable is derived from the transverse momentum and rapidity of the lepton-neutrino system and offers sensitivity to Z boson exchange in one-lepton-plus-bottom quark configurations. Additionally, it allows for a more precise determination of the $W$ boson mass, with a potential improvement of up to 10% compared to existing methods utilizing missing transverse energy. Finally, we examine the prospects for future experiments to measure the $W$ mass with this new observable. We conclude that the proposed transverse mass observable is highly sensitive to missing energy events featuring exactly one leptonic jet and a $b$-tagged jet, a sample that can be obtained at the high-luminosity LHC. The mass of the $W$ boson can be measured with a precision of approximately 15 MeV, representing a substantial improvement over the current experimental accuracy of 16 MeV. This enhanced sensitivity is particularly relevant for scenarios where new physics effects are expected to be small. Furthermore, we observe that in certain cases, this one-lepton-plus-bottom quark configuration surpasses the current best results

Telepresence robots (TPRs) are remotely operated vehicles that enable users to physically visit locations while simultaneously observing, communicating, and engaging with the environment. Given the growing adoption of TPRs across various sectors such as healthcare, education, and business, ensuring a high Quality of Experience (QoE) for remote users is increasingly critical. However, traditional video metrics are inadequate for assessing TPR performance because they evaluate only the visual feed and neglect the robot's underlying motion control. This paper demonstrates that TPR motion control is the most influential factor in determining overall QoE. We evaluate three distinct motion controllers by comparing their tracking and exploration capabilities. To do so, we introduce a new interactive QoE assessment framework that employs a broad set of experiments to test each controller's performance against human users. Our results indicate that existing video motion controllers fail to meet human expectations, offering neither smooth exploration nor effective target tracking. To address these deficiencies, we developed a learning-based trajectory controller and a feature-based target tracker, which were integrated into a new motion controller designed to better satisfy human needs. This proposed controller significantly improves target tracking and exploration efficiency. Furthermore, our interactive QoE assessment method offers a practical solution for developing future QoE-optimized TPR motion controllers. By enabling direct human evaluation, this approach facilitates the co-design of both TPR systems and their controllers. Ultimately, this study advances the creation of next-generation TPRs with enhanced motion control and target tracking capabilities. Leveraging the adaptability and utility of Bayesian modeling, this study presents a tutorial on hierarchical regression designed for individuals possessing only basic familiarity with regression analysis and Bayesian concepts. Through a series of practical examples focused on performance and price data, we illustrate how hierarchical (or mixed-effects) models surpass standard regression approaches by incorporating external information, thereby enhancing predictive accuracy and enabling the estimation of population-level characteristics alongside entity-specific effects. The tutorial demonstrates the implementation of these models using the R programming language and the rstanarm package. Furthermore, we emphasize the broader significance of Bayesian hierarchical models in addressing real-world data challenges, such as those encountered during the COVID-19 pandemic. The underlying R code is accessible at https://github.com/bayes101/r101. These materials are designed to foster interest in, and facilitate the adoption of, hierarchical Bayesian modeling. Additionally, this work serves as a component of a larger series of related materials available in R that structure the learning of statistics and machine learning into 101 topics, each corresponding to a single R script. This approach aims to demystify, simplify, and make accessible these often daunting fields for those new to statistics. For further details, visit https://bayes101.org. Mafia, also known as Werewolf, is a widely enjoyed party game that has been thoroughly analyzed from a psychological perspective in the work of K. Nakano, T. Nakano, and Y. Nakamura (Food, 2017). This paper introduces a straightforward mathematical model of the game, demonstrating its adaptability to combinatorial problems of varying complexities depending on the number of players and the game's duration. Specifically, this model allows for the determination of winning probabilities for both Mafia and Villain factions. When applied to a scenario with three mafia players and four villains, the model accurately predicts the observed outcomes of repeated game trials. Furthermore, the study explores how the game's dynamics are influenced by the number of nightly votes and analyzes the impact of random night eliminations on winning probabilities. The paper concludes with extensions of the model that account for more advanced gameplay strategies. A computer program, written in Python to assist with these calculations, is also provided. Keywords: Mafia, probability, combinatorial problem.

This study investigates simultaneous gas accretion into a binary system of giant planets using high-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations. We examine the accumulation of gas envelopes by two protoplanets, each with a core mass of 0.5 Earth masses, orbiting at 30 and 60 astronomical units from their host star within a protoplanetary disk. Our findings indicate that the distance between the two planets significantly influences the symmetry of their gas accretion. Specifically, the companion planet perturbs the disk, causing local depletions of mass and angular momentum in the circumprimary disk that affect the primary planet's accretion rate. This perturbation manifests differently based on separation: when the planets are closer (5 AU apart), the primary planet accretes more symmetrically due to enhanced mass and angular momentum in the region between them; when farther apart (15 AU apart), the primary planet experiences a more asymmetric inflow. Consequently, the secondary planet accretes gas at a rate approximately 2.5 times higher than the primary. We conclude that these interactions result in the planet pair separating by 3.6 times compared to isolated accretion scenarios. These outcomes may contribute to the formation of massive planet pairs observed in systems like HD 106906 b and c, where the secondary planets exhibit significantly higher accretion rates. Additionally, our simulations suggest that the secondary planet's gas accretion is roughly 1.5 times greater than the primary's, whereas isolated accretion models predict nearly equal mass accretion rates for both planets. This discrepancy highlights the necessity of including fluid dynamics in binary accretion studies to better understand the conditions required for the formation of massive planet pairs. Finally, we note that the migration timescales for these planets are comparable to the lifetime of a gas disk, suggesting that further research is needed to determine if the observed separation distances are the result of accretion processes or subsequent dynamical evolution. Future studies should explore the impact of disk self-gravity on these interactions. Our simulations also reveal that the gas accretion rates for both planets are at least an order of magnitude lower than those of isolated accretion models, indicating that interactions between the planets and the disk suppress accretion. This suppression is more pronounced for the primary planet, which is consistent with the observed trends in planet mass ratios. This work presents a phenomenological framework explaining electronic transport within a macroscopic armchair carbon nanotube film, specifically detailing the creation of a backgate device functionalized with 3-iodopyridine. The 3-iodopyridine sublayer serves a dual purpose: facilitating work function tuning through chemical interaction with the nanotubes and acting as an effective filter that blocks non-resonant states. We analyze conductance measurements across varying gate voltages, temperatures, and light intensities, correlating these findings with the characteristics of the 3-iodopyridine sublayer. Our results indicate that electronic charge carriers move via a phonon-assisted mechanism, as evidenced by the correlation between conductance and gate voltage, as well as the observed temperature and light intensity dependencies. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of this work in advancing the engineering of carbon-based materials, such as nanotubes and graphene, to develop materials with optimized electronic properties. This study also underscores the importance of the 3-iodopyridine sublayer in enabling precise control over the electronic characteristics of carbon-based systems. Finally, our findings demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed experimental setup for the tunable work function of carbon-based materials. These conclusions are supported by the accompanying data file. Additionally, the paper includes detailed mathematical derivations of the proposed transport theory, which can be utilized to explore the limits of this approach. This study introduces a novel fuzzy k-means algorithm designed to resolve the high-dimensional data challenge. In traditional fuzzy k-means clustering, high-dimensional features are treated with the same importance as others, often leading to the curse of dimensionality, the curse of sparsity, and curse of dimensionality. To address this, we propose simultaneously learning cluster assignments and custom weights for each dimension, ensuring that less significant dimensions receive lower weights. Inspired by the success of weighted fuzzy k-means in high-dimensional image data, we initially applied it to high-dimensional datasets; however, results showed that the model occasionally assigned zero weights to certain dimensions, rendering those features irrelevant. To prevent this, we integrated an entropy-based penalty into the objective function. By incorporating this penalty, the model can effectively identify the relative importance of each dimension while ensuring all weights remain strictly positive. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms standard fuzzy k-means and entropy-based clustering with respect to the Silhouette coefficient. The proposed approach is particularly well-suited for high-dimensional data where the number of dimensions exceeds the sample size. The implementation can be found here. Please cite this work. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a foundational technique in machine learning that integrates multiple expert models through a gating network. Although proven to be both learnable and expressive, theoretical research into efficient algorithms for learning general MoE has largely been absent. This study investigates the core challenges of the "gating first" MoE architecture, where gating determines the support for exactly one expert per input, while that expert outputs the result. We first demonstrate that standard gradient descent fails to consistently learn this model, identifying the root cause as "gradient pathologies" where gradients are disproportionately influenced by inactive experts. To address this, we propose a "gates-first" gradient descent algorithm that jointly optimizes the gate and expert support without incurring the prior drawbacks. We provide a comprehensive analysis of this method, proving that it achieves a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(n)$ for consistent learning, where $n$ represents the number of experts. Furthermore, we extend this approach to the "support first" MoE model, where the gate selects the top-$k$ experts for each input. We develop an efficient algorithm for this more complex variant and establish a sample complexity upper bound of $\mathcal{O}(k^n)$. Finally, supported by extensive experiments, we illustrate the practical effectiveness of our proposed models. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWu1996/MoE. These notes offer a self-contained introduction to chip-firing games on metric graphs, along with an overview of Jacobians and Prym varieties, and how chip-firing dynamics relate to them. Chip-firing games serve as a simple yet deep combinatorial model that effectively illustrates core concepts in algebraic geometry, including divisors, linear equivalence, Riemann-Roch, Jacobians, and abelian varieties. Notably, chip-firing dynamics on any (smooth projective) graph occur within the second cohomology group, modeled by the Jacobian, where the move corresponds to the principal divisor of a meromorphic function. Consequently, the dynamics can be analyzed using algebraic geometry, with powerful tools like Riemann's Reciprocity Theorem and the Weak Approximation Theorem playing a crucial role. The primary motivation for these notes is to extend chip-firing theory from finite graphs to arbitrary metric graphs, thereby providing a framework for new research. This material is based on a two-week mini-course titled "Chip-firing games on metric graphs" presented at the 2021 Algebraic Geometry Summer School in Madrid. The course was co-taught by the author and David Jensen, whose insightful contributions to the content are deeply appreciated. For a comprehensive treatment of these topics, readers are directed to the book "Chip-Firing Games, Abelian Varieties and Approximation in Arithmetic Geometry" by David Jensen, which emerged from the same source as this work. Additional references are available in [Dresen20], [Jensen20], and [Jensen21]. The author extends special thanks to all participants, whose insightful questions and contributions throughout the course significantly enriched the resulting outcomes. Additionally, the nLab entry on chip-firing games on metric graphs is recommended for further relevant information. Although quantum gravity is believed to severely restrict or eliminate the spontaneous breaking of global symmetries due to decoherence from gravitational interactions with quantum fluctuations, it is difficult to investigate this phenomenon empirically. We estimate the constraints on global symmetry breaking in quantum gravity by comparing our predictions with recent measurements of cosmic birefringence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these constraints can be improved to $\lesssim 10^{-2}$ in both the Planck and GUT scenarios with the implementation of future birefringence observations. This approach offers a promising pathway to explore the breaking of global symmetries in quantum gravity and to probe the energy scales of the intermediate stage between the electroweak and Planck/GUT scales, a region otherwise inaccessible to experimental study. Finally, this proposal may contribute to the broader effort of formulating testable predictions for quantum gravity. Conversely, if symmetries are broken at the Planck/GUT scale, this would support the existence of black holes in the early universe, which would scatter CMB photons and contribute to the vanishing of linear polarization in the CMB. Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) represents a significant category of Deep Learning that leverages knowledge transferability. Its effectiveness largely relies on two established beliefs: first, that knowledge transferability exists and is deeply rooted; and second, that this transferability is source-task specific, meaning pre-trained knowledge from a source task remains reusable in downstream applications involving the same input space. This study critically re-examines both of these widely accepted consensus points. To achieve this, we introduce a novel framework termed "Counterfactual Deep Transfer Learning" (CDTL), which explicitly models transferability as a function of distributional similarity and mutual information. Through a thorough theoretical analysis and rigorous empirical validation, we demonstrate that counterfactual knowledge can indeed be transferred across diverse inputs and tasks. We validate CDTL on image classification and Natural Language Processing tasks, supporting all claims with comprehensive experimental evidence. We hope this work inspires researchers to further explore the fundamental mechanisms underlying transferability in deep learning. The code and data are available at: https://github.com/Cheng-Zhang2020/Counterfactual-Deep-Transfer-Learning. The spread of information within complex networks has been examined through the lens of the contagion dynamics framework. While most existing research has focused on the equilibrium between diffusing and lost data, our investigation highlights the significance of the diffusion velocity in assessing the efficacy of information dissemination. Employing a network model comprising communities connected via a sparse inter-community backbone, our studies utilize an Erdős–Rényi graph as the internal structure for each community. We demonstrate that modular structure significantly alters information flow in a manner contingent upon the relationship between the inter-community connection backbone and the contagion's intrinsic diffusion rate. Specifically, we find that the velocity of information diffusion is substantially governed by the connectivity of this backbone, which acts as a critical determinant in distribution speed. These findings offer fresh perspectives on how network topology influences the efficiency of information diffusion. Additionally, our research underscores the necessity of addressing both equilibrium states and dynamic processes when planning information delivery across complex networks. Finally, these conclusions may have broader applications beyond data diffusion, potentially extending to other systems exhibiting self-organized behavior in complex networks. These outcomes were achieved through straightforward analytical and numerical methods, which also facilitate comparisons with prior research on equilibrium states. Notably, our approach avoids reliance on mean-field approximations, as it accommodates both mean-field and inhomogeneous scenarios. Consequently, the methodology employed herein is broadly applicable to various information-driven diffusion problems. The computational code utilized in this study is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/inter-community-information-flow. Furthermore, to support future investigations into this and related topics, we have developed a Python package named `pyflow`, available at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan1992/pyflow. This package enables the simulation of diffusion processes on complex networks, including community detection, using a variety of dynamics and topologies. It also allows for the analysis of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium states, alongside features for calculating network modularity. Pyflow is designed to be extensible, enabling users to easily add their own variants of dynamics and community detection algorithms. We anticipate that these tools will be valuable for researchers engaged in diverse diffusion problems on complex networks. Additionally, Pyflow incorporates a functionality to visualize dynamic processes, which can assist in qualitatively assessing outcomes and offering intuitive insights for users.
