The regular perturbation model is recognized as a practical method for calculating the signal-to-noise ratio in unamplified satellite links by accounting for space loss, Earth curvature, curvature gain, atmospheric attenuation, reflection loss, and antenna pointing loss. This paper demonstrates how to evaluate satellite link performance by integrating regular perturbation equations with a time-binned discrete-time channel model. Additionally, we derive a closed-form expression for the probability density function of the perturbation model and generate plots showing the statistical deviations of this approximation relative to the exact solution. Our findings are supported by simulations that validate our accuracy analysis. Ultimately, these results provide designers with discrete-time equations for C-band and Ku-band downlinks, enabling them to estimate performance limitations across various rain rates, frequencies, and link parameters. Furthermore, our analysis offers an efficient algorithm for computing C/N0 that requires minimal processing time and memory. The proposed solution for generating software is available on GitHub.

As the most widely used operating system globally, Android has become a primary target for malicious software, prompting the Android security community to develop various detection tools. Recently, machine learning-based approaches utilizing the problem-space have emerged as the leading strategy for these tools, utilizing the launch history of Android applications to predict malware. However, this survey reveals that numerous studies have previously demonstrated the easily exploitable vulnerabilities in the problem-space within the Android OS. Leveraging this knowledge, adversaries can design malware capable of bypassing problem-space-based security solutions. This paper reviews existing research on problem-space evasion attacks in Android, providing a classification and summary of these studies to facilitate a deeper understanding of the current state-of-the-art in Android malware evasion. Furthermore, we identify potential future research directions to assist in developing more robust detection mechanisms. Finally, we outline how these findings can inform risk assessment and guide efforts to strengthen Android's problem-space against such threats.

Building scalable, distributed systems is difficult and often demands constant, intricate adjustments to configuration parameters. Typically, these parameters alter the system's resource footprint, necessitating adjustments to the count of instantiated system components. Currently, executing such adaptations in production environments is manual, time-intensive, and demands specialized knowledge. This work introduces Ozy, a general-purpose orchestration container designed to automate these operations. Ozy accepts a model defining the desired resource distribution and automatically adjusts the number of system components to satisfy these targets. The feasibility and efficacy of this approach are demonstrated through three examples ranging from simple to complex: (1) configuring a distributed task executor, (2) managing distributed task accelerators, and (3) managing distributed machine learning training accelerators. To our knowledge, this represents the first effort to apply orchestration container technology to distributed systems. Our empirical findings indicate that Ozy can predict resource requirements with high accuracy, thereby enabling correct configurations for distributed systems. Furthermore, we show that Ozy can facilitate useful adaptations in live production settings with guaranteed resource safety. Specifically, correct adaptations are achieved in 99.9% to 100% of live production runs, depending on the example, with an average deviation from target resource usage of only 0.05% to 1.0%. Additionally, Ozy enables adaptations to be completed in 10 seconds or less, depending on the example, which is 1,000 to 10,000 times faster than manual methods. These capabilities allow for the automatic execution of useful adaptations in production environments, a use case not addressed by prior orchestration containers. Overall, this paper establishes a foundation for the automatic operation of distributed systems. The code and containers required to replicate this work are publicly accessible. To our knowledge, this represents the first open-source implementation of an orchestration container for distributed systems. The code and containers are available at https://github.com/emory-research-corp/ozy. The project is supported by an open invitation to contribute at https://gitlab.com/emory-research-corp/ozy/-/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md. Access to the orchestration container technology itself is also available at https://gitlab.com/emory-research-corp/ozy/-/packages/generic/container/ozy/1.0.0. Questions can be directed to https://gitlab.com/emory-research-corp/ozy/-/issues. Contributions are welcome at https://gitlab.com/emory-research-corp/ozy

Through analysis of density density correlation functions, we identify a reentrant topological phase exhibiting 5-fold degenerate edge states, supported by the calculation of the bulk topological invariant, the Zak phase. Furthermore, we demonstrate the emergence of 5-fold degenerate zero-bias modes at the sample edges. The moderate landau level mixing strength, which allows for the construction of Wannier functions, facilitates a more straightforward numerical investigation of the system's topological properties. In certain scenarios, this mismatch could lead to discrepancies in the calculation of the gravitational wave signal, although the overall impact remains negligible. Consequently, the current LIGO-Virgo constraints on primordial black holes as a component of dark matter are essentially unaffected. However, we demonstrate that evaporation reduces the cross section for black hole formation by at least ten orders of magnitude. This significantly lowers the density of black holes within the dark matter halo, implying that the effects of a black hole on spacetime geometry are minimal, thereby validating our method for calculating its effects. Furthermore, we show that the deviations of the Thakurta metric from the Schwarzschild solution are insufficient to produce observable effects on gravitational waves, even in the most extreme cases. Therefore, we conclude that cosmological black holes within dark matter halos are not well-described by the Thakurta metric from a physical perspective, despite recent claims to the contrary. Finally, we note that the formation of dark matter black holes is heavily suppressed due to evaporation, a factor that was overlooked in previous studies. This suppression suggests that primordial black holes may constitute only a small fraction of the dark matter that the LIGO-Virgo collaboration attributes to them. We also address the conceptual issues surrounding the derivation of the Thakurta metric and the validity of the inverse square law of gravity within it. Core accretion models struggle to explain the formation of Jupiter-mass planets within typical protoplanetary disk lifetimes of approximately 1 to 3 million years. However, recent findings indicate that growing planetesimals to planetary masses is significantly accelerated when they encounter gas-rich pebble streams. This paper investigates how this pebble accretion mechanism is influenced by local gas density variations caused by pressure bumps. We identify a "window of pebble accretion," meaning accelerated core formation occurs only when the planet passes through dense pebble streams rather than sparse ones. Furthermore, the intensity of icy pebble accretion peaks when the stream's density contrast matches the disk's turbulent density contrast, a condition that likely explains the observed timing of gas giants' formation. Our results suggest that Jupiter may have formed within a few million years in a pressure bump where turbulent density contrasts aligned with that of the pressure bump. Finally, our framework predicts the core mass of a super-Jovian planet as a function of both stream density contrast and turbulence strength, a relationship that can be tested using the JWST. Future observations of young, nearby T Tauri stars will be able to constrain pebble stream properties and their influence on planet formation. Consequently, our study underscores the critical role of local gas density perturbations in facilitating planet formation via pebble accretion. (Abridged)

Overparameterized models contain more parameters than degrees of freedom, leading to infinitely many solutions that minimize the training error. In deep learning, despite having access to these solutions, practitioners typically employ specific ones during testing. This behavior contrasts sharply with traditional statistically efficient methods, where the minimum training error solutions are used for inference. This discrepancy highlights a fundamental distinction between the computational environments of classical and modern machine learning. This thesis formally investigates the origins of this contrast and demonstrates that the shift toward computationally feasible inference over statistically optimal inference is driven by the need to minimize communication costs. The study reveals a direct link between communication constraints and the selection of feasible inference methods. Finally, the work examines the resulting differences between the two approaches. Although feasible methods exhibit sub-optimal statistical properties, they enable inference that is strictly causal, whereas minimum training error methods can yield non-causal predictions. Overall, this research offers a framework for understanding how communication limitations can dictate whether minimum training error solutions or computationally feasible ones should be employed in inference. This research investigates a multi-modal pretraining approach for e-commerce scenarios, emphasizing the significance of domain-specific knowledge within custom modules. A primary challenge in e-commerce multi-modal deep learning lies in data imbalance, characterized by a vast quantity of easy negative samples and scarcity of both hard negative and positive samples. This method employs a multi-source multi-head self-attention mechanism to fuse knowledge-rich negative samples, utilizing them to learn robust multi-modal representations through negative sample mining. These fused representations subsequently guide the domain-customized end-to-end model during training. Experimental results on an e-commerce dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms single-modal baselines and improves upon existing multi-modal methods by 1.4% in Average Precision. Text classification stands as a core task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), where the quality of an algorithm is primarily judged by its ability to comprehend the semantics of written or spoken text. However, processing extensive datasets independently often yields models with suboptimal performance. To address this, this paper introduces a new interaction-based recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture designed to jointly learn interaction patterns and encode interaction semantics within natural language. The study demonstrates that incorporating external general knowledge, specifically general semantics, into the training process of a dataset-specific model significantly enhances the model's performance on large-scale datasets. Experimental results on the SemEval-2007 task confirm the efficacy of the proposed interaction-based RNN framework, and the method is also applied to the Amazon Electronics review dataset for comparative analysis. Ultimately, the results indicate that the interaction-based RNN model, when augmented with external general semantics knowledge, substantially improves classification performance on both datasets. Furthermore, performance metrics such as precision, recall, and F-measure are analyzed in relation to the count of interaction terms. Finally, the paper outlines future research directions regarding the extension of interaction terms to higher orders and the investigation of their relationships with natural language phenomena like anaphora, cohesion, and coherence. Ultimately, enriching models with external general knowledge represents a promising avenue for advancing NLP research. Keywords: Interaction term, General knowledge, General semantics, Interaction pattern, Interaction term count, External knowledge, Anaphora, Cohesion, Coherence.

In correlated metals, strong electron-electron interactions can substantially enhance spin-orbit coupling (SOC), a phenomenon known as interaction renormalization. We demonstrate that this mechanism can be even more powerful in the presence of ferromagnetic order, a scenario termed interaction-amplified SOC. A straightforward illustration is a model where interaction-amplaged SOC generates a novel spin gap within half-filling exchange bosons. This discovery opens a promising avenue for investigating interaction-amplified topological phenomena, including interaction amplified superconductivity and interaction amplified topological order. Furthermore, we show that interaction-amplified superconductivity can occur without time-reversal symmetry breaking, a finding that contrasts with recent theoretical predictions. Finally, we explore the experimental implications of these findings, with specific focus on the oxide manganite La1-xSrxMnO3. This work establishes a foundation for investigating interaction-amplified topological effects using existing experimental platforms. Additionally, the proposed interaction-amplified superconductivity can be investigated via newly developed thin-film samples that break time-reversal symmetry through ferromagnetic order induced by an external magnetic field. The required Sr-doped samples are already available in various forms, such as thin films and nanostructures. We introduce a straightforward framework for producing metastable conformally coupled dark matter through collisions between heavy, metastable states. This general approach is subsequently applied to the supersymmetric dark photon scenario. In this context, the Standard Model, alongside heavy dark photon and hidden sector photon states, resides in a hidden sector that interacts with the Standard Model via kinetically mixed dark photons. These hidden sectors are engineered to be nearly conformally isolated from the standard QCD vacuum by introducing an exponential suppression factor. Consequently, the dark photon acquires a suppressed mass and serves as dark matter within a heavy metastable state. The mass of this metastable state is generated through QCD instanton effects. The abundance of dark matter is established by these heavy states decaying into dark photons during the radiation-dominated era. We derive the resulting mass of the dark photon and the lifetime of the metastable states as a function of the hidden sector's conformal anomaly. Furthermore, we examine the constraints on this framework imposed by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, Dark Matter searches, and LHC data. This framework predicts a dark matter lifetime that approaches, though does not reach strictly infinite, thereby distinguishing it from absolutely stable dark matter. The model offers a pathway to explain a specific feature observed in LHC searches for dark photons. Additionally, the framework is applicable to the QCD axion and other well-motivated dark matter candidates. The consistency of the framework is supported by the observation that the lifetime of these metastable states exceeds the age of the Universe, ensuring that decay into dark photons is complete. The analysis also explores the potential for decays into other hidden states and examines the implications of this framework for the Hubble Tension. Finally, we demonstrate that the framework can simultaneously account for the excess in BBN-derived helium-4 abundance reported by Paul et al. and the non-detection of dark photons at the LHC. This suggests that the parameter space where the lifetime exceeds the age of the Universe is not entirely excluded by experimental data. Finally, we explore the possibility of future verification of this framework through LHC experiments. Specifically, we predict that the mass of these metastable states should be approximately $10^{-3}$ times that of the top quark, with a decay width consistent with experimental upper limits. The lifetime of these states is predicted to be roughly $10^{17}$ seconds, and the fraction of dark matter constituted by these remnants is estimated to be around $10^{-2}$. Accurately forecasting the performance of AI-driven medical software when facing distribution shifts is vital for determining their real-world applicability and supporting regulatory decisions. This study introduces a framework for predicting model testing results that occur outside the training domain, specifically for binary classification tasks. Leveraging a validation set, we demonstrate how to estimate prediction probabilities and subsequently calculate the expected accuracy and false positive rate for any threshold, utilizing a test performance function grounded in type-I error control. Our approach relies on conformal prediction and nonparametric density estimation, ensuring distribution-free validity without requiring specific loss function assumptions. We highlight the benefits of this method for medical imaging applications by presenting a segmentation model trained and evaluated on histopathology data, demonstrating its capacity to accurately predict software performance under domain shift. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/ashley-chen-chen/estimating_test_performance. Furthermore, we offer an R package named MedicalAI, which includes medical imaging datasets, machine learning models, and the functions necessary to quantify performance degradation due to distribution shifts. The package can be installed via the command install.packages("MedicalAI", repos = "https://mcr.github.io") and is available at https://mcr.github.io/. Enhanced sampling via supercoiling release is a well-established method for investigating DNA conformations, yet it often yields results with insufficient sequence diversity. We present Rigid Base Biasing (RBB), a rigid-body potential applied to individual DNA base pairs that restricts their sampling to specific regions of orientation space. RBB constraints are defined by target values and a biasing strength, with targets ideally matching the unstrained conformation. We demonstrate that RBB improves sampling efficiency across various scenarios, including differentiating between AT- and GC-rich sequences, targeting equilibrium looping, and refining the generation of plectonemic-like structures. Furthermore, RBB proves effective when combined with other enhanced sampling techniques, such as metadynamics and umbrella sampling, by focusing on specific conformational degrees of freedom. Finally, we illustrate how this approach enables local reconstruction of the free energy landscape of DNA, specifically depicting the potential of mean force between base pairs during looping. RBB is readily implementable in standard enhanced sampling frameworks and is accessible as an open-source plugin for the GROMACS molecular dynamics package. By restricting sampling to target values, RBB offers a straightforward method to constrain enhanced sampling to biologically relevant conformational spaces. This facilitates a quantitative analysis of the free energy landscape of DNA, thereby elucidating the free energy costs associated with genomic looping and the resulting sequence dependence. Such insights address a fundamental question in the field: which conformational states are accessible, and which are not? This capability represents a significant advancement in sampling strategies, allowing researchers to address questions that were previously intractable. Ultimately, RBB expands the range of questions that enhanced sampling can address regarding the free energy landscape of DNA. Duraflou and Salo introduced the arithmetic number system (ANS), which maps the interval $(0,1)$ to non-negative integers in an optimal asymptotic sense. This mapping is nearly reversible, yielding an optimal bijection between the product set $\{0,\dots, N\}^2$ and the integers up to $N^2 + O(N)$. This paper presents the first extensive experimental evaluation comparing the ANSI encoder's performance against the Huffman encoder. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, the ANSI encoder operates significantly slower than the Huffman encoder, even when utilizing highly optimized C code for ANSI construction. Conversely, highly optimized Hufman encoder libraries exist. Our analysis indicates that the time complexity of the ANSI encoder is $O(m)$, where $m$ represents the bit length of the integer to be encoded, and the average time per symbol is approximately $O(\log m)$. In contrast, the Huffman encoder achieves an average complexity of $O(\log m)$ per symbol. These findings suggest that the current implementation of ANSI is inefficient and that future improvements are necessary to improve the performance of algorithms relying on ANSI. To address this, we propose an efficient algorithm for ANSI encoding, demonstrating that our method constructs the transform's right half in $O(n \log n)$ time for a probability vector of size $n$, representing a substantial speedup over the $O(n^2)$ time required by the current ANSI implementation. Furthermore, our implementation features constant-time arithmetic operations and ensures that both encoding and decoding run in amortized $O(1)$ time per symbol. The resulting ANSI encoder is approximately 10 times faster than the original implementation. In comparison to Huffman coding libraries, however, it remains 10 to 100 times slower. We attribute this slowness to the high cost of arithmetic operations within ANSI, which are necessary to maintain the algorithm's simplicity. To resolve this, we explore applying approximate computing techniques to ANSI to accelerate its execution. By leveraging the fact that ANSI is primarily used for lossless compression, we demonstrate that it can be adapted for near-lossless compression. Specifically, we prove that ANSI can compress images with zero perceptible quality loss, achieving this at the bit rate of Huffman coding with only a 0.000000001% error rate. The dielectric characteristics of micro-porous media are of significant interest for non-destructive material assessment. In this study, we simulated a representative volume element (RVE) of cement-based systems, specifically examining the dielectric response of the pore solution. By integrating the finite volume method with the Poisson-Boltzmann equation to account for high ionic concentrations, we successfully replicated the dielectric dispersion observed in concrete. Our analysis revealed that within the pore solution, ionic concentration rises sharply near solid surfaces due to ion adsorption, while it diminishes as the distance from the surface increases. Furthermore, we determined that increasing the solid volume fraction leads to dielectric relaxation, a phenomenon driven by the interfacial polarization between the solid matrix and pore solution. These findings have practical applications, including detecting micro-cracks in cement-based structures and establishing the optimal frequency for acoustic emission testing to identify damage. Additionally, our methodology can be extended to model other porous materials where the ionic concentration in the pore fluid is sufficiently high.

The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable tool for cosmological research, yet fully harnessing its potential requires developing highly efficient and precise estimators for cosmological parameters. This study introduces a new method for measuring the 3D power spectrum of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest using Gaussian process regression to model the continuous field within a Lagrangian framework. Unlike small-scale power, which is sensitive to the thermal state of the intergalactic medium (IGM), the large-scale power is primarily determined by the underlying dark matter distribution and is largely unaffected by IGM physics or the treatment of small scales. By combining these two distinct components, we achieve more robust measurements of IGM properties, specifically the He II fraction ($f_{\rm HeII}$) and the IGM temperature as a function of redshift, $T\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{dz'}\right)$. We demonstrate that the 3D correlation analysis presented here offers significant improvements in accuracy compared to 1D redshift-space slices, achieving an uncertainty of approximately 10% for $f_{\rm HeII}$ and 20% for the temperature reconstruction using a single $C=100\,h^{-3}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^3$ cubic volume. Furthermore, we show that the accuracy of the He II fraction scales inversely with the volume of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest sample, following a $V^{-1/4}$ relationship. These findings indicate that the proposed method will enable precise cosmological measurements from upcoming large-scale spectroscopic surveys, such as DESI, as well as from high-resolution simulations and targeted observations, exemplified by the upcoming COSMOS Deep Extragalactic Spectroscopy (Cosmedes) project. The code used in this analysis is publicly accessible. [abridged]

An experimental initiative at the Fermilab A0 Photoinjector has successfully demonstrated a novel technique for swapping the horizontal and longitudinal emittances of a particle beam. This achievement utilized a newly installed beamline featuring a TM110 deflecting mode cavity situated between two horizontal dispersive elements. With the transverse-to-longitudinal mode conversion cavity operating, and given specific betatron and radio-frequency (RF) phase conditions at the upstream dispersive element, the remaining beamline elements funneled the modified beam into the longitudinal phase space. The swap was accomplished at a single point in the beamline by accelerating bunched beams with reduced longitudinal emittance to higher energies. This methodology offers a streamlined approach for achieving transverse-to-longitudinal emittance transfer at the injection point of an accelerator, enabling a strategic realignment of the beam's phase-space envelope. Such an innovation holds promise for optimizing the initial beam quality of future high-energy particle colliders. A detailed description of this experiment will be published in Phys. Rev. Accel. Predicting trajectories over extended time horizons is difficult due to long-term dependencies, diverse user behaviors, and the need for accurate headway and lateral spacing. To address this, the paper introduces CSR, a method that incorporates a Socially-aware Rethinking (SAR) module based on a Sliding CVAE. The SAR module sequentially predicts headway and lateral spacing, accounting for the driver's cognitive decision-making process. A Sliding CVAE is trained to predict the distribution of the next state by combining the output from the previous time step with SAR predictions, effectively inverting the chain rule. Additionally, the model is enhanced with an attention mechanism to capture long-term dependencies. Experimental results demonstrate that CSR outperforms state-of-the-art models in prediction accuracy and realism for various driving scenarios. Furthermore, the approach shows improved robustness when dealing with varying initial states and different driving behaviors. Finally, the method is applied in a real-time path planning system, successfully generating smooth and socially compliant trajectories. Over the last thirty years, numerous theoretical metrics have been developed to characterize the complexity of information-theoretic systems. This study examines the correlation between the interpretability of various measures—such as the Fisher-Hopkins complexity ($C_{FH}$), Fisher information ($F$), and Shannon entropy ($H$)—and the simulation outcomes of Boltzmann machines. To facilitate a direct comparison among these metrics, we introduce a normalized variant termed $C_{FH}^*$, which is derived by normalizing $C_{FH}$ with the product of the means of its constituent components, $F$ and $H$. Through the analysis of Boltzmann machine simulations across varying $K$ values, we evaluate the efficacy of these complexity measures in forecasting the behavior of the simulated systems. Our findings indicate that the proposed $C_{FH}^*$ metric is a more robust indicator of the complexity within simulated systems compared to the unnormalized $C_{FH}$ and $F$ and the traditional $H$. Additionally, we have made our simulation code accessible for replicating these results at our GitHub repository: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/Comparing-ITM. This paper introduces preliminary research on a human-swell interaction system designed to facilitate natural, intuitive, and interpretable communication on demand between human operators and decentralized swarms of autonomous robots. By integrating sequential hand gesture recognition to establish a unified interaction language, operators can command robot subgroups to execute sequence-based missions, including formation flying and spatial distribution. This approach eliminates the need for continuous interaction, thereby reducing computational overhead and energy consumption within the swarm. The study validates the efficacy of this language through a proof-of-concept demonstration, which also explores advancements in gesture recognition capabilities and inter-robot coordination. The proposed methodology holds significant promise for enhancing interaction protocols across various domains, such as search and rescue operations and agricultural support. The resulting software is released under a permissive license to encourage further development and experimentation by the research community. This work is published in conjunction with ICRA 2022. Video demonstrations are available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=41111111111 and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22222222222. Corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/sergio-fernandez/MyGestureRecognition and https://github.com/sergio-fernandez/MyMultiRobotControlCode. The study aims to assess the effectiveness of neural network architectures, specifically CNN, RNN, and GNN, combined with their attention mechanisms, within a multi-model ensemble, or "committee," framework, using both original and augmented cell images. We utilized the only publicly accessible dataset dedicated to classifying ten cell types, including various stages of cell division and apoptosis. To enhance image quality and increase the sample size for rare cell classes, we applied eight image augmentation techniques. The primary goal was to evaluate whether neural models could surpass human performance in image-based blood cell classification. Our ensemble strategy involved training eight different neural networks, each processing the input data in a unique manner. The secondary objective was to demonstrate that this committee approach yields more consistent results than a single model. Finally, we examined the models' ability to identify rare and ambiguous cell types. The experimental findings indicate that the proposed ensemble method surpasses human performance by 10% and produces more consistent classifications regarding rare and ambiguous cell types compared to human experts. Additionally, we demonstrated that training on a larger dataset significantly improves model performance. Furthermore, our high-resolution images and deep learning models successfully detected rare and ambiguous cell types that were missed by human pathologists. However, the models occasionally misclassified rare cell types that were correctly identified by humans. To address this, we trained a new ensemble incorporating human classifiers, which further enhanced the overall performance of the proposed system. The proposed ensemble model outperforms state-of-the-art solutions by 10% and ensures more consistent classification results. Additionally, we developed a new tool to assist pathologists in handling ambiguous cases, which has shown promising performance. The tool's classification results are comparable to human performance, and its consistency exceeds that of human experts. Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols have become essential tools for achieving rapid and precise quantum evolution across diverse physical systems. However, implementing these schemes in realistic scenarios often requires controlling an infinite number of degrees of freedom, which limits their practical application. This study demonstrates that, specifically for preparing the ground state of the Hubbard model, one can utilize a finite set of auxiliary CD fields derived from a simplified adiabatic gauge potential (AGP). We find that even a single field successfully eliminates adiabaticity, significantly speeding up diagonalization while keeping the final energy error negligible. Furthermore, we show that the proposed CD protocol is compatible with variational quantum algorithms, marking a crucial step toward implementing these methods on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Our findings hold significant promise for advancing the development of efficient quantum algorithms capable of ground-state preparation across a wide range of other strongly correlated systems. Finally, our proposed CD protocol is expected to be universally applicable to other one-dimensional local systems, particularly those lacking internal degrees of freedom. Grayscale images are essential for numerous image processing tasks, including tone mapping, global or local contrast adjustment, and halftoning. However, converting high-quality RGB images to grayscale is more complex than simply applying a weighted linear combination of RGB channels, as colorimetrically accurate tonal mapping is difficult to achieve. This paper introduces a high-speed color-temperature-based approach for color-to-gray conversion. We present a new formula for calculating color temperature and use it to map the color spectrum of an image to a gamma-corrected one-dimensional tone curve. This mapping effectively handles not only low and saturated colors but also dark and desaturated hues. The proposed method is highly efficient and can be executed in two high-speed colorimetric operations: (1) a vectorized per-pixel calculation and (2) a separable convolution-based calculation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces visually superior color maps compared to existing techniques and reduces computational time by several orders of magnitude. The proposed algorithm is now widely used in modern tone-mapping tools, such as our free software RadianceVision, to provide users with high-quality color-to-gray conversion capabilities. The source code is publicly available at http://sourceforge.net/projects/radiancevision/. Furthermore, users can access the free software directly from http://sourceforge.net/forums/?forum=content.name2.radiancevision#radiancevision or purchase the commercial version from http://sourceforge.net/forums/?forum=content.name2.radiancevision#radiancevision. Additional details regarding the method can be found in our book, "Radiance Vision: Tone Mapping, Local Contrast Enhancement, and Halftoning," published by Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg in 2011, with the manuscript accessible at http://sourceforge.net/forums/?forum=content.name2.radiancevision#radiancevision. Finally, users may explore our free or commercial solutions via our website, http://sourceforge.net/forums/?forum=content.name2.radiancevision#radiancevision. Keywords: Color-to-gray conversion, Halftoning, Global/local contrast enhancement, Radiance Vision, Tone mapping. Citation: Y. Wang, C. Chen, and P. This paper introduces a formula that expresses differentiable complex-valued functions as a sum of exponentials, including an explicit remainder term. This approach allows for the association of an infinite series with $C^\infty$ functions, which converges to the original function under specific conditions regarding the remainder. These findings are subsequently applied to compute various infinite series containing Stirling numbers. Additionally, the study examines the convergence and divergence of this exponential series across the complex plane for several standard functions. The authors further calculate the "Taylor radius" and "Hadamard circle" for a broad class of functions. Finally, the text presents numerous examples of exponential Taylor series for familiar functions, many of which admit simple closed forms. The presentation includes historical context and concludes with open problems and challenges. The challenges section begins with finding the Taylor series and identifying the Taylor radius and Hadamard circle for the $\Gamma$ function and its logarithm. It then poses a problem concerning the pointwise convergence of the exponential Taylor series for the $n$-th derivative of a $C^\infty$ function, followed by a problem on the summation of a double sum involving Stirling numbers of the first kind. The chapter ends with determining the Taylor radius for the function $f(x)=\sqrt{\sin x}$. Keywords: Stirling numbers, permutations, Stirling transform, Taylor series, Hadamard circle. Let $S$ denote an orientable CAT($k$) sphere, where $k$ is a constant. This paper establishes that for any harmonic branched covering $f: S \to S$ of degree $n \ge 2$, the mapping $df: TS \to TS$ constitutes a non-zero eigenfunction of the Laplacian $\Delta$ on $S$ with a specific, calculable eigenvalue. Consequently, if $S$ is equipped with a Riemannian metric possessing non-negative curvature, such a map $f$ cannot exist; similarly, if the curvature is non-positive, $f$ exists only when it functions as the $n$-th power of a rotation about a fixed point. These findings offer partial progress toward resolving a longstanding conjecture by Y. B. Shulman regarding the uniformization of CAT($k$) spheres. As a corollary, we demonstrate that any harmonic function $h: S \to \mathbb{R}$ is constant, thereby extending Lichnerowick's theorem regarding the uniformization of Riemannian manifolds homeomorphic to a sphere. Furthermore, we generalize Poincaré's uniformization theorem for surfaces to the setting of CAT($k$) surfaces. Finally, we formulate and partially address a conjecture linking the uniformization of a CAT($k$) sphere $S$ to the uniformization of a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ that is homotopy equivalent to $S$. Specifically, if $S$ is uniformlyizable, then the unit sphere bundle $U_{-1}(TS)$, endowed with a suitable canonical metric, is diffeomorphic to $U_{-1}(UM)$, the unit sphere bundle of negative vectors with respect to the 1st Wiener index for the manifold $(M,g)$. Conversely, the uniformization of $S$ follows as a direct consequence of this correspondence. The proofs rely on a novel generalization of the Bochner formula for the Laplacian of the second fundamental form of a map between Riemannian manifolds. Additionally, we provide a new proof of Poincaré's theorem and characterize the Bochner tensor using the Laplacian and the stress-energy-momentum tensor of a map. The approach also recovers certain results by J. Li and Y. B. Shulman concerning the uniformization of metric graphs and catonoids. We present a photon-plasma interaction method designed to generate intense laser fields with broad bandwidths. This approach offers on-demand tunability across the infrared, visible, and violet spectra, along with high conversion efficiency. Utilizing a solid-density plasma as an intermediate stage enables the creation of photon-photon scattering events within the near-infrared range. This technique is particularly promising for driving high-harmonic generation in multi-electron atoms, thereby expanding capabilities in non-linear laser-platon physics, attocycle science, and photon-photon technology. Additionally, it serves to validate fundamental concepts in quantum electrodynamics. By providing a robust platform for future experiments involving photon-photon scattering, relativistic laser-plasma interactions, and attosecond phenomena, it may help answer pivotal questions in quantum physics. Furthermore, the method can be integrated with advanced light sources, such as free-electron lasers, to facilitate the study of non-linear light-matter interactions. This could lead to the creation of novel light sources, including non-coherent photon-photon scattering modules, and support fundamental research in quantum electrodynamics. This study investigates how the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-violating soft-breaking parameter $m_{12}$ in the Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) influences the model's sensitivity to the data exclusions of the CMS search for a Higgs-like particle, specifically the 2012 analysis by ATLAS covering the 95% CL. Our results indicate that the constraints imposed on $m_{12}$ by the non-observation of a Higgs-like particle by CMS are highly model-dependent and can be entirely absent in certain 2HDM variants. Furthermore, we demonstrate the absence of such constraints in various 2HDM scenarios using Monte Carlo simulations. These findings are particularly relevant for models featuring light CP-even or CP-odd states, such as the 2HDM with a Tunable Light Higgs (2TLL), which offer a promising framework for interpreting the absence of signals in Higgs searches conducted prior to 2012. This research is especially pertinent to 2HDM with Extended Scalar Spectrum (2HESM) models, which extend the scalar sector of the 2HDM with an additional scalar field. Additionally, we present constraints derived from LHC Run 1 data for specific 2HDM models characterized by a non-zero $m_{12}$ value. These constraints were generated within a unified framework that incorporates both theoretical and experimental considerations, thereby facilitating more comprehensive and consistent comparisons between different 2HDM models. Finally, we compare the sensitivity of various 2HDM models to the CMS exclusivity regarding Higgs-like particles in the presence of an $m_{12}$ value, revealing significant differences among the models. This outcome underscores the necessity of adopting a more comprehensive approach when analyzing 2HDM extensions of the Standard Model. This analysis should integrate both theoretical and experimental factors, such as the specific decay channels of the additional scalar states and the precise mass ranges they occupy. By incorporating such considerations, we can achieve a more accurate and meaningful assessment of the 2HDM model's ability to explain the absence of Higgs-like particle signals reported by CMS. Ultimately, our findings provide a valuable tool for future studies aimed at elucidating the nature of the Higgs boson discovered by CMS in 2012. This understanding is essential for elucidating the complex structure of the scalar sector in the 2HDM and its potential to address various phenomena beyond the Standard Model. This paper presents the first comprehensive investigation of the $t \bar t \phi$ production mode for exploring the light mass range of a new scalar particle ($\phi$) that couples to top quarks. By examining a target luminosity of 300 $fb^{-1}$ at the LHC with $\sqrt{s} = 13.6$ TeV, we examine various production channels to determine optimal search strategies. Our results indicate that for masses below 10 GeV, the most sensitive channels are the fully-muonic and semi-leptonic top topologies, which can achieve inclusive branching ratio limits of approximately $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-3}$, respectively. Additionally, we address the necessity of including these processes in interpreting the recent CMS excess observed in the top channel. Furthermore, our analysis of heavier mass regions yields scalar scalar top Yukawa coupling limits consistent with those from scalar searches at lower masses. Finally, we demonstrate that a dedicated flavor factory experiment possessing $10^7$ $t\bar t$ events could reach scalar branching ratio limits of roughly $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-4}$ for the two primary production modes, respectively. This potential experiment offers complementary sensitivity to both the LHC and future hadron flavor facilities. Overall, the $t \bar t \phi$ production mode represents a vital channel for exploring new physics at the top quark Yukawa coupling. This is particularly relevant for masses below 10 GeV, where the long lifetime of the $\phi$ particle allows for distinctive signatures that can be effectively isolated from the complex LHC background environment. Such searches are crucial for investigating potential new physics phenomena, including new flavor dynamics, dark matter, and neutrino mass mechanisms. Future studies of this process will be essential for uncovering new physics. Furthermore, the $t \bar t \phi$ mode will be highly relevant for analyzing data from a future flavor factory, which we argue should be prioritized in the coming decade. We also explore the potential of such a facility to search for heavier scalar particles, a region that remains poorly explored at the LHC. We conclude that the $t \bar t \phi$ search mode is one of the most promising avenues for discovering new physics. Finally, we argue that investing in a future flavor factory capable of producing $10^7$ top events is a strategic priority for advancing our understanding of fundamental physics. Natural language parsing is essential for numerous downstream NLP applications, yet manual annotation is labor-intensive and costly. While neural parsing models have been widely developed, achieving accurate syntax trees remains difficult due to the scarcity of high-quality trees in training datasets. This paper investigates unsupervised and few-shot parsing using pretrained language models. We introduce Tree of Fields (ToFields), a novel architecture for unsupervised and few-shot syntax tree induction rooted in the fields formalism. Tree of Fields comprises three components: a language model, an expectations network, and a tree expectations solver. The tree expectations solver, derived from the expectation-maximization algorithm, operates outside the neural network to enable few-shot learning, while the expectations network is designed to leverage pretrained language models. Experimental results on the Penn Treebank demonstrate that Tree of Fields outperforms strong baselines in both unsupervised and few-shot settings, achieving an F1 score comparable to supervised parsers. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhujingjing1994/ToFields. Our findings indicate that Tree of Fields L is the first architecture capable of parsing effectively without task-specific supervision. Furthermore, we hope that the open-source implementation will encourage further research into unsupervised and few-shot language parsing with pretrained models. High-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is essential for numerous applications, including speech-to-text services, virtual assistants, and medical ASR. While off-the-shelf ASR solutions are readily available, they often fall short for language-specific needs. For instance, general purpose ASR models typically perform poorly when processing German medical speech due to acoustics distinct from standard radio voices and while handling sentence-specific language required by medical dialogues. Although developing a high-quality, cost-effective, and efficient language-dedicated ASR solution presents significant challenges, it offers unique benefits. General purpose ASR usually demands a US English accent, whereas language-specific ASR can accommodate various accents and even accented non-native speakers. Furthermore, ASR models can be tailored to specific domains by incorporating training data from that particular field. This requires only a small amount of training data compared to a general model, resulting in a more efficient and specialized solution. However, this approach is costly and complex to implement unless an open-source ASR package supports the target language. Kaldi and Google Speech Recognition (GSR) are prominent open-source packages, yet both require extensive manual effort to achieve state-of-the-art results in less common languages. Kaldi, for example, necessitates detailed knowledge of language resources and their modification for use as test data. Google Speech Recognition, while easier to use, often fails to deliver accurate results for language-specific applications. To address these issues, we present SpeechDee, a German Open Source Automatic Speech Recognition package designed to provide a cost-effective and efficient solution for language-specific ASR. SpeechDee enables users to easily train their own German ASR models using either Google Speech Recognition or Kaldi. Our package provides a straightforward workflow for training, testing, and evaluating a German ASR model with minimal manual input. Additionally, we offer a user-friendly graphical user interface for non-programmers. We also include a German acoustic model trained on the MEDICO dataset, which supports various German accents and delivers promising results. This model can be easily adapted to specific domains by providing limited task-related training data. We demonstrate this capability by training a German medical ASR model using Google Speech Recognition and Kaldi as starting points. Furthermore, we provide a speech corpus extracted from the MEDICO medical dialogue corpus to assist users in training their own models. We also introduce a graphical user interface for SpeechDee, allowing users to train ASR models without programming knowledge. We analyze high-resolution spectra of 14 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus star cluster, which were previously observed as part of a large survey of 30 Doradus, utilizing the UVES spectrograph at the ESO Very Large Telescope. Our study examines the characteristics of these stars, addressing the nature of their winds, the physical conditions of their line-forming regions, and the potential presence of a $\beta$-Ceti-type companion. We identify 11 stars exhibiting winds with terminal velocities between 1000 and 2000 km/s. For the remaining three stars, we attribute their broad spectral lines to resonance lines from a nearby hot star rather than stellar winds. Using the method of minimizing the $\chi^2$ between synthetic and observed spectra, we determine the effective temperatures, temperature structures, and lower limits for the mass-to-radius ratios of these 11 wind-bearing stars. Our findings indicate effective temperatures ranging from 15,000 K to 18,000 K, with surface temperatures approximately 2000 K lower than the effective values. Additionally, the products of stellar mass and distance are estimated to be $1.1 \leqslant M_*\times d \leqslant 2.4 \times 10^{26} \; {\rm kg} \; {\rm m}$. Our results suggest that the observed winds in 30 Doradus are primarily driven by radiation pressure, with the stars' surfaces closely approximating their photospheres. Finally, we report no evidence of a $\beta$-Ceti-type companion in any of the analyzed spectra. These conclusions are supported by a comparison of the derived parameters with other studies. This work contributes to a series of 30 Doradus papers aimed at understanding the properties of massive stars. These data are also available to the public. Inverse text normalization (ITN) transforms automatic speech recognition (ASR) outputs from spoken to written format. Traditional handcrafted ITN rules are difficult to maintain and often fail to generalize across diverse spoken language variations. Conversely, inverse text normalization using natural language processing (NLP) has gained ground recently due to its ability to handle complex sentences and varyiform ITN. However, NLP-based ITN models often struggle with numbers appearing in text messages. This study investigates data augmentation techniques to enhance data-driven NLP-based ITN models through two main approaches: (1) generating numbers from natural text using back-translation and rule-based number generation, and (2) creating number-containing data via ASR and number generation. Our findings indicate that NLP-based ITN models are significantly improved by this data augmentation process. Specifically, the ITN model achieved a character-level edit distance of 0.021 on the CallHome Babel Corpus and 0.024 on the CommonCrawl Corpus. Furthermore, it demonstrated a zero-shot transfer capability to multiple text messages from various providers without retraining. Notably, the ASR+NLP combination (ZoomITN) outperformed NLP-only ITN in both trained and zero-shot scenarios for ITN. Overall, this research establishes a new framework for NLP-based ITN models that are robust to diverse number forms and ITN conditions. Additionally, the code is publicly available to facilitate a standardized evaluation baseline for the community. This work offers a promising avenue for developing universal NLP-based ITN models applicable to various domains. The project repository can be accessed at: https://github.com/taehyung-lee96/Universal-ITN. The models are also available at: https://huggingface.co/taehyung-lee96/Universal-ITN. Their success relies heavily on customizing kernel functions to adapt to specific domains. However, current approaches typically design a single, unified kernel for all layers, failing to account for the distinct characteristics of the learning problems and sub-domains encountered at each layer. Non-Hermitian systems exhibit distinctive characteristics, most notably the emergence of non-Hermitian topological phases marked by point gaps rather than the conventional band gaps found in Hermitian systems. These phases are typically investigated within noninteracting frameworks, where particle independence and the applicability of the single-particle framework remain unchallenged. This study introduces a comprehensive analytical approach to characterize the non-Hermitian point-gap topology of the one-dimensional Hubbard model, which displays a symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. Utilizing the exact analytical Green's function, we identify multiple topological phases and elucidate their transitions, offering insights into the impact of correlations on non-Hermitian topologies. Furthermore, our findings underscore the necessity of advancing beyond non-interacting models to fully comprehend the topologies of non-Hermitian systems. Additionally, we explore the possibility of observing these phases in cold-atom setups and provide detailed methods for detection. This research establishes a foundation for future investigations into the point-gap topology of correlated non-Hermitian systems. I demonstrate that, despite its inherent superdeterminism, ISET remains susceptible to Bell tests if one assumes that statistical independence between the choice variable (governing measurement angles) and the hidden variable (constraining outcomes) is conditioned upon specific values of that hidden variable. Such an assumption is incompatible with Bell tests that rely on factorization or minimality conditions rather than superdeterminism. Given that ISET is also ruled out by the Kochen-Specker theorem, my findings suggest that the only viable superdeterministic model capable of passing a Bell test without resorting to superdeterminism is one where the hidden variable uniquely determines the choice variable, rendering the choice variable non-random at the particle emission moment. This model is effectively equivalent to the deterministic hidden-variable framework (DHS), which is also defeated by the Kochen-Specker theorem. Consequently, I conclude that no superdeterministic model can pass a Bell test unless the Kochen-Specker theorem is addressed. Finally, I outline several approaches to overcoming this challenge. I name this specific model the Unbounded-set theory (UESet). Subsequently, I demonstrate that USET successfully avoids the flaws that undermine DHS and ISET. Furthermore, I establish that Bell tests cannot refute USET, whereas references to Bell tests must explicitly detail the statistical functions to be evaluated and the constraints on their arguments. This conclusion stems from the fact that Bell's Theorem necessitates superdeterminism, which, given the constraints of the Uncertainty Principle, can only be achieved by USET. In recent years, embedded systems have increasingly integrated high-performance processors to support diverse real-time applications. However, high-performance architectures often lack the cost-effectiveness required for low-priority applications, leading to the widespread adoption of mixed workloads—combinations of high- and low-criticality tasks. High-criticality applications necessitate strict real-time guarantees and robust timing analysis capabilities. To address the hardware cost constraints of low-criticality services, contemporary embedded systems frequently employ a shared processor for both high and low-criticality workloads. This paper introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor designed to manage the scheduling of such mixed-criticality embedded real-time systems. T-Visor allocates CPU time based on criticality levels while simultaneously enforcing low-critera-level timing guarantees through hardware virtualization features. To validate the effectiveness of T-Visor, we developed a testbed that simulates the management of high- and low-criticality virtual machines (VMs) on embedded test platforms. The results demonstrate that T-Visor successfully delivers low-criticality service with a performance degradation of under 10% compared to direct execution on a bare-metal system. Furthermore, we contend that T-Visor offers a more cost-effective solution for low-criticality services than relying solely on high-performance processors. Finally, we outline our future research directions, which include extending T-Visor's scheduling algorithm to handle dynamic criticality changes and investigating the development of a full-stack VM operating system. To facilitate future research, we will release the T-Visor source code. Our primary objective is to provide a more flexible and cost-efficient means of delivering low-criticality service. We anticipate that T-Visor will significantly contribute to the emerging research domain of mixed-criticality embedded systems. We also aim to inspire further investigation into advanced scheduling strategies, robust timing analysis, and secure VM infrastructure for mixed-criticality embedded environments. Chimeras, characterized by the coexistence of synchronized and desynchronized dynamics within a network of partially coupled groups of oscillators with varying heterogeneity, have been widely studied. This work presents numerical findings on similar chimera states in a model featuring two populations with distinct oscillation frequencies, where heterogeneity is uniformly distributed across each population. This methodological approach offers distinct benefits, enabling the investigation of chimeras with smoothly distributed heterogeneity. Notably, this setup allows for the existence of multiple chimeras, a phenomenon absent in models with monomodal heterogeneity distributions. Furthermore, the study examines the relationship between these multiple chimeras and the spatial distribution of heterogeneity. Finally, the work explores the application of control methods to transition the system from a chimera state to either full oscillation or synchronization. Various control strategies are evaluated, with the specific technique selected based on the target state and the chosen control parameter. Across all scenarios, a transition between the initial and final states is observed, with the system remaining in the selected state after the control is removed. These results demonstrate the potential for advanced control techniques to manipulate chimera states, a finding with significant implications for both fundamental research and practical applications. Model-based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) utilizes a world model to approximate the true environment and derive an optimal policy, typically offering superior sample efficiency compared to model-free (MFCBRL) methods. However, current MBRL approaches often fail to generalize effectively to unseen states during training, largely because their World Models (WMs) are trained on datasets heavily skewed toward states frequently encountered under the behavior policy. To address this, we introduce a method that first learns a mapping from prior states to future states, thereby expanding dataset diversity. Subsequently, the WM is trained on synthetic data generated by this state-expansion mapping to produce approximate WM parameters for use in policy search, rather than on the original, biased data. We demonstrate the application of this method within the PMP3 framework, showing that it significantly enhances performance in controlled settings. Additionally, we demonstrate that controlled generalization is achievable when the WM depends on states produced by a linear dynamical system. Nevertheless, we observe that controlling the distribution of unseen states is insufficient to induce robust generalization to highly complex, real-world environments, where performance remains comparable to the baseline. We attribute this limitation to the fact that the WM, trained on artificially expanded data, is exposed to a state distribution that is even more distorted from that of the real environment. Finally, we discuss how the concept of "controlled generalization" can be extended to arbitrary functions mapping prior states to subsequent ones. Overall, our findings highlight both the promise and the challenges of creating MFCBRL algorithms that can adapt to highly dynamic and complex environments. This work serves as an exploratory study aimed at advancing the goals of MFCBRL. Supplementary materials are available at: https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/Controlled-Generalization-MBRL. Various experiments across different fields have demonstrated dynamic patterns, yet the mechanisms generating or destroying this information remain unclear. This study employs a simple dynamical model to reveal the existence of a threshold in structural activity that separates regimes of increasing and decreasing entropy production rate (EPR). We demonstrate that specific potential configurations within an external trap cause a Bose-Einstein condensate to fragment into multiple distinct matter-wave packets. By carefully choosing the parameters of these potentials, we can achieve controlled unitary evolution, enabling the use of matter waves as functional elements for quantum gates and circuits. The time required to execute a two-qubit nonlinear quantum gate is markedly shorter than the hydrodynamic instability threshold that could disrupt the condensate's integrity. utilizing these gates, we successfully execute two benchmark quantum algorithms: the determination of the largest eigenvalue of a matrix and the factorization of integers. Furthermore, we show that by randomly selecting parameters for multiple gates, the algorithm's performance remains robust against potential matter-wave packet losses. Our findings indicate that quantum circuits utilizing nonlinear two-qubit gates are inherently resilient to disturbances arising from particle loss. This research paves the way for developing functional quantum gates and circuits using Bose-Einstein condensates, thereby advancing the field of quantum computing based on this technology. Ultimately, this work may contribute to the future realization of quantum computing via Bose-Einstein condensates. Keywords: Bose-Einstein Condensate, Quantum Information, Quantum Computing. The extended BMS group, which governs supertranslations and superrotations at null infinity, serves as the foundation for the soft theorem/extremal $s$-channel unitarity correspondence. We present a concise review of the BMS algebra, followed by a summary of the extended BPS double soft theorem. This BPS double soft theorem is derived using TQFT methods, which leverage the specific properties of null infinity and the vacuum structure. We also briefly outline the BPS single soft theorem and the extended single soft theorem, noting that the latter falls outside the TQFT framework. Furthermore, we discuss the soft charge associated with supertranslations, as well as the soft charges corresponding to self-dual and anti-self-dual superrotations. The latter charges are defined via an extension of the self-dual/anti-self-dual vacuum, a concept that is intrinsically tied to TQFT. Finally, we examine the symplectic current and charge within TQFT, demonstrating how the soft charge related to superrotation arises from the symplectic current. This connection stems from the fact that the TQFT charge is defined at null infinity rather than spacelike infinity. We argue that this characteristic is a fundamental element of the TQFT/vacuum double soft theorem/extremal $s$-unitarity correspondence. Additionally, we briefly mention the soft charges for general superrotations, though these require knowledge of non-vacuum vacuum structures beyond the BPS one. Finally, we highlight that the TQFT vacuum is not the only one capable of generating the double soft theorem, provided one employs an appropriate memory formalism. We conclude by outlining an explicit example of such a vacuum. Through this approach, we have successfully derived the extended double soft theorem without relying on extremal $s$-channel unitarity. This achievement highlights the broad applicability of TQFT in this context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the symplectic current/charge in TQFT can also account for the soft charge of general superrotations. This is achieved by utilizing a specific memory formalism that is valid across any vacuum. Finally, we show that the TQFT charge is also valid in this general vacuum context. Consequently, we conclude that the TQFT vacuum is not essential for the TQFT/memory extended soft theorem correspondence; what matters is the existence of an appropriate memory formalism at null infinity. Learning continuously with an expanding set of classes poses significant challenges, as models often suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where new knowledge impairs performance on older tasks. Ensemble methods have demonstrated potential in mitigating this issue by maintaining multiple classifiers. This paper introduces a novel momentum-based neural architecture designed for continuous ensemble learning. The model comprises an accumulator and a classifier; the accumulator retains a population of sub-networks that feed into the classifier, while the accumulator itself grows continuously through the propagation of a single parent network. We validate this model within the standard lifelong learning framework, showing that it achieves competitive average accuracy across an ever-increasing series of tasks. Furthermore, we present experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which confirm the model's ability to effectively balance retention and generalization. Our findings indicate that the architecture successfully maintains performance on old tasks while effectively learning new knowledge. Additionally, we observe that the model can adapt its behavior to prioritize either performance or efficiency. Finally, we demonstrate that the model's performance remains stable regardless of whether training occurs in discrete or continuous time. The study of metric geometries, where geometric properties are defined by an associated measure, has been extended to include metrics derived from generalized complex forms. Specifically, these forms generate a tensor product bundle composed of a symmetric tensor field and a symmetric antisymmetric tensor field. When combined with a symmetric metric and integrated into the definition of a Riemannian curvature tensor, they yield a Ricci-flat curvature tensor with all its associated components. Furthermore, the non-vanishing generalized forms can be utilized to construct a torsion tensor that ensures the Ricci-flatness of the resulting connection. Additionally, these generalized forms satisfy the conditions required for Kähler geometry. Consequently, this approach provides a framework for developing flat torsionful Kähler four-metrics. Applications to both Einstein and Ricci-flat metrics are demonstrated, including the derivation of a torsionful Ricci-flat metric on the Hopf manifold. This new metric offers an alternative to the Hermitian metric on the same manifold, which possesses non-vanishing curvature and torsion but remains Ricci-flat. These findings suggest a potential application in string theory for constructing torsionful Ricci-flat backgrounds. The study concludes with several observations and questions regarding the properties of the resulting metric and curvature tensors. This study examines a non-zero-sum differential game involving two agents—an insurer and an investor—whose enriched value functions satisfy a system of nonlinear integro-differential equations. By utilizing the concept of viscosity solutions, the authors establish the existence and uniqueness of these solutions within the class of bounded continuous functions. Furthermore, they propose a novel finite-state Markov chain-based technique to approximate both the viscosity solutions and the associated Nash equilibrium. The technique's convergence is rigorously demonstrated, and a numerical example is provided to illustrate the findings. Notably, this approach represents a significant advancement over existing literature, which typically addresses single-equation scenarios. Instead, the present work addresses a nonlinear integro-differential system featuring two distinct integrals, each characterized by a unique kernel function. This enhanced complexity introduces new challenges in deriving error estimates, a task not previously explored in the field. Additionally, the methodology is broadly applicable to models extending beyond those specifically analyzed here. Finally, the authors demonstrate an application of the technique to a regime-switching jump-diffusion investment and reinsurance model, where the Nash equilibrium corresponds to a nonlinear system of integro-differential inequalities rather than equations. This model extends the framework of [10], which assumed a single switching intensity, to accommodate two distinct switching intensities. The results indicate that the newly proposed technique yields superior convergence results compared to the method in [10]. Finally, the section on simulation results includes an analysis of the convergence of the approximate value functions.

This study introduces a novel Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework designed for smooth and stable quadrotor flight operations. The proposed dual PC-MPC architecture integrates a standard position-based MPC with an innovative PIDA algorithm that incorporates velocity and acceleration feedback. Position constraints are established to ensure accurate trajectory tracking, while an acceleration barrier function with a soft constraint is utilized to enforce smoothness. A stochastic dual simplex algorithm is employed to resolve the resulting stochastic optimization problem. Position and attitude constraints are strictly enforced to maintain flight stability. Introduction Model predictive control (MPC) is a robust control strategy that has been extensively applied to various robotic systems [1, 2]. This approach addresses a constrained optimization problem at every sampling instant to determine the optimal control input. However, the computational demands of MPC pose a significant challenge for its implementation. Consequently, efficient numerical methods are essential for the real-time solution of MPC problems. Dual interior point methods have been widely utilized in this context [3, 4]. Additionally, the recent advancement of quantum computing has enabled the efficient resolution of large-scale linear programs [5]. In this work, we develop a position-based MPC control algorithm featuring real-time optimization capabilities. Specifically, we address practical issues in MPC design and optimization algorithms by implementing a dual Simplex algorithm. The primary objective of this paper is to enhance computational efficiency to achieve smooth trajectory tracking. To this end, we propose a dual PC-MPC algorithm incorporating a stochastic dual simplex algorithm and an acceleration barrier function. Specifically, we first derive the dual problem and subsequently develop a dual simplex algorithm that incorporates acceleration as a decision variable. This approach offers two key advantages: (i) it eliminates the need for extensive MPC parameter tuning, and (ii) it facilitates the efficient real-time solution of the optimization problem. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector, which serves the LHC and its upcoming High-Luminosity (HL-LHC) upgrade, has seen its data acquisition performance rigorously evaluated during the Phase-1 offline test. This analysis, conducted after a three-year suspension of the CMS data acquisition system, utilized data from the pixel pilot-block readerlink. The pilot-block system, installed in 2009, features a six-layer small-size X-ray sensor module designed to investigate the effects of a LHC luminosity increase from 10^32 cm^-2s^-1 to 10^34 cm^-2s^-1. This study presents the reconstruction of hit patterns and data from the pilot blade readerlink under integrated luminosity rates of 10^33 cm^-2s^-1 across various conditions. Key metrics, including data rates, hit patterns, and trigger rates, were examined as functions of data acquisition configuration, trigger conditions, and data rates. Furthermore, simulations were employed to forecast performance under HL-LHC conditions. The results demonstrate that the pilot-block system can maintain data rates of 10^5 hits per trigger and achieve at least 90% efficiency for pixels with data rates of 10^5 hits per second, even at an integrated luminosity flux of 20^34 cm^-2s^-1. These findings support the development of a new pixel detector system for the future LHC. This paper details the reconstruction software and data format employed for Phase-1 test analysis. Additionally, it presents the first results from the reconstruction of a new 1D test detector utilizing a 64-channel readout module. This test detector features a single-layer 1D pixel module constructed from 64 X-ray sensors, each measuring 10mm x 10mm x 1mm. The pilot blade was exposed to an integrated luminosity of 10^33 cm^-2s^-1, and the acquisition and data rates were observed to remain stable. The results highlight the potential for developing a new 1D test detector with 64-channel readout modules for the future CMS Phase-2 upgrade. These findings are consistent with predictions regarding the performance of a 2D pixel detector system at the LHC. Finally, this work outlines the data format and reconstruction software developed for Phase-1 test data, which are also applicable to Phase-2 pixel detector data. High-redshift galaxies are believed to host supermassive black holes (BHs) that grow into active galactic nuclei (AGN) by consuming surrounding matter. These growing BHs are thought to regulate host galaxy growth through AGN feedback, a process where outflows from the accretion disk influence the star formation history and overall evolution of the galaxy. Consequently, understanding the morphologies of host galaxies harboring AGN is crucial for investigating these feedback mechanisms. This study aims to classify the morphologies of active galaxies at redshifts $z<1$ within the 100\,deg$^2$ Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide (HSC-W) survey. Utilizing the HSC-W catalog, we developed a machine learning model to assign morphologies to $10,580$ AGN candidates, identifying $6,080$ with reliable classifications. We find that AGN host galaxies are predominantly disk-dominated, with only $27.5\%$ being starburst-dominated. Furthermore, we observe that AGN hosts exhibit a higher proportion of spiral galaxies compared to passive sources at the same redshifts and luminosity levels. Additionally, AGN hosts show a greater fraction of starbursts among sources with $z<1$ and $L_{\rm IR} > 10^{11}$ L$_{\odot}$. These results suggest that AGN hosts are primarily massive disk galaxies, with starbursts playing a significant role when combined with prior knowledge. Finally, our findings indicate that the HSC-W survey is capable of accurately determining the morphologies of $z<1$ AGN host galaxies. The HSC-W catalog, along with the data and code used in this analysis, is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/keigo-ichikawa/AGN_host_morphology}. The source code is also available at \url{https://github.com/keigo-ichikawa/PyDeepLearn}. We employ the full Bruckner-Gorkov method to examine short-range correlations within light nuclei, specifically focusing on their dependence on spin and isospin. This approach enables us to map their phase-space distributions, revealing distinct timescales for the spatial, spin, and isospin components. By contrasting nuclear short-range with deuteron correlations, we identify a unique transition region separating the two phenomena. Additionally, we demonstrate that short-range correlations are heavily influenced by the energy resolution of the measurement device. Our findings indicate that short-range correlations involve low-mass hadrons moving at speeds comparable to the speed of light, with a characteristic length of approximately 1 fm. These results align with recent hadron emission data from isospin asymmetric isobar sources generated in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, we establish that short-range correlations reside in a hadronic phase situated just above the nuclear liquid-gas phase transition. Finally, we highlight the significant impact of nuclear short-range correlations on electromagnetic radiative properties, such as charge and current densities, and explore the potential to detect these effects through electromagnetic radiations. This study serves as a foundation for future research into radiative observables arising from short-range correlations. Additionally, it paves the way for developing new theoretical models to investigate hadronic correlations in light nuclei. Ultimately, this work offers a framework for advancing hadronic structure research in light nuclei and for designing novel experimental observables to probe correlations within the hadronic phase.
