We identified 11 low-metallicity stars with high signal-to-noise ratios from the GALAH survey to investigate abundance dispersion across different elements. By employing a Bayesian framework, we accounted for sources of dispersion arising from stellar heterogeneity and observational uncertainties. Our results indicate that observed dispersion scales linearly with stellar heterogeneity, which we characterized using the relative contributions of intrinsic sources (such as rotational mixing and accretion) versus post-main-sequence evolution. For stars with masses below $1.5\,M_{\odot}$, the model infers that the intrinsic source responsible for most dispersion is accretion, as rotational mixing is insufficient to do so. For stars exceeding $1.5\,M_{\odot}$, the model suggests a combination of accretion and rotational mixing. Additionally, we found that the dispersion of carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen abundances is higher than that of other $\alpha$-elements, implying that accreted material had a heterogeneous chemical composition. Finally, we determined that intrinsic sources of dispersion increase with stellar mass and decrease with rotation velocity. These findings support the conclusion that the majority of low-metallicity stars with masses under $1.5\,M_{\odot}$ are accreted field giants, and that the dispersion in their abundances primarily stems from the inhomogeneous chemical properties of the natal cluster gas. This study offers the first quantitative assessment of the dispersion in chemical abundances of low-mass accreted field giants. The data utilized in this study can be found at \url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7170000}. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/afg1999/AbundanceDispersion}.

Although various machine learning (ML) algorithms are now standard across diverse fields, their "black box" characteristics often raise concerns regarding interpretability and the robustness of algorithmic decisions. These issues are particularly acute in sectors like healthcare, where predictions directly impact human lives. While literature addressing the robustness of ML forecasts exists, it lacks tools for evaluating decision sensitivity across different algorithms within a single framework. To address this gap, we introduce a new R-based software package named `robustML`. This package computes robustness metrics for ML predictions by applying local sensitivity analysis in conjunction with Bayesian nonparametric smoothing techniques. We validate the effectiveness of `robustML` by examining the sensitivity of financial literacy test results derived from a large, heterogeneous dataset. Furthermore, our package offers several advantages over existing approaches, including the ability to handle categorical features, calculate robustness for predictions involving multiple outcomes simultaneously, and provide robust estimates without needing to specify a target level of contamination. The `robustML` package is released under an open-source license and is accessible at: https://github.com/QuantEcon/robustML. This repository contains illustrative examples using various algorithms applied to different datasets to demonstrate `robustML`'s utility. Additionally, a video tutorial on the package is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=14422222222. We anticipate that `robustML` will become an essential tool for researchers and practitioners in economics, statistics, and related disciplines who are increasingly adopting ML methods. Our goal is to foster greater transparency and trust in ML predictions by providing a user-friendly, well-documented, and open-access analysis tool. We welcome feedback from the community to continue enhancing `robustML` and look forward to its adoption by economists and statisticians. Finally, please cite our work as follows: B. M. Krasnok, B. We present a classification of these structures based on their contact de Rham decomposition and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for warped products of pointwise semi-slant submanifolds to form a product manifold. Our findings include both trivial and non-trivial examples, with the latter yielding a new class of points that had not been previously identified. Notably, all examples of warped product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds are non holomorphic, and we provide additional characterization criteria for warped product semi-slant submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds. Furthermore, we illustrate these concepts with examples in Kenmotsu manifolds. The PALEOCCENE concept enables the development of passive, robust, and room-temperature detectors ranging from grams to kilograms, capable of identifying low-energy nuclear recoil events. Since these recoils may result from neutron scattering, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CEvNS), or dark matter interactions, PALEOCCENE offers a versatile, all-encompassing approach for detecting such signals. This proposal outlines a detailed, incremental, and feasible roadmap for advancing the technology from current laboratory-scale demonstrations to a market-ready, large-scale system. The initial phase involves a proof-of-principle demonstration of the full detection chain, which will also serve as a functional, in-situ calibration facility for future large-scale dark matter experiments. This pilot system will integrate a 100g sample of the target material with an optimized readout system. Subsequent steps will involve scaling up to kilogram-level detectors that are ready for deployment in underground environments. To mitigate background noise, the research will explore various optical readout technologies, with a specific emphasis on superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Additionally, efforts will be made to eliminate the need for optical re-amplification. The ultimate objective is to deploy detectors in the tens of kilograms range, thereby achieving an exposure of $10^{33}$ target-nuclei-day, which will significantly enhance sensitivity to dark matter candidates with masses up to 10 GeV/c$^2$. This capability will complement existing searches conducted by the MICROSCOPE satellite, which targeted dark matter masses up to $10^{17}$ eV/c$^2$. Collectively, these initiatives aim to conduct a comprehensive search for dark matter across a detector exposure of $10^{35}$ kg$^{\rm equiv}$. We examine a system of colloidal molecules, where each colloidal particle is linked to one of two distinct active Brownian particles. When active Brownian particles reside in spatially varying fields of activity, the colloidal molecules dissociate in regions of low activity, causing the colloids to accumulate and the active Brownian particles scattered on them to gather at the gradient interfaces. By considering symmetric molecules, we derive an analytical expression for the activity threshold triggering dissociation, which aligns with numerical simulation results and can be interpreted as a balance between the commensurability of chemical potential variations and steric effects. Furthermore, analysis of asymmetric molecules reveals that increasing the size of the smaller colloid enhances stability, whereas a strong asymmetry in the type of active particles tends to destabilize the molecule. These findings reveal novel collective behaviors and can be directly observed in experiments involving colloidal molecules, such as those using colloids propelled by bacteria or bacteria themselves, within activity gradients, including those generated by phototaxis. Consequently, our theoretical insights facilitate a more effective design of colloidal molecules for application as functional materials. Finally, we explore a novel phenomenon where molecules partially dissociate, existing in equilibrium between intact and partially broken states, which represents a new method for controlling material properties. This partial breaking is particularly significant for asymmetric molecules, as it results in a collective structure that is more balanced than the individual components. Additionally, we observe that the system exhibits hysteresis, which complicates the experimental verification of predicted partial breaking but offers a promising avenue for functional materials capable of switching between different configurations. To facilitate further experimental work on colloidal molecules, we provide a flexible and extendable computational framework. This tool is broadly applicable to various molecules composed of diverse colloidal and active Brownian particles and is expected to find wide utility in materials research. A comprehensive user guide detailing the model's implementation details is also available. The fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) can be comprehended as a many-body resonance involving charged excitations known as magnetorotons, as suggested by the liquid theory. In this study, we extend this framework to encompass multiple magnetoroton solutions. Leveraging sum rules derived from current sum rules, we demonstrate that each magnetorotonic state contributes positively to theLaughlin gap. This finding contradicts earlier heuristics that anticipated a single, dominant magnetorotonic contribution at the filling factor of $1/\nu=2/5$. Given that these earlier theories struggle to account for experimental data, our revised understanding offers a more viable explanation for the observed behavior. Furthermore, utilizing sum rules, we calculate multiple structure factors, anticipating that future experiments will be capable of detecting these resonances. We also examine the implications of our findings for the existence of ground state transitions at the 2D electron gas quantum Hall nodes. Finally, we briefly address the connection between magnetorotons and excitation gaps in higher-dimensional systems. These insights collectively pave the way for a deeper understanding of the FQHE. Specifically, our work establishes a foundation for developing sum-rule-based numerical methods capable of accurately addressing numerous unresolved challenges in the field. This approach enables the systematic investigation of the stability of ground states and the characterization of the phase diagram near quantum critical points. Additionally, it facilitates the calculation of dynamical properties and the growth of magnetorotonic condensates driven by dissipation in driven-dissipative systems. This framework is essential for understanding the phase diagram of the moiré heterostructure driven by circularly polarized light. By the end of this work, we aim to have provided a robust framework for future research into the FQHE. This will be achieved by developing numerical tools that are both accurate and efficient, thereby facilitating the systematic exploration of the phase diagram in moiré heterostructures driven by circularly polarized light. Our work will provide a solid foundation for future research on the FQHE by equipping the field with advanced numerical methods that are both accurate and efficient. This will facilitate a deeper understanding of the phase diagram in moiré heterostructures driven by circularly polarized light. When analyzing data from CMB experiments, the presence of foreground emission from Milky Way structures can create artificial patterns in maximum likelihood component separation maps, specifically resembling 'X' shapes centered on bright point sources like the Galactic center. This phenomenon arises because these Gaussians of variance accurately model foreground levels between points but fail to capture their spatial distribution. To address this, the study introduces a new likelihood function that separates foreground emission from the Galactic center into its own variance component, thereby eliminating the 'X' artifacts in maps of the Galactic center. The validity of this proposed likelihood is confirmed by comparing map results against those derived from a standard likelihood function. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that modeling variance components with Gaussians of variance yields no significant loss in map quality, even when dealing with numerous sources. These findings suggest that using Gaussians of variance for foreground components is a viable approach, provided their spatial distribution is correctly accounted for. Ultimately, this work offers a new likelihood function that produces maps free from 'X' artifacts caused by foreground emission from the Galactic center. Additionally, point sources can be effectively subtracted from total emission by modeling their variance components, which is particularly advantageous when these sources are not well described by a simple dipole. The likelihood function is implemented in C++ within the SMSEMAP package. Future applications include generating maps free of 'X' artifacts and producing subtraction maps for the Galactic center and radio sources. This method could enhance the accuracy of subtraction and component separation for Milky Way foregrounds, leading to improved cosmological parameter estimation. The likelihood function serves as a viable alternative to traditional approaches for map production. Future work will explore modeling the spatial distribution of Galactic center emission and radio sources using a superposition of dipole Gaussians of variance. Furthermore, point source subtraction via Gaussian variance components could improve the accuracy of point source subtraction, leading to better subtraction results and reduced residuals. Finally, point source subtraction may contribute to the recovery of the 21 cm signal. This paper focuses solely on subtracting foreground emission from the Galactic center and radio sources, with plans to address subtraction from other Milky Way components in future work.

Training agents to execute new tasks based on natural language descriptions is a core component of building general-purpose AI systems. A critical hurdle in this area is "referential ambiguity," where different utterances refer to the same object yet trigger different agent behaviors. This paper demonstrates that this ambiguity arises because agents fail to learn consistent responses to similar inputs. We apply an ad-hoc regularization technique to a state-of-the-art language-guided goal-conditioned policy to address this issue, proving its efficacy through an instance segment anything V2 (SV) benchmark. Furthermore, we show that regularizing only the policy is insufficient to regularize the goal-condition, and we demonstrate the benefits of incorporating an auxiliary loss function that explicitly regulates the consistency of these components. Our approach yields an agent with an instruction-following capability comparable to current methods but exhibits greater robustness to variations in how commands are phrased. Additionally, we present an experiment using an expanded version of the segment anything V2 (SAM) dataset to assess the model's generalization to more complex objects. This experiment reveals significantly improved performance in handling complex object shapes, although the model still struggles with vague instructions lacking sufficient context. Quantum process tomography is essential for characterizing quantum processes, such as gates and channels. A process's "shadow" refers to a probability distribution derived from measuring many copies of an input state. The goal of process tomography is to reconstruct the distribution of a process's shadows from observations of many input states. Since a channel'sComplementary channel produces the same information as the original, we demonstrate that a set of shadows from a channel's complementary map is sufficient to fully describe the channel. Leveraging this finding, we design efficient experimental methods for quantum process tomography that utilize measurements of only one of the output systems when a bipartite state is generated by a two-output channel. Additionally, our methodology employs only projective measurements on pure states, which are more practical to implement than general positive operator measurements. Furthermore, we develop an efficient computational algorithm for this strategy, alongside demonstration experiments for process tomography. Our approach offers several advantages over existing methods, providing greater flexibility in choosing measurement settings for certain channels and reducing the number of required measurement settings for others. Finally, we provide benchmarking examples for process tomography, showing that our method outperforms the standard CHSH-based strategy in scenarios where channels provide outputs to a single system. Overall, this work provides both theoretical foundations and experimental tools for future developments in quantum process tomography. Using renormalization group (RG) techniques, we investigate a bilayer graphene system containing $N$ impurities, where each layer interacts with its own set of Coulomb repelling defects. Our analysis reveals that the bilayer coupling constant undergoes strong renormalization, causing the low-energy physics to be governed entirely by the intra-layer coupling constant. Consequently, the bilayer becomes irrelevant at low energies, and the system's behavior is dictated solely by the single-layer dynamics. Based on this renormalization property, we explore many-body effects within bilayer graphene, demonstrating that the established phenomena in monolayer graphene—such as the anomalous Hall effect, non-Fermi liquid behavior, and the quantum Hall effect—also emerge in the bilayer system. Furthermore, we examine how these effects are influenced by interlayer interactions, finding that a repulsive coupling between layers diminishes the stability of the non-Fermi liquid state. Finally, we analyze the relevance of this problem to recent experimental findings regarding double Scanning Tunneling Microscopy measurements, which indicate that while the few-layer sample behaves as a single-layer system, the interlayer coupling remains relevant. This apparent contradiction is resolved by noting that although the bilayer coupling is relevant at low energies, the system flows to strong coupling, resulting in Fermi liquid behavior. Additionally, we address the stacking configurations of bilayer systems, showing that for systems with relevant interlayer coupling, a time-reversal symmetry breaking mechanism is necessary. In contrast, an interlayer coupling with irrelevant or marginal behavior does not require such a mechanism. These findings are supported by both analytical and numerical methods. Notably, our approach offers a unique advantage over the single-layer model by enabling the study of non-Abelian anyons in bilayer systems. Finally, we discuss the potential for realizing these findings in experiments. Specifically, we demonstrate that a non-Abelian anyon state can be achieved in a 2-layer graphene structure with $N$ impurities, where the interlayer coupling is either irrelevant or marginal. This setup can be realized by applying a perpendicular electric field to break time-reversal symmetry. Our findings regarding impurities in multi-layer systems may also contribute to explaining the puzzling experimental results concerning impurities in multi-layer graphene. The behavior of molecular machines is highly dependent on temperature, yet experimental evidence regarding how temperature influences conformational changes in molecular systems remains scarce. This study experimentally investigates how temperature affects the changes in the bipartite structure of Sc2TbN@C80 on an h-BN/Ni(111) surface. At room temperature, the two Sc atoms in Sc2TbN@C80 are located on opposing sides of the C80 cage, resulting in a bipartite conformation. As the temperature rises, a transition occurs to a new configuration where the bipartite structure is absent. This transition is attributed to the rotation of the C80 cage, which serves as the C80@M3N@C80 endofullerene configuration. The observed cage rotation was quantitatively determined to occur at 350 K. Furthermore, a classical molecular dynamics simulation was conducted to theoretically analyze the mechanism behind this temperature-induced conformational change. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the conformational change of a molecular system is closely linked to temperature, providing a foundation for developing molecular machines that are controlled by thermal energy. Additionally, the findings offer a reference for understanding how molecular motors respond to thermal fluctuations. Finally, this study presents the first example of a conformational change induced by temperature in a molecular system. This indicates that classical molecular dynamics simulations are a viable approach for investigating how temperature induces conformational changes in molecular systems. Furthermore, the findings suggest that classical molecular dynamics simulations can serve as a useful reference for understanding such thermal fluctuations. Finally, classifying conformational changes according to the response to thermal fluctuations provides an example of how to classify bipartite structures. The Ramsey sequence serves as a standard model for quantum phase measurements involving spin qubits. In this context, optimizing measurement efficiency relies on carefully selecting the pre-phase measurement rotation angle, $\theta$, which can be refined using spin prior data. We introducing a sequential Bayesian experiment design protocol that utilizes an analytical form for the likelihood function to determine the optimal $\theta$. Within this analytical framework, the prior distribution is defined by two parameters. Furthermore, a specialized prior with one parameter simplifies the problem to finding the mode. Simulation results demonstrate that this sequential design method efficiently extracts spin prior information and accurately estimates measurement parameters. Additionally, this sequence design can accommodate constraints regarding measurement time. Notably, the method also applies to estimating unknown phase shifts within Ramsey sequences. Overall, this approach offers a flexible experiment design strategy applicable to various quantum measurements. Supplementary material is available. [arXiv:1905.07776v2] [quant-ph]. Centrality metrics are essential for identifying pivotal nodes and connecting communities within complex networks. However, existing centrality measures are often limited to a single scale and fail to account for the multi-scale topology of graph distances, potentially leading to misleading conclusions. To address this, we introduce Gromov centrality, which leverages Gromov's triangle inequality to assess the centrality of nodes or regions relative to network bridges. By incorporating multiple metric scales, Gromov centrality offers a more nuanced and detailed analysis. We demonstrate its effectiveness through both synthetic and real-world network examples. This study is supported by open-source software available at https://github.com/eliashahn/GromovCentrality. The corresponding source code can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7240017. Our results indicate that bridges exhibit the lowest Gromov centrality, while nodes or regions closest to these bridges display the highest centrality values. Furthermore, Gromov centrality proves effective in detecting communities, identifying critical nodes, and constructing synthetic networks. We introduce a generalized azimuthally symmetric framework for azimuthally averaged quantities that encompasses all known relativistic theories of gravity. Utilizing generalized Lagrange multipliers, we derive a comprehensive set of differential equations governing azimuthally averaged variables and demonstrate the inclusion of the standard theory as a limiting case within this generalized framework. Furthermore, we examine equations describing the azimuthally averaged behavior of a perfect fluid, which may serve as a foundation for investigating cosmological models featuring azimuthally symmetric perturbations. We also address equations relevant to a non-magnetized, electrically charged perfect fluid, potentially offering a basis for analyzing charged cosmological perturbations. Additionally, these findings are expected to be valuable for analyzing galactic disks, spiral arms, and planetary rings. The author intends to continue this series by applying the generalized azimuthally symmetric and azimuthally averaged theory to the planar motion of test particles and charged test particles in equatorial orbits. In that sequence, only the conservative part of the generalized equations will be utilized. This series of works is designed to facilitate experimental and observational tests of the generalized theory through the analysis of experimental and observational data. Generalized relativistic theories of gravity can be examined by comparing the motion of charged and uncharged test particles within the same gravitational field. Specifically, the planar motion of a charged test particle in the equatorial plane of a black ring provides strong observational evidence. Additionally, cosmological observations of large-scale structures and perturbations are anticipated to contribute significantly to this endeavor. Such efforts will involve analyzing a broad range of data, including the distribution of matter, baryon acoustic oscillations, the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and supernova remnants. This sequence of works aims to advance the understanding of the generalized theory of gravity. (For Part II, see [arXiv:2109.00022 [gr-qc]].) (For Part III, see [arXiv:2109.00023 [gr-qc]].) We examine the structure of a bundle comprising matrix pencils, where each element possesses a specific characteristic polynomial. Our primary finding states that, assuming all pencils in the bundle are non-similar (i.e., they share identical invariant polynomials but are not similar to one another), the bundle can be realized as image bundles derived from free modules over the polynomial ring. Consequently, these modules are isomorphic to free modules whose generators correspond to the bundles' characteristic polynomials. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such a bundle always admits a realization via matrix pencils that follow a cyclic pattern. Finally, we explore how certain properties of the bundle—specifically, the ranks of its image and co-kernel modules over the polynomial ring—impose constraints on the possible realizations. These findings have potential applications in control theory, particularly within behavioral theory, where matrix pencil bundles are used to represent families of systems sharing a common characteristic polynomial. Additionally, we establish that any map between matrix pencil bundles preserving characteristic polynomials can be expressed as a composition of elementary transformations. This outcome follows from our proof of the bundle's realization as image bundles over the polynomial ring. We also briefl y touch upon several open questions arising from this research. Variational quantum eigensolvers employ parameterized ansätze in quantum circuits to determine ground state energies. While the energy eigenvalues of various Hamiltonians, particularly those in quantum chemistry, can be represented as sums of excitation numbers (quasi-particles), existing ansätze typically excite both excitation and de-excitation operators. We introduce the qubit-excitation-based adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (QEV), which utilizes a more circuit-efficient qubit-excitation operator. By employing a linear Trott parameterization, QEV achieves a more balanced variational space with fewer circuit measurements compared to traditional adaptive variational quantum eigensolvers (VQE). Additionally, we demonstrate that QEV successfully calculates ground state energies for diverse quantum chemistry Hamiltonians within experimentally feasible ranges of circuit depth and qubit count. Furthermore, QEV exhibits a superior convergence rate in determining the minimum energy. These findings suggest that QEV holds significant potential for practical application on near-term quantum devices. Additionally, the linear Trott parameterization utilized in QEV is broadly applicable to other algorithms requiring multi-parameter optimization. The QEV code is publicly accessible via our GitHub repository. Deep generative models are increasingly employed to derive insights from complex data by jointly training a representation layer and a data likelihood within a unified framework. Nevertheless, decoders trained in this manner often fail to capture the intricate relationship between representations and data, leading to suboptimal generative performance. We introduce a new "map" decoder designed to enhance the training of such models. This decoder posits that for a given representation, the most probable target variable is the one closest to the mean of the local conditional distribution. Theoretically, we demonstrate that this approach yields a computationally efficient training objective while remaining statistically consistent, provided the target variables are unimodal. Empirically, our method outperforms standard dense coding schemes and competitive baselines across various generative generation tasks. Furthermore, we show that this updated objective promotes the discovery of more interpretable representations across diverse datasets. This objective targets practitioners utilizing existing "deep generative models," such as Variational Autoencoders and Auto-regressive Latent Variable Models. To facilitate adoption, we have released an open-source PyTorch implementation supporting modified versions of "Probabilistic Models of Featureless Patterns" and "Auto-regressive Latent Variable Models." These implementations utilize the new decoder objectives to foster more interpretable representations and include diagnostic tools for assessing decoder accuracy. Additionally, we have made available pre-trained models for all datasets used in our empirical evaluations. The recent NANOGrav 15-year data release indicates a common-spectrum process in the radio timing residuals of pulsar pairs, which some researchers attribute to a primordial gravitational-wave background (GWB). If the frequency of this signal matches the lowest range of NANOGrav ($f \sim 10^{-9}$ Hz), cosmological models could potentially predict the GWB at higher frequencies, such as those accessible to Advanced LIGO-Virgo ($f \sim 10^{-2}$ Hz). This study presents a minimal cosmological scenario incorporating stiff matter and gravitational wave (GW) damping, followed by transient dark energy, which can simultaneously resolve the $H_0$ tension and predict the GWB. This study details observations of Atacama Compact Array (ACA) data collected by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) of sulfur monoxide (SO) and carbon monosulfide (CS) in the coma of PanSTARRS comet C/2015 ER61. The ACA's wide field of view allowed for the creation of integrated maps of these molecules within a 1000 au radius, enabling an analysis of their spatial distribution. We constructed two-dimensional density profiles for both molecules along the Sun-comet axis and compared them to a steady-state, radial, collisional, steady-state (RCSC) model to determine production rates. The integrated ACA map revealed that PanSTARRS comet is not actively outgassing SO or CS; instead, the detected molecules are remnants of prior activity. Additionally, we identified a distinct "tail-like" structure in the CS density profile, indicating that the source of the observed CS is spatially distributed rather than originating from a single point. This distribution suggests that the comet's past activity was driven by internal processes, such as the sublimation of CS-bearing ices trapped within the nucleus. These findings support the hypothesis that PanSTARRS comet possesses a differentiated nucleus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ACA observations can significantly enhance our understanding of cometary physical and chemical processes. The ability to map coma molecules across a broad region is crucial for distinguishing between outgassing sources, such as differentiating between the direct sublimation of surface ices and the release of volatile-rich material from the nucleus. This capability will facilitate a more comprehensive analysis of the physical and chemical processes occurring in cometary comas. Ultimately, ACA observations will advance our knowledge of the formation and evolution of cometary nuclei. This research was conducted under program codes ALMA#2016.1.00020.L and ALMA#2019.1.00009.L. The data were obtained using the ALMA Observatory, which is operated by the ESO, International ALMA Partnership, and ALMA Science Partners under the ALMA Science Partnership framework, with funding from the ALMA Foundation and national funding agencies of the participating countries. Data analysis was supported by the ALMA Data Analysis Support Center (DASCO) and the ALMA Data Management Center (DMC). The authors extend their gratitude to the ACA team for their exceptional support and for providing high-quality data. We also thank the ALMA staff for their dedication

We present the inaugural unsupervised speech synthesis system, built upon two foundational concepts: the application of unsupervised learning to traditional speech synthesis and the principle that comprehensive, accurate speech synthesis models must capture the joint distribution of speech and text. To operationalize this paradigm, we propose a straightforward yet effective unsupervised learning framework that ensures the speech encoder comprehensively learns the joint distribution of speech features and acoustic labels, while the text encoder captures the correlation between text features and acoustic labels. Additionally, the diffusion model demonstrates exceptional suitability for generating the speech encoder's output noise. Experiments conducted on the TIMIT corpus demonstrate that our system achieves clear and intelligible speech synthesis using only unsupervised learning. Given its simplicity and effectiveness, this approach holds significant potential for developing large-scale, cost-efficient, and high-quality speech synthesis solutions. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in numerous real-world scenarios, yet their non-linear characteristics render them computationally challenging. Although specific solution approaches exist for MO-MINLPs, most are approximate and fail to guarantee the identification of all feasible solutions. This paper introduces a Branch and Bound (B&B) framework utilizing branch-and-cut techniques to address MO-MINLPs. The method incorporates bounding and feasibility checks enabled by the Couenne non-linear solver to manage the extensive search space. Furthermore, to avoid the frequent convergence to local optima typical of non-linear objectives, the algorithm targets a set of Non- Dominated Solutions (NDS). This objective is achieved through a Multi-Objective Branch and Bound strategy employing the Normalized Tchebycheff scalarization function. Empirical testing on both mathematical benchmarks and a real-world application demonstrates the technique's effectiveness in significantly reducing the explored search space and improving computational efficiency. The results indicate that the proposed approach successfully identifies a set of NDS within a defined scalar performance region. This outcome underscores the value of relaxing strict optimality requirements in favor of relaxed feasibility, a strategy particularly advantageous for practical applications. The paper concludes with suggestions for future enhancements to the current algorithm. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/fernandocorrea/NSGA2-BB. We generalize core concepts from the established extension of Lie theory involving Lie groupoids by recasting them within a well-adapted synthetic differential geometry model. Specifically, we introduce internal versions of source path objects, internal differentials, and internal morphism differential kernels, demonstrating that for connected Lie groupoids, each of these properties is equivalent to integral completeness. Furthermore, we prove that if a Lie groupoid is connected, then being source path connected is also equivalent to all of them. Additionally, we derive a general theorem stating that any smooth functor between locally source complete Lie groupoids that preserves structure must be a groupoid morphism. The paper also incorporates several novel constructions and findings. Our methodology builds upon earlier work by the second author and J. Strubecker, with integral completeness in this context representing a genuine generalization of the standard property found in smooth manifolds. Our findings underscore the fact that synthetic differential geometry models are exceptionally well-suited for developing the abstract Lie theory of Lie groupoids. Finally, this research marks a significant initial step toward a fully synthetic differential geometry framework for groupoids. Notably, the concept of internal morphism differential completeness emerges as a new and meaningful attribute for Lie groupoids in this setting. This concept naturally extends traditional differential completeness by incorporating information regarding source and target structures. We demonstrate that several instances of this internal morphism differential completeness can be characterized through externally defined properties, including differential kernels and smooth factorizations. Furthermore, we observe that many integral properties of manifolds, such as simply connected manifolds, admit natural extensions to Lie groupoids via these internal concepts. We have verified that numerous of these properties and their associated examples hold true within the synthetic differential geometry introduced by A. Grothendieck in his "Programme de Langue." The confidentiality of patients is safeguarded in healthcare facilities by enforcing strict network isolation, where sensitive data is kept away from general network segments. However, this strategy often hinders biomedical data sharing, as researchers must either navigate complex administrative procedures to access isolated environments or contend with firewalls that block gateway connections. To address this, we introduce a novel approach to secure and efficient collaboration within biomedical information science by utilizing specialized tools that manage data transfers between gateways and non-gateway locations without traversing network barriers. Specifically, we have developed and deployed enhanced versions of "Data Transfer Service" (dtm) and the "Biomedical Data Transfer Service" (bdts) specifically for gateway locations. These tools streamline and enhance data exchange between secured and unsecured environments, thereby significantly simplifying collaboration. Furthermore, these tools incorporate advanced security features, including end-to-end encryption, to ensure robust data protection. By integrating these tools into existing cyberinfrastructure, we substantially lower the barriers to entry for data sharing. To demonstrate their utility, we have created practical use cases in both theoretical and real-world scenarios. These examples illustrate how researchers can leverage bdts and dtm to access data seamlessly, thereby removing obstacles that have traditionally restricted biomedical data sharing. Additionally, we have developed a monitoring and usage tracking system for these tools to facilitate administration and support within real-world settings. Our current and future efforts are dedicated to expanding these tools and monitoring systems to enhance usability, reliability, and security. Ultimately, this work serves as a proof of concept for a comprehensive, integrated, and secure biomedical data sharing infrastructure. By providing a secure and user-friendly environment for collaboration, researchers can concentrate on utilizing data for discovery and innovation. Ultimately, this approach aims to improve healthcare outcomes and the lives of individuals. This paper provides a detailed overview of these tools, their deployment, usage, and monitoring capabilities. Additionally, it outlines ongoing and prospective activities to further develop, integrate, and deploy these solutions. Finally, the paper presents a comparative analysis of bdts and dtm against other data transfer methods, including WebDAV, GridFTP, and rsync. This analysis demonstrates that bdts and dtm offer superior security and usability, along with performance comparable to other methods, as evidenced by extensive benchmarking across diverse scenarios. The corresponding source code and documentation are available at http://code.google.com/p/bdts/ and http://github.com/bdts-tools/. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment polarity of specific aspects within product reviews. In this context, aspects can be explicit, such as keyword mentions, or implicit, derived from paraphrased phrases. While most existing research concentrates on capturing explicit aspects, capturing implicit aspects remains a significant challenge. To address this, we employ a supervised contrastive pre-training strategy to learn implicit sentiment representations. This approach utilizes sentiment polarity labels from large-scale datasets to generate sentiment embeddings. These pre-trained embeddings are subsequently integrated into the final model for sentiment analysis. Experimental results on the latest ABAC2020 shared task demonstrate that our proposed method implicitly models sentiment and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code for this method is available at: https://github.com/zhenghao2017/SC-ABSA. The paper can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.04001. Mediation analysis serves as a vital tool for assessing whether a specific factor accounts for a treatment's impact on an outcome, a process often supported by statistical models. While modern models have evolved from simple linear and logistic frameworks to those incorporating non-linearities and high-dimensional covariates, many existing approaches struggle with sampling designs where subgroups are selected based on outcome status. In biomedical research, case-control designs are frequently employed to reduce cost and time, although standard mediation analysis methods often fail in such settings. This paper establishes the identification conditions for mediation effects in designs featuring a binary treatment, a binary outcome, and a binary mediator under a case-control setup. Subsequently, we propose a model and estimation procedure for these identification regions, demonstrating through simulations that our approach outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we apply this framework to a design evaluating the identification and estimation of the direct effect of a treatment on an outcome through a binary mediator. Our findings indicate that the direct effect is identifiable when case-control sampling is conducted on strata defined by covariates, and we can consistently estimate this effect using our proposed approach. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of our method against an alternative proposal. Finally, we illustrate the application of this methodology in a study examining the direct effect of a surgical weight-loss intervention on quality of life, excluding the mediation role of body mass index. This example demonstrates that our method yields more accurate estimates with a narrower confidence interval compared to the alternative. Overall, our methodology enhances precision and efficiency in mediation analysis when case-control sampling is involved. The code required to replicate this work is accessible at: https://github.com/Sebastian-Beier/MediationAnalysis-with-CaseControlSampling. Keywords: Mediation analysis, Case-control design, High-dimensional data, Sparse identification.

This study examines secure multiuser communication systems enhanced by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) that are subject to hardware impairments (HIs). The primary goal is to maximize the sum secrecy rate (SSR) by jointly optimizing the RIS's reflection coefficients and the power allocation for access points (APs). To address the computational complexity inherent in SSR optimization, the authors utilize the convexity of the SSR function to formulate a second-order cone programming problem, which is then solved using the interior point method. Results demonstrate that with appropriate power allocation and RIS reflection co-design, SSR can be significantly improved compared to traditional transmission strategies. Furthermore, an efficient interior-point-based joint design is proposed to minimize the total active circuit power (TACP) within the AP, yielding outcomes comparable to those of SSR maximization. Finally, an analysis of the trade-off between SSR and TACP is provided. Simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed transmission designs, when incorporating RIS, substantially outperform the benchmark approach. Additionally, the impact of RIS placement on SSR is analyzed, and it is observed that the proposed solutions remain robust against RIS positioning. Ultimately, the proposed solutions offer a significant improvement over the benchmark, achieving a 1.5-fold increase in SSR and a 1.2-fold increase in TACP. Keywords: Hardware impairments, interior point method, optimization, power allocation, reconfigurable intelligent surface, secure multiuser communication.

Third, we apply this result to generate a new executive function (XF) policy capable of efficiently planning with resources. Finally, we present an XF agent capable of executing complex tasks by optimally planning and allocating its computational resources. Finally, we evaluate our approach on a demanding suite of benchmark tasks, demonstrating its superiority over prior executive function agents. The energy carried by the solar wind is a critical component of the solar-terrestrial system, influencing Earth's climate and space environment. This study examines energy transfer rates from the solar wind to the Earth's magnetosphere using nearly two years of high-cadence ($10$ s) solar wind data from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP), the first spacecraft to directly characterize the near-sun wind. These measurements are benchmarked against observations from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GEO-12), both located at 1 AU and representing the inner boundary of the Interspherical MHD (ISM) model. We analyze the energy flux across all three PSP field lines of sight (FLS) for each of the 10-second integration intervals, calculating the total energy flux within the solar wind and comparing it to the energy reaching the boundary of the ISM simulation. The comparison reveals that energy is conserved in approximately 50% of all PSP observations, while the other half show energy loss. This loss is primarily attributed to the neglect of magnetic pressure in the solar wind. When magnetic pressure is included, energy loss is entirely eliminated, resulting in an energy balance of 100% for all observations. This finding suggests that the ISM model requires an additional source of magnetic pressure to be balanced at 1 AU. Consequently, the magnetic pressure must be derived from the Parker Solar Probe. We propose a method to estimate the magnetic field using in-situ pressure data, which is then applied to all energy balance observations. The resulting model is balanced for 90% of all PSP observations. Finally, we compare the energy fluxes from Parker Solar Probe, ACE, and GEO-12 at the 1 AU boundary of the ISM simulation. The energy fluxes at the outer boundary of the ISM simulation are highly correlated with the energy fluxes observed by the in-situ probes, with the exception of the outer Parker Solar Probe field lines. This indicates that current global solar wind models are well-balanced at 1 AU. However, the significant discrepancy in energy balance on the outer PSP field lines suggests that the current model may be missing a physical process active in the outer heliosphere. This discrepancy may be linked to the heliospheric current sheet, which is not currently modeled. We define a concept of noncommutative (or quantum) numerable principal bundles within the context of C*-algebras, specifically for groups of homeomorphisms. Given a group of homeomorphisms $G$ acting on a commutative C*-algebra $A$, and a numerical bundle $p: {\mathcal H}_p(G,A) \to G$, we construct a new numerical bundle associated with $G$ acting on $A$. This action is characterized by the property that the resulting C*-algebra admits a faithful representation via compact operators. When $G$ consists of homotopy fixed homeomorphisms of a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$, and there exists a numerical bundle on $Hom(X,X)$, we demonstrate the existence of a principal bundle in the noncommutative sense. Furthermore, we find a one-to-one correspondence between such principal bundles and isomorphism classes of deformations of the trivial bundle. These findings extend recent work by the first and third authors regarding principal bundles in the context of deformation quantization. Additionally, we explore certain natural applications of this research. Specifically, if $G$ represents the group of homotopy fixed homeomorphisms on a locally compact Hausdorff space, and a numerical bundle on $Hom(X,X)$ gives rise to a principal bundle in the noncommutative sense, then any deformation of the trivial bundle remains trivial. This result aligns with third author's earlier work concerning principal bundles in deformation quantization. Our work also establishes a link between principal bundles in the noncommutative sense and continuous fields of C*-algebras. In the final section, we examine principal bundles in the noncommutative sense for groups acting on C*-algebras, with a specific focus on crossed products. We illustrate this by presenting a principal bundle in the noncommutative sense derived from a free action of $S^1$ on a noncommutative algebra, which generates a continuous field of C*-algebras. This construction was previously identified in the third author's work, where it was noted that the bundle is not numerable. We demonstrate that this principal bundle is indeed numerable within our framework. Moreover, our findings suggest that the principle linking continuous fields of C*-algebras and principal bundles in the noncommutative sense, previously observed in the third author's work, may be more extensive. This research examines the conditions necessary for achieving transparency with both fast and slow light, as well as the enhancement of such phenomena in a $q$deformed optomechanical system (QDM) operating in different quantum regimes. The QDM comprises two optomechanical cavities linked by a $q$deformed beam splitter (BS). We analyze the dispersion relation of the QDM to identify regimes supporting fast and slow light, as well as transparency conditions. To investigate transparency, we introduce a weak probe field within a specific configuration. Our findings indicate that both fast and slow light regimes, alongside transparency, can be controlled via the $q$deformation parameter. Furthermore, we demonstrate that employing a strong pump field amplifies these effects. These findings are confirmed through numerical simulations. Ultimately, the QDM offers a new perspective for exploring fast and slow light regimes alongside transparency, potentially advancing the development of quantum devices. In prior research, the two-rotors model, incorporating both rigid and elastic degrees of freedom, demonstrated that the R parity of rotors could mimic the effects of cranking. This yielded a negative rotational band, or negative R parity, driven intrinsically by the coupling of elastic and rotational modes, which relied on the deformation of the elastic rotor. The current study extends the rotors' characteristics by introducing additional degrees of freedom, thereby increasing the coupling between the rotor modes. We find that, in contrast to rigid rotators, the negative R parity mode transitions from an orbital scissors mode to an orbital scissors - local scissors double mode. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of negative R parity states within both the two-rotor model and real nuclei. Our findings indicate that the negative R parity orbital scissors mode in nuclei is driven by the coupling between the shape vibration of the nucleus and the rotation of both the collective elastic rotor and the single R parity of the excited particle. The contribution of the local scissors mode grows with an increased number of degrees of freedom. The sensitivity of the orbital scissors mode to the interaction between the two rotors in the two-rotor model suggests that the negative R parity orbital scissors mode in nuclei is more susceptible to the rotational motion of the particle. Consequently, the orbital scissors mode in nuclei is neither a pure orbital mode nor a pure local mode, but rather a complex state involving orbital-local and vibrational rotational couplings. The orbital scissors component is primarily driven by the rotor, whereas the local scissors component is influenced by the particle. The interaction between the local and orbital scissors modes is contingent upon the specific nucleus under consideration. Additionally, the negative R parity local scissors mode in the two-rotor model is driven by the interaction between the local mode and the rotor. The local scissors rotational vibration coupling in the two-rotor model is contingent upon the details of the rotor. The analysis of negative parity states in two nuclei confirms the validity of these conclusions. Overall, the negative parity rotational band in nuclei is driven by the particle-nucleus-rotor three-body system, while the negative parity local scissors mode is driven by the particle-rotor two-body system. The local orbital scissors mode is governed by the particle-rotor system and the particle's angular momentum. The local local scissors mode is driven by the particle-elaxed nucleus-rotor three-body system. Inspired by finite volume schemes, we introduce a neural network architecture designed to address various hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. By applying the cell-average property, this framework transforms original partial differential equations into integral constraints. Consequently, any solution satisfying these integral constraints qualifies as a cell-average based neural solution. The model's versatility extends to nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi equations and a broad spectrum of nonlinear parabolic problems, ranging from parabolic to hyperbolic-type behavior, all of which can be handled using adaptive mesh designs to handle moving domains and sharp gradients. Furthermore, rigorous existence theorems for cell-average based neural solutions are provided for both hyperbolic and parabolic cases. Additional model capabilities include the resolution of problems with discontinuities and the estimation of Lyapunov exponents for stochastic partial differential equations. Numerical examples demonstrate the model's potential applications in control theory and chaos prediction. Finally, this approach represents a significant advancement in physics-informed machine learning, offering a pathway to derive existence theorems for physics-informed machine solutions and thereby enhancing their reliability and trustworthiness. Several such examples are included in the appendix. To facilitate broader application, an open-source Python package, `cnne`, is available at https://github.com/chenjunyan1988/cnne. This package allows users to easily set up finite volume based cell-average neural networks (CVNN) and derive corresponding existence theorems for their problems. Furthermore, `CVNN` serves as a foundational step toward developing more complex, multi-physics-informed machine learning models. Specifically, it can be integrated with existing physics-informed machine learning frameworks, such as those utilizing Darcy's law, Maxwell's equations, or Navier-Stokes equations, to create adaptive mesh, multi-physics-informed cell-average neural network models. This advancement significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of physics-informed machine learning solutions. Additionally, existing existence proofs for these frameworks can inform the development of existence theories for cell-average based machine learning solutions. Finally, this work serves as a preliminary step toward establishing physics-informed, rigorous, and trustworthy machine learning solutions within applied mathematics. The Unruh effect serves as a foundational pillar in quantum field theory in curved spacetimes, yet it remains experimentally unverifiable due to the absence of external classical sources capable of generating sufficient acceleration. Consequently, it is widely believed that an equivalent phenomenon should be detectable through measurements of entanglement across the boundaries of future and past light cones within flat spacetime, a scenario often modeled using two accelerated detectors. This paper introduces a proposal to extract physical data from the entanglement between timelike-separated future and past light cones by analyzing the entanglement harvesting capabilities of time-symmetric detectors. Our findings indicate that the interaction between a future cone and an accelerated observer generates Berry curvature within the detector's internal state space, while interactions with a future cone alone yield no such curvature. The phenomenon linked to past cone entanglement shares all characteristics of the Unruh effect, including entanglement asymmetry, geometric gates, and rotational behavior in state space; we therefore designate this as the "timelike Unruh effect." Furthermore, the phase rotation associated with past cone entanglement can be interpreted as arising from a Unruh-like thermal bath. We also identify specific physical observables, such as entanglement fidelity and internal state rotation angles, that achieve their optimal values at early and late times, suggesting the timelike Unruh effect is most pronounced during the transient stage of state preparation. Finally, we demonstrate that the entanglement between future and past light cones constitutes a distinct entity from spacetime entanglement. These results suggest that the timelike Unruh effect offers a more feasible pathway to unambiguously detect and verify Unruh-like phenomena. Our findings also hold relevance for understanding quantum systems in the early universe, where the future and past light cones of an initial event horizon-like region may play a role in cosmology. Finally, we propose that the timelike Unruh effect could be detected in the near future at particle accelerators. We demonstrate that the positivity of universal characteristic forms at specific degrees can be derived from positivity conditions on universal Chern classes of increasing degrees as the dimension of the fiber rises. Furthermore, we establish positivity for universal condition forms through an inductive process utilizing universal vector bundles and their associated characteristic forms. Our approach relies on integrating geometric and algebraic perspectives, employing increasing dimensional fiber restrictions alongside a push-forward formula. Additionally, we derive positivity for universal Chern forms in degrees up to eight. Our universal vector bundles align with those constructed in \cite{Burgin}, and our positivity results extend the findings of \cite{Berg}. While our universal vector bundles may not always admit a global construction, we contend that this limitation is not essential for advancing the study of positivity. We contend that the argument's strength lies in its reliance on geometric and algebraic reasoning rather than combinatorial ones. The study examines Yang-Mills-aether theory, focusing on the implications of a non-abelian, aether-like term that induces Lorentz symmetry violation within a thermal quantum field theory framework. By employing the Thermofield Dynamics formalism to account for temperature and non-abelian screening effects, the analysis derives both the perturbative and non-perturbative propagators of the theory across various momentum regimes and temperatures. Furthermore, the temperature-dependent behavior of the theory's mass is calculated within these momentum ranges. Finally, the findings explore the physical consequences of a non-abelian, aether-like term that introduces Lorentz symmetry violation and describes the theoretical consequences of setting its coupling constant to zero. Specifically, the theory exhibits a transition from Lorentz symmetry breaking to restoration, and from non-confining to confining characteristics as the coupling constant constant increases. These results provide a foundation for investigating the physical effects of Lorentz symmetry breaking in quantum systems and for developing numerical models and simulations within numerical relativity and cosmology. Finally, the work outlines potential future research directions. Although numerous independent frameworks exist for parsing, there remains no joint solution that simultaneously produces a complete set of parse graphs covering all universal syntax and semantics. We introduce USTG, a unified algorithm for joint parsing that generates the complete parse graph (CPG). To evaluate our approach, we utilize the Joint Universal Syntax Semantics Parsing (JUSSP) benchmark, a new resource for measuring syntactic and semantic analysis. Experimental results on a small subset of CoNLL-2014 and Universal Semantic Evaluation 1 demonstrate that our method achieves a substantial increase in the covered parse graph while maintaining result quality comparable to independent parsers. Furthermore, our results align with or surpass those of separate parsers, and the coverages generated by STG and CSTG intermediate algorithms are highly competitive. Given that joint parsing is a more realistic approach than current separate methods, we believe this offers a promising avenue for future research. JUSSP and its associated code and documentation are publicly accessible. Our study compared outcomes from magnetized versus non-magnetized disks and initial conditions featuring high versus low angular momentum. In all scenarios, we found that even weak magnetic fields (initial poloidal magnetic energy $E_{Bp}$ of $\sim10^{-5}E_G$) are sufficient to launch a relativistic quenching jet, which subsequently disrupts the disk. Within our simulation timescale, these jets are transient and originate from the inner disk regions. The total energy released by the jet, $E_{jet}$, scales with the poloidal magnetic energy, $E_{Bp}$, following the relation $E_{jet} \propto E_{Bp}^{0.7\pm0.1}$. In contrast, the jet energy shows no significant dependence on the initial magnetic tilt angle or the angular momentum of the accreting matter. Our results indicate that while non-magnetized disks can re-heat and produce longer-lived, weaker jets, such a transition requires $E_{Bp}$ to reach approximately $10^{-4}E_G$. Consequently, we conclude that post-merger outflows from accretion disks are primarily magnetically driven. ASTG proposes that such a civilization might develop an independent gravitational theory derived from the same mathematical foundation. Previous work (ASTG, Part I) demonstrated that astrophysical observations are compatible with the ASTG framework. This paper extends azimuthally symmetric motion to the presence of radial gravitational components in the equation of motion. It examines the stability of this motion within astrophysical systems and shows that the equation of motion is identical to that of relativistic fluid dynamics. Furthermore, the ASTG-derived motion equation is applied to model molecular clouds, providing a new perspective on their formation. The model successfully explains the coexistence of collapsing material and star formation alongside the observed bipolar symmetric outflows. Additionally, it addresses the problem of how protostars and protoplanetary disks are formed. The resulting stellar disk model features a central black hole and exhibits hydrodynamic properties comparable to the standard Shakura-Sunyaev accretion disk model. Finally, ASTG offers a solution to the paradox of how such outflows can exist within a gravitational field. Overall, ASTG provides a robust theoretical foundation for modeling these astrophysical phenomena. The model is shown to be applicable to both the solar system and other planetary systems. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that stellar disks can be formed without requiring the assumption of superluminal fluid velocities. This study examines the optical emission characteristics of ten well-localized fast radio bursts (FRBs) with high signal-to-noise ratios, which were previously identified as fast optical transients through extensive sky searches. The optical signals from eight of these events exhibit two distinct, bright emission components separated by approximately 10 seconds, each lasting a few seconds, alongside a faint background continuum. The remaining two events display a single prominent optical component. We demonstrate that the two-component emission from eight of the ten FRBs is at least 100 times brighter than the background continuum. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit of 10⁻⁸ solar luminosities for any optical emission occurring simultaneously with the radio burst, and a limit of 10⁻⁵ solar luminosities for optical emission with a delay between the radio and optical components ranging from 0.1 to 100 seconds. These findings indicate that the radio and optical fast bursts are likely generated by distinct physical mechanisms. Additionally, the optical emission from the FRB afterglow is found to be at least 100 times fainter than the afterglow of the corresponding radio burst. Finally, the optical emission from the two-component FRBs is at least 100 times brighter than the radio burst itself, suggesting that the optical emission associated with FRBs is significantly more energetic than the corresponding radio emission. These results are consistent with the radio bursts being powered by the magnetospheric magnetization energy of neutron stars, while the optical fast bursts and afterglows arise from different phenomena, such as stellar wind shocks or accretion onto neutron stars. The two-component optical emission is best explained by a compact central engine, potentially a neutron star or black hole. The fainter optical afterglow could be attributed to a smaller ejecta mass, a lower viewing angle, or a larger distance from the central engine. The high brightness of the two-component optical emission relative to the radio burst may indicate that the radio burst is powered by magnetospheric magnetization energy, whereas the optical emission results from other processes, such as stellar wind shocks or accretion onto neutron stars or black holes. The optical afterglow is likely powered by the central engine as well. The high brightness of the two-component optical emission relative to the radio burst suggests that the magnetospheric magnetization energy of the neutron star is the primary source of the radio burst, while the optical emission is powered by other processes such as stellar wind shocks or accretion onto the central engine

High-power lasers are essential for numerous scientific and industrial applications, making their design and optimization a critical area of focus. This work focuses on creating reverse-engineering and optimization frameworks for high-power laser systems. We begin by detailing the propagation of errors from lower-level components to the final system output. Subsequently, we introduce a reverse-engineering framework utilizing automatic differentiation (AD) to estimate errors in system parameters without requiring the explicit formulation of the error propagation model. Furthermore, we develop and implement an optimization framework based on multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs). In MOEA-based optimization, fitness evaluation is a paramount challenge; we propose an efficient approach leveraging parallel computing and machine learning to significantly reduce the overall computational cost. Finally, we present numerical results from an experimental case study involving the reverse-engineering and optimization of a multi-level laser, demonstrating the effectiveness of this framework. Our comprehensive approach integrates error propagation analysis, a model-based reverse-engineering technique, machine learning, machine optimization, and parallel computing. The resulting framework is versatile and can be extended to assist in the reverse-engineering and optimization of various high-power laser systems. Although language models now excel at generating text that encodes visual controls, achieving model-agnostic, visual-centric control over text generation in a view-independent manner remains difficult. We introduce a systematic framework that integrates visual controls (like zoom and pan) directly with text generation. Our method harnesses the multi-modal integration capabilities of pre-trained large multi-modal models (LMMs) to map low-level visual parameters to semantic cues in latent space, subsequently converting these cues into token-level instructions. Specifically, latching onto the multi-modal integration strengths of models such as CLIP and mCLIP, we employ an LMM to extract semantic embeddings from natural images. Using an LLM, we map these embeddings to model-specific visual condition embeddings, which are then injected into the generation process to guide the LLM in producing context-aware, low-level descriptors. We demonstrate that our approach effectively imparts visual controllability to text generation in a view-independent fashion, even in limited data regimes, and that low-level descriptors generated by our method can accurately control an image generator. Furthermore, our method is model-agnostic and can be easily extended to other parameter-efficient, low-resource, or domain-specific generation tasks. This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a modified version of the RingCT protocol, which is a ring signature designed to ensure privacy in blockchain transactions. Specifically, it defines a new ring signature protocol named DSIG (Delegated Signature Graph), which maintains the core delegated anonymity of RingCT while significantly reducing the size of ring signatures. This reduction is achieved by utilizing a specific delegation structure for anonymous signers. We provide a formal definition and model for DSIG, demonstrate that it satisfies all necessary security properties for ring signatures, and outline a constant-time verification algorithm for the scheme. The paper also details the construction of Delegated RingCT and presents a comparative analysis of the system between the current RingCT protocol and the proposed delegation approach. The study concludes by identifying potential attack vectors targeting Delegated RingCT and proposes measures to mitigate these risks. Finally, we outline several future research directions. Although Delegated RingCT offers significant performance improvements over current RingCT implementations, it also introduces new challenges that require further investigation. Addressing these issues will be essential for enabling the widespread adoption of Delegated RingCT. Additionally, we have developed a prototype of Delegated RingCT, which will facilitate further analysis and facilitate future research in this area. We believe that Delegated RingCT holds great potential for enhancing the efficiency of ring signatures within the RingCT framework. Its application could extend beyond blockchain technology to other domains that rely on ring signatures for privacy. Furthermore, Delegated RingCT offers greater flexibility, allowing for the customization of ring signature ring sizes to suit the specific requirements of different applications. By offering these advantages, Delegated RingCT paves the way for more efficient and practical privacy solutions in various contexts. Overall, Delegated RingCT represents a significant advancement in the pursuit of privacy-preserving technologies. By balancing anonymity with efficiency, it addresses the limitations of previous RingCT protocols and opens up new avenues for future research and application. In 2018, the KEKB accelerator was successfully relinked to the SuperKEKB project, which features a highly asymmetric ring geometry with straight sections at the interaction points. This design enables the independent control of horizontal and vertical beam envelopes, a capability known as the luminosity scissoring effect. In this study, we present a method for measuring the horizontal and vertical beam sizes at the interaction region by conducting luminosity scans at various locations along the straight sections. Using this approach, we successfully characterized the horizontal beam envelope at KEKB following the relativistic quenching feedback system (RQF) installed in 2016. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of the RQF on the head-tail mode, observing a reduction in the coherent oscillation amplitude and the creation of coherent sidebands. These findings offer a new methodology for diagnosing interaction-region beam envelopes and a means to evaluate feedback system performance. We anticipate this technique will be applied throughout the KEKB ring to support the design and commissioning of SuperKEKB. Driven by advancements in machine learning, data-driven methods are increasingly applied to biomechanics. These approaches offer distinct benefits over traditional methods, including superior performance in handling nonlinear and non-stationary data, the capacity for high-dimensional feature extraction, and enhanced results when temporal correlations are significant. This tutorial reviews recent breakthroughs in data-driven biomechanics, emphasizing the emergence of cooperative techniques that synergistically combine data-driven and physics-based methods. While current applications remain limited, the field is rapidly expanding, and cooperative approaches are poised to become increasingly vital. We illustrate this with examples in gait analysis and musculoskeletal modeling. Ultimately, data-driven techniques are not meant to replace physics-based ones but to complement them, fostering stronger interdisciplinary collaboration between biomechanics and machine learning. Ultimately, the convergence of these fields holds promise for significant scientific advancements. Keywords: biomechanics, machine learning, data-driven, cooperative.

This study examines the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ ($n=1,2,3$) decays, which feature a narrow resonance at $10753$ MeV. In this framework, we analyze the impact of intermediate $\Sigma_b\bar{\Sigma_b}$ and $\Sigma_b^*\bar{\Sigma_b^*}$ loops on the decay dynamics. This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train deep neural networks using quantized weights. We begin by examining existing approaches that apply straight-through estimators (STE) within the Lagrangian framework for analog training methods. Subsequently, we identify and characterize a fundamental limitation of these techniques when applied to volume-preserving transformations, such as those found in quantized neural networks. To resolve this issue, we propose AskewSGD, an innovative training strategy for quantized neural networks that leverages interval constraints to manage the previously described rank deficiency. Our empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of AskewSGD in quantized network training and highlight its capacity to enhance test accuracy when used in an ensemble with analog training methods. Furthermore, we extend the theoretical framework developed for the 1-bit case to accommodate multi-level quantization. Additionally, we explore the connection between AskewSGD and the interval arithmetic constraint formulation recently introduced by us under the name Orthogonally Constrained Optimization. Finally, we outline the theoretical properties of the interval constraints utilized in AskewSGD. The source code will be made publicly available. The paper includes several original contributions, such as formulating analog training via the Lagrangian framework, extending the theory to multi-level quantization, and providing original theoretical insights into the interval arithmetic constraint formulation. Furthermore, our work offers the first original theoretical analysis of the interval arithmetic constraint formulation, which represents a significant contribution to the research field. Additionally, the source code is original, as it was developed alongside the newly proposed annealed interval-constrained optimization method. Finally, the test accuracy improvements achieved through ensemble training with AskewSGD constitute a novel empirical contribution. AskewSGD is anticipated to become a standard component in the training pipeline for quantized neural networks. Continuum robots, defined by their high degrees of freedom, flexible structures, and ability to perform complex maneuvers, are essential for numerous applications. Their inherent compliance enables them to operate within confined spaces and interact gently with their surroundings. However, this very compliance makes model-based control extremely challenging, as the robots are highly susceptible to disturbances and heavily influenced by contact interactions. While various control strategies exist, no single universal solution has been established to address the full range of continuum robot challenges. This article presents an up-to-date review of model-based control approaches, with a specific focus on fluidic elastoporous (FEP) robots. Our goal is to summarize current methodologies, validate established concepts, and identify critical research gaps. Furthermore, we propose several promising directions for future investigation, including the development of robust actuation and sensing systems, the adoption of new modeling formalisms, and the implementation of advanced control architectures. By addressing these areas, the field can move toward the creation of a truly universal control framework for continuum robots. To support this narrative, a comprehensive bibliography of 200 references is provided. This reference list is also made available online at https://continuumrobotreferences.com for easy access and contribution. We invite researchers to utilize this repository to facilitate a more efficient literature search and to propose enhancements to the database. Your input and participation are deeply appreciated. Finally, our team is actively seeking a Research Associate or Postdoc to join our control group, which is dedicated to advancing the theoretical and practical understanding of continuum robots.
