Power system expansion planning, particularly when integrating substantial renewable energy shares, relies heavily on optimization models grounded in various data assumptions. While literature has extensively examined model sensitivity to parameter values, the standard assumption of independent data parameters often fails, as real-world inputs like load growth, technology costs, and model structure are inherently interdependent, resulting in a multi-dimensional sensitivity landscape. This study investigates the joint sensitivity of power system models by constructing a non-orthogonal design with 120 scenarios and analyzing it through principal component analysis. We observe that carbon pricing and model structure are positively correlated with the emergence of natural gas, whereas all parameter variations are correlated with reduced wind curtailment. Furthermore, carbon pricing and model structure influence system costs, generation costs, carbon taxes, and natural gas consumption in opposite directions. Conversely, variations in all parameters shift these four metrics in the same direction. Consequently, policy recommendations derived from model analyses must explicitly account for the interdependencies among parameters. Finally, our sensitivity analysis reveals that power system expansion models are highly responsive to variations in model structure and the price of carbon. Specifically, the cost of flexible capacity, such as natural gas, is strongly correlated with the system discounted cost, while the price of wind and coal capacity are correlated with the marginal price of wind. We conclude that the sensitivity of system costs to renewable penetration is significantly amplified by the price of carbon. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that traditional sensitivity analyses are insufficient for evaluating power system models with high renewable targets, and a multi-dimensional, joint sensitivity analysis is necessary to fully capture the model's sensitivity landscape. This approach offers a more comprehensive understanding of how model outputs respond to data variations and facilitates a more robust assessment of policy implications. This methodology is now being applied to analyze the sensitivity of the open-source renewable expansion planning model, pypsa. By integrating sensitivity analysis with policy scenario design, we aim to provide a more holistic perspective on policy impacts, thereby enhancing the robustness of policy design. This represents a significant advancement in the sensitivity analysis of medium-to-large-scale power system models. Our work establishes a new framework for sensitivity analysis in power system planning, which will be made available as an open-source package. This provides a valuable tool for researchers and policymakers to better understand the trade-offs inherent in policy decisions. The sensitivity analysis code is accessible at: https://github.com/epi2030/sensitivity_analysis_for_power_system_models. This represents a step toward our ultimate goal of developing a generic sensitivity analysis tool for large-scale power system models. This tool will enable researchers

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for both the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems within bounded regions. Regarding boundary conditions, we apply specular reflection to the Vlasov equation, while imposing either homogeneous Dirichlet or Neumann conditions on the Poisson equation. For the ionic Vlasov-Poisson system with Dirichlet conditions, we demonstrate a global-in-time existence theorem for classical solutions near an equilibrium Fermi-Dirac distribution, provided the deviation is sufficiently small. Furthermore, we derive local existence results in bounded domains with low-regularity initial data. Finally, our approach extends to the Gauss-Poisson system, yielding global existence theorems in bounded domains. However, due to the boundary conditions imposed on the Gauss field, we could not prove well-posedness for the Gauss-Vlasov or ionic Gauss-Vlasov systems. Additionally, we offer a formal argument suggesting that global existence might also hold in this context. To support these findings, we present the complete proof for the ionic Gauss-Poisson system with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions as a model case. This provides essential insights for addressing global existence challenges in systems using Gauss conditions, ultimately leading to the conclusion that global existence is unlikely to be proven using the same techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that global existence can indeed be shown for the ionic Gauss-Poisson system when Dirichlet conditions are applied on the boundary of the unit ball. In this specific scenario, we also extend the result to low-regularity initial data. Notably, we show that global existence can be proven for both ionic Gauss-Poisson and Gauss-Poisson systems when the domain $\Omega$ is the unit ball and homogeneous Dirichlet conditions are used. Crucially, the primary difficulty in establishing global existence in bounded domains stems from the lack of control over boundary integrals in energy estimates. We overcome this obstacle specifically when $\Omega$ is the unit ball, as it possesses no flat boundaries, thereby significantly simplifying the problem. Conversely, this technique is ineffective when $\Omega$ includes domains with flat boundaries, such as a cube or any region in $\mathbb{R}^d$ where $d \geq 2$. Consequently, we explicitly demonstrate the failure of our method in controlling boundary integrals when $\Omega$ contains a flat boundary. Accurately mapping programming concepts to their textual equivalents is a critical component of IDEs and software development tools, as it allows developers to leverage tool support for tasks like refactoring, search, and navigation. While prior research has primarily addressed this challenge from a natural language processing perspective, we propose an alternative approach by adapting information retrieval techniques. Specifically, we introduce STRICT, a method that computes the similarity between concepts and textual text using syntactic-based representations. STRICT generates a list of candidate locations for concepts from various languages and achieves a top-5 recall of 80.2% and 79.5% for Java and Python, respectively. Furthermore, our ablation study demonstrates that STRICT surpasses the original STRICT method, which was also grounded in a source code representation approach, by delivering superior performance across all evaluated metrics. Additionally, our extensive ablation study reveals that semantic representations contribute the most to the performance of our method. Finally, we highlight that our methodology is adaptable for future applications within the field of software engineering. In summary, our key contributions are: (1) an adaptation of information retrieval techniques for concept location, which surpasses prior state-of-the-art results, (2) a novel approach that avoids the need for training data, and (3) an exploration of semantic representations for concept location that opens avenues for future research in software engineering. Our code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/strict-project/strict-project.github.io. This paper is also available as an arXiv preprint at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02010. Strict-project is also accessible at: https://github.com/strict-project/strict-project.github.io. Additionally, our arXiv preprint can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02010.

Colloidal gels, characterized by their gel-like networks, are frequently employed in rheo-acoustics, where ultrasonic vibrations are applied to adjust their structural and rheological properties. Previous research has primarily utilized ultrasound to either completely disrupt the gel or drive it into shear flow. In this study, we demonstrate that applying low-power ultrasound at specific frequencies can progressively weaken a gel network, thereby continuously modifying its mechanical and flow properties. We introduce the concept of "rheo-acoustic" gels, achieved by subjecting a colloidal gel to controlled ultrasonic vibrations. The magnitude of acoustic energy determines the extent of gel weakening, a phenomenon explained by the extent of primary particle separation caused by ultrasonic scattering. We examined how these acoustic-induced structural changes influence mechanical and flow behaviors, including yield stress, yield strain, and the size of yielding clusters. Furthermore, we explored how varying the ultrasonic frequency and position within the gel sample allow for the spatial tuning of both structural and rheological characteristics. This ability to controllably weaken, rather than fully liquefy, a gel network may offer new opportunities for advanced applications in rheo-acoustic gels. Additionally, our findings provide insights into the mechanisms of structural evolution in ultrasonically induced gel weakening. Finally, we propose a method to determine the primary particle size in colloidal gels by analyzing the non-Newtonian behavior of "rheo-acoustic" gels. This approach is validated using a model system of hard-sphere colloids. We anticipate that this technique will facilitate the determination of particle sizes in various complex fluid systems. Collectively, these findings offer valuable insights into how ultrasonic vibrations affect the structure and behavior of colloidal gels. Furthermore, they pave the way for developing new materials that can be precisely tuned for specific applications through controlled ultrasonic exposure. This research was conducted using a novel ultrasonic device that enables the application of precisely controlled and tunable acoustic energy to colloidal gel samples. The device features an integrated rheometer, allowing for the simultaneous measurement of acoustic energy and gel rheology. This innovative apparatus is poised to advance investigations into the structure and behavior of "rheo-acoustic" gels. Additionally, it can be adapted for use in other experimental settings, such as microscopy studies. Finally, the device is expected to facilitate further exploration of how ultrasonic vibrations impact the structure and behavior of colloidal gels. Let $X$ be a subset of a metric space $M$. According to Collatz, if every sequence of positive integers $n$ for which the symmetric difference $|X \Delta T_n|$ is finite implies that $|X \cap X_n|$ is infinitely divisible, then the closure $\overline{T}$ must be either discrete or dense within $M$. The objective of this paper is to enhance Collatz's result by substituting the condition that $|X \cap X_n|$ is divisible by every integer with the weaker assumption that it is the product of distinct primes. Furthermore, to align with this refined finding, a new definition for the term "regular" will be proposed, replacing the conventional definition. This work also explores several applications of these findings and examines the challenges associated with the inverse problem. Specifically, for any given set of primes $\{p_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$, can we construct a set $X$ such that $|X \cap X_n|$ equals the product of the first $n$ primes, $\prod_{i=1}^n p_i$? The answer is affirmative; such a set $X$ exists if and only if the sequence $\{p_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ includes an infinite subsequence of primes that are either all greater than 2 or all greater than 3. Additionally, the concept of a polynomial set is introduced, characterized by the property that $|T_n \cap X_n|$ is the factorial of $n$, and the relationship between primes and polynomial sets is explored. Finally, the paper addresses the question of whether a metric space can be partitioned into a finite number of dense sets. The answer is affirmative: if a metric space possesses a countable base, then every subset with a finite Hausdorff dimension is dense. Consequently, such a space can indeed be divided into a finite collection of sets, each having a finite Hausdorff dimension and being dense within the space. The proofs for these statements are supported by two computer programs written in Maplesoft. The first program verifies Collatz's theorem for the case where $M$ is the unit interval, while the second verifies a generalized version of the theorem. Categorizing documents by subject is vital for managing large-scale information flows. Although this task appears straightforward, it is highly complex, particularly within specialized domains like medicine and mathematics. In such fields, understanding the semantic and meaning-based nuances of discipline-specific terms is essential for accurate classification; however, standard classifiers often overlook the relationships between these entities. This study leverages mathematical entities to enhance STEM document classification, offering transparency into the models' decision-making processes. We introduce MathXLS, a mathematics entity linker that extracts mathematical symbols from raw text and connects them to a knowledge base of meaningful entities. Our findings indicate that utilizing mathematical entities improves the accuracy of multi-class classification, and we have made our findings, source code, and trained models publicly available. The experimental results and documentation for the entity linker can be accessed at: https://mathxl.github.io/MathXLI/ (last accessed: 10/10/2021). The experiments were conducted under the supervision of the MathXLI project (https://mathxl.github.io/) and are part of the Natural Science Computing (NSC) initiative (https://www.nsc.uni-bielefeld.de/). This work was conducted by students at the University of Bielefeld, Germany. Future efforts will focus on expanding the knowledge base with entities from other specialized domains. The decision-maker (DM) in a stable matching scenario chooses from multiple independent agents, where each agent can form at most one relationship. Agents may be single-minded, requiring specific DM partners, or flexible, accepting a range of choices. Over time, the DM discovers agent types and receives feedback on potential matches. Drawing from the multi-armed bandit framework, we investigate the DM's challenge of selecting which agent proposals to submit. Our findings include:
*   A novel multi-armed bandit problem featuring multiple "pull" options per arm and "lazy" feedback, which reduces to the "peek" problem when relationships are single-minded. We establish new convergence rates for both issues and identify the key difference driving this connection.
*   For general flexible stable matching, we present the first convergence guarantees when arms yield multiple pull opportunities.
*   We develop algorithms with provable guarantees for both problems and conduct extensive experiments to assess their practical performance.
*   We evaluate several real-world datasets to determine their suitability for these applications.
*   An important insight emerges: our algorithms surpass current state-of-the-art methods by over 100% across all datasets.
*   We release an open-source software package that enables reproducible research and facilitates the discovery of new algorithmic improvements. This package allows researchers to replicate our results and test their own proposals against the existing state-of-the-art. Specifically, we introduce "PyStableMatch," which offers an open-ended user interface for specifying preferences and generating initial proposals. Additionally, PyStableMatch provides a suite of algorithms proven to outperform current alternatives. Users can access the code via the project's public repository to explore the algorithms, compare them against existing solutions, and test their own proposals. Our goal is to foster new discoveries and encourage the community to enhance PyStableMatch. This paper serves as a launch point for that effort. By making PyStableMatch publicly available, we aim to enable researchers to leverage its capabilities and contribute to its ongoing development. Summary generation models are typically trained to align with human quality standards, yet current evaluation metrics serve as approximations of these standards and fail to correlate strongly with model performance. To address this limitation, we present SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation metric grounded in the cross-encoder architecture. This approach integrates content-based and language-fluency scores to provide more accurate quality assessment. Extensive experiments across English and 11 Asian languages demonstrate that SummScore achieves superior human performance correlation compared to existing metrics. Additionally, SummScore is computationally efficient, offering an order-of-magnitude cost reduction relative to current methods. The SummScore source code and API are accessible at https://github.com/summa-tech/SummScore. SummScore is released under the Apache 2.0 license and can be utilized as an open API to assess summary quality across various languages and domains. By facilitating accurate model evaluation, SummScore aims to enhance summary quality and ultimately improve user experience. We invite the community to provide feedback on this new metric to facilitate its adoption in future tasks. Additionally, we welcome contributions, such as additional languages or domains, to further expand SummScore's applicability. For more details, please visit https://summscore.github.io. This work investigates the reconstruction of real signals using complex quadratic measurements. We demonstrate that for real signals, the complex quadratic model yields superior recovery guarantees compared to linear frameworks like compressed sensing. Specifically, we derive an exact recovery condition for real signals drawn from discrete uniform distributions (including uniform sparse vectors) and a conditional probability of recovery for signals selected via standard isotropic random matrices. In both scenarios, our condition allows the noise level in the measurement model to be positive. Notably, this recovery guarantee holds without requiring the measurement matrix to be complex; a real matrix is sufficient. We utilize the full quadratic model rather than a hybrid approach combining linear and quadratic data, as the latter increases the measurement count to levels where phase retrieval becomes infeasible. Furthermore, the proposed condition relies on the $\ell_2$-norm of the difference between pairs of signal supports, which closely relates to recent progress in phase retrieval. Finally, the section on efficient recovery outlines a polynomial-time algorithm capable of reconstructing real signals from complex quadratic measurements. This algorithm is based on a semidefinite program augmented with a cut condition, which modifies the problem into a simpler eigenvalue optimization that can be solved in polynomial time. For real signals, this solution corresponds to the global minimizer of the original program. In the complex case, we suggest a method to obtain a good approximate solution. Numerical results, which confirm the theoretical findings, are presented in the associated paper. To facilitate these results, we introduce a new norm for vector spaces, which may have independent applications. This norm is defined as the limit of a sequence of functions representing the maximum recovery rate given specific support configurations. We also examine its relationship with the standard $\ell_1$-norm. To support these findings, we present a variety of examples, some of which are counterexamples. Many of these examples are adapted from existing literature on phase retrieval. To ensure reproducibility, we have made our code available on GitHub. Additionally, we observe that our definition of the maximum recovery rate for vector spaces is equivalent to the exact recovery condition for sparse vectors, as demonstrated in our examples. This equivalence suggests that existing algorithms for sparse phase retrieval could be interpreted as solving a semidefinite program modified by a cut condition. We also demonstrate that these algorithms successfully recover sparse vectors in practice. However, we note that the specific algorithm presented in this paper does not perform as well as others available in the literature for sparse vectors. We provide an analysis of energy dissipation in incompressible, three-dimensional fluid turbulence, incorporating the effect of all three kinematic turbulent numbers: the Reynolds number ($Re$), the Péclet number ($Pe$), and the Prandtl number ($Pr = 1/Pe/Sc$). Our approach integrates inertial fluid turbulence with the dissipative turbulence arising from thermal fluctuations. By examining both the magnitude and sign of thermal effects, we demonstrate how these influences vary across different turbulence ranges. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our model for numerical fluid simulations that utilize thermal noise as artificial dissipation, specifically when $Pr$ is set to a constant value of 1. In this scenario, we identify the distinct regimes of dissipation-range turbulence, which include either thermal turbulence or both thermal and hydrodynamic turbulence, depending on the magnitude of the Reynolds number. Finally, we relate our findings to the accuracy of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in describing energy dissipation. We conclude that for $Pr=1$, as often assumed in computational fluid dynamics, and for $Re$ values within the relevant range, the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations fail to account for the energy dissipation mechanism inherent in compressible fluids. Consequently, we advocate for the use of compressible fluid models in computational fluid dynamics. Additionally, we note that our compressible model simplifies to the correct thermal fluid model under the low-$M_a$ limit of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations; therefore, computational fluid dynamics simulations should employ a thermal model derived from compressible Navier-Stokes equations rather than the incompressible version. This ensures that any observed physical effects are not merely artifacts of the incompressibility approximation. We also address the potential for thermal transpiration, which may be detectable in microfluidics, and offer suggestions for relevant experimental investigations. Finally, we relate our conclusions to the validity of the classical Kolmogorov-Obukhov theory regarding energy dissipation. Specifically, we highlight that the thermal model reduces to the Kolmogorov-Obukhov model in the low-$Pe$ limit, suggesting that thermal effects on energy dissipation remain a valid hypothesis for further investigation. We also address the possibility of thermal effects on energy dissipation, which could be tested through experiments involving the forced relative motion of two parallel plates separated by a fluid, where temperature varies with position. This work provides a comprehensive numerical characterization of the spatial and temporal evolution of a thermal profile within a liquid subjected to a pump laser, with the aim of facilitating the interpretation of experimental data. The liquid's thermal response is modeled by solving the heat diffusion equation using specific parameters for CS$_2$, a common nonlinear optical liquid. For illumination by a Gaussian laser beam, the resulting transverse profile depends on the laser's local heating rate, heat dissipation rate, and the observation time. Numerical simulations demonstrate that, depending on the specific values of these parameters and the duration of laser interaction, the resulting transverse profile can exhibit either a single-peak or a minimum-peak structure. These outcomes are directly reflected in "diffraction-in-time" patterns generated by injecting a probe pulse during the laser-induced modification of the liquid's refractive index. The study confirms that both the type of self-induced spatial structure and the time required to form a significant feature are governed by the pump laser's wavelength and intensity, as well as the liquid's thermal properties. Furthermore, the presence of a thermal wave creates an intermediate transient regime that offers insights into the mechanism producing a single or a pair of intensity peaks in the probe signal. Finally, the study addresses a common misconception by clarifying that the spatial profile of a localized heat source does not inherently mirror its spatial intensity distribution. These findings are broadly applicable to experimental setups that rely on the manipulation of time-dependent, localized heating sources in liquids. Additionally, the numerical approach is transferable to other liquids and numerical frameworks where heat diffusion dominates over volumetric nonlinearity. This establishes a "time lens" mechanism in liquids capable of focusing temporal wave packets and performing temporal imaging. Potential applications include the investigation of time-lens nonlinearities and temporal self-focusing in liquids, which may generate a temporal minimum within the probe wave packet. Moreover, the formation of a temporal "time lens" can be observed via spatially resolved detection. The present analysis serves as a valuable preparatory step for conducting a systematic study of the interaction between localized heat sources and temporal wave packets in liquids. In this context, the pump laser acts as a localized heat source, while the probe wave functions as a temporal wave packet. Furthermore, the pump laser's spatial localization enables the study of the temporal lens's spatial properties and spatial wave packet manipulation. Ultimately, the proposed numerical description offers a universal approach for analyzing the interaction between localized heat sources and temporal wave packets in liquids, where heat diffusion dominates over volumetric nonlinearity. Developer interactions and conversational data from software systems offer a rich source of insights into a system's evolution. However, natural language barriers make it difficult to directly extract actionable knowledge from design discussions. This study introduces a natural language pipeline to identify and classify changes to the current design. The proposed pipeline employs two transformer-based models to sequentially perform design entity recognition and design pattern recognition, which are followed by a rule-based event detection system to identify stability-changing events. Conceptually, we frame design changes as a form of temporal reasoning, where the impact of an event on stability is determined by its arguments and antecedent conditions. To validate this approach, we developed a dataset of design discussions, annotating them for natural language events and consistency with the existing stability assessment. Experimental results demonstrate that the pipeline effectively captures semantic information from design discussions, with both individual components and the overall pipeline achieving performance that meets requirements for practical application. Furthermore, an analysis of real-world data indicates that stability does not necessarily decline over time, though various factors can influence it. This research paves the way for more effective mining of design discussions through natural language processing. The associated dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/ashra/Conclusion.
Index Terms—Consistency mining, design changes, developer discussions, natural language processing, software design evolution.

This paper presents H-STREAM, an open-source hybrid in-memory storage engine and query processor designed for real-time analytics on billion-scale data streams. It also offers a comprehensive case study examining the technical hurdles and innovative solutions required to bridge the gap between batch and stream data processing. Recently, there has been a resurgence of interest in Top and Bottom Partners, which are the lightest states associated with the Standard Model top and bottom quarks within the 5D Hosotani mechanism. These states have been investigated in the context of 5D models featuring global symmetry breaking, where such symmetries offer a theoretical framework for explaining the naturalness of the electroweak hierarchy and baryon asymmetry. This study examines the production of top and bottom partners at the LHC and a future 100 TeV proton-proton collider. Specifically, we calculate the dominant vector-like particle production diagrams involving top and bottom partners up to next-to-leading order in the $\alpha_s$ expansion. We present the results of these calculations as a function of the virtual gluon momentum in the transverse plane, which is a crucial variable for optimizing the transverse kinematics of transverse-momentum dependent parton distributions. Furthermore, we provide the leading-order cross sections for various relevant final states. These findings are intended to serve as a reference for interpreting future LHC and high-energy collider data. Additionally, we explore potential applications for future experiments aiming to investigate the origin of electroweak symmetry breaking. We also address the necessity of including final-state radiation in the initial stage of calculations. Finally, we offer recommendations for experimental searches for top and bottom partners at the LHC and upcoming high-energy colliders. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems translating English to SPARQL representations of knowledge base entities must incorporate SPARQL triplets into their generation; however, these triplets are not naturally present in the input context. To address this, the proposed solution utilizes a copy mechanism for handling base language elements, enabling the model to directly copy tokens from the input context for the generation process. Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach substantially enhances performance compared to standard NMT models for knowledge base translation, as well as outperforms previous methods featuring enhanced copy mechanisms. Furthermore, an analysis of the experimental findings reveals that the copy mechanism is frequently employed during generation to produce base language elements. Additionally, since copy mechanisms can be readily integrated into various sequence-to-sequence frameworks, this work has the potential to benefit other Neural Machine Translation tasks that necessitate the handling of base language elements. A dataset and implementation of the proposed solution are available at https://github.com/DeepMind/TrieNet-KB. Our code and data will be made publicly accessible upon request. This new approach is detailed in our paper published at the 2019 European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV). Furthermore, we have collaborated with a contributor from Facebook AI Research to implement a neural model that integrates entity-retrieval enhanced generation with our TrieNet copy mechanism for handling base language elements. It begins by outlining techniques for establishing the safety of neural network controllers alongside adaptive agents. Finally, we summarize recent advancements by presenting a learning-based optimal control application that utilizes formal verification to establish the safety of its neural network controller. The paper concludes by identifying key research gaps and proposing future directions for learning-based control systems integrated with formal methods. Overall, learning-based control is projected to become a vital component of next-generation cyber-physical systems. This study introduces a novel, operationally defined functorial framework for clustering. The initial component, termed overlap clustering, utilizes overlap groups to capture both direct and indirect data similarities. This approach is followed by a second stage, called merge clustering, which applies a specified clustering functor to the resulting overlap clustering. To illustrate the efficacy of overlap clustering, several examples and multiple novel methods are provided. Furthermore, the functorial nature of merge clustering ensures that the final clustering data set remains entirely dependent on the input to overlap clustering, thereby guaranteeing that no information is lost during this intermediate step. The functorial approach offers a flexible foundation for developing new merge clustering techniques and serves as a useful reference for addressing various clustering challenges. Notably, this method resolves a long-standing issue in distance metric clustering regarding how to address strictly singletons. Additionally, a reverse construction is proposed to address a current limitation in overlap groups concerning multiple data similarities. This paper provides a comprehensive exposition of these issues and solutions. The developed theory offers a fresh perspective for creating merge clustering methods with broader applicability. Ultimately, this work aims to inspire the formulation of new overlap clustering methods that draw from diverse data similarities. Tensor completion leverages low-rank structures to reconstruct missing data in incomplete tensors. While streaming algorithms complete incoming data efficiently, existing methods struggle to recover pre-streaming data due to the significant computational burden of rank estimation on large tensors. This paper introduces a patch tracking-based streaming tensor ring completion algorithm that utilizes patch-wise low-rank structures to reduce the cost of rank estimation on incoming data. Specifically, new streaming algorithms for tensor ring completion are developed based on both batch and stream observations. These algorithms support two modes: online completion for new streams and global update for existing streams, leveraging patch-wise low-rank characteristics to enable rapid rank estimation. Furthermore, an adaptive learning rate strategy is proposed to enhance convergence speed and stability. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms significantly outperform current methods in both recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we establish that any Yetter--Weber $W$-module $V$ satisfying these conditions must be one-dimensional. Consequently, we characterize all finite Gelfand--Kazhdan Yetter--Weber $W$-modules in types $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$, and $D_n$. Additionally, we determine the Gelfand--Kazhdan dimension and Poincaré series (relative to $W$) for Yetter--Weber $W$-modules with trivial $W$-action. Our analysis demonstrates that in types $A_n$, $B_n$, and $D_n$, the Gelfand--Kazhdan dimension aligns with the Poincaré series (as defined by $W$) observed in non-trivial cases within specific low-dimensional instances. Finally, we present examples of Nichols algebras with finite Gelfand--Kazhdan dimension that arise within these classical families. Notably, in each instance, the Yetter--Weber module is constructed from a sub-fusion of irreducible yet non-trivial $W$-modules. These examples encompass all possible Yetter--Weber structures for $C_3$, as well as those for $B_2$ and $A_3$. Furthermore, we detail various structures of Yetter--Weber $C_3$ and $B_2$ modules that yield finite Gelfand--Kazhdan Nichols algebras, alongside several other examples. We present numerical findings regarding energy transfer and the inverse cascade in three-dimensional Taitelbaum turbulence. In this scenario, the direct energy cascade (characteristic of random phase turbulence) is abruptly halted at a specific Reynolds number, contrary to the continuous power-law decay predicted by the model of Zakharov, Nazarenko, and Belanovsky. Instead, a single inverse energy cascade emerges, supporting the hypothesis that three-dimensional inertial waves follow the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. To elucidate the mechanisms behind energy transfer, we examine the interaction between random and quasi-geostrophic components. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the energy cascade in three-dimensional turbulence is influenced by the maximum ellipticity angle, which quantifies the mixing of barotropic and baroclinic modes. These insights are corroborated by an analysis of energy transfer across scales. Our findings suggest that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum may also be relevant in geophysical flows, such as the Jupiter Great Red Spot. Additionally, the numerical framework employed here is applicable to investigating the stability of rotating convective flows. Finally, the impact of supercritical rotation on stability and energy transfer requires further investigation. The impact of electrical gating on the thermodynamic characteristics of monolayer graphene has been investigated. Specifically, we computed the specific heat, energy, and Debye temperature across various gating levels, examining their dependence on both temperature and chemical potential. findings indicate that raising the electrical gating level enhances specific heat at low temperatures within the first and third bands while reducing it in the second band. Conversely, at high temperatures, an increase in the gating level leads to reduced specific heat across all bands. Furthermore, electrical gating level raises results in a decrease of the Debye temperature across all bands. These thermodynamic parameters were also evaluated for their potential use as thermosensors at low temperatures. Additionally, our data demonstrates that adjusting the electrical gating level can enable graphene to function as a super-thermosensor at low temperatures in the second band. Finally, we calculated the energy for all bands, observing that the energy decreases as the gating level increases. Consequently, this electrical control over graphene's thermodynamic properties offers new avenues for designing effective thermosensing devices at low temperatures. Notably, these adjustments can be achieved without altering the physical structure of the graphene. To our knowledge, this represents the first study to examine the gating effect on the specific heat of monolayer graphene using the many-body Hamiltonian method. Furthermore, our calculations reveal that the many-body effects are more pronounced than those predicted by the tight-binding approximation. Graphene's exceptional thermal conductivity has made it a promising material for thermosensing applications, driving growing interest in developing efficient thermosensors. However, existing thermosensors are limited to operating only in the very low temperature range. This work aims to investigate whether gating-induced modifications to graphene's thermodynamic properties could facilitate the creation of thermosensors for low-temperature applications without requiring a change in the graphene's structure. To address this, we employed the many-body Hamiltonian (MBH) method to calculate the heat capacity, Debye temperature, and energy of graphene monolayers at different gating levels. Our results show that the heat capacity of a graphene monolayer is highly sensitive to changes in the gating level. Specifically, the heat capacity decreases when the Fermi level shifts from the second to the third band due to gating. This suggests that the heat capacity of a graphene monolayer can be effectively tuned by modifying the gating level. To validate our calculations, we compared our results with existing literature. We report on low-frequency observations of the M dwarf system CR Draconis, consisting of two late M stars with periods of 1.6 and 3.7 days, spanning from 2018 to 2021. Our radio data indicate that M dwarfs can sustain magnetospheric radio emission for extended durations. We estimate the minimum average radio power at 22 MHz to be approximately 10^19 W/Hz, comparable to levels detected during active nights. This emission is likely generated via the electron-cyclotron maser instability, a mechanism typically associated with much more active M dwarfs. Additionally, we provide an updated list of low-frequency radio sources in the CR Draconis region, including three new detections. CRD1 exhibits polarized emission with a fraction of roughly 10% at 22 MHz, while CRD2 is detected only at 37 MHz. The polarized emission from CRD1 is likely of magnetospheric origin, whereas CRD2 may represent a synchrotron emission from a relativistic jet. We conclude that low-frequency monitoring is essential for comprehensively understanding M dwarf activity. Future observations of CR Draconis at even lower frequencies are expected to significantly enhance our understanding of this unique M dwarf binary. We introduce a complete system designed to create photorealistic virtual avatars capable of performing complex movements, tracking facial expressions, and recovering audio. Our approach utilizes a closed-form solution to model joint kinematics, which significantly reduces the size of the neural network required to render facial and bodily expressions, all while preserving high-fidelity appearance and speech. Specifically, we develop a compact, data-driven key pose library for joint angles, which appears sufficient to capture a wide range of human movements. By applying these library poses via linear combinations guided by an attention mechanism, we effectively minimize the parameter count of the appearance network without compromising the richness of motion or visual quality. We validate our method's efficacy by reconstructing characters from various sources, including controlled capture sessions, generated skeletons, and jpeg images, and providing full-body animated sequences with audio. Furthermore, we establish a new benchmark for virtual avatar synthesis in the First Person Shooter gaming domain. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art models, particularly in generating complex bodily movements, while using approximately ten times fewer neural network parameters. Additionally, we release the largest publicly available dataset for virtual avatar synthesis to date, comprising over 100 hours of controlled capthure data. This dataset includes diverse individuals with varied appearances, voices, and speaking styles, providing controlled inputs for head and body pose, jaw position, and speech. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our method for character animation by applying it to skeleton animations from popular motion capture libraries. We investigate the impact of extreme image transformations on both human and machine visual perception. These transformations include geometric shifts like rotation and perspective changes, as well as photometric variations such as brightness and color adjustments. While humans often maintain object recognition under these conditions, it remains uncertain whether machines perform similarly. Our study involves 50 experiments conducted by 32 participants, covering a broad spectrum of images and transformations. We present the results and offer a concise guideline for the tolerances of human visual perception. Subsequently, we evaluate model performance against human capabilities using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViT). Although state-of-the-art models demonstrate robustness to many extreme transforms, they exceed human limits in specific cases, whereas humans outperform models in others. This research aims to foster a more nuanced understanding of the distinctions between human and machine vision. By clarifying the boundaries of human visual perception regarding these transforms, we can identify critical design constraints for computer vision systems. Furthermore, this understanding aids in the development of evaluation protocols that ensure fair and meaningful benchmarks. Finally, our extensive dataset of experimental results can facilitate the creation of new synthetic data for training computer vision models. The code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/robust-perception/Extreme-IT.

The paper investigates the relationship between Chern-Simons theory, knot invariants, and the Askey-Wilson (AW) algebra. Specifically, it demonstrates that the Askey-Wilson algebra, along with its subalgebras the $q$- and $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2)$-Calogero-Sutherland (CS) algebras, arises naturally from the Chern-Simons path integral. This connection extends to the two-point correlation function and the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov (KZ) correlator. By employing the CS model's partition function, the authors derive recurrence relations for the Jones polynomial that mirror those of the $q$- and $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2)$-CS models. Consequently, this approach elucidates specific recurrence relations of the Jones polynomial and establishes a link between the Jones polynomial and the Askey-Wilson polynomial. Furthermore, the study derives recurrence relations for the Kauffman polynomial from the path integral and proves its invariance under the Whitehead move. Finally, the authors derive recurrence relations for the HOMFLY polynomial and the full family of integrable difference equations governing it. Finally, the paper demonstrates that recurrence relations of the Jones polynomial are a consequence of the q- and U_q(\widehat{sl}_2)-Calogero-Sutherland models, thereby clarifying various discovery processes of the recurrence relations of the Jones polynomial. We present findings from quantum Monte Carlo simulations utilizing the quantum cluster Monte Carlo method to investigate the two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnet, which consists of strongly coupled triangular units (trimers) arranged on a square lattice. By analyzing the pair correlation function, spin structure factor, and the low-temperature excitation spectrum, we examine the system's ground state and low-energy excited states. Our results indicate that both the ground state and low-energy excitations can be understood as resulting from the antiferromagnetic superexchange interaction between trimers. Furthermore, our data suggests that the spin structure of the ground state transitions from a spin glass state to a long-range-ordered state with long-wavelength modulations as the system moves from the weakly-coupled to the strongly-coupled regime. In the weakly-coupled limit, the system is expected to correspond to a critical point where extended Dirac fermions are generically generated. The spin structure of the low-energy excited states is identified as a long-range-ordered state with double-wavelength modulations, which can be explained by the antiferromagnetic superexchange interaction. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between this system and the 2D Dirac fermion system. Finally, we compare our findings with the numerical results reported by Senthil and Fisher [Phys. Rev. B 60, 2701 (1999)]. Our calculated spin structure aligns with their result, whereas the spin spectrum differs from their prediction of a spin gap of $k_F\pi/4$. The origin of this discrepancy is attributed to the cluster size used in their study. We conclude that our method is capable of accurately reproducing the spin spectrum. Finally, we discuss the potential to calculate the central charge of the low-energy effective Hamiltonian for the system. To achieve this, we introduce a technique to extract the low-lying degenerate eigenstates of the system's Hamiltonian from the quantum cluster Monte Carlo method. Using this approach, we successfully obtain the low-lying eigenstates and their corresponding energy gaps, and we calculate the central charge as $c=1$, which matches the expected result. This demonstrates that our method is capable of accurately computing the low-lying eigenvalue spectrum. Finally, we discuss the utility of our approach for studying other frustrated systems. By accurately calculating the low-lying eigenvalue spectrum, our method can provide quantitative support for field-theoretical predictions regarding the critical point of 2D Dirac fermion systems. Large pre-trained language models (LLMs) like GPT-3 have demonstrated an remarkable capacity to learn diverse tasks with minimal supervision, yet current approaches often rely on dataset tuning that lacks generalizability. This study investigates whether it is possible to adapt models using tuning data from different tasks. We contend that a straightforward method for integrating tuning data into LLMs involves treating it as a pseudo-pretraining corpus, emphasizing the preservation of original task structures. Furthermore, we explore how to most effectively leverage this pseudo-pretraining in a zero-shot framework, introducing the concept of dataset prompt alignment. Our findings indicate that pre-training on a collection of tasks, paired with prompt alignment and simple downstream prompting, enables competitive performance across a broad range of benchmarks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Notably, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the Natural Questions multi-task learning benchmark and achieve promising performance on other significant zero-shot benchmarks. Additionally, we analyze the effects of pseudo-tuning and prompt alignment on pre-trained LLMs, offering insights for future research. We anticipate these techniques will assist researchers in adapting LLMs for zero-shot scenarios and provide a foundation for further developing fully unsupervised learning capabilities. We investigate the impact of $Z_3$ symmetry, which prevents a $\mu$-term in the superpotential, on the viability of a strong first-order electroweak phase transition and Higgs Hubble consistency. This analysis is conducted within a scenario where both the gravitational wave signal from a strong phase transition and a dark matter candidate are present. To ensure a robust first-order phase transition, we find that dark matter must reside on the coarsening mode, with the lightest neutralino and lightest stau excluded as candidates. Furthermore, we determine that for a strong phase transition to align with Hubble data, the dark matter mass must fall below $1\TeV$. Finally, we estimate the potential signal intensity of gravitational waves detectable by LISA using the parameters established for this analysis. We conclude that while the observed signal may not be definitive, it should remain a strong candidate for confirmation by future missions such as LISA. Additionally, we highlight that our study successfully demonstrates that a strong first-order phase transition and Hubble consistency can coexist, yielding a gravitational wave signal detectable by LISA. Our findings also confirm that a scenario with a strong first-order phase transition and Higgs Hubble consistency is feasible, with a phase transition temperature of $100\GeV$, an expansion velocity of the bubble wall at $0.6c$, and dark matter mass below $1\TeV$. These results are consistent with the LHC cross-section, direct, and indirect detection limits. Consequently, this study offers a comprehensive framework for detecting the gravitational wave signal. We anticipate that the LISA collaboration will soon release updated information regarding the signal's intensity and the likelihood of its detection. We introduce High-z Sudoku, a two-step diagnostic framework designed to verify redshifts for (sub)millimeter sources at $z>1$ via the 21cm Hydrogen Line via the ALMA. In the first step, we apply a two-component Gaussian fit to source spectral energy distributions (SEDs) across multi-wavelength (sub)mm data to isolate redshift candidates. In the second step, we simulate observations using the first-step candidates as input redshifts for the 21cm Hydrogen Line, generating four mock zCOSMOS-bright galaxy catalog images for ALMA. We then solve a z-Sudoku puzzle using these mock images to identify robust redshifts, which are subsequently cross-matched with input sources. We demonstrate the Sudoku solver and illustrate its effectiveness using 210 input sources from the SCUBA-2 Large Programme. Our results show that 87% of these sources are robustly redshifted with confidence intervals of $\Delta z=0.1$ for $z<1$ and $\Delta z=0.2$ for $z>1$. Additionally, 13% of the input sources remain un-solved; 7% of these are missed due to incorrect input redshifts, while 6% are missed because they lack detectable 21cm emission in the mock ALMA observations. We conclude that High-z Sudoku is a highly effective and efficient tool for identifying (sub)mm redshift candidates, with the primary limitation being the availability of (sub)mm flux data. We argue that High-z Sudoku will significantly enhance the (sub)mm redshift identification process, thereby increasing the number of confirmed sources and improving source matching. Future applications of this tool are anticipated to substantially boost the (sub)mm redshift identification rate. The High-z Sudoku code is publicly available at https://github.com/kevinmccreight/High-z-Sudoku. This project utilized the zCOSMOS Bright Galaxy Catalog (BGC) data release v.8.1. Utilizing large-scale quantum spin dynamics simulations, we investigate the thermodynamic properties of the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice to identify the characteristic signatures of the 120-degree ordered state and the spin-liquid phase. Our analysis centers on the dynamical spin structure factor $S(k,\omega)$ and the correlation function $C(r)$, which exhibit distinctive characteristics within the spin-liquid regime. Specifically, low-energy excitations in the spin-liquid phase consist of gapped, highly damped magnons, a finding that contrasts sharply with the well-established properties of 120-degree ordered and spin-glass phases. These results are derived from simulations of increasingly larger spin systems and progressively longer time evolution intervals. The emergence of distinct dynamical signatures serves as a robust verification mechanism for the spin-liquid ground state in certain frustrated antiferromagnets. Furthermore, we observe that $S(k,\omega)$ retains significant spectral weight at the 120-degree ordering wave vector even within the spin-liquid phase, suggesting a substantial overlap between the two phases in the parameter space. This biphase boundary is notably sensitive to finite-size effects, necessitating corrections based on the system size. Consequently, our study underscores the critical role of extensive system sizes in accurately determining the phase diagram of this model. Finally, our methodology is broadly applicable to other frustrated magnetism problems, offering a quantum simulation tool capable of delivering qualitative and quantitative insights into dynamical properties. This serves as an essential complement to static spin structure data, which alone is often insufficient to differentiate between the 120-degree ordered and spin-liquid phases. Ultimately, our findings provide compelling evidence supporting the existence of the spin-liquid phase in this model. This study examines the confinement and deconfinement transitions within $3-3$ Higgs theory, a framework where the $SU(3)$ gauge group couples to a Higgs field in the adjoint representation. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we track the behavior of the baryon loop to differentiate between center symmetry breaking and confinement. By analyzing the dependence of the baryon loop on the mass of the Higgs field—the parameter conjugate to the chemical potential—we observe that the theory exhibits volume-independent string tension, indicating a confining interaction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the deconfinement transition occurs as a first-order phase transition. These findings are contrasted with the predictions of the $3-3$ Gross-Witten-Witten (GWW) model. Additionally, we report on finite density phenomena, specifically the disappearance of string tension and center symmetry breaking when the chemical potential reaches the Higgs field mass. Finally, we explore the potential for connecting these numerical results with an $SU(3)$-invariant effective model. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the chiral phase transition. Cr2OCl2 has been identified as a high-temperature nematic antiferromagnet. Within the hexagonal Cr2OCl2 layer, the exchange interactions between the Cr ions generate a unique anisotropy in the exchange field, resulting in a novel type of G-type antiferromagnetic ordering. This study employs x-ray magnetic scattering to investigate the in-plane magnetic structure of the closely related compound Cr2Al. The measured magnetic Bragg peaks correspond to a complex arrangement of spins on the hexagonal lattice, consistent with the expected antiferromagnetic structure. The exchange interactions derived from this analysis are presented for the first time. The analysis indicates that the exchange interactions in Cr2 are comparable to those in Cr2OCl2, suggesting that the emergence of the nematic antiferromagnetic state in Cr2OCl2 is driven by the exceptional anisotropy of the exchange field. Furthermore, the results suggest that the previously reported magnetic structure in Cr2Al is of the simple ferromagnetic type. This finding is significant because it demonstrates that the magnetic structure of Cr2Al is not solely determined by the anisotropy of the exchange field. The first-principles calculations conducted in this work support these experimental outcomes. Ultimately, Cr2Al is established as a new representative of G-type antiferromagnets. These materials are expected to exhibit a wide range of unique phenomena, including a complex array of spin excitations and a rich variety of non-Hermitian topological states. Additionally, the exchange interactions in Cr2 are shown to be comparable to those in other well-known magnetic materials, such as Cr and Mn. This underscores the potential of Cr2 as a promising candidate for developing new functional magnetic materials. To facilitate this development, the comprehensive set of exchange interactions and the magnetic structure of Cr2 are provided in this work. These datasets are expected to serve as a valuable reference for future research into the intrinsic properties of Cr2. The detailed procedures for calculating the exchange interactions and magnetic structure from first principles are also included in the supplementary material. This ensures that other researchers can easily reproduce the results and apply the same methodology to investigate the magnetic structures of other materials. The inclusion of these calculations in the supplementary material is intended to enhance the reproducibility of the study and facilitate further research into functional magnetic materials. The availability of the exchange interaction data and the magnetic structure of Cr2 is expected to contribute significantly to the understanding of the intrinsic properties of Cr2 and advance the field of functional magnetic materials. We introduce a kinetic model utilizing a velocity-dependent collision frequency to analyze monatomic rarefied gas flows. In this framework, the distribution function is represented as a superposition of plane waves, with relaxation rates for the collision term determined by temperature and the collision radius. This model is evaluated against the classical linearized Boltzmann equation, the S-model, and the Maxwell model using the exact analytic solutions for plane parallel shear flow discovered by Torrance and Keller. The results demonstrate that this proposed model effectively captures the dependency of rarefied gas flow parameters on intermolecular potential. Furthermore, the model's computational efficiency and ease of implementation make it highly suitable for engineering applications. Finally, an extension of this model is introduced to describe weakly non-equilibrium gas flows. The findings indicate that this model serves as a valuable tool for both scientific research and practical engineering. Finally, the computational implementation will be released as an open-source project. Semantic parsing is a critical challenge in natural language processing, aiming to translate natural language queries into query languages. Although semantic parsers for standard datasets like Spider and SchemaText have demonstrated significant advancements, they still encounter issues with hallucination and delusion. This paper introduces an end-to-end training approach for large-scale natural language models using natural text as supervision. By leveraging extensive external text resources, our method shows promising results on both schema-based (e.g., Spider) and non-schema-based (e.g., WikiHow) datasets. Leveraging the text-generation capabilities of GPT-3, we demonstrate that even models as small as T5-base can achieve performance comparable to larger, more complex architectures such as NeuRA and DALI on the Spider test set. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/alexpaulos/natural_sup_sem_parsing. Furthermore, we release our results on additional datasets, including WikiHow and crawl4web, which were not included in the original study. We aim for this work to inspire research into semantic parsing with limited data, moving beyond the traditional reliance on specialized, manually annotated corpora. Our system ranks among the top performers on Spider v2.0, achieving a execution accuracy of 59.2% with an average Hallucination Rate (HR) of 1.2, compared to the original T5-base model's 59.0% execution accuracy and 2.6% HR. Additionally, by prompting smaller models with fewer parameters, we enable the deployment of high-performing semantic parsers on resource-constrained edge devices. Future research should focus on developing more efficient large language models that balance performance with computational efficiency. Finally, we emphasize the need for greater transparency regarding the limitations of text-generation models in semantic parsing, particularly their tendency to produce hallucinated outputs. Addressing these hallucinations remains a critical area for future investigation. Overall, this work represents a significant step toward creating more robust and reliable semantic parsers. By demonstrating the potential of natural language supervision, we hope to drive further research into data-efficient semantic parsing and the mitigation of associated challenges. Through this approach, we aim to build more trustworthy and dependable systems for practical deployment. Additionally, we stress the importance of ensuring that limited-data research contributes to the advancement of the field rather than perpetuating misconceptions about the feasibility and reliability of such approaches. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aims to investigate the internal structures of nucleons and nuclei, as well as particle formation mechanisms within high-energy collisions. A forward silicon tracking detector is proposed for the EIC to measure forward charged particles, determine particle identification, and measure track curvature. Given the EIC's unique capabilities, such as measuring the electric charge carried by identified pions, neutrons, and protons, its scientific output is anticipated to be groundbreaking, thereby offering a platform for discoveries that will advance our understanding of the strong interaction. However, the extreme radiation environment of the forward region poses a significant challenge to silicon detectors. Consequently, there is an urgent necessity for novel detector technologies, including advanced sensor designs, radiation-hardened materials, and superior readout electronics. Furthermore, the EIC's high luminosity demands the integration of these new technologies with efficient readout and fast data acquisition systems. This paper outlines the current status of R&D efforts regarding the EIC forward silicon tracking detector and highlights key findings and outcomes from the 2021 Silicon Detector Technology Workshop for the EIC. A series of specialized workshops on silicon detector technology for the EIC were held in the spring of 2021, and this volume includes a selection of research papers resulting from those meetings. These papers address various aspects of the detector, such as sensor development, radiation damage, readout systems, and data acquisition. Additionally, the paper presents results from an experimental campaign conducted at CERN SPS in May 2021, which involved irradiating and testing a silicon tracking detector using the ADT test stand. Finally, the acquisition and analysis of test stand data are presented, with a focus on the performance of the readout system and data acquisition. Ultimately, the development of the EIC forward silicon tracking detector serves as a valuable benchmark for the design and implementation of future high-energy physics experiments. Through the advancements and innovations undertaken for the EIC, the broader high-energy physics community will be well-prepared for the next generation of large-scale particle accelerators. Keywords: Electron-ion Collider, silicon tracking detector, radiation hardening, data acquisition.

This study introduces multi-epoch, multi-wavelength observations of the nearby, low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) NGC 4103, spanning from 2017 to 2019. The data encompass optical and near-infrared (NIR) imaging, broad-band spectroscopy, and high-resolution spectroscopy, with a specific focus on the 2017 epoch. By analyzing the 2017 NIR images, we identified a significant brightening in the AGN continuum within a single epoch, an event we classify as an eruption. Furthermore, the high-resolution spectra reveal broad H$\alpha$ emission lines with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of approximately 1000 km/s, which exhibit substantial flux variability. These findings imply a rapid timescale for AGN nuclear variability and support the existence of a highly variable accretion disk. Our results align with recent high-resolution spectroscopic studies of AGNs, yet they contrast with earlier low-resolution work that reported narrow emission lines. Additionally, the variability observed in the broad H$\alpha$ lines is not well-explained by standard accretion disk models. We propose that the AGN corona is the primary source of this variability, potentially resulting from either eruptions or oscillations. Our analysis of the 2019 epoch indicates a decline in the AGN continuum flux, which we interpret as a coronal eruption occurring between 2017 and 2019. These results offer a compelling explanation for the substantial flux variability seen in AGN, while also being consistent with and contributing to the broader body of research on AGN variability. Ultimately, our work underscores the necessity of high-resolution spectroscopy for investigating AGN variability. The datasets used in this analysis are publicly accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7100000. The code utilized for this analysis can be found at https://github.com/akshaykumar1999/variability_in_agn. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD58260 conducted using the ESPaDOnS instrument at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope. The sample includes emission lines of neutral calcium and titanium, alongside the previously examined absorption line of neutral iron. By employing the "solar method," we analyzed the line profiles to determine the magnetic field geometry. Our results indicate that the iron absorption line originates in a region with a radial magnetic field gradient, while the titanium and calcium emission lines form in zones characterized by smaller gradients. The most precise cross-field gradients derived are 22% for Fe I 617.3 nm, 8% for Ti I 630.2 nm, and 4% for Ca I 656.3 nm. These findings confirm the presence of a magnetic field gradient within the stellar atmosphere of HD58260. Furthermore, the magnetic field strength and gradient magnitude decrease as the magnetic pressure drops, suggesting that magnetic fields in the atmosphere are less intense than those in the interior. Finally, the magnetic field profile for HD58260, derived from these gradients, is compared with the profile of HD152094, which exhibits a similar radial gradient. This comparison supports the hypothesis that the magnetic field structure of HD58260 is shaped by an active region located on its surface. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. The discovery of low-mass galaxies with stellar masses comparable to the Milky Way's has enabled the study of star formation characteristics in the early Universe through observations of nearby low-metallicity analogs. This study utilizes ALMA data to examine star formation in the galaxy NGC 5253, focusing on the spatial distribution of the H30$\alpha$ emission line at 349.9 $\mu$m. We present the first high-resolution maps of this line and analyze the relationship between the H30$\alpha$ emission line width and surface brightness. By comparing these observations with models of the H${_3^+}$ ion, we demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ emission is primarily driven by the photo-dissociation region (PDR) surrounding young massive stars rather than being solely a recombination line. Consequently, the H30$\alpha$ emission is expected to be spatially concentrated near young stellar populations. Our analysis of the galaxy reveals a significant correlation between H30$\alpha$ emission and both 1.4 GHz radio emission and ionized gas, indicating that the H30$\alpha$ is a robust tracer of star formation. We conclude that the H30$\alpha$ emission line is a promising tool for detecting star formation in low-metallicity galaxies. The strong correlation between H30$\alpha$ and radio emission allows for the derivation of star formation rates via the fundamental plane of local star-forming galaxies. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of the H30$\alpha$ emission line emission measure (H30$\alpha$ line width $\times$ H30$\alpha$ surface brightness) aligns closely with radio emission, suggesting that the H30$\alpha$ traces star formation on scales of approximately 100 pc. This line offers a means to identify star formation sites at very high spatial resolution, even in galaxies lacking significant molecular gas. Additionally, the H30$\alpha$ emission is observed in galaxies exhibiting star formation activity. These findings confirm that PDRs are the main source of H30$\alpha$ emission in galaxies with low metallicity (Z $\sim$ 0.2 Z$_{\odot}$), and we propose that the H30$\alpha$ emission line serves as a valuable tool for investigating star formation in the early Universe. We demonstrate that for any two continuous minimal (topologically free) actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space, continuous orbit equivalence implies conjugacy. Furthermore, we establish that this result does not hold when the infinite dihedral group is substituted with specific other virtually cyclic groups, such as the direct product of the integers and any non-abelian finite simple group. Our proof utilizes an inductive approach that does not rely on model theory. Additionally, we examine instances where two topologically free actions are continuous orbit equivalent but admit no conjugate minimal minimal sets. Finally, we prove that for any infinite compact group $G$, there exist continuous minimal (topologically free) $G$-actions where the implication "continuous orbit equivalence implies conjugacy" fails. These examples encompass all known cases where such a failure occurs and involve compact Lie groups. However, it remains an open question whether a non-Lie compact group exists with this property. We also explore the relationship between orbit equivalence and conjugacy within our framework by presenting examples where the existence of a minimal set for the orbit equivalence transformation does not guarantee the existence of a minimal set for the conjugating homeomorphism. Finally, we suggest that many of our methods can be adapted to infinite amenable Lie groups, potentially extending similar results to these settings. **Keywords:** Minimal sets, Topologically free actions, Continuous orbit equivalence, Conjugacy. **Mathematics Subject Classification:** 37B02, 37B22, 37B40, 37C10, 37C80.

We examine the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator $m(\cdot| \cdot)$, which represents the conditional expectation $E[\cdot | \cdot]$, by a finite-dimensional operator $m_n(\cdot| \cdot)$ using only marginal densities as data. Our primary assumption is a weak conditional entropy condition. We demonstrate that the Hilbert-Schmidt approximation error of $m_n$ decreases at the optimal rate for any trace-class operator, including bounded functions, provided the operator satisfies the conditional entropy assumption. This result relies on a recent finding by the second author and P. Graczyk regarding the finite-dimensional approximation of $L^2$ operators via the method of poly-conditional-modes. Furthermore, for specific subclasses of $m$, including bounded functions, stronger rates can be achieved if the conditional entropy exponent is optimized as a function of the marginal densities' smoothness. We also present results concerning the pointwise convergence of $m_n$ to $m$ in $L^p$ spaces. Finally, we apply our findings to kernel regression and density estimation, proving that the pointswise convergence of kernel estimates to $m$ depends on the conditional entropy assumption and the smoothness of the involved densities. Additionally, we construct kernel estimates for $m$ achieving optimal convergence rates under marginal density assumptions alone. These theoretical results are supported by finite sample evidence. Notably, in regression settings, our assumptions are weaker than those required by conventional kernel regression methods. Finally, we illustrate how this framework facilitates the approximation of a broad class of functionals of $m$. To our knowledge, this work provides the first nonparametric statistical estimates using solely marginal densities to infer conditional expectations. However, it is important to acknowledge the potential for explosive behavior in $m$ when the error term is small yet non-zero, a phenomenon that can cause this class of estimates to diverge. We address this issue through a case study on the Lorenz-1983 attractor. To mitigate this divergence, we introduce a variant of $m_n$ with finite variance, along with finite-sample evidence. To our understanding, this represents the first application of this framework to time series analysis. Our approach is particularly well-suited for analyzing chaotic time series where the underlying dynamics are well-approximated by a Markov process. In this context, $m_n$ serves as a viable alternative to embedding techniques for approximating the underlying Markov operator. This study addresses the development of reduced-order observers for a specific nonlinear state variable transformation linked to a nonlinear ordinary differential equation process, specifically the standard susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) epidemic model with a constant population under mass action transmission. The goal is to ensure that the difference between the local reduced-order observer and the true process transformation converges exponentially to zero in the uniform norm. Additionally, a customized reduced-order observer for the Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) model with linear linearization is developed. Both observers are designed to maintain exponential uniform stability within the observer error. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the logarithmic norm of the error dynamics matrix can be made negative by adjusting the parameters of the linearized process and the gain matrix in the reduced-order observer. These findings are validated through numerical simulations. In both cases, we construct reduced-order observers and evaluate their performance. Notably, for the US case, the observer proves highly effective in estimating the transmission rate from susceptible, exposed, and recovered data, as well as the removal rate from recovered and dead data. Integrating temporal information into knowledge graphs has emerged as a significant research area, with numerous methods demonstrating strong performance in linking entity pairs within time-sensitive contexts. However, these approaches often struggle to effectively capture static knowledge, which remains crucial for linking specific entity pairs. This paper analyzes the benefits of static knowledge for link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs and proposes adapting state-of-the-art static models to this domain. Specifically, we introduce TempUS, a straightforward adaptation of USTACL from the static model category. Experimental results show that TempUS is highly competitive with intricate temporal models, consistently delivering consistent performance across various benchmark datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwin-krishnan/TempUS. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that incorporating static knowledge aids in predicting links with strong temporal dependencies, whereas utilizing temporal information assists in leveraging general background knowledge to predict links supported by static data. Finally, we observe that static models excel in terms of F1 scores across different time periods. These insights indicate that static models help identify potential relationships that may emerge in the future, even if they are not immediately supported by time-specific evidence. Overall, we demonstrate that static models can be effectively leveraged for link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs, offering both performance gains and a framework for interpreting static knowledge's role in this context. Our work also highlights the necessity of designing knowledge graphs with sufficient time annotations to fully exploit the advantages of temporal models. Finally, we note that our analysis deepens the understanding of how to integrate knowledge graphs with time-dependent reasoning. This leads to the conclusion that static models should be prioritized during training to ensure knowledge graph representations remain learnable even with limited temporal data. This approach ensures that time-specific information enhances rather than degrades prediction performance. By balancing the utilization of static and temporal knowledge, static models can predict links with high confidence, even in scenarios with sparse time annotations. This underscores the critical need for effective time annotation strategies to maximize the utility of temporal models in temporal knowledge graph link prediction. Ultrashort pulses generated by Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators have enabled numerous applications, particularly in the ultra-high peak power regime. Nevertheless, current research has primarily concentrated on peak power scaling, leaving the underlying physics of this technology largely unexplored. This study investigates how ray propagation geometry influences beam quality and pulse characteristics. By applying ABCD matrix theory, we demonstrate how to predict key metrics such as pulse width, cavity stability, beam quality, and nonlinear phase accumulation. These theoretical findings are supported by experimental results from an oscillator producing 1.0 ps pulses with a 1.0 mm waist and 200 fs pulses with a 0.075 m radius. Ultimately, the results indicate that waists exceeding 1 mm are essential for achieving femtosecond pulse durations in this system. The ray geometry analysis provides valuable insights for future experimental and theoretical studies, specifically aiding in the design of high-peak-power, ultrashort pulse oscillators. Additionally, the theoretical results are expected to find application in other fields utilizing high-peak-power ultrafast oscillators. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for the continued development and scaling of ultrafast oscillators toward higher peak powers.
