This paper introduces and examines a stochastic Newton approach designed for homogeneous distributed stochastic convex optimization. In this framework, individual machines compute stochastic gradients and stochastic Hessian-vector products—derived from unbiased estimates of the population objective's Hessian applied to arbitrary vectors—multiple times between communication intervals. We demonstrate that this method lowers both the quantity and frequency of necessary communication rounds relative to current techniques, maintaining equivalent performance. This claim is supported by convergence analysis for both homogeneous and heterogeneous data scenarios. Specifically, we establish convergence rates regarding the distance to the population optimality region, drawing parallels to the analysis of stochastic gradient descent, with convergence velocities comparable to those of stochastic gradient methods. Furthermore, we prove that the method converges to a Kullback-Leibler divergence ball matching the rate of stochastic gradient descent, and for inhomogeneous data, we demonstrate convergence to a specific weighted average of population optimality regions as defined by minimization over time. Finally, we apply the proposed algorithm to stochastic logistic regression and include numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets to validate the theoretical findings. The results indicate that the method rivals state-of-the-art centralized methods while offering significant reductions in both computation and communication costs. Additionally, we present an empirical analysis of how both sufficient and asymptotic homogeneity impacts convergence behavior.

This study presents the initial effort to address the challenge of detecting hate speech in multiple Indian languages, specifically Bengali and Hindi. We introduce a comprehensive dataset comprising comments scraped from Twitter, alongside a standardized procedure for their annotation. Our methodology employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) to develop both uni-lingual and multi-lingual models, with a specific focus on transfer learning. The acquired data has been made publicly available. Additionally, we present the first detailed analysis of the effects of transfer learning on Hindi and Hindi-on-Hindi multilingual tasks. Finally, we benchmark our model's performance against existing methods and conclude that transfer learning yields the most significant improvements, particularly when annotator consensus is low. The dataset and associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/HatE-SCRAPE.

High-sensitivity gas Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) serve as the primary detectors for numerous fundamental particle physics experiments, including those investigating dark matter, majorana neutrinos, neutrinoless double beta decay, and nuclear forces. These fundamental investigations frequently depend on identifying the specific element of detector recoil atoms. This capability is crucial for cross-validating results across different TPC experiments, correlating findings from multiple target isotopes in a single experiment, and for distinguishing between various target impurities in dark matter searches. This document series outlines methods for achieving element identification in gas TPCs by measuring the specific ionization ($dE/dx$) of recoil particles. Specifically, Part 1 examines the statistical analysis of $dE/dx$ distributions from particle-anticorrelation data to achieve element identification. Part 2 then details the optimization of $dE/dx$ measurement resolution through pattern recognition and data analysis techniques. The primary metric for evaluating the effectiveness of these approaches is the fraction of recoils successfully identified as belonging to a specific element. Ultimately, the scenarios presented in this series are tailored to the constraints of upcoming large-scale gas TPC experiments, where recoils are expected to have low energies (typically a few keV or less) and low ionization yields (ranging from a few to a few hundred ions). These conditions result in significant statistical uncertainties regarding the number of ions per recoil, making element identification challenging. Consequently, this document series offers a comprehensive overview of the techniques necessary for achieving such identification. We anticipate that the methods discussed herein will prove valuable for gas TPC researchers engaged in searches for dark matter, neutrinoless double beta decay, and nuclear forces. Furthermore, we expect these techniques to provide a robust foundation for future large-scale gas TPC experiments. For instance, in gas TPC experiments utilizing multi-isotope targets such as xenon, this approach could facilitate the identification of the majority of the xenon component in the total recoil population. This would substantially aid in calibrating the neutrinoless double beta decay search and assist in separating the target from contaminants such as majorana neutrinos, solar neutrinos, and other impurities. Ultimately, these advancements could help resolve long-standing discrepancies in the field. To achieve this, we anticipate that over 90% of the detector's xenon recoils will be identified as xenon. Similarly, for gas TPC experiments searching for majorana neutrinos, we expect that over 90% of the detector's indium recoil population will be successfully identified

Commercial driving represents a complex, hazardous occupation that demands extensive training and experience. Recent advancements in computer vision and deep learning have significantly enhanced safety by enabling intelligent vehicle systems to detect pedestrians and facilitate automated braking and obstacle avoidance. Despite these progressions, the widespread adoption of such systems in commercial driving remains hindered by their "black box" characteristics, which make them difficult to interpret and trust. This study investigates the specific incidents of braking and pedestrian detection where machine decisions deviate from human experts' judgments, offering insights into the necessary refinements for intelligent vehicle systems. Through an extensive analysis of over 100,000 decisions across more than 25,000 datasets, we demonstrate that existing machine outputs require substantial adjustment to align with human expert evaluations. Furthermore, the paper offers actionable recommendations for improving machine decision-making to achieve a fair assessment of commercial driving performance. Specifically, we propose incorporating context-aware expert moderation to align intelligent decisions with human norms and establishing a continuous feedback mechanism to support expert training and enhance machine learning capabilities. The goal is to enable intelligent vehicles to navigate real-world contexts with greater accuracy and reliability. This approach not only advances safety and reliability but also fosters a more equitable future for work in commercial driving. The datasets utilized in this study can be accessed via Github. By offering a comprehensive and practical understanding of how to improve decision-making in intelligent vehicle systems, this research serves as a vital contribution to the fields of computer vision, deep learning, and automated driving. Ultimately, the findings provide valuable insights for developing safer, more reliable, and equitable intelligent vehicles for real-world application. This paper details the final outcomes of the Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) Challenge, an ECMI initiative funded by the Portuguese Foundation for Science and Technology. The primary objective was to assess and compare various methods for handling OOV words during NLP tasks, specifically document classification and machine translation, using limited OOV information. The competition concluded with nearly 150 submissions across both tracks. This report highlights key observations regarding OOV handling strategies and OOV representation techniques. Furthermore, we present a novel OOV representation utilizing OOV frequency distributions across training document sets, OOV stem frequency, and OOV bit-parallel indexing. We validate the experimental results through an analysis of the top-performing submissions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/fgalao/OOV-Challenge. Our track record includes first place in all OOV evaluation metrics for both challenge tasks, achieving F1 scores of 0.694 and 0.712 for classification and machine translation, respectively. We present a mathematical framework for defining a metric on a random field manifold by utilizing geodesic distance among its realizations. This approach applies broadly to any space where an probability measure and a set of distance functions are defined between elements. We examine the fundamental characteristics of this random field manifold, including its dimension, metric properties, and the linearity of its geodesic paths. Furthermore, we outline applications within pattern recognition and cluster analysis, demonstrating that this framework yields alternative pattern classifiers and suggests new methods for determining the optimal number of clusters. Simulations confirm that these proposed methods achieve superior performance compared to established alternatives. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of the metric within deep learning by enhancing the generalization capabilities of Convolutional Neural Networks. Finally, we evaluate the performance of this metric on real-world datasets used in astrophysics and biology. These applications demonstrate that the proposed methodology either matches or exceeds the accuracy of existing methods while significantly reducing computational costs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ClusterRecognition/GeodesicClustering. Similar to other intrinsic cluster metrics, our method relies solely on inter-point distances within the data, ensuring model-agnosticism. Consequently, it is particularly well-suited for applications involving non-Euclidean data, such as those found in astrophysics, biology, and machine learning. Specifically, we show that the geodesic distance effectively identifies and separates bimodal distributions in manifold space that are indistinguishable using other clustering techniques. Our findings indicate that this approach offers a valuable tool for cluster analysis, for defining a meaningful metric on random field realization spaces, and for developing novel pattern recognition techniques. Supplementary materials are available at supplementary-materials.zip, which includes Jupyter notebooks containing detailed examples of applying the geodesic distance to real datasets in astrophysics, biology, and machine learning. Another application concerns clustering single-cell RNA sequencing data to identify distinct cell types. Finally, we highlight the use of the geodesic distance metric in deep learning, specifically showing how it aids in the generalization of Convolutional Neural Networks. We conduct Rayleigh-Taylor Instability experiments by employing magnetic levitation to induce a controlled initial perturbation. We observe that the periodicity of the resulting periods is contingent upon the initial perturbation amplitude, with distinct regimes of behavior identified across various orders of magnitude. A theoretical framework is proposed to characterize the predicted period, offering an explanation for the observed results. The impact of the Lebedev magnetic levitation technique is also examined. Furthermore, the failure to predict system behavior using a simple model based on the period and perturbation amplitude is addressed. Finally, the development of a robust, high-resolution high-speed camera is described, which is essential for future research. This equipment will facilitate the measurement of profiles and the determination of the effective reduced mass ratio. We conclude that this capability will enable a more precise validation of existing theories and potentially lead to the identification of additional behaviors. Let $F$ be a cuspidal Hecke eigenform for $Sp_n(Z)$ and $\chi$ a Dirichlet character, defining the standard $L$-function $L(s,F,\chi,St)$. Boecherer established that the denominators of the algebraic components of $L(m,F,\chi,St)$ at critical values $m$ remain bounded as $\chi$ varies. This paper presents a refined version of that theorem and extends a similar conclusion to products of Hecke $L$-functions associated with primitive forms for $SL_2(Z)$. We further explore applications of these findings to the study of supercongruences for the Ramanujan $\tau$-function. Additionally, we examine the broader boecherer-strassens question and the analogous problem posed by Li, Yeung, and Zudilin regarding the denominators of the $p$-adic interpolations of these $L$-values. Finally, our findings offer a partial resolution to a conjecture by Li and Zudilin concerning the denominators of $\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \binom{2p}{4k}^4$. This work is a partial fulfillment of the author's thesis under the supervision of Prof. Dr. B. Grossenbacher. This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for weakly nonlinear and monotone operators defined on Banach lattices of multivariate functions. The findings address convergence almost everywhere, convergence in measure, and convergence in $L^{p}$-norm, with several examples provided to demonstrate the theoretical framework. Additionally, the authors aim to extend the theorem's applicability to more general function spaces, such as vector lattices, by presenting several open problems for future research. Finally, the paper illustrates that the developed theory is relevant to various fields, including statistics, stochastic processes, and machine learning. Specifically, an application involving the estimation of a multivariate probability density function via kernel estimates is included. This estimator is proven to be non-decreasing on its support and to converge pointwise and in $L^{p}$ to the target density under specific conditions. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that smoothing these estimates within weakly nonlinear and monotone operators preserves the convergence properties. This learning application represents the first instance where the theory is applied to multivariate probability density estimators based on kernels with bounded kernels. While analogous applications exist for kernel approximations of non-increasing functions, the current work extends the scope to multivariate functions that are either non-decreasing or non-increasing along individual variables. The authors intend to explore this application with multivariate regression functions in a subsequent paper. Both applications rely on establishing weighted inequalities and applying them to the specific kernel smoothing method employed. These weighted inequalities hold significant independent interest and are also utilized in the theory of nonlinear and monotone operators on Banach lattices. Given their broad applicability, they are expected to be valuable in other areas involving the approximation of functions or operators on Banach lattices. To demonstrate this, an appendix includes multivariate functionals that preserve linearity, monotonicity, and mean continuity, which do not fall under the category of weakly nonlinear operators. Approximating these functionals serves as an alternative example to the weakly nonlinear operators discussed in the main text. This discussion begins by considering functionals on one-dimensional functions and subsequently examines their extension to higher dimensions. This approach underscores the broader applicability of the theory, as it addresses nonlinear and monotone operators on Banach lattices of univariate functions. Overall, this work represents a step toward developing a comprehensive theory for the approximation of weakly nonlinear and monotone operators on Banach lattices of multivariate functions. A graph with $n$ vertices is defined as pancyclic if it includes a cycle of every length $l$ where $3 \le l \le n$. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that for a Hamiltonian graph on $n > 4k^4$ vertices with an independence number of $k$, the graph is necessarily pancyclic. He subsequently proposed that the condition $k = o(n)$ is both sufficient and required for this conclusion to hold. This study confirms the sufficiency of that condition by proving that any Hamiltonian graph with an independence number $k \le 2.622 \frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ is pancyclic. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the condition $k = o(n)$ cannot be strengthened further, as there exist Hamiltonian graphs where $k \approx 1.61 n$ that are not pancyclic. Additionally, the paper investigates the pancyclicity of graphs that are Hamiltonian via a specific type of closure operation, revealing that determining when such graphs are pancyclic is significantly more complex than the original problem. Finally, the results establish new, tighter bounds and identify numerous open questions and conjectures within this domain. Notably, the paper concludes by demonstrating that no Hamiltonian graph exists with an independence number exceeding $n - 2$ that is not pancyclic, thereby resolving an issue first raised by Erdos in 1976. Finally, the topic of fractional independence numbers and their connection to pancyclicity is examined. Specifically, it is shown that every Hamiltonian graph with an independence number of $0.5n$ is pancyclic, advancing previous work by Erdos and others on bipartite graphs and non-bipartite graphs with independence numbers of $0.5n - 1$. The validity of this result for graphs with independence numbers strictly less than $0.5n$ remains an open question. The term "fractional independence number" was originally suggested by Erdos. The proof strategy for the main theorem draws inspiration from Erdos's own approach, yet represents a more sophisticated version of his original argument. Ultimately, the findings suggest that $k = o(n)$ serves as the tightest possible condition for guaranteeing pancyclicity in Hamiltonian graphs. The term "pancyclic" was also suggested by Erdos. This study details the directed flow of charged pions, kaons, and protons generated in $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}$ = 200 GeV Au+Au and isobar collisions, as measured by the PHOS detector at the RHIC PHENIX experiment. Systematic trends regarding the influence of charged hadron production sources are examined as a function of charged pion, kaon, and proton rapidity. The analysis reveals that the slope of the directed flow versus rapidity ($dv_{1}/dy$) for pions, kaons, and protons decreases with increasing transverse momentum ($p_{\textrm{T}}$) across all rapidity intervals. These experimental findings are compared with simulations derived from viscous hydrodynamic models coupled to hadronization frameworks. The results indicate that the directed flow of light hadrons at negative rapidity is primarily determined by the equation of state and the topological structure of the QCD phase diagram, whereas heavy hadrons exhibit a stronger directed flow. Furthermore, the study confirms that the spin-orbit interaction between quarks and the quark-meson model can account for the observed directed flow of light hadrons. A key distinction between RHIC and LHC conditions is that the slope of $dv_{1}/dy$ for protons exceeds that of pions at negative rapidity in RHIC collisions, whereas this trend reverses at LHC energies. Additionally, the data show that the ratio of $p/\pi$ directed flow slopes is independent of charged kaon to proton directed flow ratios, suggesting that the directed flow of heavy hadrons is driven by the initial spatial anisotropy of the collision system. Finally, variations in the directed flow slopes among Au, $^{150}$Nd, $^{124}$Xe, and $^{129}$Xe+Yb are linked to the mass and charge of the participating ions. Overall, this work enhances our comprehension of directed flow generation mechanisms and highlights the critical role of spin-orbit interactions in heavy-ion collisions. The combined experimental and theoretical approach employed here establishes a foundation for future investigations into directed flow. The adaptive spectral Koopman (ASK) method has recently demonstrated superior performance compared to standard spectral kernel methods by achieving high accuracy with fewer collocation points. This paper extends the ASK framework to handle high-dimensional systems more efficiently. We introduce a sparse-grid-based adaptive spectral Koopman method that offers a substantial computational advantage over traditional ASK approaches. These spectral kernel methods are designed to generate low-rank approximations of the full-rank Koopman operator. Numerical experiments utilizing both low- and high-dimensional nonlinear systems validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. Additionally, the method is applied to reconstruct the full set of invariant manifolds within a nonlinear normal form system. The available code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongliangchen/sparsegridKoopman. This study investigates the use of exterior complex scaling (ECS) within relativistic density functional theory (DFT) for systems subjected to constant electric fields. The relativistic ECS approach is established, achieving convergence with a scaling angle of 1.57 rad (~90 degrees) applied in a region 20 Bohr radii distant from the origin. The method's accuracy is validated by comparing molecular orbital energies and electron densities against numerical differentiator (ND) results derived from relativistic DFT. Furthermore, the ECS approach demonstrates successful modeling of relativistic DFT nodes in scaled space. Finally, the efficacy of the external complex scaling technique is illustrated through calculations of relativistic relativistic stabilization zones (RSZ) and relativistic butterfly structures (RBS) for various diatomic molecules under DC fields. The findings confirm that both RSZ and RBS exhibit symmetry under reflection across the plane perpendicular to the field direction and along the field axis when the two atomic species are identical. Additionally, it is observed that these zones and structures vanish at sufficiently high field strengths. These observations align with non-relativistic calculations regarding the presence or absence of such regions. However, a key distinction arises from relativistic effects: while non-relativistic molecules display RBS structures on both sides of the z=0 plane, relativistic structures appear only on one side due to spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, the observed relativistic threshold for field-induced dissociation is lower than the corresponding non-relativistic threshold. These results provide a comprehensive framework for future calculations utilizing the external complex scaling method alongside relativistic DFT. The proposed approach is also applicable to molecules in strong magnetic fields and atoms or molecules without external fields. Finally, the paper includes a supplementary appendix detailing the minimal basis set, numerical integration scheme, and exchange-correlation functional employed in these computations. This work serves as a foundational reference for future studies employing external complex scaling with relativistic DFT. Keywords: exterior complex scaling, relativistic DFT, relativistic stabilization zones, relativistic butterfly structures, relativistic density functional theory, constant electric field, constant magnetic field. The Sinkhorn algorithm is the leading approach for addressing the Schrödinger problem; this study examines its behavior in scenarios where no valid solution exists. We demonstrate that, provided the optimal relaxation remains bounded, the Sinkhorn iterates converge almost surely to a specific limit corresponding to a fixed point of an associated operator that minimizes the asymptotic free energy. Furthermore, we establish analogous findings for a gradient descent method applied to the logarithm of free energy, highlighting that these two limiting fixed points generally differ. Finally, we present numerical examples to illustrate these theoretical results. Notably, in the case of Gaussian distributions commonly discussed in the literature, the Schrödinger problem admits a solution, rendering these convergence guarantees redundant. Consequently, our analysis concentrates on more complex cases, specifically involving gamma distributions, although the method itself is broadly applicable. Additionally, while prior literature often assumes square marginals for Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma distributions, we demonstrate that this assumption is not universally necessary. To the best of our knowledge, this specific case has not been previously addressed in the literature. Our theoretical findings rely on the convexity of the gamma function and the properties of Gamma distributions, suggesting that these conclusions may extend to other distribution types, including those governed by the beta function. We have also formulated a distinct set of assumptions for handling general marginals. Furthermore, we introduce a novel concept termed "local free energy," which facilitates the analysis of gradient descent convergence within a neighborhood of a fixed point and supports our theoretical framework. These results are deeply interconnected with stochastic processes, a relationship we also explore. Finally, we compare the performance of various fixed-point solutions and discuss their potential practical applications. Our numerical experiments indicate that the gradient descent algorithm may require more iterations than the Sinkhorn algorithm to converge, a contrast to typical applications of the Sinkhorn algorithm. However, we also observe that, in certain instances, the gradient descent method converges significantly faster than the Sinkhorn algorithm. These findings underscore the necessity of theoretical convergence proofs for the Sinkhorn algorithm in the context of the Schrödinger problem, a task that remains an open challenge. To our knowledge, such proofs are currently limited to scenarios involving Gaussian distributions with full rank covariances. In these cases, we note that the free energy is known to be convex, a property that likely does not hold in more general settings. This work serves as a preliminary investigation into the convergence of the Sinkhorn algorithm when no solution to the Schrödinger problem exists. Although most energy transfer research focuses on systems beginning near or within their local minima, investigating launches from elevated energy states offers distinct benefits, including simpler dynamics and observables. This study examines counter-intuitive energy transfer phenomena that arise from high-energy conditions. We demonstrate that selecting an appropriate launch point enables non-rapidity coupling between adjacent systems, allowing the inner one to retain energy for extended periods. Furthermore, we uncover a counter-intuitive relationship where increasing the launch height initially accelerates the equalization of the coupled systems, before eventually slowing it down. These mechanisms hold significant promise for applications ranging from vacuum insulation to energy storage. The findings are derived from both numerical simulations and experimental data. Additionally, the associated video highlights the striking asymmetry in energy transfer within the coupled system. A supplementary document is available for readers interested in the specific release mechanism. Finally, to ensure reproducibility, all code and data are provided in a public repository. \newline

Urban interactions are fundamental to the sustainability of human societies. Recent research indicates that public health measures introduced to curb the spread of SARS-CoV-2 may have caused shifts in how people engage with one another. By applying movement data from over 50 cities across 15 nations, we demonstrate that income diversity within urban encounters deteriorated under these lockdown policies. This finding implies that while lockdowns may have served their primary goal of limiting virus transmission, they risked undermining the core objective of cities to foster social coexistence. Consequently, this presents a significant challenge for future urban urbanism. Furthermore, this study highlights the potential of movement data for conducting scientific social studies. To ensure the reproducibility of these findings, the code is accessible at https://github.com/leostill/lockdown-lockdown. City-specific results can be found in the supplementary materials. Given the global impact of the pandemic, the associated Github repository is expected to grow continuously. The authors gratefully acknowledge the contributions of all data providers. This research introduces two nonlinear field-splitting preconditioners tailored for two-phase flow within heterogeneous porous media. We evaluate and contrast these new methods against two existing nonlinear field-split and field-split preconditioners. Assuming access to efficient solvers for single-phase flow in heterogeneous environments, both of our proposed preconditioners leverage such a solver to handle the resulting single-phase systems. All four preconditioners are resolved using the fixed-point Black-Oil model. Numerical experiments demonstrate that one of our new approaches, which utilizes a linear least-squares optimization method identical to that in a prior field-split preconditioner, offers a substantial reduction in CPU time compared to all other options, while also exhibiting superior robustness for the specific class of problems under consideration. Since all field-split preconditioners require a substantially higher number of inner linear solves than our new least-squares approach, we argue that this characteristic serves as a critical metric for assessing preconditioner efficiency. Finally, we extend one of our new preconditioners to a three-phase scenario, observing a moderate decrease in the number of outer iterations required for convergence. However, we note a significant increase in inner linear iterations for this three-phase case, resulting in no overall time savings. Consequently, we contend that evaluating two- and three-phase systems using distinct single-phase solvers is essential for achieving an efficient field-split preconditioner in highly heterogeneous two- or three-phase flow cases. Our field-split preconditioners described herein are intended for highly heterogeneous systems where capillary-dominated least-squares solvers are unsuitable. We acknowledge that these solvers could be incorporated into our work for less heterogeneous systems, though that is beyond the scope of this study. This paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec:model} presents the mathematical model, and Section \ref{sec:methods} details the algorithms. Section \ref{sec:results} reports numerical results comparing the four preconditioners, followed by Section \ref{sec:conclusion}, which offers conclusions and suggestions for future research. These future directions include developing efficient field-split preconditioners for three-phase flow with moderate heterogeneity and creating a unified single-phase solver for both two-phase and three-phase systems. These issues are addressed in our ongoing and upcoming work. We introduce a new class of optical cavities featuring single-handed chiral components, characterized by their exceptional ability to generate, manipulate, and detect single-handed chiral light. Specifically, we highlight the distinct maximal/minimal optical axis ellipticity and the pronounced circular/linear/bilinear polarization anisotropy that arise from the properties of these cavities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that single-handed chiral cavities exhibit single-handed optical anisotropy, defined as either preferential absorption of one handedness of linearly polarized light or the absolute absorption of linearly polarized light with a specific ellipticity and optical axis. Additionally, we find that these cavities display the absolute depolarization of incident coherent light within a single-handness polarization state, accompanied by the preservation of ellipticity and the maximal or minimal projection onto the Fresnel ellipsometric circle. Finally, we propose single-handed chiral cavity enhanced circular dichroism spectroscopy and emphasize that single-handed chiral optical cavities hold both fundamental and practical significance. We anticipate that this proposed concept will inspire further advancements in chiral optics and technologies. The findings in this Letter were published in Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 113801 (2019). The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/zhaozhijun1982/Single-handness-chiral-optical-cavities. This paper investigates the relationship between Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity on two-dimensional anti-de Sitter spaces and the semiclassical limit of $c<1$ two-dimensional string theory. The world-sheet theory of the latter comprises a space-like Liouville CFT coupled to a non-rational CFT defined by a time-like Liouville CFT. We demonstrate that their actions, disk partition functions, and annulus amplitudes are in perfect agreement, with one minor caveat: a specific counter-term in the Liouville CFT action is essential for the latter description. Additionally, we derive a relationship between the JT gravity and 2D time-like Liouville CFT central charges, finding that time-like Liouville central charges correspond to the central charge of a specific boundary JT gravity. Finally, we identify a matrix model dual to our proposed two-world-sheet theory using a double-trace deformation. We anticipate that this finding will facilitate further connections between 2D quantum gravity and conformal field theory. Our findings suggest that low-energy 2D quantum gravity demands a more intricate theoretical framework than previously assumed. *Note: This work was completed before the release of arXiv:2105.04006.* (See Acknowledgements for details.) The Alcubierre metric defines a spacetime geometry enabling superluminal travel through a "warp drive" effect,achieved by contracting and expanding space ahead of and behind a moving packet of negative energy. Originally formulated within the 3+1 ADM formalism using a 0+3 decomposition, this paper extends the original solution to include the cosmological constant. By employing the 3+1 formalism, we derive the minimal energy conditions associated with the generalization. The resulting line element represents a perfect fluid solution where the fluid's 4-velocity is aligned with the timelike Killing vector, and the metric depends on all four coordinates. This approach allows for the efficient calculation of energy conditions via line integrals. Furthermore, this decomposition facilitates the direct computation of the ADM mass for the system. We specifically analyze the lines of action for all perfect fluid components and examine the Schwarzschild case, demonstrating that all conditions can be satisfied within a finite region. Finally, we investigate how the warping of the fluid flow arises from the interaction between the fluid components and the spacetime curvature. These findings may contribute to the theoretical development of theoretical frameworks for warp drives. Notably, all conditions remain satisfiable within a finite region when the cosmological constant is present. Advancing urban planning, design, and management necessitates the integration of data from diverse sources, including sensors, satellite imagery, and existing government records. The GUIDES (Geospatial Urban Infrastructure Data Engineering Solutions) initiative is envisioned as a framework that enables the combination of this varied data. While numerous individual projects have successfully created high-quality data within the city of Utrecht, these datasets often utilize incompatible formats, coordinate reference systems, and schemas, thereby obstructing their interconnection. This paper outlines the initial steps of GUIDES to develop a unified data foundation for Utrecht. Building on this approach, the GUIDES foundation aims to facilitate: 1) enhanced data interoperability; 2) more efficient data management; 3. reduced application development costs; and 4. significant cost savings. Establishing such a foundation is essential for advancing Data-Driven Cities. GUIDES serves as a prototype that can be adapted for the broader implementation of urban data foundations. Establishing a city-wide data foundation presents numerous challenges, including the management of data quality, the definition of appropriate metadata, and the selection of foundational data assets. This article provides practical insights into the specific issues encountered during the development of the GUIDES foundation for Utrecht. Additionally, it proposes a process for identifying foundational data assets and methods for harmonizing data through the use of intermediate tables. The paper concludes by discussing how to generalize this process for the development of urban data foundations. Keywords: Smart City, GUIDES, data foundation, intermediate tables, foundational assets, data harmonization. The GUIDES foundation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/GUIDEs-org/GUIDEs. We establish an experimental framework to measure the local, mode-by-mode thermal population of a two-dimensional Paul trap using spin-dependent ion motional coupling. By applying spin-depending Doppler cooling and laser heating, we examine how different methods of thermalization impact the classical occupation numbers ($\bar{n}$) of trap modes. We find that while global heating rates are similar, the background mode population $\bar{n}_0$ and heating behaviors differ significantly based on the thermalization method. Furthermore, we quantify the inhomogeneity of $\bar{n}$ across the ion chain, which can reach magnitudes of $|\Delta \bar{n}/\bar{n}_0| \sim 10^3$. This measurement technique offers a versatile approach for characterizing the thermal state of arbitrary motional modes in large-scale trapped-ion quantum simulators. Additionally, we explore how these findings influence the interpretation of thermalization processes in quantum spin models, demonstrating that different experimental signatures arise from varying roles of local versus delocalized trap modes. We introduce and justify fully quantum mechanical approaches designed to investigate the light–matter interaction within Time-Resolved Enhanced Raman Scattering (TERSR) spectroscopy. Our treatment of the electronic structure explicitly incorporates the Jahn-Teller effect. This theoretical framework is validated using the fully hydrogenated silicon cluster (SiH$_8$) as a case study. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the light-matter interaction strength and the spatial characteristics of the silicon-hydrogen bonding orbitals. Additionally, our findings suggest that TERS can facilitate the observation of weak light–matter interactions in systems where such interactions are typically un detectable in standard spectroscopy. We also explore the challenges associated with extending these methods to larger molecular systems. Finally, we outline strategies for enhancing computational efficiency through effective core potentials and by limiting the size of the basis set required to describe the light–matter interaction. Last but not least, we address the phenomenon of electromagnetic enhancement in TERS. To our knowledge, this represents the first fully quantum mechanical examination of the non-resonant light–matter interaction within the same theoretical framework used to describe the electronic structure of the molecule under study. We conclude by discussing the necessity of such an approach to accurately analyze the non-resonant light–matter interaction in TERS. Finally, we outline future prospects for developing fully quantum mechanical theories in this critical experimental technique. These efforts aim to deepen our understanding of the physical phenomena underlying TERS and to foster a stronger connection between theoretical and experimental research in this vital field. To facilitate these goals, we have made our code publicly accessible. Specifically, the code required to reproduce the results presented in this work can be found at: https://github.com/SebastianKuhn/PyQTE. Additional codes relevant to this field are also available at: https://github.com/SebastianKuhn/pyQTE-TERS. We also provide a tutorial on how to utilize these codes to reproduce our findings. We conducted observations of 27 nearby galaxies using the Sardinia Radio Telescope to detect Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) in the K-band at 20.53 GHz. Our findings indicate that 26 of these galaxies exhibit spectral energy distributions (SEDs) consistent with conventional radio emission mechanisms, such as synchrotron and free-free emission, alongside thermal dust emission. No evidence of AME was found in any of the observed galaxies. By utilizing K-band data, we established upper limits on AME for 26 galaxies, while one galaxy, NGC 4435, shows lower limits. The derived AME upper limits range from approximately 10$^{-10}$ to 10$^{-8}$ W m$^{-2}$ sr$^{-1}$. These results, combined with previously published AME upper limits from the XXT-FAST survey, cover a broad spectrum of surface brightness values. Furthermore, the XXT-FAST data align with the AME amplitude and surface area values reported by Miville-Allaire et al. (2017) for galaxies within the COSMOS field. This suggests that utilizing K-band observations of nearby galaxies is an effective method for investigating AME. Additionally, the SRT data demonstrate that using higher frequencies for AME searches is a viable approach. Future observations with the SRT are expected to further enhance our understanding of AME. The K-band spectral index values ($\alpha_K$) for the 27 galaxies were also calculated. Finally, the SRT data enable the study of AME in various galaxy types, including starburst galaxies, interacting systems, and dwarf galaxies. The data are accessible via the CDS archive.

Ammonium sulfate ((NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$) exhibits a substantial electrocaloric effect, likely due to the ferroelectric nature of its entropy. To investigate the ferroelectric characteristics of this material, we conducted first-principles calculations on its high-temperature cubic phase, which transitions into a low-temperature tetragonal phase. Our findings indicate that the large entropy change observed during the ferroelectric transition stems from the ferroelectric polarization of the sulfate anion, rather than the ammonium cation. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this polarization arises from hybridization between oxygen $p$ orbitals and sulfur $p$ orbitals. The significance of the sulfur anion's polarization in (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$ distinguishes it from most other hydrogen-bonded molecular crystals, where proton donor/acceptor groups typically drive polarization via hybridization between the donor/acceptor and the group's central atom. Additionally, our analysis of the electronic structure reveals that the ferroelectric transition involves a symmetry-breaking orbital reconstruction, a feature that sets it apart from the hydrogen bond rearrangement seen in other molecular crystals. The orbital reconstruction is linked to a soft mode that is both symmetric under the ferroelectric displacement and Raman active, a unique property not commonly observed in other molecular crystals. Finally, our calculations confirm that the entropy associated with the sulfate anion significantly exceeds that of the ammonium cation, providing a microscopic rationale for the large entropy change of (NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$ and explaining its exceptional electrocaloric response. This study highlights the existence of a previously unknown class of molecular crystals, in which the central atom of the functional group plays a pivotal role in determining the ferroelectric properties. This discovery expands the landscape of molecular crystals and offers a novel category of materials with high energy efficiency for solid-state cooling applications. To further explore the physical properties of the sulfate anion, we computed its vibrational entropy, polarizability, and charge transfer. Our results show that the polarizability of the (SO$_4$)$^{2-}$ anion is approximately 4.0 A$^3$ e$^{-2}$, a value comparable to that of perovskite oxides, suggesting that the (SO$_4$)$^{2-}$ anion could be a viable candidate for use as an anion in complex oxides or double perovskites where a large electrocaloric effect is desired. Individual differences in personality traits influence the balance between behavioral flexibility and habit formation. While midbrain neurons encode reward-related signals that govern the learning of habits, the extent to which distinct personality dimensions correlate with these brain mechanisms remains unclear. This study investigates the connections between subscores of a personality inventory and neural activity during reinforcement learning. We developed a method to extract individual-specific, subscore-wise learning rates from functional magnetic resonance imaging data, accounting for hemispheric variations. Our results indicate that subscores from both the "agreeableness" and "conscientiousness" dimensions of the Big Five Inventory exhibit significant correlations with midbrain activity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that suboptimal learning strategies, characterized by a reduced exploration-exploitation trade-off, correlate with an attenuated association between the discount parameter and the midbrain. These findings suggest that the midbrain's role in signaling reinforcement learning rates is influenced by specific aspects of individual differences in personality. The Wigner function, defined over the complexifications of the 240 elements of the $E_8$ root system, exhibits quantum-like properties, including non-contextuality violations analogous to Bell's inequalities. This manifestation of quantum behavior appears in the distribution's value distributions relative to three coplanar, equidistant (separated by 60 degrees) roots, as well as in the probability amplitudes of anti-podal (opposite) pairs. Furthermore, these special root triples facilitate quantum-like transitions between them and facilitate the decomposition of the fundamental representation into a direct sum involving a one-dimensional subspace. This capability to express "anti-rotations" of the $E_8$ root system aligns with characteristics found in both quantum mechanics and artificial neural networks. The discovered properties of the $E_8$ root system offer promising avenues for developing architectures and machine learning algorithms with quantum features, potentially enhancing the performance of machine learning tasks. Additionally, the $E_8$ root system demonstrates additional quantum-like traits, such as the value distributions emerging from the superposition of seven plane waves associated with seven linearly independent roots. This finding is significant because it reveals that quantum behavior arises not only in specific configurations of a few roots but also within the broader structure of the entire set. Consequently, this suggests that quantum effects are deeply embedded in the fundamental algebraic structure of the $E_8$ root system. These results may advance our understanding of the fundamental nature of quantum mechanics and its relationships with algebraic geometry and Lie algebra theory. Finally, the $E_8$ root system holds relevance for string theory, as its 240 elements correspond to the massless states of the low-energy effective theory of the second bosonic string. This connection may provide insights into the fundamental nature of the quantum world. Finally, this work introduces a new field of study termed "quantum-like mathematics." Root systems, including $E_8$, serve as fundamental mathematical structures in this endeavor, offering valuable insights into the nature of quantum mechanics. This approach may yield new perspectives on the foundations of quantum theory. The paper concludes with several open questions and potential avenues for future research. Specifically, recent findings indicate that the quantum-like behavior observed in the $E_8$ Wigner function extends to other exceptional Kac-Moody (extended) Lie algebras, such as those associated with the affine Dynkin diagrams of $E_6$ and $E_7$. This research investigates the core challenge of multilevel approximate near-neighbor (ANN) search under continuous Fréchet distance. We introduce an algorithm for discrete time series (with fixed dimension $d$) that achieves Fréchet $c$-approximation, $k$-approximate query time, and $s$-approximate recall, supported by $s$ precomputed data structures of size $f(d, c, k, \epsilon, (1-\sigma)n)$. Our findings establish that for any $k > 1$ and $c, \epsilon, \sigma > 0$, the recall parameter $s$ must satisfy $s = \Omega(\min\{n^{1/k}, \sqrt{n}\})$ and the memory usage must be $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. Furthermore, for the specific case where $k=2$, we demonstrate an algorithm (with $s=2$) featuring query time $O(q(d, c, 2, \epsilon, \sigma))$ and memory consumption of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. Notably, the first result supports the first lower bound established by the author, whereas the second finding refutes a conjecture proposed by Carmi et al. (2021). Additionally, we examine the complexity of this problem through the lens of fine-grained hardness assumptions. Finally, we present an algorithm for approximate 1-ANN search under continuous Fréchet distance for Euclidean time series of length $n$ and dimension $d$. This approach attains a Fréchet 1-approximation with query time $O(n^{2/d} \log^3 n)$ and recall $O(n^{1/d})$. For the practical scenario where $d=2$, the resulting query time is $O(\sqrt{n} \log^3 n)$. Our experimental evaluation indicates that the algorithm performs efficiently in practice, surpassing the theoretical worst-case bounds. This success is largely attributed to the fact that our algorithm does not explicitly compute the Fréchet distance between query pairs. Instead, it constructs a metric tree based on a specific embedding of shapes into a Banach space, leveraging the fact that continuous Fréchet distance corresponds to the Hausdorff distance within this embedding. The algorithm utilizes B-trees to perform range searches, which then identify query neighbors. Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) represents a post-processing approach designed to handle systematic readout errors that persist despite extensive mitigation efforts. While most prior MEM studies have focused on algorithms tailored for scaled circuit sizes, we demonstrate that this constraint is unnecessary. By applying an iterative Bayesian unfolding algorithm readout-by-readout to a scalable scalable MEM protocol, we show that complete state readout errors can be reversed. Our results indicate that the algorithm converges rapidly within three iterations on circuits ranging from 1 to 100 qubits when using synthetic data, and within five iterations with real noisy quantum data. Furthermore, the method proves its scalability by achieving convergence rates on 100-qubit circuits comparable to those observed on 10-qubit circuits. Finally, we observe that the approach maintains robust performance even under varying levels of stochastic noise. Collectively, these findings suggest that complete and robust mitigation of state readout errors is achievable, even in the presence of significant systematic and stochastic noise. Additionally, the ability to mitigate readout errors on large circuits with minimal overhead opens the door to extracting full fidelity information from quantum experiments that previously lacked the scale to report such data. When humans operate robot arms, the robots must infer the user's intentions. Recent research highlights that users significantly streamline this inference process by aligning their movements with the robot's own motor commands. This phenomenon, termed "shared autonomy," implies a symbiotic relationship where the robot serves not only its human operator but also anyone who might temporarily assume control. In this study, we demonstrate that shared autonomy can facilitate communication between humans and robots by integrating into the signals any data necessary for the robot to grasp an object. Through a participatory study, we gathered twelve sets of conventions from our laboratory, and our results indicate that these shared autonomy conventions are statistically more effective than those proposed by other methods, such as geometric approaches. Furthermore, we observe that shared autonomy acts as a bridge between high-level conventions and low-level gestures. Finally, we explore the broader implications of using shared autonomy to design human-machine interaction systems. Autonomous navigation within unknown settings is crucial for mobile robots, yet it remains challenging due to the dynamic and imbalanced nature of sensor data. We introduce HiTMap, a new map representation that offers a hierarchical, hierarchical topological structure, paired with HiTNav, a corresponding navigation strategy. Furthermore, utilizing a UAV to gather global map information enables the system to relocalize and restructure the map online. Extensive experiments and a real-world demonstration on a campus show that this approach significantly improves navigation performance in terms of efficiency and path optimality. The rapid advancement of wireless communication technology has created a demand for novel coding schemes capable of significantly lowering signal interference and enhancing system capacity. Z-complementary array codes represent a newly developed class of 2-D codes designed to mitigate interference in array signal processing and wireless communications. This paper introduces two methods for generating these codes via multivariable functions. The first approach constructs Z-complementary array code sets grouped into inter-group complementary code sets (Z-ACCSSICCS) by defining multivariable functions within finite fields. The second approach develops 2-D Z-complementary arrays derived from 1-D Z-complementary arrays; this is achieved by designing specific functions using a matrix iteration method and a direct product operation. Furthermore, specific instances (N=2, 4) of the second code set are categorized as implicitly designed Z-complementary array derived from 1-D Z-complementary arrays (IDZ-ACCSSICCS), demonstrating that the maximum size of this code set surpasses the 1-D case. Additionally, the implicit multi-group IDZ-ACCSSICCS represents a novel code set that expands the existing code pool. Finally, Z-complementary array patterns are generated through a tensor product operation, resulting in a new type of 4-D Z-complementary array derived from IDZ-ACCSSICCS. Simulation results confirm the validity of the proposed schemes. Notably, all code sets discussed in this work are constructed using multivariable functions, marking a significant advancement over previous research that relied on single-variable functions. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study represents the first application of multivariable functions to the design of Z-complementary array code sets. Furthermore, the resulting 4-D Z-complementary array constitutes a new code set, with its generation method representing a first-time achievement in the field. Overall, this work introduces novel coding schemes that expand the existing code pool and offer substantial theoretical and practical value. The proposed methods provide a new approach for constructing multi-dimensional Z-complementary array codes, a development that has not been achieved in prior literature. These schemes hold the potential to advance the development of various practical applications. Notably, Z-complementary array codes can be directly applied to array signal processing, wireless communications, and other practical domains. This paper also provides a detailed analysis of the spectral efficiency of 2-D Z-complementary array codes. Computed Tomography (CT) images suffer from severe artifacts when imaging objects with high-contrast boundaries. Although material decomposition (MD) can mitigate this issue, it demands greater computational resources. Consequently, we introduce a model combining total variation (TV) and demixing to achieve both noise reduction and MD within a single CT reconstruction framework. This approach utilizes latent variables and an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem. Furthermore, the proposed model is adaptable to various x-ray energy spectra, including polyenergetic scans. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques in both image quality and material separation accuracy. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/zhonghao1992/NonConvexMD.

This study examines how electron spill-out and nonlocality influence light propagation within the gap separating two semi-infinite metallic regions. We contrast a local response model, which accounts solely for spill-out, against a quantum hydrodynamic model capable of incorporating both effects. Our findings indicate that only the quantum hydrodynamic model accurately predicts the system's behavior as the gap closes; in contrast, the local model exhibits an unphysical amplification of light by several orders of magnitude in this limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain materials, such as gold, exhibit local-field effects that are sufficiently strong to invalidate the common assumption of negligible electron spill-out even at very small separations. These insights are crucial for the faithful interpretation of imaging results obtained using techniques like scanning near-field optical microscopy. Finally, we establish that valid results can be obtained using the parabolic (free-electron) band model when utilizing a local model, provided that local-field corrections are properly applied. The methodologies employed are also applicable to other scenarios involving light propagation in the nanoscale vacuum spaces between materials. The rise of NLP tasks involving the generation of rich textual descriptions of entities (such as in Wikipedia) has significantly increased the demand for systems capable of retrieving relevant entities based on natural language queries. Existing research in this area typically employs broad web search methods that perform Nomadic Named Entity Retrieval (NNER), in which an entity can migrate between documents. To address this, we introduce a document-level nomadic named entity retrieval technique. Our approach utilizes a relevance feedback loop that identifies similar examples from the corpus using a query's closest semantic neighbors, allowing those terms to replace general words in the embedding space during subsequent searches. We demonstrate that our method surpasses baseline approaches in terms of ranked retrieval quality, measured by Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Recall@K. Furthermore, through an ablation study, we highlight the effectiveness and interpretability of our proposed solution. Finally, we present insights into the characteristics of the dataset employed. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ashwin-krishnan/nler. Such interactivity is vital for data analysts to comprehend data transformations and their effects, fostering trust in multivariate time series (MTS) visualizations and supporting multivariate temporal data analysis (MTDA). The richness of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offers immense potential for uncovering novel disease insights. While Deep Learning (DL) models have demonstrated efficacy in handling tabular data, they often overlook inherent relationships between features. Heterogeneous graphs provide a suitable framework for representing both entities and relations, yet current approaches fail to capture entity similarity effectively. To address this limitation, we introduce the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), a novel graph neural network designed for EHRs. This work not only introduces a new method for probabilistic inference on EHR data but also details a unique dataset for biomedical research in the CardioMed center. This study examines the electric double layer adjacent to a charged soft surface within an electrolyte solution by deriving a mean-field model that accounts for inhomogeneous solvent polarization. Using the Grand Canonical potential, we determine conditions for thermal equilibrium between the surface and the solution. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium conditions for both the electrolyte and the polarizable solvent. We analyze how variations in surface charge density and the dielectric constant of the solvent influence the electric double layer. Additionally, we explore the relationship between water density and the surface charge density. These findings could prove valuable in analyzing systems involving charged soft matter immersed in polarizable electrolyte solutions. Specifically, the parameter $K_w$, representing the product of proton and hydroxide ion concentrations, is observed to influence anionic and cationic concentrations, as well as water and ion densities within the electric double layer surrounding a polyelectrolyte. Consequently, this research is also applicable to polyelectrolyte systems. Finally, within the framework of the mean-field model, we investigate the density profiles of anions, cations, and both anions and cations in the presence of a polarizable solvent. These results are expected to be significant for understanding the behavior of polyelectrolytes in solutions. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to incorporate solvent polarization into a mean-field model describing a charged soft surface in an electrolyte solution. Finally, the derived conditions for the polarizable phase of the solvent may be relevant for studying liquid-liquid phase separation in electrolyte solutions. This study investigates the energy efficiency of a network coding system operating under a single-relay power allocation framework. Initially, the network coding power is determined based on the geometric mean of the two involved relays. Subsequently, the problem of minimizing total transmission power, subject to a specific distortion constraint, is addressed through joint relay scheduling and power allocation. This is accomplished by formulating the issue as the minimization of the sum of two convex functions, a task resolved using the subgradient method. Finally, simulation outcomes demonstrate the benefits of joint relay scheduling and power allocation when applied to energy efficiency via network coding. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is validated through comparisons against the optimal relay selection and power allocation benchmark, as well as the existing cooperative network coding approach. To the best of the authors' knowledge, joint relay scheduling and power allocation within the context of network coding have not been previously explored. Consequently, the findings of this paper may serve as a foundation for future research in these areas. Notably, this paper's primary objective is to achieve energy efficiency through network coding, rather than focusing on achieving high data rates or performance gains. Therefore, the proposed relay selection and power allocation schemes within this context may not be directly applicable to other research areas such as high data rate transmission. However, this does not diminish the value of the proposed approaches for achieving energy efficiency via network coding. Finally, the authors intend to extend this research by considering the more general scenario of multiple relays. Specifically, future work will involve formulating the energy efficiency minimization problem as the reduction of the sum of multiple convex functions to determine an optimal relay selection and power allocation scheme. Additionally, the authors aim to develop an efficient and practical algorithm capable of solving the resulting convex optimization problem in distributed network coding environments. In this extended scenario, relays would independently adjust their power levels using the proposed multiple-level power allocation scheme, thereby enhancing the algorithm's practicality. Furthermore, relays would only need to share power levels with their immediate neighbors, significantly reducing the communication overhead associated with the relay selection algorithm. Finally, the authors plan to examine the case where network coding is not employed, specifically analyzing the benefits of the multiple-level power allocation scheme in this context. To the best of the authors' knowledge, multiple-level power allocation in cooperative communication systems has also not been previously investigated. Consequently, this paper may also provide a basis for future research into power allocation techniques within cooperative communication frameworks. Overall, this research aims to serve as a foundational step toward achieving high performance within cooperative communication systems utilizing network coding.

We introduce a fully quantum mechanical, first-principles theory based on the density functional theory framework to investigate magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces. Utilizing a realistic model system consisting of body-centered cubic niobium superconductors and 4d transition metal adatoms, our calculations successfully reproduce the characteristic spin-split Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. These states emerge from the hybridization between the magnetic impurity's localized $d$-orbitals and the superconducting conduction electrons, manifesting as in-gap peaks in the spin-projected local density of states. Our analysis reveals that these in-gap YSR states are predominantly spin-polarized, with their unique characteristics, including energy and total magnetic moment, varying based on the specific impurity and its location within the superconductor. Furthermore, our theory accurately predicts experimental measurements, including recent scanning tunneling microscope observations of YSR states on an Mn-Sq tip coupled to a Nb superconductor. Finally, we examine a simple dimer configuration to explore the potential for spin-transfer phenomena and propose a mechanism for detecting the local magnetic moment of the adatom. This theoretical framework is broadly applicable to studying the interaction between local magnetic moments and unconventional superconductors. Additionally, it can be extended to investigate the interaction between a magnetic moment and a superconducting quantum dot embedded in a Josephson junction. In that context, YSR physics is anticipated to play a crucial role in the proposed proposal for detecting the Majorana zero mode in a superconducting quantum dot. Consequently, this theoretical method is expected to be valuable for investigating the correlation between the Majorana zero mode and the YSR state. Ultimately, our findings regarding the in-gap YSR states underscore the necessity of employing quantum mechanical, first-principles methods to investigate the interaction between a magnetic moment and a superconductor. This approach is essential for elucidating the fundamental physics governing magnetic moments in superconducting hybrid devices, a topic currently under intense experimental investigation. Such understanding is critical for realizing the Majorana zero mode, which holds promise for topological quantum computing. This approach offers an alternative to conventional modeling techniques. Our findings indicate that when each photon is absorbed by a single electron, the method accurately reproduces XANES data from solid copper, including effects attributed to transient electron populations and interband transitions. Consequently, we argue that pulse energy, energy density, pulse energy density, and repetition rate are critical parameters that must be explicitly reported in x-ray absorption studies. Deep neural networks (DNNs) offer significant promise for enhancing modulation classification performance under adverse conditions, such as additive noise, signal power variations, and spectral masking. However, emerging research indicates that adversarial attacks can bypass these DNN-based classifiers, potentially compromising the integrity of automated systems. This study investigates the impact of adversarial perturbations that exploit a DNN's susceptibility to misclassify modulated signals. We present experimental findings demonstrating the resilience of DNN-based modulation classifiers against such attacks, followed by the introduction of a novel GAN-based defense mechanism designed to counter adversarial threats. Our results show that this defense strategy effectively mitigates the risks associated with adversarial attacks in deep neural networks. Furthermore, we observe that combining a defense system with multiple DNN models yields superior results compared to using either approach in isolation. Overall, this research advances the understanding of adversarial vulnerabilities and explores innovative solutions to safeguard deep learning systems within communication environments. We introduce a novel metric comparison, analogous to Alexandrov's, and demonstrate its significant link to the continuity of optimal transport for regular measures on Riemannian manifolds, especially concerning the $L_1$-distance. Furthermore, we apply this new comparison to establish key results regarding the existence and monotonicity of optimal transport maps within the $L_1$-framework. Specifically, by considering a family of Riemannian metrics, we show that a continuous optimal transport map (characterized by absolute continuity and a non vanishing focal function) exists precisely when the bipolar comparison holds; in this scenario, the map maps geodesics to geodesics and preserves length in an Alexandrov sense. Additionally, our findings provide a partial resolution to an open question posed by Loeper regarding the relationship between the Alexandrov and bipolar comparisons. Finally, we illustrate a crucial distinction between the Alexandrov and bipolar comparisons by presenting an example where the Alexandrov comparison indicates CAT(k) while the bipolar comparison does not. This example serves as a counterexample to several conjectures found in existing literature. To achieve this, we construct a specific example of a CAT(0) group acting on a tree that fails to preserve lengths in the Alexandrov sense. This establishes the existence of a CAT($\infty$) Riemannian manifold where geodesics are not uniquely determined by their endpoints, yet the bipolar comparison still holds. Our example involves two finitely presented groups acting isometrically on a Riemannian manifold, one of which exhibits properties closely resembling hyperbolic groups. This allows us to address another of Loeper's questions by showing that the curvature condition required for the Alexandrov comparison is not necessary for the bipolar comparison to hold. To reach this result, we also needed to establish that the bipolar comparison is stable under taking subgroups and passing to quotients, a result of independent interest. Finally, our work suggests that the concept of comparison angles, which underpins the definition of the bipolar comparison, is valuable in various geometric contexts, such as CAT($\infty$) spaces and CAT($\epsilon$)-spaces, rather than being restricted to geodesic spaces. Consequently, we have extended the standard definition of comparison angles to apply to complete metric spaces and investigated the relationship between this extended concept and geodesic completeness. This study introduces a method for applying behavioral machine learning to capture nonlinear system dynamics. By integrating behavioral modeling with structural modeling, we enhance the robustness of identified models. We present high-resolution (0.1 arcsec) 1.2 mm continuum images of the Dragon infrared dark cloud (D253-2), revealing a compact core with a radius of roughly 30 au. By combining these images with $^{13}$CO J=1-0 and C$^{18}$O J=2-1 line data, we calculated dust emission from the mm continuum and gas velocity fields from the isotopologues. Our analysis indicates that the velocity fields are governed by the internal dynamics of the core rather than the surrounding envelope, with a central region of 100 $\times$ 100 au showing no signs of rotation. The Dragon core's mass (300 M$_{\odot}$) and radius (30 au) align with the Bonnor-Ebert instability criterion, suggesting that gravitational instability drives core expansion. This process may facilitate the formation of dense, compact cores and the subsequent development of protostars and stars. Additionally, we identified a new compact structure within the envelope, characterized by a mass of 100 M$_{\odot}$ and radius of 1000 au, which is likely a shock-compressed region. This structure appears to result from the interaction between the envelope and a dense molecular ridge. The discovery of the expanding core in the Dragon cloud offers new insights into the link between the internal dynamics of mm continuum-emitting cores and the early stages of star formation. Furthermore, the observed core expansion in the Dragon core may help explain the lack of a central condensation in the radial distribution of the 1.2 mm continuum emission. These findings also help clarify the apparent contradiction between the observed low central density and the high central temperature in the core. Finally, the observed expansion in the mm continuum emission may be linked to the lack of a central temperature peak in the 1.2 mm continuum emission. These results are consistent with the model of Meeus et al. (2010), which predicts that the core radius grows over time. The Dragon cloud is thus an ideal target for studying the early phases of star formation. We introduce a novel simulation exploring the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) as a potential dark matter candidate. This simulation utilizes PopSyCLE, a new code tailored for modeling early universe structure formation that works in tandem with existing PBH mass spectrum calculations to predict the resulting PBH mass function. Although the derived mass spectrum fails to account for the entirety of dark matter, it indicates that PBHs may constitute a significant fraction of it, potentially resolving issues related to dark matter annihilation. Our PopSyCLE framework can be readily expanded in the future to investigate other PBH scenarios as potential dark matter sources. Additionally, we examine how alternative inflationary models could impact the mass and abundance of PBHs. Finally, we discuss how future observational constraints from the Euclid satellite and the Roman Space Telescope will limit the fraction of dark matter composed of PBHs with masses around $10^{-6}M_{\odot}$. This mass range corresponds to peaks in radiation density perturbation power spectra generated by the reheating phase that follows inflation. Furthermore, we note that such masses align with the peak in radiation density power spectra produced by the standard model of structure formation, aside from the well-documented scenario involving supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies. In that latter case, the relevant process is the direct collapse of massive gas clouds into massive black holes, rather than the formation of supermassive black holes from smaller seeds during the earlier stages of galaxy evolution. We also address how the Euclid and Roman surveys will constrain the fraction of dark matter made up of slightly less massive PBHs, a scenario arising from the decay of massive particles shortly before or during recombination. While the current constraints on the mass fraction of PBHs relative to the total dark matter density remain relatively weak, the upcoming Euclid and Roman space missions are expected to significantly tighten these limits, thereby enhancing the viability of PBHs as a dark matter candidate. Additionally, we highlight that the PBH mass function derived from the standard model of structure formation exhibits a sharp cutoff at lower masses, a feature also present in the mass function derived from our PopSyCLE simulation. Finally, we compare the constraints on PBHs as a dark matter candidate with results from other observational tests. Our findings suggest that future constraints on PBHs will improve substantially, which could establish PBHs as a compelling dark matter candidate. We employed Monte Carlo simulations to investigate equilibrium systems featuring local nematic order built from hard wedges, where each wedge consists of a sphere with a sector removed. Each molecule occupies a single wedge, which inhibits rotational motion around the binormal. For a system of hard neutral wedges, the modulation type observed experimentally in attractive samples was not found at temperatures where neutral phases exist; instead, only a critical phase exhibiting splay modulation and Poisson distributed dislocations appeared. This indicates that geometric phases of this nature can be classified into subtypes based on whether nonconvexity is concentrated at the leading or trailing edge of the wedge. Furthermore, we examined charged phases and identified two distinct charged splay blocks, corresponding to charged samples with short and long interaction ranges, respectively. In both neutral and charged scenarios, the equilibrium charged splay block with the longer interaction range displays Poisson distributed dislocations. Additionally, we identified a charged twist modulation, though it remains uncertain if this represents a distinct phase or merely the charged equivalent of a critical phase. Finally, we contrasted these findings with previous studies on phases in models featuring both transverse and leading-edge nonconvexity.

Finally, extensive experiments across diverse pretrained language models, domains, and methods reveal that PASTA consistently outperforms prior parameter-efficient approaches, achieving up to an 84% reduction in the number of trainable parameters. This research investigates the challenge of inserting an element into an ordered set, a fundamental operation in operating systems and spreadsheet applications. We examine a scenario where a new item is added to a dataset representing user preferences, and the resulting sequence must be reordered based on that preferred relationship. We evaluate two strategies for solving this issue: a non-contextual approach, which orders items solely based on their pairwise comparisons, and a contextual method, which considers both pairwise preferences and the item's initial position. Our findings indicate that the contextual approach typically requires fewer comparisons than its non-contextual counterpart. Furthermore, we present a benchmark suitable for researchers to assess the efficiency of various algorithms addressing this fundamental problem. Finally, we develop a contextual algorithm as a proof of concept, demonstrating that it is more efficient than existing state-of-the-art solutions that ignore context.
