Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a prominent method for integrating prior physical knowledge into machine learning. By utilizing the principles of physics as a regularizer, PINNs enhance the interpretability and reliability of their inferences. The efficacy of PINNs in high-dimensional parametric optimization tasks has been validated across diverse application areas. However, the standard PINN approach relies on minimizing a loss function that includes both a data term and a residual term. The challenge arises from the fact that these PINN objectives are not inherently interpretable. Consequently, the primary goal of this study is to establish a rigorous connection between PINN objectives and their corresponding approximate solutions. We achieve this by employing the weak formulation of partial differential equations (PDEs) to derive an equivalent weak formulation for the PINN objective. Leveraging this equivalence, we develop an a posteriori error estimator for the PINN solution. This estimator utilizes the residual of the weak PDE formulation, where test functions are replaced by the PINN itself. We demonstrate that this estimator is reliable, meaning the true error is bounded by the estimator up to a constant factor, and that it can effectively guide the optimization process. Our findings indicate that the proposed a posteriori error estimator serves as a valuable supplementary tool for the certified machine learning of high-dimensional parametric optimization problems utilizing PINNs. A key advantage of our approach is its compatibility with both smooth and non-smooth PDE solutions. We validate the efficacy of our method through examples involving both smooth and non-smooth solutions to the heat equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's utility in high-dimensional parametric optimization by applying it to a cancer therapy scenario. In this application, we employ our error estimator to determine an optimal treatment protocol, where the PINN output functions as the test function to compute the residual. The results show that our approach yields more optimal treatment protocols and achieves higher cure rates for both healthy and malignant cells. Finally, we provide a summary of the method's advantages and outline potential future research directions. Specifically, we aim to extend the method to other emerging techniques, such as operator learning and graph neural networks. Additionally, we intend to apply the method to other PINN applications, including high-dimensional non-linear inverse problems and other cancer therapy problems. Ultimately, we aim to create a unified framework for solving various PINN problems. Ultimately, our findings establish a foundation for the certified machine learning of high-dimensional parametric optimization problems using PINNs. In contemporary epidemiological research, the integration of air pollution models, geostatistics, and machine learning has become essential. This introduction briefly outlines recent progress and key advancements in these critical domains. Regarding air pollution models, both chemical composition and physical characteristics have improved significantly. For instance, high-resolution air quality models now reach 1 km, enabling the disaggregation of national-scale outputs to support epidemiological studies. Additionally, models simulating particle penetration and deposition within the human respiratory system have been developed, offering quantified estimates of alveolar and extrathoracic fractions. Geostatistics, the statistical discipline governing spatial data, has also advanced substantially. Bayesian spatial models now facilitate the spatial interpolation of air pollution data, a vital component when high-resolution measurements are sparse. Furthermore, machine learning techniques have been increasingly applied to enhance air pollution modeling and spatial interpolation. Collectively, these innovations hold the potential to substantially boost the accuracy of spatially interpolated air pollution data. Consequently, this accuracy is a primary factor influencing epidemiological findings, including the magnitude of health effects, the spatial distribution of disease burden, and the identification of vulnerable populations. This paper aims to provide an overview of these advancements and their implications for air pollution epidemiology and public health. It begins by examining recent progress in air pollution modeling and geostatistics, including critical issues and innovative solutions. We establish a regret bound for the full exploration linear bandit setting that is superior to any bound achievable by bound-based algorithms, thereby revealing the limitations of these methods. Specifically, while bound-based algorithms achieve a regret upper bound of $O(dH\log|\mathcal{F}|\log T)$—where $d$ represents dimensionality, $T$ is the number of rounds, and $H=\sqrt{\frac{\pi^2}{6}\sum_{t=1}^T |\mathcal{F}|\kappa_t^2}$ with $\kappa_t$ denoting the trace of the Gram matrix—we derive an regret lower bound of $\Omega(dH\log|\mathcal{F}|\log T)$ for any exploration algorithm. This result demonstrates that full exploration strategies necessitate exploring the entire action space rather than relying solely on an ellipsoidal region centered at the origin as done by bound-based approaches. Furthermore, we analyze how the lack of localization in full exploration algorithms impacts Eicker-Huber-robustness-augmented algorithms, which combine standard and robust estimators. We prove that these hybrid algorithms fail to achieve $d\log T$ regret when the number of corrupt rounds approaches $d\log T$. Additionally, we present an algorithm achieving $d\log T$ regret that remains robust against any constant fraction of corrupt rounds. We provide an efficiency guarantee for this algorithm when applied to bounded loss functions and investigate how the sparsity of $\mathcal{F}$ influences the regret of robustness augmentation. Finally, we establish an $\Omega(d\log T)$ regret lower bound for any algorithm that is robust against an arbitrary constant fraction of corrupt rounds. Collectively, these findings indicate that robustness-augmented algorithms are inefficient for full exploration, and that full exploration linear bandits are intrinsically difficult. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the efficiency of robustness-augmented algorithms within the general linear bandit framework. Our work underscores the necessity of carefully selecting the balance between robustness and exploration to mitigate the trade-offs inherent in these approaches. Finally, we examine the impact of adversarial noise on the efficiency of robustness-augmented algorithms in linear bandits with an unbounded action set. We prove that noise can compromise the efficiency of these algorithms by degrading their regret performance. Gapped graphene has been suggested as a promising system for observing the valley Hall effect, a transport phenomenon involving distinct, oppositely charged valley currents in a spatially uniform electric field. The necessary inversion symmetry breaking can be achieved through various methods, such as nanoribbon confinement, strain, or chemical functionalization. However, a common limitation across these approaches is that sample defects and edge roughness render experimental detection of the valley Hall effect in nanoribbons particularly difficult. In this study, we propose an alternative method to break inversion symmetry in a large graphene sheet, yielding an anisotropic band structure and the associated valley anisotropy. This approach avoids issues related to sample imperfections and is compatible with a gate voltage for carrier doping. We show that valley Hall currents can be experimentally realized through the Kerr effect in graphene. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect, a nonlocal response to a uniform electric field, is a more robust alternative to the valley Hall effect, as it is driven by a nonlocal potential difference. This makes the orbital Hall effect viable for detection via Kerr spectroscopy or Kerr microscopy, unlike the valley Hall effect, which remains unobservable in Kerr spectroscopy due to valley degeneracy. Additionally, we show that the orbital Hall effect is significantly enhanced by applying a spatially varying potential. Finally, we illustrate that the orbital Hall effect in graphene is primarily governed by valley anisotropy, a property that can be tuned via a Hall gate. Our findings suggest that the orbital Hall effect in graphene is more accessible for experimental verification than the valley Hall effect. Moreover, our results indicate that orbital Hall effects, despite their nonlocal nature, could be detected using local probes like Kerr microscopy. This is because the orbital Hall effect is intrinsically linked to the nonlocal potential difference, allowing for the generation of a large, local transverse electric field through the insertion of a potential barrier. Such an insertion can amplify the orbital Hall effect by orders of magnitude, thereby enabling its detection via Kerr microscopy. Ultimately, our findings provide a promising pathway for further investigating the orbital Hall effect in graphene. Specifically, they may facilitate the discovery of spin-orbit coupling mechanisms, spin-orbit interactions, and the spin Hall effect within graphene. Additionally, our findings may help explain the recently observed orbital Hall effect in graphene sheets featuring a spatially varying potential. Our work paves the way for exploring orbital transport in graphene, a field that has been largely overlooked. Data poisoning represents a well-known security risk in machine learning, where malicious actors embed malicious samples into training datasets to compromise model integrity. While graph data is frequently encountered in real-world applications, existing research on graph-based data poisoning primarily focuses on static graphs and tends to overlook the inherent graph structure. In contrast, this study examines dynamic graphs within the context of data poisoning. We introduce a method leveraging reinforcement learning to disseminate malicious samples across specific nodes and edges, ensuring they exert a stronger negative impact on the target class while causing minimal damage to non-target classes. Experiments on the Cora and Citeseer datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves significantly higher attack success rates compared to current methods. Furthermore, we observe that the data poisoning attack success rate peaks when the attacker controls both nodes and edges. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our method in attacking diverse graph neural networks, including GCN, GAT, and GraphSAGE. Ultimately, our findings highlight the necessity of developing defenses capable of addressing dynamic graph poisoning threats. Catalogue matching serves as a critical method for identifying repeated observations of the same celestial object across multiple images, a prerequisite for astrophysical research such as photometric variability studies. This process involves two stages: estimating object coordinates and performing catalogue matching. The accuracy of coordinate estimation is heavily influenced by the signal-to-noise ratio of the data. Consequently, low signal-to-noise objects are often excluded from catalogues generated during the coordinate estimation phase, which subsequently limits the scope of later catalogue matching. This limitation is particularly problematic for studying the variability of low-luminosity sources. To address this, we developed an innovative catalogue matching algorithm that integrates photometric data to detect objects with weak signals. In our approach, an initial catalogue is created using photometric information to ensure the inclusion of faint sources during matching. We evaluated this new method against three established techniques and tested it on real data from the Kepler mission, demonstrating that our approach significantly improves match completeness in regions with low signal strength. The methodology is fully automated and accessible at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez-castro/catalogue_matching. Furthermore, we have developed a novel catalogue matching utility that incorporates photometric information, releasing it under the MIT license as part of the photutils package within astropy. This release also features a new star catalogue generator that utilizes our innovative matching algorithm. More details can be found at https://astro.physik.uni-kiel.de/~apc17/. Ultimately, providing catalogue estimates for low-luminosity sources in photometric surveys will facilitate their study through variability analysis. Therefore, releasing our package will enable users to generate catalogs that estimate coordinates for low-luminosity sources, thereby enhancing the quality of astrophysical research in this field. This includes, for instance, identifying active stars that exhibit photometric variability, which is a key factor in stellar activity. These active stars are of significant interest due to their impact on the habitability of exoplanets in their systems. The primary challenge in studying stellar variability is reliably detecting low-luminosity active stars within large datasets. Thus, our package offers a valuable tool for variability analysis, facilitating the identification of active stars with low signal strength. This capability is essential for the broader goal of characterizing the Sun and other stars to better understand their influence on life. This paper identifies a hypergraph's infinite minimal vertex cover through the inclusion of its finite minimal vertex covers. Specifically, for a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, the union of the sets comprising all its finite minimal vertex covers constitutes a minimal vertex cover of $\mathcal{H}$. Furthermore, this set constitutes a vertex cover if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ is $\mathcal{M}$-free, where $\mathcal{M}$ represents the collection of all finite minimal vertex covers of $\mathcal{H}$. These findings extend and refine several results previously established by Tuza [J. Combin. Theory. Ser. A 49 (1989) 161--171]. Additionally, we demonstrate that this result fails to hold when the term "minimal" is substituted with "inclusion-minimal." Finally, we examine methods for constructing the minimal vertex covers of a hypergraph based on those of its sub-hypergraphs. Specifically, if the union of the vertex covers of a finite family of sub-hypergraphs of $\mathcal{H}$ (with edges disjoint from the others) forms the edge set of a sub-hypergraph $\mathcal{H}'$, and $\mathcal{H}'$ possesses a unique minimal vertex cover $C$, then $\mathcal{H}$ includes a minimal vertex cover $S$ such that $S \subseteq V(\mathcal{H}) \setminus V(\mathcal{H}') \cup C$. This approach yields partial solutions to an inquiry posed in [Discrete Appl. Math. 160 (2012) 2623--2632]. Lastly, we present an algorithm that, given any hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, constructs a vertex cover of $\mathcal{H}$ using the inclusion of all its finite vertex covers. This algorithm operates in polynomial time, and the resulting vertex cover is inclusion-minimal provided $\mathcal{H}$ is finitely generated. To our knowledge, the $\mathcal{M}$-free condition identified herein is both necessary and natural; to our understanding, no stronger condition exists. In the context of infinite hypergraphs, this conclusion remains valid even if $\mathcal{M}$ denotes the set of all minimal vertex covers. Ontologies serve as formal models of concepts and their intricate interrelations, predominantly utilized within knowledge management and information systems. Because of this formal structure, ontology visualizations must accurately depict only the valid semantic connections. This work introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization that departs from conventional ontology graphs by depicting non-hierarchical associations between large collections of classes and properties. In OntoPlot, classes are positioned on vertices while properties form the edges, enabling users to explore associations across domains without visual clutter. The study also examines the limitations of traditional visualization techniques and evaluates OntoPlot through three case studies. The findings indicate that this approach is more scalable than alternatives for visualizing large ontologies, and user testing suggests that OntoPlot aids in comprehending ontology structures and identifying redundant or potentially erroneous associations. We introduce a method for enhancing end-to-end automatic speech recognition (EEASER) through a semi-supervised framework that leverages unsupervised domain adaptation (UNDA) and inter-domain losses. UNDA enables the training of a model on a source domain using data from multiple target domains, after which an adapter model is trained to map features from these target domains into the source domain's feature space. To improve feature representation, we employ discriminators that ensure the adapter produces source-domain-like outputs, alongside inter-domain losses that increase similarity between sources and targets while maintaining distinctions between different target domains. This approach allows for unsupervised training on extensive target domains and utilizes supervision from diverse source domains to enhance representation quality. Applied to EEASER, this technique ensures the model focuses on learning acoustico-linguistic mappings rather than domain-specific invariances. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art UNDA techniques and yields significant gains over supervised EEASER when supervision is limited. Specifically, in transcribing US news with 10 hours of data, we reduced Word Error Rates (WER) from 19.1% to 17.3%. Furthermore, we achieved a 15.6% relative WWER reduction compared to a strong semi-supervised EEASER baseline that performed cross-domain adaptation on the same 10 hours of data. These findings highlight the efficacy of semi-supervised learning with UNDA for speech recognition, offering a pathway to higher performance through superior feature representations. Active inference serves as the theoretical framework explaining how biological agents perceive and interact with their environment. Recent studies have demonstrated that artificial neural networks can master complex tasks, such as navigation, by adhering to the core principles of this theory. However, most existing research relies on simple, flat network architectures that fail to incorporate the hierarchical organization found in biological brains. This paper introduces the principles of deep active inference and demonstrates, for the first time, that a multi-level hierarchical recurrent architecture can navigate an agent through a 2D grid world. Furthermore, we present novel architecture and learning mechanisms that endow the agent with the capacity for self-supervised learning of a hierarchical representation of its surroundings. Our findings indicate that this multi-level system not only navigates effectively but also explores the environment and discovers skills consistent with the predicted developmental trajectory of active inference agents. Overall, our work paves the way for developing autonomous, self-learning robotic systems. We open-source our code at https://github.com/DeepActiveInference.

Keywords: Deep active inference, autonomous robot navigation, autonomous robot learning, hierarchical reinforcement learning, recurrent neural networks, robotic self learning, robotic autonomy, deep active inference.

Using non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations, we examined the Soret effect in binary mixtures of dimers and monomers, specifically isolating the contribution of the dimer's internal degree of freedom to the Soret coefficient. Our results indicate that as the interaction between dimers becomes softer, the contribution from the internal degree of freedom increases. This phenomenon is interpreted as follows: in mixtures with softer intermolecular potentials, a stronger temperature gradient leads to more frequent collisions, causing the system to deviate further from thermal equilibrium. Consequently, the likelihood of dimers dissociating into monomers rises, thereby enhancing the impact of internal degrees of freedom on the Soret coefficient. Additionally, we investigated the link between the potential width and the internal degree of freedom contribution, finding a strong correlation: softer potentials yield larger contributions. Finally, we demonstrated that the internal degree of freedom has the greatest effect on the Soret coefficient when the two constituent species are nearly symmetric. These findings offer valuable insights for both experimental and theoretical analyses of the Soret coefficient. Furthermore, our methodology is applicable to the molecular design of functional materials where the separation of large and small molecules is crucial. We anticipate that our results will serve as a reference for the molecular design of polymers, peptides, and other functional molecules. To facilitate this, we provide the simulation code at https://github.com/taekyungkim/Soret_Simulations. Finally, to ensure reproducibility, we have made the input files for the simulations used to derive the results in this study available. Automated Essay Scoring (AES) represents a multidisciplinary intersection of education and Natural Language Processing (NPS), focusing on identifying metrics that differentiate high-quality essays from inferior ones. This study proposes using Language Models (LMs) to address AES, specifically fine-tuning state-of-the-art transformer-based LMs, which rely on a "self-attention" mechanism to predict the probability distribution of the next word in a sequence. The primary objective is to analyze learning curves and determine the most efficient balance between model performance and computational costs when data is limited. To achieve this, we introduce two new AES datasets, both derived from real essays submitted by students in grades 3 through 12 across various countries. The first dataset, NLP4Education AES 2021, sourced from the NLP4Education Challenge, is smaller and suited for initial exploratory research. The second, AES2021, is a larger collection designed for final model evaluation. Both datasets provide simultaneous, independent evaluations from two educators for each essay. We evaluate multiple transformer-based LMs, demonstrating that fine-tuning a pre-trained, sparsely-sparse encoder-only BERT model on a smaller corpus yields the best results, whereas a larger corpus may necessitate a hybrid encoder-decoder architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that enhancing model performance can be achieved through pre-tokenization techniques, such as adding special characters to tokens. Finally, we emphasize the necessity of careful hyperparameter selection and feature engineering to fully leverage the potential of these datasets. Overall, this work underscores that fine-tuning pre-trained LMs offers a highly effective solution for AES, presenting a promising avenue for NLP research in the education sector. The datasets and code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/rodrigoalvesaev/NLP4Education-Essay-Scoring. The data was utilized in the AES 2021 competition at the NLP4Education Challenge, which took place from May 10 to May 14, 2021, as part of the 22nd International Conference on Computational Linguistics & Philosophy of Language. Additional context regarding the competition can be found at https://competitions.codabench.org/competitions/59. Low-quality music recordings, commonly found on social media, often suffer from mixed audio and recording degradation. This study introduces the first automatic method for separating and enhancing such music files. The proposed system utilizes a dual encoder-vocoder architecture. First, a four-stem audio source separation model, adapted from images, partitions the mixed input audio into individual instrumental tracks. Subsequently, various neural networks, also adapted from image-based super-resolution models, process each track to remove noise. Finally, the vocoder combines the enhanced individual stems. The model's performance was evaluated using traditional audio quality metrics, including Signal-to-Perceived-Distortion Ratio, Spectral Distortion, Log Sin similarity, and Sin Similarity. Additionally, a human study was conducted to assess the perception of the quality improvement, with results indicating that the model is highly effective at enhancing mixed music recordings. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first attempt to apply image translation techniques and vocoding to music enhancement. This paper introduces a motional editing technique that transfers amplitude and rotation data from a donor motion to a recipient. The system operates by identifying a point of release on the donor trajectory, extracting the kinematic properties at that instant, and propagating motion details along a new trajectory defined by the release location, point, and velocity, as well as throw angle. The core algorithm is driven by a combination of a general purpose differential equation solver, a spring-damper model, and a motion detail filter. Qualitative results demonstrate that editing a motion with an incorrect release point can yield visually convincing outcomes. The paper also reviews related work in throwing motion synthesis, discusses design decisions, and outlines potential future applications. A collection of video demonstrations is available at http://www.cs.uaf.edu/~jg/fauthrow/. The authors intend to release the system as open-source software in the near future. Although Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have demonstrated strong performance, they often fail to generate syntactically accurate outputs because they lack an explicit framework for controlling syntax. To address this, we propose a top-down tree-structured decoding algorithm with syntactic connections, which integrates a standard NMT model with a parse tree of the target language to constrain the decoding process. Furthermore, we have derived two enhanced variants of this algorithm by incorporating a Noun Phrase (NP) sub-lexicon and integrating syntactic from both top-down and bottom-up perspectives; these improvements have yielded notable gains. Experiments conducted on NMT tasks utilizing the CoNLL 2014 German Treebank 2 demonstrate that our methods can significantly boost NMT performance. For instance, on sentence-level tasks, BlueNMT achieved a 0.76% increase, while on dependency tasks, DepNMT saw a 2.07% improvement over NeuralMT. Additionally, we have evaluated the proposed algorithms on English-to-German and German-to-English translation pairs, finding that they improve performance across various sentence types, including long and short sentences, as well as sentences with complex syntactic structures. Finally, to support the reproducibility of our work, we have released the source code and the German Treebank 2 dataset at https://github.com/ChenchenLi2017/Syntactic-Connections-Code. The accuracy of astrochemical models relies heavily on the binding energies of molecules to dust grains. This study presents the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), a database containing quantum chemical calculations for molecular binding energies. These values were derived using the M06-2X/6-311++G(3df,3pd) method and corrected with the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVTZ single-point energy. BEEP includes over 100 molecular species and their corresponding water-ice grain binders. All energy values in BEEP are rigorously corrected for energy conservation issues, basis set superposition error (BSSE), and the relaxation of periodic systems. The platform's utility was assessed by comparing its binding energy distributions against those in the literature and the NIST database. Results indicate that the binders employed are more diverse than those typically used in quantum chemical studies, and the generated binding energy distributions align well with existing literature. Furthermore, these distributions exhibit a narrower range than those reported in the literature. Finally, a suite of Python tools is provided to facilitate the efficient querying of BEEP. The platform is accessible at http://www.phy.ustc.edu.cn/bEEP. Future updates will expand the database to include species from the recent NIST NIST88 database. The study examines a multiplicative stochastic process constrained by a lognormal lower bound. A model for this process is developed, deriving its distribution function—which relies on four parameters—and associated statistical characteristics. By analyzing the distribution, the analysis identifies the mechanisms influencing the four parameters and proposes an approach to establish an appropriate lower bound using historical data. A simulation utilizing synthetic data validates the theoretical results, while additional outcomes from real-world data on Bitcoin and Ethereum further illustrate the practical applicability of multiplicative stochastic processes with sample-dependent lower bounds. The findings indicate that this lower bound effectively filters noise in time series, retaining only significant fluctuations that drive price evolution. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that this filtering mechanism can be identified from historical data and utilized to construct a stochastic process that accurately represents real-world price dynamics. Consequently, these results provide a valuable framework for developing processes capable of replicating the behavior of real assets. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Specifically, it notes that the current study does not address the upper bound of the distribution; however, extending the analysis to include an upper-bound model is feasible. Such an approach could refine the proposed method for selecting lower and upper bounds, potentially leading to a stochastic process that constrains price evolution within a specific interval. Developing such a process would offer a new tool for analyzing the price dynamics of real assets. Additionally, while this work focuses on validating the properties of a stochastic process through distribution and statistical analysis, it does not address the development of new processes for stochastic differential equations. Future research will explore the application of this approach to financial modeling, aiming to derive processes from historical data that can be used to price financial derivatives. Furthermore, future studies will investigate the application of these processes to time series analysis, including volatility forecasting. In that context, the lower bound serves as a volatility proxy, and the authors will explore time series models that incorporate this proxy to forecast future volatility. We introduce a new class of circuits designed to advance expectation estimation under low-depth constraints. Our primary findings demonstrate that these circuits achieve substantial expectation estimates with circuit depths scaling as $\mathcal{O}(n^2/d^3)$, where $n$ represents the qubit count and $d$ denotes the target error tolerance. Our circuit designs are founded on random Clifford circuits modified by measurements on a fixed subset of qubits. We establish that the Shallow Shadow protocol yields a $1/d$-level set of 2-design measure, ensuring that the remaining unestimated observables possess nearly classical probability distributions. This property ensures that expectation values can be accurately approximated through a reduced number of measurements. Additionally, we present an alternative circuit construction achieving a $k$-design measure for classical distributions, where $k$ scales as $\mathcal{O}(n/d)$. We validate the practical utility of our proposals by successfully estimating a broad range of expectation values, including ground state energies for the transverse field Ising model, $Z$-eigenvalues, and magic state generators. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to near-term quantum processors, offering low-depth solutions for problems such as expectation estimation and property prediction. We anticipate that our results will pave the way for future advancements in expectation estimation. Finally, we discuss extensions of our protocols to scenarios involving higher levels of noise. In this context, we demonstrate that the random Clifford circuit can be truncated at a depth of $\mathcal{O}(n/d)$ without significantly compromising accuracy, even in the presence of constant noise, thereby retaining the $1/d$ classical probability set measure. We conclude by outlining several promising directions for future research. Specifically, we propose extending our protocols to many-body systems where ground states are highly entangled, as well as to many-body systems exhibiting significant many-body dephasing. In this regard, our protocols are particularly well-suited for execution on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. We also explore potential extensions to the field of expectation estimation, including applications to many-body systems with high entanglement and those subject to substantial dephasing. Achieving robustness to adversarial examples is a primary objective in natural language processing. This study explores sibylvariant transformations (SBTs), a collection of syntactic variants designed to simulate adversarial texts. We process these transformation sets using a transformer-based model to train a classifier that produces predictions consistent across all of them, thereby enhancing overall adversarial resilience. Our experimental results indicate that a classifier utilizing SBTs outperforms both the standard baseline and the state-of-the-art TextDefenses approach on two text classification benchmarks, with statistical significance confirmed at the 0.05 level. Additionally, we introduce TextFisher, an open-source Python library that integrates multiple SBT methods and defines the robust classification problem. We also present an extensive array of generated sibyltransformations, offering a new resource for robustness research. Meta-learning has recently demonstrated significant success in classification tasks. In the context of non-stationary environments, the goal of meta-learning with linear representations is to determine an optimal prior linear representation that minimizes empirical risk across multiple tasks. This study focuses on high-dimensional, low-sample-size (HDLSS) scenarios where the number of samples per task is finite but the number of tasks is potentially infinite. We derive an explicit formula for the optimal representation and develop a multi-task gradient descent algorithm to compute it efficiently. We present both finite-sample and asymptotic theoretical guarantees regarding the convergence rate of our algorithm, confirming that it achieves global optimality. Furthermore, our theoretical findings indicate that the convergence rate of gradient descent is influenced not only by sample size and feature dimension per task but also by the "spectral gap"—the ratio of the minimum to the second-largest eigenvalue of a specific kernel matrix. Finally, numerical experiments substantiate our HDLSS theoretical results and demonstrate the practical utility of the spectral gap. Specifically, in cases where the spectral dimension is low, our method surpasses existing approaches; conversely, when the environment fluctuates rapidly, it becomes more advantageous to fine-tune the model on each task rather than relying solely on a shared prior representation. Additionally, we provide a proof of a generalization bound and utilize it to design an efficient model selection strategy. Unlike the test set method, which fails in HDLSS settings due to estimation errors, our proposed selection method leverages training data from numerous tasks to identify a suitable model. Finally, we discuss how to extend this multi-task gradient descent approach to handle cases where the number of tasks is finite. By computing the exact optimal representation and employing the conjugate gradient method, we achieve the same performance as the infinite-task scenario while reducing computational costs. Additionally, by applying multi-task learning only during the initial pre-training phase and retrieving task-specific representations via standard fine-tuning in high-dimensional settings, our method offers a practical solution for large-scale deep learning applications. Empirical results confirm the efficacy of this large-scale multi-task learning approach. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zhonghaochen1992/provable-meta-learning. Keywords: Meta-Learning, Generalization, Linear Representation, Gradient Descent.

Although current image captioning models generate diverse descriptions, they often fail to capture multiple valid perspectives of an image due to limited expressiveness. To address this and enable the generation of varied yet accurate captions without changing the model weights, we introduce Prompt Controllable Image Captioning (PCIC). Our approach directly incorporates prompts into the model input and utilizes a generated caption as a reference to steer the model toward producing a new variation. Specifically, during inference, users can input different prompts to generate captions with varying degrees of diversity or controllability. Extensive experiments on the COCO- captions dataset demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms strong baselines in both accuracy and prompt-following capabilities, effectively breaking the previously established accuracy-diversity trade-off. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that the proposed double-negative prompt mechanism is highly effective. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/brandon-wu/PCIC.

We present the first comprehensive and principled investigation of harm within causal semantic mapping. By establishing a categorical distinction between agentive and non-agentive harms, we introduce a unified semantic model that accounts for (1) differential sensitivity to causal premise variations, (2) semantic gradient effects across cause types, and (3) cause type gradient impacts on negated statements. Our extensive manual annotation of over 2,000 cases reveals that agentive harms exhibit greater inter-annotator agreement regarding their cause types compared to non-agentive harms, suggesting that agentive cases rely on shared lexical knowledge, whereas non-agentive cases utilize diverse knowledge sources. Furthermore, we demonstrate that current neural network models struggle to differentiate between agentive and non-agentive harm types, indicating that these models lack an understanding of the causal mechanisms underlying events. Finally, we offer theoretical insights into the causal nature of non-agentive harms, proposing that their causes are characterized by high dynamism, animacy, and proximity. We argue that agentive causes function as true triggers of the harm event, whereas non-agentive causes act as pre-requisites that enable the necessary dynamism, animacy, and proximity to generate the event. This distinction explains the higher interpretability of agentive causes and accounts for the fact that removing agentive causes leaves harm events unchanged, while removing non-agentive causes typically prevents the harm from occurring. Our findings underscore the critical role of causal knowledge in causal semantic mapping and suggest that future models must explicitly model causal mechanisms to effectively handle negation and the diverse cause types associated with non-agentive events. To facilitate this, we propose the use of detailed causal models that capture the dynamism, animacy, and proximity of non-agentive causes. We conclude by arguing that a causal grammar framework offers the ideal foundation for representing such detailed causal structures. Overall, this work provides deep insights into the nature of non-agentive causes and establishes a path toward the next generation of causal models capable of representing non-agentive causes. To enhance the performance of zero-shot speech translation, this study employs a dual strategy: first, it investigates the impact of training data volume and statistics, specifically the languages selected as source and target languages; second, it addresses a critical deficiency in prior research, which neglected the utilization of audio features to bridge gaps between similar languages during inference. These strategies collectively improve the efficacy of zero-shot speech translation. Accurate short-term load forecasts are essential for the efficient management of low-voltage networks. This accuracy is particularly critical as the integration of distributed energy resources introduces uncertainty into grid operations. Consequently, utilities and large consumers often require their demands to remain below specific demand caps, such as the highest load recorded over the previous 24 hours. However, the presence of multiple subscribers and unstable components like solar panels and batteries complicates the aggregation of individual loads into a single network load, while subscriber mobility further distorts total consumption by altering subscriber profiles and locations. To address these challenges, we propose a network probabilistic load forecasting framework that combines long- and short-term projections using the forecast fusion technique. Furthermore, to evaluate the impact of specific load components and ensure compliance with demand caps, we utilize the probability distribution of aggregated loads, conditioned on whether those caps will be exceeded in the future. Finally, extensive empirical results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework. Our findings indicate improvements in both point and interval load forecasting accuracy through the application of the proposed forecast fusion method. Additionally, the analysis of aggregated load probability distributions reveals how the proposed network probabilistic load forecasting framework can help utilities and large consumers manage their loads effectively. This is achieved by understanding the characteristics of the load mixture and identifying the specific subscribers contributing the most to the aggregation. Ultimately, this enables the development of strategies to mitigate demand peaks. These insights are operationalized through a real-world case study of the Smart Grid Demonstration District in Eindhoven, which includes 1,024 smart homes equipped with smart meters and smart home controllers. This demonstration district offers a valuable opportunity to test and validate the proposed framework in a real-world setting. By analyzing the local network's load, utilities can better manage its peak demand, thereby mitigating the stress on the distribution grid. This capability is crucial for ensuring the reliable supply of electricity to end-users. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader goal of achieving a sustainable energy future. Furthermore, effective peak demand management can enhance energy security by reducing reliance on foreign energy sources and ensuring a stable supply of electricity to meet the needs of communities and industries. Although significant advancements have been made in radiomics for non-invasive diagnosis and treatment planning for COVID-19, two critical issues remain: the potential for class imbalance in deep learning models and the absence of reliable segmentation methods. To address both challenges, we introduce a weakly-supervised, unbiased framework for localizing segmentation. Specifically, we develop a weakly-supervised localization network that identifies unbiased COVID-19 lesions in chest X-rays, followed by a segmentation network trained specifically on these labeled lesions. Both models are trained in an end-to-end manner using only bag-of-instance labels. Quantitative results across three independent cohorts demonstrate that (1) our localization model accurately detects unbiased lesions, achieving an average Dice score of 0.80±0.11, and (2) the weakly-supervised segmentation model performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods, reaching an average Dice score of 0.85±0.11. Furthermore, we show that our segmentation model outperforms weakly-supervised baselines by an average Dice score margin of 0.05±0.01. These findings indicate that weakly-supervised learning holds promise for delivering high-quality, unbiased, and reliable segmentation in clinical settings. Finally, we release the largest publicly available, multi-institutional COVID-19 dataset to date, comprising 1,000 chest X-rays with confirmed lesions and expert annotations. This dataset will facilitate future research in COVID-19 lesion localization and segmentation. The code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/leeyu12345/COVID19-lesion-localization-and-seg. Automatic vertebra localization and identification is essential for tasks such as vertebral age estimation and spine fracture detection. This study introduces a method that employs an end-to-end, anatomically-constrained network for labeling vertebral segments within the spine. The approach first reorients the vertebral segment along the central ray of the CT volume and then conducts vertebral identification within the resulting cross-sectional slices. Furthermore, the vID-LSTM module utilizes recurrence to extract and aggregate spatially dependent features for determining vertebral labels. The model is trained exclusively on synthetic data, eliminating the need for any manual design of convolutional kernels. We evaluated the proposed method using CT scans from the Medical Image Challenge 2018: Vertebrae Age Estimation (MICCAI-VAE) dataset. Our results demonstrate a vertebral identification (vID) accuracy of 92.5% and achieve a state-of-the-art performance of 95.5% on the validation set. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yzhang12/VertebraeAge. This work aims to streamline age estimation and reduce the manual effort required for vertebral localization and identification. The method is designed to be easily adaptable to other vertebral analysis tasks, including age estimation, diagnosis, and treatment. The name vID-LSTM reflects the core components of this approach: vertebral identification (vID) and the variable-length sequence characteristics of vertebrae, which are effectively modeled using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. We investigate single-electron scattering within a cavity where electromagnetic field vacuum fluctuations are intensified. Our findings indicate that the electron's interaction with these amplified vacuum fluctuations causes scattering resonances, onsets, and steps to shift. Notably, when the electron's energy aligns with a Fano resonance, dynamical stabilization occurs; the otherwise degenerate continuum of scattering states is effectively frozen, enabling the formation of a stable, localized bound state. This phenomenon is particularly significant in regimes such as the ultrastrong coupling regime, where electromagnetic quantum vacuum fluctuations play a crucial role in the formation of bound states. Furthermore, we explore the experimental feasibility of observing this effect in the context of the Jaynes-Cummings model. This theoretical framework is highly relevant to emerging quantum technologies, including superconducting qubits, as it addresses fundamental questions regarding electron behavior in regions with enhanced electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations. Additionally, we examine the potential for developing novel devices that utilize electron scattering within electromagnetic vacuum field "hot spots." In this scenario, the ultra-short lifetime of the excited state is a critical factor. The principles of ultra-short excited-state lifetimes and ultra-fast dynamics are also vital to the field of ultrafast science. Finally, we address the fundamental issue of whether electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations can be considered "real" by analyzing the one- and two-particle density functions. These concepts are essential for understanding quantum field theory and the quantum nature of the vacuum. Recent nature-inspired machine learning approaches have enhanced the dexterity and performance of robotic systems, yet the specific benefits of elasticity in locomotion robots remain underexplored. The primary obstacle to utilizing neural network control for biomechanically inspired, elastic-legged robots is the high dimensionality of the state space, which makes learning difficult. To address this, we introduce the concept of "elastically coupled feet," which significantly reduces the state dimension. This paper investigates the advantages of this architecture through simulations of quadruped walking and running. Our findings indicate that the proposed learning-based controller, employing elastically coupled feet, successfully replicates biological gait patterns and delivers superior disturbance rejection compared to controllers without such coupling. Additionally, our elastic controller can maintain stable gaits at higher walking speeds and can gauge terrain conditions to adaptively select between running and walking gaits. Our results show that these elasticity effects result in superior performance for quadruped locomotion. The proposed elastically coupled foot architecture holds promise for enhancing the performance of other legged robots, and we plan to extend these results to real-world scenarios in future work. We introduce the variational separability verification (VSV) algorithm, a quantum method designed for the determination of state separability. An expression for the entanglement monotone is constructed, and the VSV algorithm is formulated based on the principle that the minimum of this monotone characterizes separable states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that VSV can be implemented using only single-qubit gates and measurements in the computational basis. We establish that VSV achieves the optimal measurement complexity, matching that of the relative entropy of entanglement when computed via variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). Additionally, we show that any separable state constitutes a unique global minimizer of the VSV objective function. We also examine the algorithm's convergence properties and its capability to approximate the minimum for certain highly entangled states. Finally, we present experimental results from superconducting circuits confirming that VSV successfully identifies both separable and entangled states. The source code for VSV is available at https://github.com/QuantinTech/icvsa. This work extends the application of VQAs to entanglement verification, enhancing the utility of quantum computing for fundamental research in quantum information science. Specifically, the proposed VSV algorithm offers a new approach to leveraging quantum computational resources for solving fundamental problems in quantum information science. Furthermore, the VSV objective function is characterized by a simple analytic expression, enabling quantum computers to efficiently determine the minimum without the need for complex circuit simulations or approximations, a limitation present in existing VQA applications. Consequently, VSV establishes a novel link between fundamental quantum information problems and quantum computational resources. The demonstration of VSV's capacity to verify the separability of Bell-like states and entangled states generated through entanglement witnesses underscores its potential as a building block for future entanglement verification methods. This study examines the initial development of small-scale tearing modes within the collisionless collisionally dominated plasma regime. Through the analysis of linear theory equations, we demonstrate that this initial linear phase is characterized by anisotropic magnetic field reconnection driven by the kinetic current drive mechanism. Our findings indicate that, unlike the intermediate tearing mode, this initial linear growth does not exhibit magnetic field exponential stretching. Additionally, we show that the initial linear tearing mode is susceptible to nonlinear anisotropic reconnection, a process also responsible for the growth of the intermediate tearing mode. Finally, the lines of force associated with the magnetic field display a figure-eight shape, which is consistent with previously reported results. These outcomes provide a foundation for future investigations into the non-linear evolution of small-scale tearing modes, the scenarios in which they may arise, and their potential influence on the overall plasma system. Furthermore, the identified figure-eight structure in the lines of force could serve as a new diagnostic tool for detecting small-scale tearing modes in both current and future fusion devices. Specifically, this structure may be observable in current tokamaks, in the edge plasma of future steady-state fusion reactors, and in the edge and core regions of the ITER plasma. Additionally, small-scale tearing modes may be observable in the solar corona, where they could contribute to the heating of the chromosphere and the acceleration of solar flares. In space environments, they could be present in the magnetosphere, contributing to the heating of the plasma sheet during substorms. Finally, these modes may be detectable in the solar wind, potentially contributing to the heating of the interplanetary medium. In all these contexts, the observed small-scale tearing modes could influence the level of magnetic field line braiding and, consequently, the rate of energy transfer to the non-helical component. This, in turn, could affect the rate of energy transfer to the helical component through inverse cascade. Such a scenario could be a factor in the generation of the Parker spiral and the large-scale magnetic field of the galaxy. Consequently, small-scale tearing modes could play a significant role in the overall evolution of the magnetic field. This possibility could be investigated through space missions, such as the Solar Orbiter and the Magnetospheric MultiScale missions, as well as current space weather forecasting models. Driven by increasing demands for image-based systems, particularly in e-commerce, we introduce a novel approach for fashion image retrieval utilizing a pre-trained Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN). By leveraging the DCNN's intermediate layers, we reduce the model's complexity and extract local spatial information that standard DCNNs overlook. Although DCNNs are typically trained via supervised back-propagation, our method employs semi-supervised training, requiring only that samples in the query set remain unchanged from the pre-trained state. This strategy significantly lowers the labeling expenses associated with the search database. In the retrieval framework, queries are transmitted to the network to extract key features that guide image ranking. To enhance ranking accuracy, we incorporate Local Weighted Ranking (LWR) and Attribute-level Attribute Manipulation (AAM) to replace the conventional pairwise ranking method. Experimental results on the PolyU PolyFashion dataset demonstrate that our proposed system outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/1234567890zhang/semi-supervised_fashion_image_retrieval. Furthermore, to support future research in the field, we release the LWR and AAM datasets in our LWR-AAM dataset. This dataset features images with consistent shapes and colors but distinct attributes, alongside the corresponding LWR-AAM data files. This work introduces a dual gradient flow to address stochastic variational problems linked with linear ill-posed equations within Banach spaces. The derived solution flow is a gradient regularized deconvolution method, formulated using the dual norm of the gradient of the data misfit functional. Findings from prior studies on this approach in Hilbert spaces are extended to the broader setting of Banach spaces. Numerical experiments confirm the method's superior noise reduction capabilities, demonstrating its effectiveness as a competitive technique for denoising stochastic ill-posed problems. Additionally, the study investigates the strong convergence of the dual gradient flow solution to the stochastic variational solution, specifically in the case of Gaussian noise. Finally, the paper examines the case of general noise, highlighting the necessity of modifying the variational problem and subsequently analyzing the convergence of the dual gradient flow solution under this adjustment. Furthermore, the document explores local optimality for the variational problem, a factor that influences the selection of Banach spaces for practical applications. The theoretical findings are complemented by numerical examples that validate these results. The accompanying code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/SebastianKlauer1992/DualGradientFlow}. Notably, the code also employs Banach space regularizers on infinite-dimensional spaces. The results for infinite-dimensional spaces were presented at the 2022 International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2022) \cite{klauer2022dual}. Constructing the matching cost map is a pivotal step in the light field (LF) depth estimation framework. Conventional LF depth estimation frameworks typically rely on simple metrics, such as the median or contrast-based costs, for the cost construction phase. However, these straightforward metrics often yield suboptimal results, particularly when dealing with complex regions like occlusions. To address this limitation, we introduce an occlusion-aware cost constructor. This approach first generates a simple cost map using the contrast-based cost constructor. Subsequently, an OC map is created through a non-local anti-occlusion operator, leveraging spatial and angular correlations to assign minimal values to cost values in angular views at depth maps derived from extreme depth maps. Finally, a complex cost map is produced by multiplying the complementary products of the differences between the minimum and original cost values and their respective OC values. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across various datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, we have developed a dataset comprising 45 LF lances, derived from 9 high-resolution RGB images at 6 views each, to support depth map evaluation. Finally, our code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-chen2000/LF-Depth-Completion.

This paper examines the Fokas-Lenells equations using a bilinear method. We demonstrate that the dark, bright, and trigonometric solutions correspond to specific Gray-blacksolitons, Gray-black-lumps, black-lumps, bright-lumps, bright-lumps-on-lumps, and double-lumps, respectively. Furthermore, we illustrate that the focus and defocus FL equations support lump-type solutions of these described types. Additionally, we note that two- and multi-lump solutions of various configurations exist within the focus and defocus FL equations, although these lumps do not exhibit the breathing phenomenon observed in other systems. Finally, we provide the exact solutions for the focus and defocus FL equations. These findings significantly expand the scope of integrable nonlinear equations possessing lump-type solutions and enhance the understanding of lumps in both physical and mathematical contexts. Notably, our results contradict the claim previously made by other authors regarding the existence of lumps in the FL equation. To enhance Home WiFi performance, this study introduces a protocol-aware extension utilizing the IEEE 802.11k/v standards. We developed an algorithm named Channel Load Aware AP selection (CLAPA), which enables stations to dynamically choose the Access Point (AP) offering the lightest channel load. By integrating k/neighbourhood information with the velocity standards, CLAPA allows a station to: 1) identify an AP with a lower channel load than its current one, 2) mitigate co-channel interference caused by a moving obstacle by switching to a more suitable AP, and 3) accelerate the association process. Extensive simulations across three distinct home environments demonstrate that, for a given channel load threshold, CLAPA surpasses existing extension schemes in these key areas by achieving higher goodput, reduced packet loss, and lower end-to-end delay. Furthermore, the algorithm successfully converges to a stable network state, ensuring no single AP is overwhelmed with too many connected stations. Finally, performance analysis using real-world Channel Load data confirms that, for a given threshold, CLAPA delivers superior results compared to existing solutions. Human Subject Experiments also validate that CLAPA achieves higher goodput than other approaches for the same number of mobile users. Furthermore, in terms of perceived quality, users employing CLAPA report higher satisfaction regarding perceived speed, visual quality, and overall experience compared to those using other AP selection methods. Finally, to demonstrate the benefits of the IEEE 802.11v velocity standard under various mobility profiles, we propose a velocity-aware extension scheme that significantly outperforms profiles not incorporating the 802.11v standard. In this velocity-aware scenario, CLAPA achieves higher goodput, lower packet loss, and reduced end-to-end delay compared to solutions that rely solely on the 802.11k standard. Additionally, users utilizing the velocity-aware scheme report higher satisfaction with perceived quality and perceived smoothness compared to solutions based only on the 802.11k standard. In contrast, users of the k/neighbourhood approach experience higher packet loss, goodput degradation, and increased end-to-end delay compared to the velocity-aware approach. These findings indicate that incorporating 802.11v velocity standards substantially improves perceived quality and user satisfaction. Finally, the CLAPA scheme successfully identifies velocity profiles, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling mobile user dynamics.
